The proposed framework not only enhances the interpretability of spectral data but also paves the way for integrating diverse spectroscopic datasets for comprehensive molecular analysis.

papers.title: Accumulation of enzymes on the lipid-oleosin membarnes
papers.abstract: Engineering the spatial organization of proteins offers a powerful strategy for controlling biochemical reactions and material properties in synthetic cells. However, dynamically organizing multiple proteins at the nanometer scale remains challenging. We developed asymmetric lipid–oleosin hybrid vesicles in which engineered oleosin molecules served as membrane-forming scaffolds with two orthogonal conjugation systems. External chemical stimuli rapidly recruited two distinct proteins to individual oleosin molecules, generating persistent nanometer-scale proximity, as demonstrated by single-molecule tracking. In an alditol oxidase–horseradish peroxidase cascade, organization of both enzymes on the same oleosin scaffold enhanced product formation compared with intermolecular membrane recruitment. This localized cascade further drove stimulus-responsive polymerization to form membrane-associated cytoskeleton-like structures, increasing vesicle resistance to hypertonic stress. This programmable membrane scaffold couples external signals with molecular organization, enhanced biochemical reactions, and membrane mechanics, providing a framework for engineering synthetic cells that convert chemical inputs into programmable reactions and material outputs.

papers.title: Finite-Field Second Hyperpolarizability via Adaptive Bayesian Quantum Phase Estimation for Early Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers: Ground-State Energies Beyond Chemical Accuracy
papers.abstract: The static second hyperpolarizability governs third-order nonlinear-optical responses but is difficult to compute by first-principles methods because finite-field extraction requires a fourth-order energy derivative. The resulting error amplification demands sub-µHa ground-state energies, far beyond conventional chemical accuracy. Standard multi-qubit QPE can in principle meet this precision but requires a wide ancilla register, while single-ancilla iterative QPE (IQPE) is limited by a binary-grid quantization floor. We develop an adaptive Bayesian QPE (BQPE) workflow that uses a single ancilla, terminal measurements, and real-time classical feedback to estimate the eigenphase through a continuous posterior rather than a fixed binary grid. For a linear H4 chain in the STO-3G basis, represented by a six-qubit parity Hamiltonian with one ancilla, BQPE reaches a ground-state energy error of ≈ 10−7 Ha at controlled-U depth mmax ≈ 215, about two orders of magnitude below the IQPE floor. Propagated through the finite-field stencil and Richardson extrapolation, these energies recover the second hyperpolarizability within ±10% of the FCI reference over the stable field-strength plateau, whereas IQPE at the same depth fails to do so. These results indicate that grid-free Bayesian phase estimation can make nonlinear-optical properties accessible on early fault-tolerant quantum computers.

papers.title: Machine Learning Optimization of Polymeric Complex Coacervate Micelles Reveals Cell-Type-Specific Formulations for Enhanced mRNA Delivery
papers.abstract: The cell-type dependent transfection heterogeneity of polymeric mRNA delivery remains a fundamental barrier to their broad translation. The field has historically addressed this by optimizing the cationic component itself, refining amine identity, density, and block architecture to maximize transfection. Even highly optimized cationic carriers, however, still transfect some cell types well and others poorly, because no single cation chemistry can simultaneously match the internalization and cytoplasmic trafficking biology of every target. Rather than seeking a universally optimal carrier chemistry, we instead sought a tunable formulation framework capable of adapting charge balance and interfacial properties across distinct cellular environments. Here, we report a multicomponent complex coacervate micelle platform in which a cationic oligoamine-functionalized A7 amphiphile , an anionic poly(carboxyethyl acrylate) (CEA) homopolymer, and a neutral-anionic poly(ethylene glycol)-b-poly(carboxyethyl acrylate) (PEG-CEA) diblock are co-assembled into a single carrier, with the anionic and stealth components associating electrostatically with the cationic micelle as external corona species. Closed-loop multi-objective Bayesian optimization (qNEHVI) of the A7/CEA/PEG-CEA formulation simplex over three rounds in HEK293T cells identified a productive ternary region that increased effective efficiency (delivery × viability) from ~0.35 for the A7 homomicelle to approximately 0.8 for the best mixed micelle. The resulting 35-formulation library was directly screened across six additional cell types (A549, MDA-MB-231, HuH7, OVCAR8, HEK001, and primary patient-derived fibroblasts), where the best mixed micelle outperformed all polymer-based commercial reagents in every cell line. The winning composition was different in every cell line, establishing tunability rather than a single fixed optimum as the platform's central practical advantage. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) attribution on Random Forest surrogates then converted these cell-line-specific winners into transferable design rules, identifying which formulation descriptors drive delivery and viability in each cellular context. Together, this work delivers a tunable polymeric transfection platform and a framework for cell-type-aware design of mRNA carriers.

papers.title: Environmental benefits and trade-offs of dry coating for battery electrode production
papers.abstract: Dry coating is an emerging, scalable alternative to traditional slurry coating for manufacturing lithium-ion battery electrodes. It offers significant energy savings, eliminates the need for toxic solvents, and is consequently often regarded as an environmentally more benign process. Dry coating exploits the fibrillating properties of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), substituting the polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder employed in slurry coating. As replacing slurry coating with dry coating involves different production processes and materials, a comprehensive life cycle assessment (LCA) study was performed for an accurate comparison of the environmental impacts. The results of our LCA show that dry coating has the potential to reduce environmental impacts across all assessed impact categories except for the ozone depletion potential, which increases by a factor of 1.8 when PVDF is replaced by an equal mass of PTFE. For LiNi 0.8 Mn 0.1 Co 0.1 O₂ (NMC811) cathodes, dry coating typically enables a reduction in binder content by a factor of two, which offsets the higher ozone depletion potential of PTFE with respect to PVDF and results in a comparable impact at cell level. For LiFePO 4 (LFP) cathodes and graphite anodes, state-of-the-art processing relies on aqueous, non-fluorinated binders, typically a combination of carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) and styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR). Dry coating therefore introduces PTFE into a process that is currently free of fluorinated materials, lowering CO 2 emissions but increasing ozone depleting emissions. We also highlight knowledge and data gaps associated with the polymerization of PVDF and PTFE, which currently prevent a robust comparison of toxicity-related impact categories, and discuss the potential of non-fluorinated binders for dry coating. Overall, our study provides a foundation for understanding environmental benefits, trade-offs, and remaining data gaps identified for dry coating technologies, supporting informed decisions on their future development and scalable implementation in lithium-ion battery manufacturing.

papers.title: Melt-State Ligand Addition Generates a Near-Infrared-Emissive Coordination Polymer Glass
papers.abstract: Meltable coordination polymers (CPs) combine liquid-phase processability with the structural and functional diversity of crystalline coordination compounds, but methods to install targeted local coordination environments and photophysical functions in CP glasses remain limited. Here, we demonstrate that 1,10-phenanthroline (phen) reacts with the 1D-extended Cu I -CP Cu(ipim) (Cuip; ipim − = 2-isopropylimidazolate) in the melt, converting half of the linearly coordinated Cu I sites into pseudo-tetrahedral [Cu(phen)(ipim) 2 ] − units while preserving chain topology and the interchain-separation melting mechanism. Depending on thermal history, the resulting phen 0.5 Cuip forms either a melt-quenched glass or crystalline polymorphs, whereas pristine Cuip invariably recrystallizes on cooling. X-ray total scattering and spectroscopic analyses show that the local Cu I -phen motif is retained across the phases, while the coordination geometry, interchain order, and phen···phen π-stacking interactions differ. Ligand addition transforms the photophysics from green phosphorescence in Cuip to broad near-infrared emission centered at approximately 850 nm in both crystalline and glassy phen 0.5 Cuip. The pronounced temperature dependence of this emission is consistent with a thermally activated delayed fluorescence mechanism. Calculations indicate that the extended CP environment restricts flattening of the pseudo-tetrahedral [Cu(phen)(ipim) 2 ] − units after metal-to-ligand charge-transfer (MLCT) excitation, thereby limiting access to non-radiative decay pathways. Melt-state ligand addition thus provides a route to construct molecular-complex-like functional units during processing, linking reactive CP melt chemistry to targeted photophysical design in CP glasses.

papers.title: Morphology-Dependent Excited-State Dynamics in Hollow Sphere Poly(Heptazine Imide) Photocatalysts
papers.abstract: Photocatalytic oxygen reduction to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) over stable, earthabundant materials is attractive for solar energy conversion. The question how photocatalyst morphology governs photocatalytic performance remains, however, poorly understood, as the contributions of surface area and charge-carrier dynamics are convoluted. Herein, we investigate a series of hard-templated hollow potassium poly(heptazine imide) (PHI) spheres (KPHIS) with varying shell thickness and porosity. The photocatalytic H2O2 production is benchmarked against bulk KPHI and correlated with excited-state dynamics probed by steadystate and time-resolved photoluminescence and femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy under quencher-free and donor-containing conditions. Notably, whilst all KPHIS outperform bulk KPHI, the activity varies non-monotonically with shell thickness and excitation wavelength, whereby the thickest-shelled sphere ‒ not the one with the highest specific surface area and pore volume ‒ is most active at 365 and 406 nm, with apparent quantum yields up to ~3.9%. These experiments reveal that the activity is governed not by porosity alone but by the kinetic competition between donor-mediated hole extraction (least efficient in the most porous sample at low wavelength irradiation) and stabilization of long-lived reduced states that drive O2 reduction. Shell thickness should be co-optimized with light penetration depth and donorconditioned charge dynamics, rather than maximizing porosity alone.

papers.title: Applicability-Domain-Aware Evaluation of Machine-Learning NMR Chemical-Shift Prediction in Small drug Molecules: GT-NMR for 13C and CASCADE for 1H
Engineering a Carboxylesterase for Acyl Transfer to Amines
papers.abstract: Within the mechanistic realm of centralized catalysis (chemical catalysis), reactivity activation is site-centered on reactant functional groups and site-driven from catalytic centers, leading to a low-resolution catalytic architecture with low catalytic activity and catalytic efficiency. In contrast, within the mechanistic realm of decentralized catalysis (biological catalysis), reactivity activation is reactant-spanned on both functional groups and appendage groups and enclosure-driven from catalytic cavity, offering a high-resolution catalytic architecture with high catalytic activity and catalytic efficiency. Herein, as a proof-of-concept illustration for reactant-spanned and enclosure-driven enzymatic catalysis (as exemplary for biological catalysis), we report the engineering of a carboxylesterase for acyl transfer from carboxylesters to amines. The precision disjoint presentation activation of acyl group and amino group has empowered the achievement of an expansive reactant scope of both carboxylesters and amines. As a demonstration of the synthetic utility, a pharmaceutically relevant agent has been constructed on the gram scale. As a manifestation of the synthetic potential, a quantitative or near-quantitative S-enantioselectivity has been established for the kinetic resolution of secondary amines. The high catalytic activity and catalytic efficiency showcased herein promise decentralized catalysis as a powerful, generic mechanistic basis for the highly effective programming of reactivity activation. Keywords: Centralized Catalysis; Decentralized Catalysis; Chemical Catalysis; Biological Catalysis; Carboxylesterase; Acyl Transfer; Carboxylester; Amine; Kinetic Resolution.

papers.title: Advanced HILIC-MS Analysis of Therapeutic siRNAs with Non-Canonical Backbones and Conjugate Scaffolds
papers.abstract: The evolution of small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapeutics toward increasingly complex chemical architecture has created analytical challenges for structural characterization. Confident sequencing and site-specific localization of modifications by tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) remain difficult due to non-canonical backbone chemistry, diverse chemical modifications and attached conjugates, all contributing to heterogeneous fragmentation. We present an ion-pair-free hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (HILIC–MS/MS) workflow that enables non-denaturing and denaturing analysis of conjugated, heavily modified siRNA constructs through temperature-controlled separation. Under non-denaturing conditions, duplexes can be evaluated to assess therapeutic integrity and stability, whereas elevated temperatures achieve duplex dissociation, permitting chromatographic separation and MS/MS analysis of sense and antisense strands. The method was benchmarked using multiple siRNA therapeutics of increasing structural complexity, including the unconjugated duplex ATU027, patisiran, a Huntingtin (HTT)-targeting siRNA containing an extended nucleic acid (exNA) backbone, and a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA drug, fitusiran. Complementary activation methods, including collision-induced dissociation (CID), higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD), and ultraviolet photodissociation (UVPD), produced extensive backbone fragmentation and high sequence coverage while also revealing conjugate-specific fragmentation pathways for GalNAc siRNA. Customized Nucleo-SAFARI software supported confident localization of chemical modifications, non-canonical backbone chemistries, and conjugation sites. These results establish temperature-controlled HILIC–MS/MS as a versatile analytical framework for robust structural characterization of complex therapeutic siRNAs.

papers.title: Catalytic Phosphorus-Based Hydrogen Atom Transfer via a Phosphinoyl Anion Relay
papers.abstract: We report the first catalytic phosphorus-based hydrogen atom transfer system. Using an iridium photocatalyst and 10 mol% diphenylphosphine sulfide, we achieve decarboxylative reduction of diverse carboxylic acids—including peptides and pharmaceuticals—to C–H products in up to 95% yield, without stoichiometric reductants. Mechanistic studies reveal an unprecedented anionic relay: a phosphoryl radical is reduced to a phosphinoyl anion, which upon protonation regenerates the P–H catalyst. This work establishes catalytic turnover in phosphorus-based HAT and identifies a new elementary step in main-group radical chemistry.

papers.title: Catalytic Phosphorus-Based Hydrogen Atom
papers.abstract: We report the first catalytic phosphorus-based hydrogen atom transfer system. Using an iridium photocatalyst and 10 mol% diphenylphosphine sulfide, we achieve decarboxylative reduction of diverse carboxylic acids—including peptides and pharmaceuticals—to C–H products in up to 95% yield, without stoichiometric reductants. Mechanistic studies reveal an unprecedented anionic relay: a phosphoryl radical is reduced to a phosphinoyl anion, which upon protonation regenerates the P–H catalyst. This work establishes catalytic turnover in phosphorus-based HAT and identifies a new elementary step in main-group radical chemistry.

papers.title: alchemy: systematic enumeration and thermodynamic screening of small-molecule radical reaction networks
papers.abstract: Automated construction of chemical reaction networks is limited by the combinatorial growth of possible molecules, intermediates, and formal transformations. We present alchemy, an open-source Python workflow for systematic enumeration and screening of small-molecule radical reaction networks. Within an explicitly bounded graph space, alchemy generates connected, neutral C/N/H molecular graphs with single, double, or triple bonds and specified radical counts; RDKit sanitisation and canonicalisation then remove graph-invalid and duplicate records. Reaction candidates are constructed without learned reaction templates by combining bond-dissociation records into rearrangement and transfer stoichiometries. Parallel generation, disk-backed storage, machine-learning prediction of molecular Gibbs free energies, and Kuzu graph representation make the resulting formal network searchable. In a trimethylamine case study limited to at most five heavy atoms and one unpaired electron per reaction side, the workflow generated 41,735 unique molecular graphs and 60,035 first-generation radical-transfer records. A PaiNN model trained and tested on OpenBabel-generated QM9 geometries supplies rapid ranking scores, but QM9 contains no open-shell species and therefore cannot validate predictions for the radical chemistry enumerated here. alchemy therefore provides a reproducible route to efficient reaction-space enumeration while retaining practical filters for chemical plausibility and downstream mechanistic analysis.

papers.title: Unveiling the Potential of Biobased Bifuran unit in Conjugated Polymers: Synthesis, Thermal Properties, Photophysics, and Comparative Study with Phenylene and Thiophene Analogues for OLED Applications
papers.abstract: The bifuran unit is an attractive biobased building block for organic electronics, however its potential in electroluminescent devices has not been explored. In this study, a series of bifuranbased conjugated polymers, PBFAr1–PBFAr9, was synthesized via Suzuki–Miyaura polycondensation to evaluate the effect of the bifuran unit on thermal, photophysical, and electrochemical properties. For comparison, analogous polymers containing phenylene (PSPhAr1), biphenyl (PBPhAr1), and bithiophene (PBTAr1) units were also synthesized. Characterization showed that the bifuran-containing polymers exhibit varied thermal stability, emission in both solution and the solid state. Specifically, the photoluminescence quantum yield of chloroform solution of PBFAr1 was 43%, which was higher than the 39% observed for the bithiophene-based analogue, PBTAr1. Kelvin probe measurements indicated an energy-level alignment with the ITO anode that may facilitate hole injection. Solution-processed OLEDs with an ITO/PEDOT:PSS/emissive polymer/LiF/Al architecture were fabricated, and the PBFAr1-based device exhibited bright cyan electroluminescence at 484 nm. These results suggest that bifuranbased conjugated polymers have potential as emissive and p-type semiconducting materials for organic optoelectronic applications.

papers.title: Hypermolecule: Chemically Synthesized Three-dimensional Macroscopic Molecular Moiré Superlattices
papers.abstract: Recently, moiré superlattices in two-dimensional (2D) systems have attracted significant attention owing to their tunable optical, electronic and quantum properties. Nevertheless, the studies of moiré systems were mostly limited to 2D systems, which make scalability and reproducibility an important issue. Here, we report evidence for the formation of moleculebased macroscopic three-dimensional (3D) moiré superlattice superstructure. We define the isolated 3D assembly as a hypermolecule that has no known natural or synthetic molecular analogue. The time-dependent evolution of the 2D moiré assemblies was investigated using transmission electron microscopy, UV-visible spectroscopy and photoluminescence studies, revealing the hierarchical progression of twist-stacked 2D moiré superlattices towards the growth of macroscopic moiré systems. In addition, X-ray diffraction characterization methods were pursued to elucidate the structural characteristics of the resulting 3D assemblies and establish the correlation between the 2D and 3D superlattices. The macroscopic moiré superlattices – in addition to the 2D structures – exhibited chiroptical behavior, which was further investigated using circularly polarized luminescence study. These observations provide essential insights, and an open platform for further developments in pursuing deeper mechanism underlying their formation at the molecular level and their application potential.

papers.title: PORMAKE2: Topology-Based Generation of Hypothetical Metal-Organic Frameworks through Single-Metal Nodes and Symmetry-Aware Linker Rotation
papers.abstract: Topology-based hypothetical metal–organic framework (MOF) generators enable scalable exploration of chemical space beyond experimentally reported structures, but their accessible design space is constrained by the building blocks and assembly rules they encode. Here, we present PORMAKE2, an upgraded topology-based hypothetical MOF generator designed to improve both access to small-pore structures and geometric fidelity. PORMAKE2 introduces an expanded buildingblock library, including single-metal nodes, and implements symmetry-aware linker rotation for higher-fidelity framework assembly. These upgrades substantially expand the accessible small-pore MOF space and enable MOF designs that were inaccessible to earlier workflows, including ZIF-type and CALF-20-like structures with improved geometrical agreement. Carbon dioxide direct air capture (DAC) and Xenon/Krypton separation are included as case studies demonstrating that improved generator framework can influence downstream screening outcomes. These results establish PORMAKE2 as a more expressive and chemically faithful front-end platform for hypothetical MOF generation.

papers.title: Non-bridging oxygen as the master variable linking structure to the elastic, electronic, and photonic properties of heavy, polarizable cesium silicate glasses
papers.abstract: Cesium silicate glasses, (Cs2O)x(SiO2)1−x, are candidate hosts for optical, dielectric and nuclear-waste-immobilization applications, yet the large, polarizable Cs+ cation is poorly described by conventional potentials. We combine a firstprinciples reference with a single, composition-transferable machine-learned force field for the full range x = 0–0.30, built by pooling the ab initio data of all compositions with no empirical parametrization. First-principles calculations show wide-gap insulators whose gap narrows from 5.9 to 3.3 eV, while the static dielectric constant nearly doubles and the refractive index and optical basicity rise, in agreement with experiment. The pooled potential then scales these cells to nanometre-sized glasses, reproducing the density (within ∼2%, and 5% at x = 0.20), the intact SiO4 network, and the bridging-to-non-bridging-oxygen conversion and Qn depolymerization. Its elastic constants agree with Brillouinscattering experiments, and its pair-correlation functions and structure factors match the ab initio reference. A single structural variable, the non-bridging oxygen, governs these trends quantitatively: the moduli decay exponentially to a stiffness floor with a common non-bridging-oxygen scale and the gap narrows linearly with it, making it a quantitative descriptor linking structure to the elastic, electronic and photonic properties and a transferable basis for designing heavy-alkali silicate glasses.

papers.title: Impact of SEI Formation History on Lithium Metal Electrode Stability at Elevated Temperatures
papers.abstract: Solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) is critical for stabilizing lithium metal anodes, yet its evolution under thermal stress and the role of its formation history remain poorly understood. Here, lithium plating and stripping on Cu electrodes were investigated in 1.0 and 5.0 M lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI)/propylene carbonate electrolytes at 25 and 80 °C using electrochemical measurements, Raman spectroscopy, hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (HAXPES), and X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS). Raman spectra showed that the bulk solvation structure changed little with temperature, whereas HAXPES and XAS revealed that elevated temperature accelerated LiFSI decomposition, inorganic enrichment, and SEI growth, leading to increased interfacial resistance and unstable cycling. Electronic-structure calculations showed that increasing LiFSI concentration enhanced the FSI− contribution to the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO), while elevated temperature lowered FSI−-derived unoccupied states, favoring anion reduction. Pre-cycling at room temperature markedly improved subsequent operation at 80 °C, particularly with the concentrated electrolyte. These results demonstrate that high-temperature stability is governed by the combined effects of electrolyte concentration, temperature, and SEI formation history, providing a mechanistic basis for controlling SEI formation and stabilizing lithium plating and stripping under thermal stress.

papers.title: High-pressure allotropes of tellurium: Evolutionary structure prediction
papers.abstract: The high-pressure structural evolution of elemental tellurium in the 30–400 GPa range has been systematically investigated using the USPEX evolutionary algorithm combined with first-principles density functional theory calculations. The constructed enthalpy–pressure diagram reveals a previously unresolved phase transition sequence Im-3m → I4/mmm (P63/mmc) → Fm-3m that reconciles long-standing discrepancies in the literature. The body-centered cubic Im-3m allotrope was identified as the thermodynamically stable ground state from 30 to 290 GPa. Above 290 GPa, it becomes energetically unfavorable, yielding to two competitive lower-symmetry structures: I4/mmm (stable) and P63/mmc (low-energy metastable). A distinct crossover occurs at 330 GPa, stabilizing the dense face-centered cubic Fm-3m allotrope. The results provide a definitive structural framework for understanding the pressure-dependent properties of tellurium, and a fertile ground for exploring the intricate interplay between crystal structure, electronic topology, and emergent quantum phenomena in elemental systems under pressure.

papers.title: Decoupling Morphological and Electronic Effects of Ni-Doped Ruthenium Oxide Oxygen Evolution Catalysts for PEM Water Electrolysis
papers.abstract: Proper assessment of oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalyst performance requires recognising that doping can introduce simultaneous changes to structure, morphology, and electronic properties that together influence the observed electrochemical behaviour. In this study, Ni-doped RuO2 is used as a model system to systematically investigate how dopant concentration and synthesis temperature affect catalyst morphology and electronic structure. These trends are correlated with OER mass activity (MA), intrinsic activity, and stability enabling the morphological and intrinsic electronic contributions to catalyst performance to be distinguished. The acid-stable limit for bulk Ni incorporation in RuO2 is found to be approximately 10 mol%. Ni incorporation affects the rutile structure and inhibits particle growth, while lower synthesis temperatures decrease particle size. The best-performing Ni-doped RuO2 catalyst here shows up to a tenfold increase in OER MA compared with undoped RuO2. Surface area-based normalisation of MA reveals that this enhancement is partly caused by increased accessible surface area and includes an additional contribution from increased intrinsic OER activity. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy reveals Ni-dependent changes in the Ru 3d and O 1s regions (electronic effect), which correlate with the increase in intrinsic OER activity. S-number measurements further indicate an approximately twofold improvement in catalyst stability caused by doping.

papers.title: Contrastive Reward Based Reinforcement Learning for Goal Directed 3D Molecular Design
papers.abstract: Although three-dimensional flow-matching models have become powerful tools for efficient sampling of high-quality 3D molecular structures, reward-based reinforcement learning for flow-matching models is complicated by the absence of a tractable trajectory likelihood for hybrid molecular states comprising categorical features and continuous coordinates. Existing policy-optimization strategies address this difficulty by stochasticizing the generative process or constructing likelihood surrogates, introducing additional approximations. Here, we present ReCoFlow, a novel trajectorylikelihood-free reinforcement learning framework for reward-contrastive post-training of pretrained molecular flow-matching models. Within ReCoFlow, reward-favored molecules provide positive endpoint supervision for the flow-matching model, whereas reward-disfavored molecules are used to construct reference-guided negative targets. Additionally, an anchor loss to an exponential moving average (EMA) reference model constrains the drift of the fine-tuned model. In benchmarking studies including physicochemical property optimization, three-dimensional shape optimization, and pocket-conditioned 3D molecular generation, ReCoFlow consistently improved the performance of flow-matching models over reward-weighted and surrogate-ratio optimization schemes while maintaining high molecular validity. These results suggest that ReCoFlow could be an effective reinforcement-learning strategy for goal-directed molecular design.

papers.title: Reliable Machine Learning for DPPH Antioxidant QSAR: Scaffold- and Study-Aware Validation with an Out-of-Domain Sulfonamide-Tyr-Gly Case Study
papers.abstract: Machine-learning QSAR models can prioritize antioxidant compounds, but apparent accuracy depends strongly on how chemical data are partitioned for validation. This study develops a reproducible DPPH antioxidant QSAR workflow using 1,891 curated molecules from a public 30 min DPPH dataset. Molecular structures were represented by nine RDKit physicochemical descriptors and 2,048-bit Morgan fingerprints (radius 2), giving 2,057 combined features.Random Forest regression was evaluated as the primary model,with Extra Trees as an independent ensemble comparator.Random Forest achieved mean R-squared = 0.712 and MAE = 0.297 pIC50 units under random five-fold cross-validation, but performance decreased to R-squared = 0.447 and MAE = 0.433 under Bemis-Murcko scaffold-aware validation, and to R-squared = 0.124 and MAE = 0.545 under DOI-grouped validation. In an internal held-out set, molecules with scaffolds represented during training performed better than those with unseen scaffolds(R-squared=0.824 versus 0.580).Nearest-neighbour Morgan Tanimoto analysis further separated structurally supported predictions from extrapolation: inside-domain molecules achieved R-squared = 0.830, whereas outside-domain performance was R- squared =-0.031. The workflow was then applied to two experimentally investigated sulfonamide-Tyr-Gly derivatives. Both had low maximum Tanimoto similarity(0.364 and 0.333), unseen scaffolds,and were overpredicted by approximately one pIC50 unit.The results show that random-split performance alone is insufficient for judging DPPH-QSAR reliability and that chemically informed validation and applicability-domain analysis are necessary when predictions are extended to structurally novel compounds.

papers.title: Is Bioorthogonal Pretargeting Superior to Conventional Targeted Photosensitizers? A Comparative Study of Chlorin Delivery Using Biotin Vectors
papers.abstract: Bioorthogonal pretargeting offers a modular approach to targeted photodynamic therapy (PDT), but its advantages over conventional ligand-photosensitizer conjugates remain insufficiently explored. Here, we aimed to directly compare preformed biotin-containing conjugates with sequential biotin-mediated bioorthogonal delivery. DFT calculations were used to guide the design of new tetrazine dienes with tuned electronic properties for inverse-electron-demand Diels-Alder (IEDDA) chemistry. The selected tetrazines were synthesized and paired with BCN- and s-TCO-functionalized chlorin photosensitizers, and their reactivity was characterized by second-order rate constants and photophysical measurements. In vitro, sequential pretargeting produced substantially higher intracellular fluorescence than administration of preformed 1:1 ligation products; however, this advantage did not translate into enhanced photodynamic activity. Moreover, neither accumulation nor PDT efficacy consistently correlated with SLC5A6 expression in SMVT-high SK-BR-3 versus SMVT-low MDA-MB-231 cells. Free-biotin competition produced heterogeneous, combination-dependent effects, indicating that SMVT is unlikely to be the sole determinant of uptake.

papers.title: Phase-Dependent Thermally Activated Self-Discharge of β-NiOOH and γ-NiOOH Electrodes
papers.abstract: Nickel oxyhydroxide electrodes undergo spontaneous self-discharge that is strongly accelerated at elevated temperature. Although detrimental to alkaline batteries, this reaction is central to electrochemical–thermally activated chemical (E‑TAC) water splitting. The process operates in two distinct steps: electrochemical charging of Ni(OH)2 in cold (~25 °C) alkaline electrolyte and hydrogen generation at the cathode, followed by spontaneous regeneration of the charged NiOOH anode in hot (~80–100 °C) alkaline electrolyte, with concurrent oxygen evolution. A key unresolved question is how the charged-phase composition of NiOOH affects this thermally activated self-discharge. Here, we prepare phase-pure cobalt-doped β-NiOOH and γ-NiOOH electrodes using tailored electrochemical charging protocols and compare their short-term self-discharge in hot alkaline electrolyte simulating the TAC step in the E-TAC cycle. X-ray diffraction and iodometric titration show that phase-pure β-NiOOH undergoes little or no measurable structural or oxidation-state change after 5 min in 5 M KOH at 80 or 100 °C. In contrast, phase-pure γ-NiOOH exhibits substantial self-discharge, corresponding to 43-46% of the charge transferred during the preceding charging step, accompanied by partial transformation to α-Ni(OH)2. These results demonstrate that thermally activated self-discharge in charged nickel hydroxide electrodes is strongly phase-dependent under E-TAC-relevant conditions. More broadly, they show that γ-NiOOH, which is usually regarded as an undesirable overcharged phase in alkaline batteries, is closely associated with rapid chemical regeneration and therefore should be considered a key design variable in E-TAC anodes.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction and Multi-Ensemble Gradient Boosting for Subtype-Selective Binding Affinity Estimation Across Human Adenosine Receptors
papers.abstract: Subtype selectivity across human adenosine GPCRs remains an intractable medicinal chemistry challenge. The four orthosteric binding pockets share over 70% sequence homology across transmembrane helices III, V, VI, and VII. Consequently, standard QSAR models fail prospectively. They suffer from systemic scaffold leakage, overestimating held-out affinity while producing point estimates that lack calibrated error bars. We built an open-source, leak-free computational platform to solve both failure modes. The architecture combines XGBoost gradient boosting with MAPIE Jackknife+ cross-conformal prediction, Random Forest, and LightGBM, trained on 9,589 curated ChEMBL v34 and GPCRdb bioactivity records. Under strict Bemis-Murcko scaffold partitioning (N_train = 6,332; N_test = 1,583), the ensemble achieved an overall R2 of 0.693 and MAE of 0.390 pChEMBL units. On active compounds alone (N_test = 3,771, structural decoys removed), accuracy reached an overall R2 of 0.865 and MAE of 0.314. Per-subtype R2 values reached 0.753 for A1, 0.884 for A2A, 0.912 for A2B, and 0.886 for A3. Conformal intervals delivered 85.80% empirical coverage at a 90% nominal confidence level. Uncertainty quartiles scaled monotonically with absolute prediction error. A GINE graph neural network trained on identical scaffold splits managed only R2 = 0.248 overall, demonstrating that curated physicochemical descriptors decisively outperform deep graph convolutions in low-to-medium data regimes. Twenty-fold Y-randomization confirmed genuine structure-activity relationships, with all permuted R2 values falling below zero (p < 0.001). External blind validation on 15 novel GPCRdb ligands yielded a 75% selectivity recall accuracy. TreeSHAP features attributions verified that model decisions follow interpretable electrostatic and steric properties. All source code, curated data splits, model weights, and interactive deployment are publicly available.

papers.title: Performance of Highly Coarse-Grained Chain Models with Extremal Measures for a Configuration-Dependent Hydrodynamic Diameter in Rheological Flow Fields
papers.abstract: In the presence of fluctuating hydrodynamic interactions (HI), coarse-grained beadspring models are known to show large deviations in rheological predictions relative to finely resolved chain models. In a recent study, we formulated a modified bead-spring approach where the bead hydrodynamic diameter increases proportionally to the mean spring stretch. Significant improvements were observed in the resulting predictions for rheological flow fields for models with many springs. In the new approach, a balanced accuracy across flow types was obtained with the harmonic mean strategy to obtain the mean stretch. In this study, we explore the limits of this approach with highly coarse-grained models consisting of very few springs. Additionally, we test the behavior of two extremal measures to set the bead hydrodynamic diameter. Note, due to the computational complexity with HI, minimizing the number of beads is highly preferable for any application. Surprisingly, our results show the validity of the approach for high degrees of coarse-graining up to only 3 springs, even with the extremal measures, particularly for extensional flows. Predictions in shear flows become better with increasing number of springs, with a good agreement observed with 10 springs.

papers.title: Effects due to the solvent density distribution on the dynamics of polymer coils in solution under rheological flow fields
papers.abstract: We study the behaviour of highly resolved polymer chains under rheological flow fields encompassing varying levels of hydrodynamic interactions (HI) using dissipative particle dynamics (DPD) simulations. The chains are discretized to a single Kuhn step, while the spring lengths set the level of HI. While the overall trends agree with Brownian dynamics (BD) simulations of similarly resolved chains, the balance of drag and restoring spring forces is unable to explain the chain stretch obtained for DPD simulations with higher HI (lower spring length) at moderately large flow rates. For compact coils showing high levels of HI in DPD simulations, the solvent density remains low deep inside the coil, which persists to some extent even as the chains stretch at higher flow rates. In contrast, the solvent density remains nearly constant, at the bulk value, across expanded coils with larger spring lengths. We show how this density distribution has implications for the viscosity of the interface between the polymer coil and solvent and provides a correction to the viscosity used in the drag force expression, which explains the chain stretch values observed in simulations. CFD simulations show the decay of the influence of one sphere on another beyond a separation of one diameter and the persistence of the same for a linear array of spheres, which allows the assumption of a thin cylinder for the drag force.

papers.title: Deployability-First Benchmarking of LFIA Innovation: A Framework and COVID-19 Literature Audit
papers.abstract: Lateral flow immunoassays (LFIAs) are operationally simple, enabling low-barrier, decentralized testing. Their reported performance should therefore be interpreted in relation to the deployability of the required workflow. LFIA innovations often seek improved detection performance, commonly expressed as lower limits of detection (LODs), but workflows can differ substantially in burden and testing conditions. To guide experimental planning, interpretation of results, and formulation of performance claims, we developed a deployability-first benchmarking framework. At the planning stage, the intended deployment setting guides selection of a compatible workflow, while the performance question guides the type of evidence needed to address it. The framework distinguishes low-burden, enhanced lowburden, and higher-burden workflows. Once results are available, the implemented workflow, sample context, measured endpoint, LOD definition, and any comparator help determine what conclusions and comparisons are supported and how the claim should be framed. We applied these principles retrospectively to 96 COVID-19 LFIA innovation articles. Nearly two-thirds of workflows supporting the selected primary performance claims were higher-burden, requiring instrumentation, trained users, or laboratory conditions. Direct like-with-like benchmarking was often limited by differences in workflow burden, sample context, endpoint, LOD definition, readout mode, and comparator conditions. We operationalized result interpretation and claim framing as a claim-level checklist. Applied retrospectively to the same 96 selected primary claims, about 40% were supported as written, whereas about 60% required narrowing or reframing. COVID-19 served as a literature test case; the framework and checklist contain no COVID-19-specific criteria and were designed for medical and non-medical LFIA settings.

papers.title: Entropy-Guided Dataset Reduction for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) deliver near-quantum-mechanical accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost. Their performance depends on the quality and composition of the training data: the training set must cover the range of atomic environments the model will encounter, yet unnecessary redundancy increases training cost without improving accuracy and can inadvertently introduce training biases. Dataset pruning (i.e., selecting a compact, representative subset from a larger collection) has emerged as a practical strategy for building high-quality training sets. Recently, methods based on informationtheoretic diversity measures such as QUESTS (Quick Uncertainty and Entropy from STructural Similarity) have shown significant promise, however, QUESTS requires specification of a lengthscale parameter (kernel bandwidth) that controls how similar two atomic environments must be before one is considered redundant. We show that operationally useful values of this parameter vary across structurally distinct phases, making naive automated pruning of heterogeneous datasets challenging. We present a pruning framework that addresses this problem by adapting the bandwidth independently for distinct thermodynamic subsets of the training dataset using an automatable elbow criterion applied to QUESTS informationentropy metrics. Farthest-point sampling (FPS) is then applied within each group to select maximally diverse atomic environments. Using the Small Carbon ChIMES 2.0 dataset comprising diamond, graphite, and liquid carbon spanning a broad range of thermodynamic conditions, we show that use of a single global bandwidth yields pruned datasets that can be strongly dominated by a single phase, particularly when the distribution of environments varies significantly between phases (e.g., liquid vs crystalline).1,2 Relative to global pruning at the same retained fraction, group-aware adaptive pruning reduces test force-MAE by up to 37% for diamond and 26% for graphite for models trained on only 5% of the original training data, with corresponding improvements in radial distribution function (RDF) fidelity. Benefits are smaller in structurally heterogeneous conditions where a single thermodynamic label encompasses multiple distinct local bonding environments with different characteristic length scales, indicating that finer grouping is the natural remedy in such regimes. Across crystalline conditions, the elbow-selected bandwidth aligns with the onset of rapid error growth as the dataset is pruned, providing a practical, model-agnostic guide for pruning decisions that requires no model training.

papers.title: Cationic Selenuranes Enable Direct Linchpin Formation in Arenes
papers.abstract: The formation of linchpins is a powerful strategy for increasing molecular complexity. Chalcogenonium salts have become valuable intermediates for molecular diversification, owing to their exceptional chemoselectivity in arene C–H functionalization and a synthetic versatility comparable to that of halides and pseudohalides. Sulfonium group introduction through an isohypsic process from S(IV) precursors requires activation with strong acids or anhydrides. Here, we report the direct synthesis of selenonium salts from bench-stable Se(III) cationic selenuranes using a simple dump-and-stir protocol. The transformation proceeds under air at ambient temperature and requires no exogenous activators. Mechanistic investigations reveal high sensitivity to electronic effects (ρ = −10), whereas site selectivity is determined by the rate-limiting deprotonation step (kH/kD = 2.3). The method is scalable to 10.0 mmol (>6.2 g) and provides direct access to selenonium salts derived from complex molecules. The resulting selenonium salts serve as versatile linchpins for photochemical, nucleophilic, and transition-metal-catalyzed transformations, enabling late-stage molecular diversification.

papers.title: Evolution of primary loops in vitrimers
papers.abstract: Covalent adaptable networks (CANs) comprise dynamic covalent bonds that allow topological reconfiguration. While this behavior underlies the reprocessability and recyclability of CANs, its influence on network topology, including defects, remains poorly understood. Prior simulations and indirect experimental studies suggest that dynamic exchange decreases the prevalence of primary loops, but direct experimental quantification has remained elusive. Here we use network disassembly spectrometry (NDS) to directly measure topological evolution during dynamic exchange. Surprisingly, activation of exchange at constant composition reveals two distinct concentration-dependent regimes. At concentrations above ~0.2 M, primary loops decrease upon activating exchange, whereas at lower concentrations, loop content increases, leading to gel-sol transitions. Temperature-dependent experiments and coarse-grained simulations suggest that these trends arise from competing entropic contributions that favor either loop formation or consumption depending on concentration. Changes in topology are accompanied by measurable changes in mechanical properties, demonstrating a direct relationship between network structure and macroscopic behavior. Furthermore, the concentration-dependent transition enables topology-mediated recycling, in which materials reversibly transition between gel and sol states through network rearrangement alone. These results provide the first direct experimental evidence of topology evolution in covalent adaptable networks and establish network topology as a measurable and tunable design parameter in dynamic polymer systems.

papers.title: Unlocking Ligand-Centered Redox Activity in an Indenyl Framework through Phosphorus Substitution
papers.abstract: Herein, we show that a phosphonium-substituted diphosphaindenylide (PPIPh) functions as a genuine two-electron redox-active π-ligand. The cationic manganese complex [Mn(CO)3(η5‑PPIPh)][BArF24] ([1][BArF24]) undergoes a reversible two-electron reduction to afford the isolable anionic complex [K(18c6)][Mn(CO)3(η3‑PPIPh)]·([K(18c6)][BArF24])n (n = 1 – 5). This constitutes the first isolable and structurally characterized two-electron redox couple of an indenyl-derived manganese complex, which has previously eluded isolation with purely carbocyclic indenyl ligands. Computational studies establish manganese in the +I oxidation state in both complexes, demonstrating that the redox process is exclusively ligand-centered. The redox-activity of the ligand also translates into chemical reactivity, with the anionic complex affording 91% yield in the hydroboration of 2-acetonaphthone, compared to only 7% for [1][BArF24].

papers.title: Chemical Accuracy for Carbapenem Breakdown by Class A beta-Lactamases Using a Transferable Embedded Machine-Learned Potential
papers.abstract: Bacterial resistance to carbapenems (potent β-lactam antibiotics) is a critical global health threat. The primary cause is β-lactamase enzymes that hydrolyze antibiotics. Previously, carbapenems resisted breakdown, making them ‘last resort’ antibiotics, but enzymes with carbapenemase activity have become widespread. Understanding and predicting the activity of β-lactamases will help in developing antibiotics and inhibitors, and combating antibiotic resistance. Effective prediction requires methods that are both accurate and computationally efficient. Multiscale combined quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) molecular dynamics simulations of reactions can discriminate between class A β-lactamases (the most widely distributed group) with or without carbapenemase activity, and identify determinants of activity. but face an accuracy/efficiency tradeoff: approximate semiempirical QM methods do not predict reaction barriers accurately, but higher level QM calculations require extensive computer time and resources, making them impractical for rapid predictions. Here, we develop and test a transferable ML/MM framework for the deacylation reaction of the carbapenem meropenem, using the electrostatic machine learning embedding (EMLE) scheme. This model gives free energy barriers to within 1 kcal/mol of values derived from experiment, for four different class A β-lactamases. Crucially, the model was trained only on active site structures from QM/MM simulations of a single enzyme. It did not require retraining to generalize across Class A β-lactamases. It is both faster and more accurate than semi-empirical QM/MM simulations. The ML/MM simulations capture the structural and electrostatic determinants of carbapenemase activity, including oxyanion stabilization and active site electric fields, that differ between enzymes. This work establishes transferable EMLE-based ML/MM simulation as a practical route for accurate, efficient modelling of enzyme-catalyzed reactions.

papers.title: Temporally decoupled electrochemiluminescence breaks the sensitivity–portability tradeoff in water toxicity sensing
papers.abstract: Multiple technologies have been developed to reconcile the trade-off between sensitivity and portability, which is a persistent fundamental challenge in chemical sensing. Among them, electrochemiluminescence (ECL) has the advantages of simple device configuration and outstanding sensitivity based on the transduction of electrochemical signals into optical readouts. However, this is based on multi-step interfacial electron transfer, wherein the concomitant efficiency losses and areadependent signal intensity inherently constitute the primary limitations. Herein, a novel photochargeable wireless ECL (PC-Wireless-ECL) system is established based on a bifunctional carbon nitride (CN). This strategy boosts the ECL signal intensity by eliminating the dependence on the electrode dimensions and decoupling the excitation and emission processes temporally. By constructing portable bifunctional CN vials coupled with a miniaturized light intensity sensor, this system revolutionizes the conventional ECL measurement paradigm and realizes on-site, rapid, and highly sensitive screening of water toxicity, thereby offering a new strategy for next-generation in-field analytical technologies.

papers.title: From Materials to Metalloenzymes: Superconducting Microresonators for Characterization of Thin Films
papers.abstract: Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy is a widely used technique for the characterization of paramagnetic centers across a wide range of disciplines. Yet, the detection limits of conventional 3D microwave resonators hinder the application of EPR to nanoscale and magnetically dilute thin films relevant to quantum, catalytic and biological devices. Here we show that high temperature superconducting spiral microresonators fabricated from YBa2Cu3O7-x enable pulse EPR measurements on diverse thin films with a sensitivity improvement of two to three orders of magnitude over commercial resonators. Templated 50 nm films of copper phthalocyanine (CuPc) diluted in metal-free phthalocyanine (H2Pc) deposited onto the microresonator were detectable in echo-detected EPR field sweeps with the templating effect clearly visible from narrowing of the spectrum compared to powder samples. The number of Cu(II) spins present in a single thin film of CuPc on a microresonator with 400 μm diameter was ~1011, as determined by measurement of coherence memory times (Tm) and longitudinal (T1) spin relaxation times. The Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) sequence was also employed, enabling improved SNR by averaging multiple echoes obtained from echo trains. To demonstrate biological application, Cu,Zn superoxide dismutase (SOD) was incorporated into trehalose films of ~3.7 μm average thickness, containing ~1012 Cu(II) centers. Hyperfine spectroscopy (ESEEM and HYSCORE) was successfully performed on the SOD films, producing spectra that match conventional measurements taken with ~104 times more enzyme. These results establish superconducting microresonators as a versatile high-sensitivity platform for pulse EPR of ultrathin and volume-limited films. The transformation of EPR from a ‘bulk’ to a ‘surface’ technique will facilitate the study of quantum materials, catalytic interfaces and bio-integrated devices.

papers.title: Olympic-patterned pentaboron emitter featuring highly distorted geometry enables efficient solution-processed ultrapure green OLEDs
papers.abstract: Efficient, ultrapure green organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) fabricated via wet processing are crucial for ultrahigh definition displays but remain highly challenging due to the paucity of suitable emitters. Herein, we developed Oly-BN, a novel multipleresonance thermally activated delayed fluorescence (MR-TADF) emitter featuring a distinct Olympic-patterned boron-distribution. The zigzag doped heteroatom polycyclic aromatic framework enables near-degenerate singlet/triplet excited states. Integrating para-N-π-B motifs helps regulate the triplet manifold and emission color point, enabling energetically accessible higher lying triplet excited states with enhanced spinorbit coupling, while also suppressing low-frequency structural relaxation and modulating the optical bandgap. Oly-BN in toluene exhibits vivid green emission at 522 nm with a narrow full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 17 nm, a photoluminescence quantum yield of 95%, and a fast reverse intersystem crossing rate constant of 6.9×106 s−1. Additionally, its highly twisted conformation weakens intermolecular interactions and favors bright, solid-state emission. The nonsensitized solution-processed OLEDs deliver ultrapure green electroluminescence with a CIEy value up to 0.73, and achieves an optimized maximum external quantum efficiency of 39.4%, which remains high at 29.9% at 1000 cd m-2. This work not only provides a promising highly saturated green emitter for solution-processed OLEDs but also demonstrates the importance of precisely integrating heteroatoms in modulating photophysical properties of MR-TADF emitters.

papers.title: Synthesis, Spectroscopic Characterisation, and Structural Elucidation of Ni(II) and Cu(II) Complexes of a Novel N,N’-Diaminophthalamidoxime Ligand
papers.abstract: A new N,N’-diaminophthalamidoxime (NAD) ligand was synthesised by reacting hydrazine hydrate with diethyl phthalate to give phthalic dihydrazide, which was subsequently reacted with hydroxylamine to yield the target ligand. The ligand was reacted with Ni(II) and Cu(II) salts to give [Ni(NAD)2]Cl2 and [Cu(NAD)2(OAc)2], respectively. The ligand and its complexes were characterised by solubility studies, melting point determination, complexometric metal analysis, room-temperature magnetic susceptibility, and infrared and UV–Visible spectroscopy. The free ligand was soluble in DMSO, DMF and hot ethanol, but insoluble in chloroform, ethyl acetate, acetone, methanol, dichloromethane and distilled water, and all three compounds showed high thermal stability (>300 °C). Diagnostic infrared bands at 3572 and 3524 cm-1 (νNH2 and νOH) and UV bands at 48,300, 36,630 and 28,985 cm-1 (n→σ*, π→π* and n→π*, respectively) confirmed the identity of the free ligand. Complexometric titration gave experimental metal contents of 9.92% (Cu) and 9.82% (Ni), in good agreement with the theoretical values of 10.09% and 10.15%, consistent with 1:2 metal-to-ligand stoichiometry in both complexes. Coordination through the azomethine nitrogen was indicated by shifts in ν(C=N) to 1651 cm-1 and 1634 cm-1, together with new ν(M–N) bands at 435 cm-1 and 487 cm-1 for the Cu(II) and Ni(II) complexes, respectively. [Ni(NAD)2]Cl2 displayed an effective magnetic moment of 4.83 BM and a d–d transition at 25,000 cm-1, consistent with a high-spin tetrahedral d8 environment, while [Cu(NAD)2(OAc)2] gave a magnetic moment of 2.27 BM and a d–d transition at 15,267 cm-1, consistent with a Jahn–Teller-distorted octahedral d9 environment. Together, these results establish the NAD ligand as an effective bidentate N-donor for first-row transition metal ions.

papers.title: A Distributed Diffusion Landscape Governs CO2 Coproduct Release from Fatty Acid Photodecarboxylase
Accelerating the Design of New Natural Deep Eutectic Solvents with Supervised Variational Autoencoders
papers.abstract: The rational design of natural deep eutectic solvents (NaDESs) is hindered by the vast combinatorial space arising from the possible combinations of hydrogen bond donors and acceptors. This enormous design space limits the systematic experimental exploration of their physicochemical properties. In this work, we propose a supervised variational autoencoder (SVAE) framework to efficiently explore this chemical space by coupling generative modeling with property prediction. The model is trained on a curated dataset of deep eutectic solvents to learn simultaneously the latent structural representations and correlations with target properties, including melting point, density, and viscosity. The SVAE generates virtual NaDES candidates characterized by molecular descriptors, component ratios, and target property values. To associate these virtual candidates with real molecules, a descriptor matching strategy is applied using the COCONUT natural product database. The resulting NaDES candidates are subsequently validated using predictive models trained on experimental DES data. The results show strong agreement between the SVAE-generated target property values and the corresponding predictions of the regression models (R2 = 0.89, RMSE=21.7 K for melting point; R2 = 0.91, RMSE = 0.04 g·cm-3 for density; and R2 = 0.89, RMSE=0.47 cP for ln(viscosity)). This workflow demonstrates how guided generative models can be combined with machine learning models to accelerate the discovery of sustainable solvents. Beyond NaDESs, the proposed strategy provides a general and transferable framework for the rational design of other chemical systems, where combinatorial complexity limits conventional experimental approaches.

papers.title: Polyelectrolyte Solutes, Gels, and Coacervates Differentially Impact Proto-Metabolic Ni-Catalyzed Bicarbonate Reduction.
papers.abstract: Reactions using metal and mineral catalysis likely provided vital organic feedstocks for the process of life’s origination, accessing early metabolic pathways, building proto-metabolism, and providing avenues for compartmentalization. Towards proto-cellular encapsulation, a growing pool of multiply-charged solutes and polymers, as well as organic-rich phases, would have influenced the operation of Earth’s proto-metabolic pathways. Here, we employ quantitative NMR and model molecules containing relevant carboxylate, amine, and phosphate moieties to describe their effect on the catalytic reduction of bicarbonate to formate, the first step in ancient carbon fixation, such as via a precursor reductive Acetyl-CoA (Wood-Ljungdahl) pathway or reductive tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. We find that this proto-metabolic carbon fixation process is relatively robust to build-up of organics, maintaining yields within about twofold despite relatively high concentrations of organic additives. Solute effects are not simply predicted by charge or solute size but depend on adsorption, participation in competing reactions, and solute-solute interactions. Combinations of solutes have a nonadditive effect, with certain pairs resulting in unchanged, intermediate, or increased formate yields compared to either solute alone; for example, sequestration of a yield-suppressing co-solute, adenosine monophosphate (AMP), partially alleviates yield suppression.

papers.title: Plasma Protein Binding Prediction under Scaffold Split: Tree Models, ChemBERTa, Graph Networks, and Late Fusion
papers.abstract: From idea generation to testing, drug discovery is a lengthy and expensive process. Rather than chasing all of their molecule ideas, scientists prioritize certain molecules that are more likely to be successful, from synthesis to safety to therapeutic use. Machine learning and AI enable researchers to narrow their candidate choices by predicting important properties such as ADMET (Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity). This study uses the Plasma Protein Binding (PPB) dataset from DeepChem’s MoleculeNet, with several graph neural networks (GNNs), ChemBERTa (a language model for SMILES strings of molecules), and fusions of these models. The performance of these neural models is compared against two standard tree-based models: Random Forest (RF) and XGBoost. Instead of random splitting of the dataset, this study evaluates the models based on scaffold splitting that separates molecules by the Bemis–Murcko scaffold and puts the entire group into only the training, validation, or test set. This study demonstrates that for the PPB dataset, GNNs and ChemBERTa models perform better than the tree models. On a mean basis, the fusion models perform better than the individual GNNs or ChemBERTa-only models. Random splitting on the RF model exhibits a better R2 score than on a scaffold-split dataset. Because under scaffold splitting the model predicts on unseen cores, the task becomes more difficult than under regular random splitting.

papers.title: Chemoproteomic mapping of active glycan-processing networks in a defined gut microbiome
papers.abstract: Microbiome studies typically infer function from gene content or expression, but these measurements do not establish which enzymes are catalytically active or what substrates they recognise. Here we use a multiplexed panel of mechanism-based glycosidase probes to map active glycan-processing enzymes directly from caecal samples of mice colonised with a defined, 14-member, human gut microbiota. Activity-based protein profiling identifies host and microbial enzymes involved in starch, β-glucan, xyloglucan and xylan degradation and links them to defined taxa and loci. Decorated probes resolve branch and substitution preferences within active enzyme families, revealing xylanase activities poorly detected by bulk substrate assays. Several prominent activities are assigned to low-abundance Bacteroides species, while enzyme deployment differs among animals sharing a common inoculum and diet. These results establish activity-based chemoproteomics as a complementary layer to metagenomics, transcriptomics and proteomics for defining functional glycan-processing states in host-associated microbiomes.

papers.title: What actually moves virtual screening performance: two measured resolution limits and six pre-registered interventions
papers.abstract: Reported improvements to structure-based virtual screening are usually differences in AUROC or enrichment between two protocols on one benchmark. We asked what a benchmark of typical size can actually resolve, and then measured six interventions against that limit with the reading rule for each committed to version control before the data existed. Two limits, not one. Scoring the same Vina poses with a second implementation of the same scoring function — agreeing at r = 0.970, no compound differing by more than 2 kcal/mol — moves AUROC by 0.020 [95% CI 0.011, 0.029]. Re-running the whole protocol at a different search effort and scoring it the same way moves AUROC by 0.039 [0.024, 0.056]. The first bounds a comparison of scoring functions on fixed poses; the second bounds a comparison of protocols, which is what most published improvements are. Both fall inside the range in which docking improvements are typically reported. On SARS-CoV-2 Mpro: changing the scoring function on identical poses moved AUROC +0.140, repairing a receptor preparation defect +0.045, scoring the pose ensemble rather than the top pose +0.055, supplying the correct binding site to a co-folding model −0.013, and eight-fold search effort −0.019. Two clear the relevant floor, one is marginal and two fall inside. The sixth — substituting DiffDock-L pose generation — is not evaluable on this panel: DiffDock places a fifth of the compounds outside the binding site, and that fifth is heavier and more often active than the panel, so any comparison on the remainder is biased. These are distributions over cross-validation fold assignment, not point estimates: we previously published the pose-ensemble arm as +0.019 and refuted, and it proved to be the 2nd percentile of a distribution centred at +0.031. The search-effort result is the sharpest either way: its measured effect is smaller than the run-to-run reproducibility of the protocol it was measured in. Docking adds nothing demonstrable over seven free physicochemical descriptors on either panel we assembled: on Mpro it significantly subtracts (−0.002 [−0.004, −0.000]) and on Factor Xa its +0.015 [−0.003, +0.034] crosses zero. Applying the same descriptors to LIT-PCBA gives a median AUROC of 0.7260 across 15 targets against published AutoDock Vina at 0.581 and GNINA at 0.611–0.616. These descriptor baselines are supervised on each benchmark's own labels while docking is not, so this is a bias control in the sense of Sieg et al., not a claim that descriptors are a deployable substitute. On the AVE-debiased variant the descriptor median falls to 0.6510. One method exceeded the floor. Boltz-2, an open-weights co-folding model scoring compounds from sequence and SMILES alone, does not beat the descriptor baseline on its own (Mpro +0.026, Factor Xa +0.019, both intervals spanning zero) but adds +0.093 [+0.062, +0.125] and +0.075 [+0.051, +0.099] respectively when combined with those descriptors. Its advantage is not that it is less property-driven — descriptors explain 63% of its score and 63% of Vina's — but that on Mpro its residual, the part orthogonal to those descriptors, ranks actives at 0.657 where six docking scores residualised the same way sat between 0.494 and 0.573. Both descriptor comparisons are supervised on each target's own labels; transferred cold to the other target the descriptor model ranks actives below chance , and the standalone Boltz-2 score — which requires no labels at all — is the only configuration usable on a target with no known actives. Across twelve cross-validation fold seeds the two do not overlap on Mpro: the highest docking residual observed is 0.581, the lowest Boltz-2 residual 0.644. On Factor Xa the residual result replicates in direction — 0.5882 [0.5789, 0.5975] against that target's own Vina arm at 0.5733 — but the margin is +0.015 rather than +0.083 and the ranges touch at their extremes, so the size of the effect does not replicate. One point outside a band is not a generalisation, so we pre-registered a third scoring approach to test it. FlashBind, an EGNN affinity head over learned docking poses, residualises to 0.538 [0.529, 0.546] — inside the docking band — with all three pre-registered controls passing and a pocket-agreement check ruling out the confound that the band is a property of our docking box. The claim that this ceiling belongs to the scoring approach rather than to these panels therefore remains untested rather than supported.

papers.title: Advancement of triphos-Ru catalyzed C–O bond disconnections and its challenges
papers.abstract: Cured epoxy resins are crosslinked thermoset materials with applications including carbon-or glass-reinforced composites, but whose extensive C–O and C–N bond networks renders recycling challenging. Previously, our group has reported a Ru-triphos-catalyzed system for the chemical deconstruction of amine-cured epoxy resins, enabling recovery of bisphenol A (BPA) under relatively mild conditions. Subsequent mechanistic studies identified slow catalyst activation and catalyst deactivation as key limitations. Herein, these insights were used to develop improved catalytic systems through pre-catalyst and reaction design. Replacement of the original triphos-Ru-TMM pre-catalyst enabled improved catalytic performance, while ligand design enabled the use of H2, instead of isopropanol, as reductant. Despite these advances, the improved performance observed for model compounds did not translate directly to cured epoxy resins. Reaction optimization revealed pronounced dependencies on substrate concentration, and polymer accessibility, while computational studies suggest changes in catalyst speciation imposed by conformational constraints. Together, these findings demonstrate that the bottlenecks governing epoxy-resin deconstruction can change due to constraints imposed by the polymer matrix. The mechanistic insights obtained herein provide a foundation for the development of next-generation thermoset deconstruction strategies.

papers.title: Vicem: Automating Molecular Mechanics Modeling of Solvation Dynamics with Applications to Time-Resolved X-ray Scattering
papers.abstract: Time-resolved X-ray solution scattering (trXSS) probes molecular-scale structural dynamics in solution, but its interpretation requires efficient computational methodologies and models for assessing how changes in solute structure and charge distribution affect the surrounding solvent shell and the resulting scattering signal. We present VICEM, an OpenMM/ASE-based software suite for constructing solvated molecular models, running molecular dynamics simulations, inspecting and analyzing the resulting trajectories, while exposing solute geometry, partial charges, Lennard–Jones parameters, and bonded terms as editable variables for model refinement. VICEM includes an approximate restrained-solute model designed for rapid solvent-shell sampling around prescribed solute geometries, together with utilities for correcting the potential energy along selected intramolecular coordinates. We benchmark the restrained model against established force fields for 244 systems comprising neutral organic molecules, charged organic solutes, and transition-metal complexes. Across 5018 solute-water radial distribution functions, the effect of restraining the solute structure on the solvent shell is generally comparable to differences between established flexible force fields, and diagnostic cases are scrutinized to identify when reference geometry, nonbonded assignment, or suppressed solute flexibility controls the solvent response. For a prototypical iron complex, VICEM is used to scan candidate geometries and quantify the effect of the structure on solvent-shell radial distribution functions and the corresponding scattering signal, showing how VICEM can be used to tune molecular models for structural refinement. VICEM is therefore shown to provide a platform for reproducible solvent-shell modeling and targeted force-field refinement with particular focus on trXSS analysis.

papers.title: THIOETHERS AS POTENTIAL ANTIBACTERIAL AGENTS AGAINST METHICILLIN-RESISTANT STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS (MRSA)
papers.abstract: The emergence and rapid spread of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) have created an urgent need for new antibacterial agents capable of overcoming established resistance mechanisms. Among the diverse sulfur-containing scaffolds, thioethers have attracted increasing attention because of their structural versatility and ability to modulate antibacterial activity through incorporation into different pharmacophores. This review provides a comprehensive overview of synthetic, semisynthetic, and natural or natural-product-derived thioether compounds evaluated against MRSA, with emphasis on their structural features, structure-activity relationships (SAR), antibacterial potency, and mechanisms of action. The major classes discussed include aminoglycoside-derived thioether amphiphiles, membrane-active small-molecule thioethers, quinazolinone and quinoline thioether scaffolds, pleuromutilin thioether derivatives, SecA-targeting thioethers, chalcone and oxazolidinone derivatives, FtsZ-targeting thioethers, anti-virulence and antibiofilm agents, antimicrobial peptidomimetics, and natural-product-derived thioether compounds. The studies demonstrate that sulfur-containing motifs can contribute to anti-MRSA activity through membrane disruption, inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis and targeting of essential non-ribosomal proteins. The available SAR evidence highlights the scaffold-dependent nature of thioether activity and supports their continued exploration as versatile structural motifs for the development of new therapeutic strategies against drug-resistant MRSA.

papers.title: Directed Evolution of a Non-Heme Iron Enzyme for Enantioselective Dearomative Nitrene Transfer: Synthesis of 3a-Aminopyrroloindoline Alkaloids
papers.abstract: Enzymatic nitrene-induced dearomatization represents an unexplored area of biocatalytic reactivity. Here, we report the directed evolution of AsqJ, a non-heme iron enzyme from aspoquinolone biosynthesis, to catalyze the first biocatalytic asymmetric dearomative nitrene transfer into indoles to furnish enantioenriched 3a-aminopyrroloindolines — a privileged scaffold in bioactive indole alkaloid natural products. Obtained through iterative semi-rational engineering and structure-informed mutagenesis, the final variant achieves up to 98% yield and >99% ee. The reaction accommodates a range of indole substrates, affording up to 86% isolated yield on preparative scale with consistently high enantioselectivity. Molecular dynamics simulations suggest that directed evolution established a new substrate-binding conformation that is distinct from the starting variant through a reorganized hydrogen-bonding network within a more preorganized active site. The synthetic utility of this platform is demonstrated through the total syntheses of two natural products, (+)-psychotriasine and (+)-psychotrimine. This work establishes asymmetric dearomative nitrene transfer as a new biocatalytic modality, extends the catalytic repertoire of non-heme iron enzymes to encompass asymmetric dearomatization, and provides a foundation for applying new-to-nature biocatalytic reactions in complex natural product synthesis.

papers.title: From Proteins and Molecules to Cats and Dogs: Visualization as Scalable Minimum Spanning Trees
papers.abstract: Dimensionality reduction and data visualization are essential for analyzing highdimensional datasets, yet traditional projection methods obscure local structural relationships. We present TMAP2, a scalable rewrite of TMAP that maps highdimensional data as a minimum spanning tree. TMAP2 accepts diverse input types, including continuous embeddings, sparse fingerprints, and precomputed graphs, and applies to single-cell, image, chemistry, or protein-language-model data. Every line on the map is therefore a real nearest-neighbor relationship, and exactly one path joins any two points. The number of edges along that path, its hop count, works as a coordinate along a progression: it recovers a pancreatic cell’s developmental age (Spearman 0.90), tracks the collection date of a SARS-CoV-2 spike sequence built from raw sequence alone (Spearman 0.86), and traces a smooth morph from a Persian cat to a Yorkshire terrier that crosses species at a single edge. On 3.6 million CAZyme sequences the same tree separates taxonomic domains and, within the family GH43, sorts sequences by catalytic activity, revealing an anchor enzyme annotated as one activity sitting among a cluster of another. TMAP2 extends the original TMAP from fingerprints to any embedding, at up to one million points with 95–99% recall.

papers.title: Interface-Engineered MXene/TMD Heterostructures for Efficient Hydrogen Evolution: Progress, DFT-Guided Mechanisms, and Perspectives
papers.abstract: The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) requires efficient, durable, and earth-abundant electrocatalysts to reduce reliance on platinum-group metals. MXene/transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterostructures offer a promising platform by combining the abundant, tunable catalytic sites of TMDs with the high electrical conductivity, hydrophilicity, and versatile surface chemistry of MXenes. This review critically examines recent advances in the synthesis, interfacial engineering, and HER performance of MXene/TMD heterostructures, with particular emphasis on how interfacial interactions govern catalytic behavior. The roles of phase engineering, defect and heteroatom incorporation, surface terminations, and heterointerface construction are discussed in relation to interfacial charge redistribution, electronic-structure modulation, hydrogen adsorption energetics, active-site accessibility, and reaction kinetics. Experimental HER performance across representative MXene/TMD systems is compared to establish structure-interface-performance relationships and identify the origins of enhanced activity and stability.
