The review first discusses the main mechanisms of shear thickening, namely hydrodynamic interactions, hydrocluster formation, frictional contact activation and stress dependent jamming and then critically reviews constitutive and theoretical models used for description of continuous and discontinuous shear thickening. Then, we discuss the effect of particle size and shape, volume fraction, surface chemistry, carrier fluid properties, temperature, confinement and boundary conditions on particle rearrangement, formation of frictional contacts, jamming and macroscopic rheology. Formulation stability, sedimentation, reproducibility, processing and scale-up, as well as experimental and computational approaches to characterize and predict STF behavior are emphasized. Recent advances in STF-based composites

papers.title: Visible Light-Mediated Homoallylic Radical Rearrangement for the Intermolecular Synthesis of 1,2-Biscyclopropanes
papers.abstract: 1,2-Biscyclopropanes are privileged structural motifs found in natural products, pharmaceuticals, and functional materials, yet their assembly remains challenging. We report the first radical intermolecular strategy for the synthesis of highly functionalized 1,2-biscyclopropanes. Visiblelight-mediated energy transfer (EnT) provides access to a triplet diradical species that, through an ordered intermolecular radical addition, furnishes a rare bis-homoallylic diradical intermediate. This strategy activates the 3-exo-trig radical cyclization triggered by an irreversible intersystem crossing (ISC) step. The method is compatible with naturally occurring functional groups, providing efficient access to polycyclic architectures bearing otherwise inaccessible protic functionalities. Furthermore, the resulting products serve as versatile intermediates for downstream diversification. This work marks a milestone in the development of new mechanistic approaches for the synthesis of highly challenging molecules, highlighting the potential of EnT-enabled diradical reactivity to overcome longstanding limitations in the construction of small rings.

papers.title: QSARmil: A Package for Molecular Multi-Instance Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Numerous Python tools are available for molecular machine learning, typically built around core modeling paradigms such as descriptor-based approaches (“RDKit + scikit-learn”), deep neural networks, graph neural networks, geometric deep learning, and foundation models. Multi-instance learning (MIL) was originally inspired by the drug discovery problem, where a molecule can adopt multiple conformers and the biologically active one is unknown. Despite its clear relevance, MIL has not yet been supported by a dedicated and comprehensive Python platform for molecular applications. Here, we present QSARmil, a Python package designed for molecular multi-instance machine learning, that provides an integrated workflow including instance generation (e.g., conformers), 2D and 3D descriptor calculation, implementation of diverse MIL algorithms, and key instance identification. By bringing these components together in a unified and user-friendly framework, QSARmil makes it straightforward to apply multi-instance learning to any molecular property prediction task.

papers.title: De Novo Linear Peptides as Potential Recognition Elements and/or Aggregation Modulators of Amyloid-β42 in Alzheimer’s Disease
papers.abstract: The development of deep learning algorithms for de novo protein design has opened the way for novel in silico strategies to develop peptide binders targeting protein aggregation implicated in neurodegenerative diseases. When combined with molecular simulations, these approaches provide a promising framework for investigating protein-peptide recognition and its impact on aggregation. Herein, we studied, through molecular dynamics, four de novo peptides of sizes ranging between 7 and 15 residues, generated with RFdiffusion, combined with ProteinMPNN and AlphaFold, using different constrained sequences of the Aβ42 peptide and a common hotspot region (residues 16-22). The shorter peptides formed cross-β sheet structures with the hotspot sequence, whereas the longer peptides adopted α-helical conformations. The hotspot sequence in trans and the segment Aβ42(16-20) linked to an hexalysine sequence were also investigated. Aβ42 was modeled using CHARMM36m (C36m) and AMBER99SB-DISP force fields, with the latter showing an aggregation propensity comparable to C36m under 8 M urea denaturing conditions. The peptides’ potential to modulate aggregation was assessed for C36m Aβ42 model tetramers at 1:1 peptide-to-monomer ratios. Although none of the peptides prevented the formation of all possible oligomeric species (i.e., dimer, trimer, and tetramer), several, selectively inhibited or delayed tetramer formation within the simulation timescale, resulting in less compact assemblies. The underlying mechanisms differed among peptides, with some altering intermolecular β-sheet organization through persistent interactions with the C-terminal region and others influencing tetramer formation with limited participation in βsheet interactions. The behavior of the peptides 16-22 (KLVFFAE) and the 16-20-KKKKKK closely reproduced experimental observations. At high temperatures none of the peptides precluded tetramerization, suggesting that enhanced hydrophobic interactions outweigh peptide-mediated inhibition. Notably, charged peptides showed the strongest effects on tetramer formation, indicating an important role for electrostatic interactions in inhibiting Aβ42 aggregation.

papers.title: Reactive Molecular Dynamics Simulations of Mechanochemical Ammonia Production
papers.abstract: Green ammonia production will be crucial to achieving global net-zero emissions. The current dominant technology for producing ammonia, known as the Haber-Bosch process, requires extreme temperatures and pressures. One promising alternative is mechanocatalysis, where mechanical energy is used to promote reactivity and reduce energy consumption. Ammonia production via mechanocatalysis has recently been demonstrated at the laboratory scale. A deeper understanding of the kinetics and mechanism of this reaction is necessary to facilitate scale-up of this process. However, this is challenging to obtain inside ball mills, the most commonly used devices for mechanocatalysis. Here, we use molecular dynamics simulations to study mechanocatalytic ammonia production. A reactive force field is employed to investigate the effect of applied stress on nitrogen dissociation and hydrogenation on an iron catalyst. We find that the activation energy of the nitrogen dissociation step decreases from 56 kJ/mol in the thermally activated process on Fe(111), to 29 kJ/mol under a normal stress of 5 GPa. For the less reactive Fe(110) surface, the reduction is even more significant, from 117 kJ/mol to 35 kJ/mol. The larger activation volume for Fe(110) than Fe(111) is due to deeper penetration of the nitrogen molecules into the more open surface. The hydrogenation step was also accelerated under applied stress, although the effect was less pronounced than for nitrogen dissociation. These trends are quantified using SATA equation framework, providing the first SATA analysis of mechanochemical ammonia synthesis. We also reveal the atomic-scale mechanism of this stress-enhanced reactivity, which does not require increased defect density in the iron catalyst. The mechanistic analysis reveals that normal stress promotes Fe–N bond formation, which weakens the N–N bond and lowers the activation barrier. This is distinct from non-catalytic mechanochemistry, where normal stress typically inhibits bond-breaking reactions. Nitrogen dissociation can be further accelerated by the application of shear stress, which can promote the reaction at room temperature. These results provide an improved fundamental understanding that could help to guide further improvements in the efficiency of mechanochemical ammonia production.

papers.title: Framework-Defined Microenvironments Differentiate Molecular CO2 Reduction Sites
papers.abstract: Molecular catalysts offer well-defined active sites for electrochemical CO2 reduction to CO, while immobilization in metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) can increase catalyst loading and organize these sites within a porous environment. This strategy often assumes that repeated molecular sites remain functionally equivalent after framework incorporation. Here, using DFT-benchmarked, site-resolved empirical valence bond–free energy perturbation (EVB–FEP) simulations in an explicit electrode-supported Co-porphyrin MOF, we studied four elementary CO2-to-CO reactions across eight matched boundary and inner sites and four progressively assembled electrochemical environments. Framework embedding produces the dominant energetic redistribution and establishes a persistent boundary–inner differentiation in CO2 adsorption. We identify its microscopic origin as a site-dependent local axial electric field generated by different balances of solvent, ion, and neighboring-framework electrostatics. Boundary and inner sites therefore stabilize the same reaction through different microscopic environments. Regional CO2 mobility further shows that intrinsic reactivity and transport accessibility provide separate constraints on site function. Together, these results show that framework incorporation creates a spatial distribution of functionally distinct catalytic microenvironments rather than simply multiplying an equivalent molecular catalyst. By combining high densities of well-defined molecular active sites with spatially heterogeneous yet synthetically tunable environments, framework materials provide a bridge between molecular and heterogeneous catalyst behavior. Once the microscopic origins of site-dependent reactivity are captured by suitable descriptors, this mechanistic understanding can inform materials screening and guide framework design toward balancing reaction energetics and accessibility.

papers.title: Probing Electronic Structure of Chiral Unsaturated Hydrocarbons at the Carbon Edge
papers.abstract: Core-level spectroscopies provide an atom-specific probe of electronic structure, including the effects of molecular geometry and chirality. This contribution investigates the carbon K-edge electronic structure in a series of conjugated hydrocarbons and their chiral derivatives using frozen-core core-valence-separated equation-of-motion coupled-cluster methods with single and double excitations (fc-CVS-EOM-CCSD). Core ionization energies, X-ray absorption spectra (XAS), and X-ray circular dichroism (XCD) are analyzed for ethylene, benzene, toluene, butadiene, and stilbene derivatives. The computed XAS reproduce the main features of available experimental spectra and reveal how molecular structure and π-conjugation modify core-level transitions. Chiral substitution lowers molecular symmetry, activates transitions that are dipole-forbidden in the parent molecules, redistributes oscillator strength among framework-centered states, and introduces additional substituent-centered core excitations. Comparison of XAS and XCD demonstrates their complementary character. Whereas closely spaced transitions often merge into a single XAS band, their signed rotatory strengths can produce distinct, sign-alternating features in XCD. Consequently, XCD reveals electronic structure that can remain hidden in congested XAS spectra. These results demonstrate how high-level simulations of carbon K-edge XAS and XCD can connect local core-level electronic structure with molecular structure, conjugation, and chirality.

papers.title: Interpretable Machine Learning Disentangles Pore Confinement Across Multiple Zr-MOF CO2 Capture Targets
papers.abstract: Pore confinement in zirconium-based metal–organic frameworks (Zr-MOFs) is often described using the cage–window ratio (ΓCW), the largest cavity diameter divided by the pore-limiting diameter (Df), yet whether this composite coordinate carries information beyond Df alone remains unclear. We modeled CO2 uptake, heat of adsorption (HoA), and CO2/N2 selectivity for 239 Zr-containing MOFs at two pressures relevant to vacuum-swing adsorption using structure-grouped machine learning with SHAP interpretation, reaching test R2 values of 0.77–0.88. Although ΓCW correlated positively with all three targets, controlling for Df weakened these associations and reversed their sign, while the reciprocal analysis left the Df associations largely unchanged and a difference-based formulation produced no significant association. Df played different roles across the three targets, indicating that the apparent confinement effect mainly reflects the limiting aperture rather than relative cage–window architecture.

papers.title: Confinement physics of highly anisotropic supramolecular assemblies in thin liquid films: A perspective on amyloid fibrils
papers.abstract: Amyloid fibrils derived from non-pathogenic proteins are among the most efficient protein-based stabilizers of foams and emulsions, yet the physicochemical basis of their colloidal performance remains incompletely understood. Substantial progress has been achieved in elucidating amyloidogenesis pathways, high-resolution fibril structures and the behaviour of fibrils at soft interfaces. Nevertheless, the physicochemical mechanisms through which fibril attributes and emergent interfacial self-organization are translated into macroscopic colloid stability remain fragmented and largely empirical. Here we propose a conceptual framework for advancing this problem. We argue that a major limitation arises from overlooking a decisive hierarchical level: the thin liquid film separating interacting foam bubbles or emulsion droplets. Such a film constitutes the physical locus where coalescence may be arrested through confinement-induced colloidal interactions leading to overall colloid stabilization. Beyond the problem of colloid stability, examination of such interactions in amyloid fibril-based systems exposes a broader physicochemical question concerning the behaviour of highly anisotropic supramolecular assemblies under film-confinement conditions. This Perspective identifies the principal knowledge gaps limiting mechanistic understanding of amyloid fibril-mediated colloid stabilization and discusses how its physicochemical description can be achieved through resolution of the identified knowledge gaps. We propose that amyloid fibrils should be viewed not only as high-performance colloidal stabilizers but also as experimentally mature model systems for exploring the confinement physics of highly anisotropic surface-active supramolecular entities.

papers.title: Potential-Dependent Redox Speciation in Substituted MnIII and CrIII Phthalocyanines
papers.abstract: We performed a comprehensive electrochemical and spectroelectrochemical study of three transition metal phthalocyanine (Pc) complexes, Pc n-OBu (2−)Mn III Cl, Pc tBu (2−)Mn III Cl and Pc tBu (2−)Cr III Cl (Pc tBu is the dianion of 2,9(10),16(17),23(24)-tetra- tert -butyl-phthalocyanine and Pc n-OBu is the dianion of 1,4,8,11,15,18,22,25-octa-n-butoxy-phthalocyanine), that are relevant for a variety of bond-breaking and forming reactions. Syntheses were optimized for previously reported tert -butylated species. Solvent-dependent voltammetry, spectroelectrochemistry, and for the first time for Mn III and Cr III Pc derivatives, spectroelectrochemical magnetic circular dichroism (MCD), were used to assess ligand- versus metal-centered redox events, electrochemical and chemical reversibilities of electron transfer, and effects of axial ligand coordination in dichloromethane or chloroform (DCM or CHCl 3 ) versus N,N -dimethylformamide (DMF). Comparisons are made to previously reported voltammetry and spectra of both Pc(2−)Mn II and chemically prepared oxidation states of Pc(2−)Cr II . We observe differences in localization of reduction events in P c n-OBu (2−)Mn III Cl versus Pc tBu (2−)Mn III Cl, with a more electron-rich ring promoting formation of MnI over Pc-centered reduction. We observe unique reduction behavior in Pc tBu (2−)Cr III Cl that points towards a mixture of ligand- and metal-centered character. To the best of our knowledge, these studies represent the first complete solvent-dependent spectroelectrochemical characterization of both Mn III and Cr III phthalocyanine derivatives across up to six different oxidation states.

papers.title: Weak Anion Hydration Drives LCST Behaviour in Ionic Liquid–Water Mixtures: Insights from Calorimetry and Neutron Diffraction
papers.abstract: Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) combined with neutron diffraction and isotopic substitution (NDIS) has been used to elucidate the molecular origins of lower critical solution temperature (LCST) behaviour in the tetrabutylphosphonium 5-phenyltetrazolate/water ([P4444][Ph−tet]/H2O) system. Comparison with the structurally similar but fully water-miscible analogue, tetrabutylphosphonium benzoate ([P4444][Bz]) reveals a much smaller negative enthalpy of mixing with water. This is indicative that weaker solvation of the [Ph−tet]–anion drives an entropy-dominated desolvation process upon heating, leading to phase separation into IL-rich and water-rich domains and is supported by observation from NDIS that the [Ph−tet]–anion is only weakly hydrated by water.

papers.title: Improved efficiency for better resolved solid-state NMR studies of Aluminum sites in materials
papers.abstract: In solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy of materials, a multiple-quantum magic angle spinning (MQMAS) experiment is routinely employed to characterize quadrupolar nuclei. It provides high-resolution isotropic spectra correlated with anisotropic quadrupolar lineshapes that contain valuable structural information. For aluminum (27Al, spin 5/2), a key constituent of active catalytic sites in zeolites, quintuple-quantum magic angle spinning (5QMAS) NMR spectroscopy provides substantially increased frequency dispersion in the isotropic dimension relative to its conventional triple-quantum (3QMAS) counterpart. However, the enhanced resolution of 5QMAS remains largely underexplored due to prohibitively low sensitivity for most samples. To overcome this limitation, optimal control (OC) method was used to design highly efficient excitation and reconversion pulses for both 3QMAS and 5QMAS sequences. Using Al(acac)3 reference sample, experimental 3QMAS and 5QMAS spectra acquired with specifically tailored OC pulses yielded 3.4- and 18.5-fold higher signal intensities relative to conventional rectangular pulses, respectively, at magnetic field strength of 9.4 T and MAS frequency of 12.5 kHz. Analogous measurements conducted at 14.1 T and MAS frequency of 55.555 kHz provided corresponding signal enhancements of 5.2- and 50-fold. Although broadband OC pulses optimized over broader distributions of quadrupolar coupling parameters and chemical shifts exhibit lower relative signal enhancements, OC-5QMAS for a hydrated MFI zeolite sample yielded a 6-fold intensity enhancement relative to the conventional 5QMAS experiment. Furthermore, the OC-5QMAS spectra exhibited a signal-to-noise ratio superior to that of traditional 3QMAS spectra, thereby enabling routine 27Al solid-state NMR characterization of tetrahedral sites with both improved sensitivity and larger frequency dispersion to potentially resolve crystallographically distinct framework positions.

papers.title: Saturated (Hetero)cyclic α-Fluoro-β-Keto Esters for the Scalable Synthesis of Advanced Fluorinated Building Blocks For Drug Discovery
papers.abstract: Cyclic α-fluoro-β-keto esters were used as common precursors to two classes off luorinated building blocks: α,β,β-trifluorinated (hetera)cycloalkane carboxylic acids and their functionalized derivatives, and cyclic α-fluorinated β-amino acids. The key precursors were prepared via the Selectfluor-mediated α-fluorination ofthe commercially available cyclic β-keto esters. Deoxo fluorination of α-f luoro-β-keto esters with SF 4 in anhydrous HF gave α,β,β-trifluorinated esters, which were converted into a series of building blocks (carboxylic acids, alcohols, bromides, and amines). Reductive amination of the same key precursors with benzylamine proceeded cis -selectively for the six-membered scaffolds and, after debenzylation, hydrolysis, and N -Boc protection, delivered cyclic α-fluorinated β-amino acids and their protected derivatives. The 2–5-step reaction sequences were operationally simple and scalable, with individual steps performed on up to 150 g scale. α,β,β-Trifluorination lowered the carboxylic acid p K a by 1.24–1.90 units, whereas its effect on Log P was small and scaffold-dependent; in both cases, the α-F and β,β-F 2 contributions were non-additive. In the cyclic α-fluorinated β-amino acids, α-fluorination decreased the carboxylic acid p K a by 0.66–0.87 units and the ammonium p K a by 1.39–1.85 units relative to the non-fluorinated analogs.

papers.title: The Influence of Pressure on the Carbon Dioxide Absorption in Ionic Liquids
papers.abstract: In this work, we systematically investigate the pressuredependent CO2 absorption behavior in ionic liquids and a switchable solvent using density functional theory calculations under hydrostatic pressure, combined with ab initio molecular dynamics simulations. A diverse set of ionic liquid anions was examined to identify structural motifs that govern the absorption behavior. Pressure was found to significantly affect reactivity, allowing access to chemically bound anion–CO2 complexes that are not observed under ambient conditions. We identified fully reversible, irreversible, and purely physical CO2 absorption with the application of external pressure. Nitrogen-rich heterocyclic anions were shown to predominantly exhibit irreversible CO2 absorption, whereas oxygen-based anions with moderate nucleophilicity mostly show reversible pressure-switchable behavior. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations of a representative ionic liquid system confirmed pressureactivated CO2 absorption at the dynamic condensed-phase level. The pressure-induced CO2 absorption mechanism was further validated using the switchable solvent N,Ndimethylethanolamine, which is known to bind CO2 reversibly with the application of pressure. These results provide molecular-level insights into pressure-induced CO2 absorption and establish design principles for tailoring ionic liquids specifically for tunable, energy-efficient CO2 capture applications.

papers.title: Electrostatic Encoding Enables Simultaneous Dual Labeling of Proteins by a Single Sortase A Enzyme
papers.abstract: Site-specific dual labeling of proteins provides access to multifunctional biomolecular constructs for applications ranging from imaging to the development of next-generation therapeutics. Currently, enzymatic dual labeling strategies rely on workflows involving multiple (semi-)orthogonal enzymes or temporary protection/deprotection schemes. Here, we present a one-pot strategy for protein dual labeling that relies on the single sortase A pentamutant (SrtA-5M) enzyme. By rationally designing complementary charged modules on the protein substrate and labeling reagent, we exploit electrostatic interactions to selectively guide the simultaneous installation of two distinct labels at the N- and C-termini of recombinant proteins without the need for multiple ligases, protecting groups, intermediate purification steps, or large reagent excesses. The efficiency of the approach is demonstrated on protein substrates and affords dually labeled products with high selectivity under mild reaction conditions. Beyond its practical utility, this study provides new insights into the influence of the P2 residue x within the sortase recognition motif (LPxTG) relative to glycyl nucleophiles, revealing an important role in governing sortase-mediated transpeptidation outcomes.

papers.title: Supramolecular Metallohydrogels of Fe(III) and Zn(II) with 3-Aminopropan-1-ol as Low Molecular Weight Hydrogelator: Unveiling Self-healing activity, rheological dynamics, and stimuli-sensitivity
papers.abstract: Two different metallohydrogels of Fe(III) and Zn(II) have been synthesized through the use of low molecular gelator and water as a polar protic fluid medium, encapsulated in distinct metallohydrogel networks. 3-Aminopropan-1-ol is executed as the potential LMWG for achieving non-covalent interaction-guided supramolecular soft -flexible scaffold formation. The mechanical stability and the flexible-features of different metallohydrgel have been explored through exhaustive rheological experimental studies covering shear strain sweep studies, angular frequency sweep investigations, and time sweep based experiments. The rheo-reversible dynamics of both metallohydrogels are examined through current attempts. The self-healing features of different metallohydrogels have been explored. The expression of distinct metallohydrogels under the impacts of diverse externally added stimuli has been thoroughly explored through the work. In a comparative vision the mechanical stability and stimuli effects, the Zn(II) metallohydrogel showed more predominant effect.

papers.title: Efficient NMR Signal Enhancement of Heteronuclei via Reversible Exchange at Millitesla Magnetic Fields
papers.abstract: Signal amplification by reversible exchange (SABRE) is a versatile hyperpolarization technique providing NMR signal enhancement by five orders of magnitude. The sensitivity gain offered by SABRE hyperpolarization of 13 C and 15 N heteronuclei in biologically relevant molecules enables various emerging in vivo applications, including metabolic profiling of cancerous tumors and cellular models. The pioneering spin physics developed for heteronuclear SABRE favors nano- and microtesla field range, which requires magnetic shielding of the Earth’s field, representing the key instrumentational and cost disadvantages of this method. Herein, we introduce a novel approach for heteronuclear SABRE, operating at static magnetic fields of tens to hundreds of millitesla, conveniently achieved in the fringe field of an NMR spectrometer or an MRI scanner and also readily accessible by low-cost purpose-built Halbach magnets. This approach, dubbed “SABRETACHE” (SABRE Transfer of Alignment to Coupled HEteronuclei), is effective if a substrate molecule contains two J -coupled chemically inequivalent heteronuclei, at least one of which is also J -coupled to a parahydrogen-derived hydride in a SABRE-active Ir complex. Theoretical description of SABRETACHE shows that polarization transfer results from a coherent spin mixing at level anti-crossings, which, for this type of spin systems, take place at millitesla fields. Experimental validation using the example of [ 15 N 3 ]nimorazole (clinically approved antibiotic) demonstrates that SABRETACHE can provide higher polarization levels than the well-established SABRE-SHEATH approach. Furthermore, SABRETACHE enabled sub-second high-resolution 15 N MRI. We envision SABRETACHE as a technically simple, robust and efficient hyperpolarization approach, which can serve as a viable alternative to the already established hyperpolarization techniques.

papers.title: A Rapid Chemical Relithiation Method Using Solvated Electrons for the Direct Recycling of Lithium-ion Battery Cathodes
papers.abstract: Due to the increasing adoption of electric vehicles, there is an imminent surge in waste lithium-ion batteries which will intensify resource depletion, environmental concerns, and supply chain vulnerability. Direct recycling is an energy-efficient, environmentally friendly solution that nondestructively regenerates spent cathode active material, bypassing downstream cathode resynthesis from raw materials and securing critical minerals within the supply chain to meet growing battery demand while mitigating battery waste. Here we present a rapid solution-phase relithiation mechanism, inspired by Birch reduction chemistry, for the direct regeneration of spent LiNi0.5Mn0.3Co0.2O2 active material. Our method addresses limitations of direct recycling related to process intensity and scalability. A highly stable solvated electron solution, composed of pure Li metal and condensed liquid ammonia, efficiently delivers electrons to oxidized transition metals and supplies Li ions to vacancies within the crystal lattice, replenishing stoichiometric Li content. After a short annealing, the regenerated cathode material exhibits a restored bulk and near-surface crystal structure. The regenerated material demonstrates enhanced electrochemical performance relative to the pristine material when cycled to 4.3 V (159.49 mAh/g and 94.10% capacity retention after 100 cycles), highlighting its strong long-term cycling stability. Our system demonstrates the successful application of solvated electrons for efficient, sustainable battery recycling.

papers.title: Flat Amino Acid Surrogates Induce Turn Conformers: Synthesis, Nitrogen Chirality, Conformation and Biomedical Applications of N-Amino Triazolone (Nat) Peptides
papers.abstract: 4-Amino-1,2,4-triazol-3-ones are relatively flat but shown to serve as turn inducing amino amide surrogates in peptides. Model N-amino triazolone (Nat) peptides were first synthesized and shown by NMR studies in solution to exhibit diastereotopic glycine methylene protons indicative of chiral nitrogen with inversion barriers around 17-18 kcal/mol, as well as solvent shielded amide protons indicative of involvement in intramolecular hydrogen bonds in -turn conformers. In crystal structures packing forces likely perturbed intramolecular hydrogen bonding, but Nat residues exhibited dihedral angles characteristic of the i+1 central position of certain -turn structures. Introduction of Nat residues as turn surrogates into antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory peptide analogs gave respectively comparable activity against Gram positive and negative microorganisms as well as potent ability to mitigate Toll receptor agonist effects on cytokine and chemokine levels by the modulation of the cluster-of-differentiation-36 receptor (CD36) in

papers.title: The Intrinsic Photochemical (in)-Stability of Lead Halide Perovskites
papers.abstract: The intrinsic photochemical and thermodynamic stability of lead halide perovskite, as influenced by the A-site cations, is evaluated: for Methylammonium (MA), Formamidinium (FA), and Cesium (Cs). To bridge the gap to 25-year commercial viability, MA should be excluded from commercial perovskite designs. A research and development focus on FA/Cs mixed-cation materials, or on fully inorganic Cs based materials is better (the latter being the most photostable option). However, also FA based materials show signs of intrinsic photochemical instability. Fully inorganic triple halide perovskites represent the best materials for tandems on silicon, regarding photo-stability, but, I 2 formation can still occur due to the intrinsic nature of charge transport and has to be suppressed. Exclusion of oxygen and humidity is a first prerequisite for longevity. Failures in the field of silicon solar panels are generally not related to the Si semi-conductor, implying that only an intrinsically photostable semi-conductors can result in acceptable solar panel breakdown statistics.

papers.title: Electrifying Oxygen Atom Transfer Reactions: Utilizing OER and ORR Pathways for Organic Synthesis
papers.abstract: Oxygen atom transfer reactions (OAT) are a key transformation for the synthesis of commodity and fine chemicals, with existing processes relying on stoichiometric oxidants and sometimes harsh reaction conditions. Electrifying these reactions (e-OAT), to run at room temperature and to replace chemical oxidants with cheap electricity and the sustainable O-atom donors water or O 2 can reduce environmental impact. At the same time, conceptually separating thermodynamic driving force provided via electricity from the identity of the oxygen atom source holds potential for unique selectivity that cannot easily be achieved with chemical oxidants. In order to spark new developments in the field of e-OAT, this perspective summarizes fundamental mechanistic aspects and successful examples of chemical OAT, to highlight connections as well as development potential of e-OAT reactions across epoxidation, C–H hydroxylation, sulfoxidation, N-oxidation and phosphine oxidation. Covering both, homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts, the state of the art and most recent developments of these e-OAT reactions are included. We elaborate on the role of different reactive intermediates types and design principles for catalysts and reaction conditions, outlining how to achieve high reaction selectivity for e-OAT processes over parasitic side reactions such as O 2 evolution, as well as strategies for challenging reactions such as partial methane oxidation to methanol. To inspire innovation, we visualize an overlap between active intermediates of e-OAT with OER and ORR catalysis platforms, with opportunity for repurposing existing successful catalysts for e-OAT. Finally, we showcase with selected examples that the successful application of e-OAT catalysis will eventually require a combined control over catalyst species as well as reactor design in essential combination, to reach demanding target reactions, such as epoxidation, methane hydroxylation or oxidative N 2 fixation at full performance.

papers.title: Near-Complete Synthon Library via Retrosynthetic Analysis for Automated Organic Synthesis
papers.abstract: As idealized structural fragments for guiding bond disconnections, synthons are considered the conceptual backbone of retrosynthetic analysis. Yet retrosynthesis can be difficult because the choice of synthons requires extensive experience in organic synthesis, which prevents non-experts from accessing desired products. Here we address this knowledge gap by constructing a curated, machine interpretable database of commercially available synthon equivalents (hereafter valid synthons) distilled from large-scale retrosynthetic analysis. Mining over 40 million molecules from PubChem, we identify 1,617 essential valid synthons. These synthons, organized into (i) molecular backbones, (ii) functional groups, and (iii) linker motifs, were obtained via iterative retrosynthetic decomposition and stringent frequency based filtering tied to documented reaction precedents. The resulting set enables the in silico reconstruction of over 94% of these 40 million molecules. We demonstrate that such synthons reduce dependence on expansive reagent inventories, even though the routes themselves are non-conventional and algorithm-generated: using only seven representative valid synthons, we accessed three structurally and functionally divergent targets (melatonin, a natural sleep hormone; an azo dye; and a photoactive melatonin derivative), illustrating the breadth and practicality of a synthons to products methodology in the context of automated synthesis for non-experts in organic synthesis.

papers.title: Advancement of triphos-Ru catalyzed C–O bond disconnections and its challenges
papers.abstract: Cured epoxy resins are crosslinked thermoset materials with applications including carbon-or glass-reinforced composites, but whose extensive C–O and C–N bond networks renders recycling challenging. Previously, our group has reported a Ru-triphos-catalyzed system for the chemical deconstruction of amine-cured epoxy resins, enabling recovery of bisphenol A (BPA) under relatively mild conditions. Subsequent mechanistic studies identified slow catalyst activation and catalyst deactivation as key limitations. Herein, these insights were used to develop improved catalytic systems through pre-catalyst and reaction design. Replacement of the original triphos-Ru-TMM pre-catalyst enabled improved catalytic performance, while ligand design enabled the use of H2, instead of isopropanol, as reductant. Despite these advances, the improved performance observed for model compounds did not translate directly to cured epoxy resins. Reaction optimization revealed pronounced dependencies on substrate concentration, and polymer accessibility, while computational studies suggest changes in catalyst speciation imposed by conformational constraints. Together, these findings demonstrate that the bottlenecks governing epoxy-resin deconstruction can change due to constraints imposed by the polymer matrix. The mechanistic insights obtained herein provide a foundation for the development of next-generation thermoset deconstruction strategies.

papers.title: Integrated Raman Spectroscopy and Supervised Imaging for Label-Free Identification and Mapping of Oral Pathogens in Complex Biofilms
papers.abstract: Although Raman spectroscopy has demonstrated excellent performance for the identification of isolated bacterial cells, its application to spatially resolved analysis of complex polymicrobial communities remains a major analytical challenge. Here, we present a transferable supervised Raman imaging workflow that integrates spontaneous Raman spectroscopy, confocal Raman microscopy, and PCA-LDA chemometric analysis for the label-free identification of clinically relevant oral bacteria. The proposed framework uses Raman spectra acquired from isolated bacterial cells to train a supervised classifier that is directly transferred to hyperspectral Raman images, enabling quantitative pixel-wise bacterial identification without fluorescent labels or molecular probes. The workflow was validated using four representative oral bacterial species (Streptococcus oralis, Actinomyces naeslundii, Fusobacterium nucleatum, and Porphyromonas gingivalis), spanning the ecological transition from oral health to periodontal disease. The PCA-LDA classifier achieved 99.8% accuracy for binary classification, maintained an overall accuracy of 93.8% after extension to four bacterial species, and successfully identified P. gingivalis at bacterial ratios as low as 1:6000 within mixed populations. Importantly, the classifier, trained exclusively on planktonic single-cell Raman spectra, was directly transferred to Raman images of mixed bacterial communities and increasingly complex biofilm models without retraining, achieving classification accuracies of approximately 98%. The Raman-based classification was independently validated by morphology-based segmentation and Gram staining. These results establish a scalable and transferable analytical framework for quantitative Raman imaging of polymicrobial communities. By combining supervised machine learning with hyperspectral Raman microscopy, the proposed workflow provides a versatile strategy for label-free bacterial identification and spatial mapping, representing an important step toward Raman-based precision microbiology and future optical diagnostics of oral infectious diseases.

papers.title: Cation-Dependent Ion Dynamics and Morphology in Metal-Contaminated Nafion Membranes
papers.abstract: Metal cation contamination of Nafion proton-exchange membranes (PEMs) remains a persistent durability and performance issue in water electrolyzers as well as fuel cells. Contaminant metal cations originating from insufficiently deionized feed water, coolant leaks, or corrosion of metal cell components can bind to the sulfonate groups of Nafion, thereby interfering critically with proton transport. This work is the first joint experimental-simulation study that systematically elucidates the atomistic processes behind the metal-cation-based inhibition of proton conductivity in Nafion. The impact of humidity, metal cation charge, and temperature on morphology and ion transport is studied. Combining in-plane conductivity measurements of various metal cation impurities with classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations reveals different water uptake at constant relative humidity (RH) driven by the chemical potential. The ion dynamics decrease from Li+ to K+ at constant RH, which is the exact opposite to the trend observed in bulk water. The apparent contradiction is identified as a consequence of the cation-water interaction dominating the water uptake and consequently the extent of percolation pathways. In contrast, the cation-sulfonate interaction is the decisive factor describing how the charge of metal cations impact conductivity in Nafion. By multidentate interaction of multivalent metal cations with multiple sulfonate groups, the pore is locally constricted disconnecting percolation pathways and inhibiting ion transport.

papers.title: Synthesis of Quinoline- and Tetrahydroacridine-based SNN Ligands for Fe-catalyzed Olefin Hydrosilylation
papers.abstract: We report the synthesis of a series of thio-iminoquinoline and thio-iminotetrahydroacridine SNN ligands for application in Fe-catalyzed hydrosilylation of olefins. In the hydrosilylation of styrene, the iminoquinoline ligands provide higher yields than the iminotetrahydroacridine derivatives. However, the acridine-based Fe catalysts have longer catalyst lifetimes and at low catalyst loadings (0.5 mol% Fe) provide higher turnover numbers (up to 2000 TON). The SNN-iron catalysts provide good yields in the hydrosilylation of both styrenyl and terminal olefins but fail to hydrosilylate 1,1- and 1,2- disubstituted styrenes, hindered and electron rich styrenes, or internal alkenes.

papers.title: Structure-Property Relations on Exchange Couplings in distorted Halidebridged Gd(III) Complexes
papers.abstract: In comparison to transition metals, the connection between the bridging geometry and the magnetic exchange coupling constant J remains vague for Gd(III)-Gd(III) magnetic couplings. However, such couplings are an important feature, for example for compounds showing a strong magnetocaloric effect. In this study, a series of Gd2X6 (X=F, Cl, Br, I) was systematically distorted and the magnetic coupling calculated using Broken-Symmetry DFT. We find an inversely exponential metal-metal distance dependence as well as the dependence on a second structural parameter, either the Gd-X distance or the Gd-X-Gd angle. We compared these structural dependencies with different DFT-features. We furthermore find that the nature of terminal ligands has neglectable influence. Using these results, we showed that such simple model complexes can be used to predict the coupling in experimentally investigated complexes with the same bridge. This lets us conclude that it may be possible to effectively extract reasonable exchange coupling constants and Spin-Hamiltonians for larger Gd(III)-clusters.

papers.title: Closed-loop optimization in an industrial R&D lab
papers.abstract: In industrial research and development, autonomous closed-loop reaction optimizers have the potential to significantly accelerate processes, but they must be robust and flexible, encompassing both hardware and software components. This paper presents a versatile system developed and deployed within a research unit of an industrial R&D lab, designed to address a variety of industry-relevant challenges rather than functioning as a one-off demonstrator. Unlike traditional systems that may focus on specific chemical processes, our approach facilitates the optimization of reactions across multiple organic synthesis research groups. We illustrate the system’s capabilities through three case studies, showcasing its adaptability and effectiveness in real-world applications. By prioritizing configurability and reusability, this work aims to contribute to a more sustainable and efficient approach to chemical engineering practices in industrial settings where interdisciplinary collaboration is key.

papers.title: Integrating Theory–Experiment Active Learning and Mechanistic Insights for High-Entropy Alloy Design Toward Efficient Alkaline Hydrogen Evolution
papers.abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) offer diverse local coordination environments for modulating hydrogen adsorption and water activation in alkaline hydrogen evolution, but their highdimensional compositional space remains difficult to explore efficiently. Theory-experiment closed loops can accelerate this search, yet theoretical prior and candidate sampling are commonly coupled, obscuring their individual contributions. Here, we developed a theory-experiment activelearning (TEA) framework that independently varies theoretical priors and candidate sampling strategies for AuCuPdPtIr HEAs. Under identical experimental throughput, the theoretical prior provided transferable performance trends across composition space, whereas the proposed adaptive sampling strategy broadened effective compositional coverage. After three iterations involving 120 compositions, the framework identified Au16Cu5Pd35Pt35Ir9, which required only 16 mV overpotential to reach 10 mA cm-2 in 1 M KOH. An anion-exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE) cell using this catalyst as the cathode reached 1 A cm-2 at 1.647 V and 60 °C and operated stably for 1000 h. Model interpretation, operando infrared spectroscopy, machine-learning-potential molecular dynamics (MLP-MD) simulations, and charge-density analysis further associated Ir/Cu-related local environments with a weaker interfacial hydrogenbond network and more Volmer-like water configurations. This work connects controlled module comparison, data-efficient compositional optimization, and interfacial-water mechanisms, providing a general strategy for complex multicomponent electrocatalysts.

papers.title: A retrieval-augmented agent bridges virtual screening and automated synthesis
papers.abstract: Translating virtually designed drug molecules into executable synthesis protocols is essential for connecting computational discovery with automated synthesis. However, most retrosynthesis methods focus on precursor generation, offer limited route diversity, and lack the detailed reaction conditions required for executable protocols. Here, we present Syn-RRAG, a retrieval-augmented LLM-driven synthesis agent connecting virtual screening with automated synthesis and validation. Syn-RRAG integrates initial retrosynthetic prediction, reaction-precedent retrieval and hierarchical refinement to generate structured protocols with complete experimental parameters. Its local generative model searches over complete reaction hypotheses rather than relying solely on token-level beam search, enabling exploration of feasible routes with distinct reaction classes and bond disconnections. It achieved strong retrosynthesis performance on two patent-derived reaction datasets. Syn-RRAG further generated executable plans for three virtually screened drug candidates, all of which were synthesized and validated on an automated platform. These results establish a workflow connecting virtual molecular design, synthesis planning and experimental validation.

papers.title: An Efficient Temperature-Jump Method for the Calculation of Heat Capacities
papers.abstract: We demonstrate a new method for calculating the heat capacity of molecular systems by means of highly parallel molecular dynamics simulations. In an approach using dynamical non-equilibrium molecular dynamics, a temperature perturbation is applied to the system, enabling enhanced sampling of equilibrium phase space. Calculation of the isochoric heat capacity of TIP3P is used as an example to validate this method.

papers.title: Location is information: an engineering framework for subcellular biology
papers.abstract: The cell is not a well-mixed bag of molecules; its functions are compartmentalized across the nucleus, cytoplasm, and organelles. Despite this, the single-cell and spatial revolution has largely resolved cells only as wholes, averaging away the subcellular detail that drives cellular behavior. Resolving where a molecule resides within a cell, and keeping that information linked to the originating cell, is a next frontier of single-cell measurement. Contemporary approaches span physical compartment fractionation, live-cell microsampling, coordinate-defined imaging, low-loss single-cell mass spectrometry, and barcoded multiomics. Physical compartment fractionation directly preserves subcellular origin of measured material, whereas coordinate-defined methods span cell-level spatial mapping to true subcellular measurement; low-loss single-cell mass spectrometry and barcoded multiomics generally collapse subcellular origin; however, these methods establish current benchmarks for molecular depth and multiplexing scale. Because these modalities optimize different readouts and report different performance metrics, direct comparison across technologies remains challenging. In this Critical Review, we compare these technologies by how they preserve the link between a readout, its subcellular source and the originating cell rather than by the molecule measured. We introduce a framework that maps 32 platforms according to two axes, the indexing mechanism (molecular barcode, spatial coordinate, physical address, or tracked cell) and the type of information preserved, from subcellular location to global molecular depth and scale. The framework defines four classes including coordinate-defined subcellular measurement, physical subcellular access, low-loss molecular profiling, and molecular indexing for global multiomics. The latter two serve as adjacent reference classes that inform the recovery and scale requirements for future subcellular platforms. Comparison of these technologies identifies deep, organelle-resolved measurement that remains indexed to the cell of origin at biologically relevant throughput as a central unmet capability. We conclude with engineering guidelines and minimum reporting metrics to guide the development of platforms that address this gap. 1. Introduction Population-level assays average over molecular differences among individual cells, obscuring heterogeneity in cell state, regulatory potential and spatial organization. Single-cell technologies were developed to recover this variation and now measure RNA, chromatin accessibility, proteins, metabolites and tissue location at single cell resolution (1-4). Yet many biological processes are organized below the scale of the whole cell. Nuclear-cytoplasmic partitioning, organelle remodeling, localized RNA translation, compartment-specific protein signaling and spatially restricted metabolism depend on where molecules reside within a cell, not only on whether they are present (5-9). Microscopy has long resolved molecular localization within individual cells, with highly multiplexed imaging methods such as MERFISH and seqFISH+ extending this capability to hundreds to thousands of molecular targets (10,11). The challenge is therefore not only to measure more molecular features per cell, but to preserve the relationship between a molecular readout, its subcellular source and the cell from which it came.

papers.title: Anisotropic Metallosupramolecular Crystals for Autonomous Energy Transduction
papers.abstract: Manifestation of a flexible and environmentally compatible multifunctional energy harvester (MEH) is achieved through the use of a noncentrosymmetric metallosupramolecular crystal (MSC). Here, we report the design and synthesis of non-covalent interactions-mediated synthetic strategy of a MSC system using Cu(II) salt, allylmalonic acid, and 2,2ʹdipyridylamine system. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction and Hirshfeld surface analysis reveal a distorted square pyramidal geometry organized into an oscillatory 1D hydrogen-bonded chain, which ultimately perform the acentric polar nature of MSC crystals. This unique structural anisotropy enables high-efficiency multimodal energy harvesting. A flexible MEH was fabricated by employing MSC-system for the exploration of autonomous energy transduction. The MEH demonstrates superior piezoelectric performance, yielding a peak-to-peak short-circuit current (ISC) of ~ 1.2 µA and an opencircuit voltage (VOC) exceeding ~3.6 V under periodic mechanical excitation. The device exhibits a remarkable dual-sensitivity profile in low-pressure regimes and a peak power density of ~0.15 µW/cm

papers.title: Adaptive Discovery of Uncharted Zeolitic Imidazolate Frameworks
papers.abstract: Discovering new zeolitic imidazolate framework (ZIF) structures remains a major challenge because their assembly depends on the nature of the linker and synthesis conditions. Here, we introduce linker width as a design parameter for ZIF synthesis. We designed 4-substituted benzimidazole linkers with expanded width and combined them with smaller linkers in an adaptive machine-learning (ML) high-throughput strategy. This adaptive discovery scheme yielded nine new mixed-linker ZIFs, including six adopting the previously unrealized bcv topology. Single-crystal structural analysis reveals ordered linker distributions in which the wider 4-substituted benzimidazolate linkers code for the formation of 10-membered-ring needed for the apertures of the bcv cage. Comparison with representative mixed-linker ZIFs further identifies the width of linkers and the extension ratio as steric descriptors of topology selection. These results establish chemically interpretable design principles for mixed-linker ZIF assembly and demonstrate how linker design coupled with ML-guided synthesis can access unexplored regions of chemical space.

papers.title: FCmini: Simple and Efficient Franck–Condon Simulations of Vibronic Spectra
papers.abstract: Vibronic structure plays a crucial role in determining the shape and width of molecular absorption and emission spectra. Existing methods for modelling vibronic structure are often computationally demanding, and their results can be difficult to interpret. With this in mind, we present FCmini, a minimal model for simulating vibronic progressions in typical “well-behaved” organic molecules. The approach explicitly treats dominant modes via Franck–Condon theory while modelling the remaining modes through a semi-classical approximation. This hybrid strategy, implemented within our MATILDA toolbox, yields a computationally efficient method that provides transparent insight into which modes govern spectral features. We demonstrate the approach on two contrasting systems: anthracene as a benchmark molecule with a characteristic vibronic progression and mDICz as a narrowband emitter relevant to organic light emitting diode design. For anthracene, we show that its vibronic progression and even the fine structure of the peak shapes emerge using only a small subset of the vibrational modes. For mDICz, we accurately reproduce the remarkably low Stokes shift (<0.02 eV) and narrow spectral width (<0.08 eV). The efficiency of the method allows us to investigate a variety of methodological influences, including the effect of the density functional, the solvation model, and the Tamm-Dancoff approximation to TDDFT revealing that excitation energies, spectral shapes, intensities, and lifetimes all depend critically on these. Generally, we obtain good results for all quantities using the PBE0 functional in the full TDDFT formalism with implicit solvation. In summary, we believe that FCmini will present itself as a useful tool not only for spectra predictions but also for structure-property relations and methodological investigations.

papers.title: Revisiting the Katz-Thompson Relationship Between Permeability, Electrical Resistivity, and Formation Factor for Cementitious Systems
papers.abstract: Fluid transport is important for determining the durability of concrete structures. Fluid transport modeling approaches in cement-based materials are powerful but require the intrinsic permeability (K l ), which is often challenging due to experimental limitations. Therefore, K l is typically estimated using its established relationship with various parameters representing porous structure, such as the Katz-Thomson formulation, which relates K l to formation factor (F) and the square of the critical pore diameter (d c ). However, obtaining d c , from either direct or indirect experimental methods, is rather challenging, and these measures often show a high degree of variability. This study re-evaluates the fundamental relationship between K l and the pore structure of cement-based materials without relying on conventional d c measurements. Experimental data show that intrinsic permeability is inversely proportional to the square of the formation factor (K l ∝ F -2 ), which is in line with earlier studies on non-cementitious porous media where K l was proportional to F -m without any dependence on d c . The specific proportionality holds across all tested mixtures in three separate studies although the relationship varies in each paper. This may be due to variations in the experimental procedures or the presence of aggregate and ITZ. This alternative formulation can be very powerful in enabling practical and accurate durability predictions for concrete infrastructure.

papers.title: Applications of Nanomaterials in Sports Clothing
papers.abstract: Nanotechnology is increasingly being integrated into sports clothing to enhance performance, durability, and physiological comfort. This review explores the various methods by which nanomaterials are incorporated into sports textiles. This includes nanofiber production via solution and melt electrospinning, and functional surface modifications using nanocoatings such as sol-gel, physical vapor deposition (PVD), and layer-by-layer (LbL) techniques. Each method offers distinct benefits depending on the polymer system, desired property, and application. For instance, solution electrospinning enables the formation of nanofibers with high surface area and porosity, suitable for moisture-wicking and breathability. On the other hand, melt electrospinning provides a solvent-free, scalable approach for embedding nanoparticles like TiO2 or silver directly into polymer matrices. Nanocoatings provide antimicrobial properties, UV protection, waterproofing, and temperature regulation through the use of nanoparticleenhanced surface treatments. Materials such as zinc oxide, silica, graphene, and hydroxyapatite are used to tailor the performance characteristics of garments for specific athletic environments. Applications range from antibacterial performance in polyamidebased garments to superhydrophobic outerwear using silica treatments. However, the same nanoscale properties that improve function also raise questions about long-term health and environmental safety. While many studies confirm the biocompatibility of common nanoparticles like ZnO and TiO2 under standard wear conditions, others raise concerns about dermal penetration and leaching during washing. This review emphasizes the need for lifecycle assessment and regulation to ensure performance gains do not compromise human or environmental health.

papers.title: Probabilistic dynamics operators for path-entropy-guided nonequilibrium control of self-assembly
papers.abstract: Self-assembly is inherently dynamical, with competing pathways, metastable intermediates, and kinetic traps influencing which structures ultimately form. The resulting dynamics can be irreversible and generate entropy, providing potentially useful information about how a system progresses toward an assembled state. However, data-driven approaches for controlling self-assembly commonly optimize structural observables that provide limited information about these nonequilibrium dynamics. Here, we introduce a probabilistic dynamics operator (PDO) that learns the time evolution of probability distributions in a reduced collective variable space. The learned operator provides both an efficient dynamical surrogate compared to molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and access to probability fluxes from which entropy production can be quantified. We validate the PDO using discrete Markov ring and continuous triple-well systems and show that models trained exclusively on fixed-temperature trajectories also predict dynamics and accumulated entropy production under unseen, time-varying temperature protocols. We then apply the PDO to patchy particles that competitively assemble into rhombohedral () and trihexagonal morphologies, using the PDO as a surrogate environment for reinforcement learning of temperature protocols. A -morphology-only objective produces yields of 62% comparable to the best fixed-temperature MD simulations, whereas augmenting the objective with a moderate contribution from excess entropy production substantially increases formation to 90% in explicit MD simulations. The optimal temperature control policy exploits transient melting and reorganization before promoting renewed growth, while excessive weighting of entropy production suppresses assembly. These results demonstrate that path entropy-dependent thermodynamic information can provide a useful signal for controlling self-assembly when productive pathways require nonequilibrium reorganization.

papers.title: Computationally Guided Discovery of Cannabinoid Derivatives for Antiviral and Anticancer Applications: From Chemical Space to Experimental Validation
papers.abstract: Cannabinoids represent a chemically diverse and structurally tunable class of natural and synthetic compounds that have attracted growing interest as molecular scaffolds for therapeutic discovery. However, their extensive chemical diversity, polypharmacology, conformational flexibility, and complex pharmacokinetic properties make the systematic identification and optimisation of therapeutically useful derivatives challenging. Recent advances in computer-aided drug discovery (CADD), molecular simulation, quantum chemistry, quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) modelling, and artificial intelligence (AI) provide opportunities to interrogate the chemical space of cannabinoids in a systematic and mechanistically informed manner. This review examines computational strategies for the discovery and optimisation of cannabinoid derivatives with potential antiviral and anticancer applications, emphasising the integration of complementary computational approaches rather than reliance on isolated in silico predictions. A hierarchical computational workflow is described, progressing from cannabinoid chemical-space generation and ligand preparation to disease-relevant target identification, virtual screening, molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, binding free-energy estimation, quantum-chemical analysis, and ADMET/drug-likeness prediction. For antiviral discovery, computational investigations of SARS-CoV-2 targets, including the main protease (Mpro/3CLpro), papain-like protease (PLpro), spike protein, and spike–ACE2 interface, are discussed alongside emerging host-directed targets. For anticancer applications, computational studies involving EGFR, HER2, VEGFR, PI3K/AKT, MAPK, apoptosis, autophagy, oxidative stress, and cell-cycle regulation are evaluated. Particular emphasis is placed on the complementary roles of docking and MD simulations in characterising binding modes, interaction persistence, conformational stability, and molecular recognition, while MM-PBSA/MM-GBSA and related approaches provide additional energetic criteria for candidate prioritisation. QSAR and AI/ML-assisted approaches are further considered as complementary tools for expanding chemical-space exploration, predicting biological activity and ADMET properties, and enabling multi-parameter candidate prioritisation. Importantly, computational affinity scores are not treated as sufficient evidence of target inhibition or therapeutic efficacy. Instead, the review emphasises a progressive validation framework in which computationally prioritised candidates are evaluated through biochemical target-engagement studies, cellular assays, and, where appropriate, in vivo models. Experimental observations can subsequently inform structure–activity relationship analysis, lead optimisation, and iterative computational rescreening, establishing a closed-loop strategy for integrating molecular recognition, dynamic behaviour, binding energetics, pharmacokinetic properties, toxicity, and biological activity during cannabinoid lead development. The review critically examines key limitations of current computational approaches, including incomplete treatment of ligand flexibility, scoring-function limitations, protein conformational heterogeneity, limited experimental validation, dataset bias in AI/ML models, and translational challenges associated with cannabinoid solubility, bioavailability, metabolism, receptor promiscuity, psychoactive liabilities, and off-target effects. Collectively, current evidence indicates that computationally guided cannabinoid discovery is a promising but predominantly preclinical strategy. Further progress will depend on integrating CADD, molecular simulation, AI-assisted molecular design, uncertainty-aware prediction, and experimental validation into iterative multi-objective optimisation frameworks that jointly address potency, selectivity, pharmacokinetics, toxicity, and translational relevance.

papers.title: ChiroptMap: Orbital-Cube-Free Transition-Moment Density Maps from Gaussian and ORCA
papers.abstract: Earlier cube-based workflows generated electric-and magnetic-dipole transition-moment maps from molecular-orbital cubes exported with Gaussian cubegen from formatted-checkpoint data. ChiroptMap instead evaluates canonical orbitals and analytical derivatives blockwise from Gaussian WFX or an ORCA output/JSON/WFX bridge, eliminating intermediate orbital cubes while retaining final visualization cubes and S1–S6 CPL CSV values. Across ten Gaussian S1 TDA/TD-DFT cases, the median MDTM norm discrepancy decreased from 1.214% to 0.0541%, whereas EDTM recovery was unchanged; five S1/TDA cross-engine benchmarks gave mean field differences of 1.061% (electric) and 1.774% (magnetic), and the retained footprint decreased by 99.17%. Independent coefficient-print and spatial-grid tests support IOp(9/40=4) for the tested state while requiring both sources of numerical convergence to be assessed.

papers.title: Anion effects on pKa values of organophosphonium salts in o-difluorobenzene and implications
papers.abstract: Herein, the anion effects on p K a values of organophosphonium salts in o -difluorobenzene are reported. Using the autoprotolysis constants of 2-(4-trifluoromethanesulfonato)phenylmalononitrile as an anchor, the p K a values of eight organophosphonium bistriflimides are experimentally determined in three polar fluorinated arenes via 31 P{ 1 H} NMR spectroscopic titration. Subsequently, the p K a values of eight corresponding organophosphonium tetrafluoroborates and eight corresponding organophosphonium tetraphenylborates soluble in o -difluorobenzene are further experimentally determined. These p K a values show significant differences due to different counter-anions. Further DFT calculations reveals that the anions BF 4 – and NTf 2 – in o-difluorobenzene form hydrogen-bonded contact ion pairs with organophosphonium cation, but BPh 4 – forms contact ion pairs via Coulombic interactions with it. In addition to providing important guidance for future improvement of DFT and AI for predicting p K a values and thermodynamic analyses in low dielectric constant solvents, this work also provides a more comprehensive understanding of anion effects in organic and inorganic X–H bond breaks and formations.

papers.title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Predicting Cytochrome P450 Mechanism-Based Inhibition
papers.abstract: Cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes play a crucial role in the metabolism of endogenous and exogenous compounds, and their inhibition can lead to clinically significant drug–drug interactions and adverse effects. Mechanism-based inhibition (MBI) is a time-dependent form of CYP450 inhibition in which enzyme-mediated bioactivation of an inhibitor can result in persistent or irreversible enzyme inactivation. Early identification of compounds with MBI liability is therefore important for reducing metabolic and drug–drug interaction risks during drug discovery. In this study, a curated dataset of 569 unique MBI compounds was compiled from the literature, while non-mechanism-based inhibitors (NMBIs) were obtained from PubChem. To construct a chemically diverse negative dataset, Butina clustering-based sampling was employed. Molecular representations based on RDKit and Mordred descriptors, MACCS keys, and ECFP fingerprints were evaluated using five machine learning algorithms, with feature selection and model optimization applied systematically. CYP-aware stratified splitting was employed to ensure appropriate representation of CYP isoform–class combinations across the training and test sets, and its performance was compared with random stratified splitting. Among the evaluated molecular representations, RDKit descriptors generally provided the strongest predictive performance, with optimized models achieving test-set ROC-AUC values of up to 0.92 in the CYP-aware evaluation. Applicability-domain analysis further demonstrated higher prediction accuracy for compounds within the defined chemical space, supporting the reliability of predictions for structurally represented compounds. In addition, structural-alert analysis identified class-associated structural motifs, including statistically significant alerts preferentially associated with MBI compounds, providing chemically interpretable information complementary to the machine learning models. Evaluation using the expanded MBI569 dataset further assessed the robustness of the predictive models across different dataset sizes and splitting strategies. Overall, this study demonstrates a systematic and interpretable approach for predicting CYP450 mechanism-based inhibition, with potential utility for the early identification of MBI liabilities during drug discovery.

papers.title: Heme-catalyzed Endogenous Activation of N-oxide Prodrugs
papers.abstract: N-oxides are prominent functionalities in bioorthogonal prodrugs activated by exogenous stimuli such as boron reagents, X-ray, and ultrasound. However, N-oxide optical probes that are activated by endogenous heme and hemoproteins are recently reported, which has caused the existence of endogenous activation mechanism of N-oxide prodrugs to be overlooked or remain disputed. Here, we report a systemic study to examine the endogenous activation of N-oxide prodrugs in vitro, in liver microsomes, and in mice. We prepared four N-oxide prodrugs based on the synthetic molecule IOX5 and natural product derivative SN-38 with stable N-oxide moieties. We found that all the prodrugs could be catalytically reduced by heme and hemoproteins in vitro. The pharmacokinetics results indicated that all prodrugs could release the parent drugs in liver microsomes and animals. Notably, N-oxide prodrugs of SN-38, 7-1 and 8-40, exhibited dramatically improved oral bioavailability (23.3% and 18.7% for released SN-38) compared to SN-38 itself (0.07%). In the acute myeloid leukemia mice, oral administration of 7‑1 markedly reduced the leukemia burden and the percentage of leukemia stem cells, significantly prolonging the survival rate of leukemia mice. Overall, this study not only discloses that N-oxide prodrugs could be activated by endogenous heme, without any exogenous reagent or specific physiological condition, but also provides a modular and promising prodrug strategy to improve the oral bioavailability of poorly water-soluble drugs.

papers.title: Remote C(sp3)–H Functionalization via Visible-Light-Mediated Generation of Amidyl Radicals from Readily Accessible Arylsulfonamides
papers.abstract: Remote C(sp3)–H functionalization via amidyl radical-mediated 1,5-hydrogen atom transfer has emerged as a powerful strategy for the synthesis and late-stage modification of structurally complex molecules. However, practical methods for amidyl radical generation that combine easily prepared precursors with mild reaction conditions remain highly desirable. Herein, we report a visible-light-mediated method for generating amidyl radicals from readily accessible arylsulfonamides through precise tuning of the reduction potential of the arylsulfonyl group. Systematic evaluation of arylsulfonyl groups identified the benzothiazolesulfonyl group as an efficient precursor for amidyl radical generation. The reaction exhibited broad substrate scope, including for amino acid and peptide derivatives, and was readily applicable to continuous-flow synthesis. Mechanistic studies support a pathway involving single-electron transfer from the photocatalyst and provide insight into the roles of additives in product formation.

papers.title: Iridium Oxidation-State Dynamics during Transient Operation under PEM Water Electrolysis Single-Cell Conditions Revealed by Time-Resolved Operando XAS
papers.abstract: Resolving the oxidation-state dynamics of Ir oxide anode catalysts during individual potential transients in proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) single cells remains challenging. Here, we developed an operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) cell based on a modified lab-scale single-cell design and performed super quick XAS (SQXAS) measurements with a time resolution of ca. 200 ms. The cell enabled evaluation of catalyst-coated membranes (CCMs) with an active area of 1 cm 2 and exhibited current-voltage performance comparable to that of conventional single cells at an elevated temperature (45 °C), indicating that a realistic electrochemical environment was established. Operando Ir L 3 -edge SQXAS measurements were performed using this cell for two CCMs, one with crystalline IrO 2 and the other with amorphous IrO x anode catalysts. Operando SQXAS during cyclic voltammetry indicated continuous oxidation of Ir above certain potentials and an oxidation-state plateau below them, with the behavior being more pronounced for amorphous IrO x . These results are consistent with previous half-cell-based operando XAS studies, suggesting that their fundamental findings may extend to more realistic environments. Operando SQXAS was also performed during transient potential changes simulating PEMWE startup and shutdown. In both cases, changes in the Ir oxidation state rapidly followed the applied potential for rutile IrO 2 as well as amorphous IrO x . These results not only reveal the dynamics of Ir oxidation states under such transient operations but also provide guidance for designing effective accelerated stress tests for Ir oxide catalysts.

papers.title: Selective Mono and Diborylation of Aromatic Pentafluorosulfanyl Compounds by iridium-catalyzed C–H Activation
Hydrogen Pretreatment Programs Oxidative Surface Reconstruction for Enhanced Lattice-Oxygen Reactivity in Co3O4
papers.abstract: The oxidation activity of reducible oxides is closely linked to the nature of lattice oxygen species, and reductive treatments are often used to tailor the low-temperature reactivity by modifying the surface coordination environment. Here, using Co3O4 and the oxidation of 2-propanol as a model reaction, we demonstrate that a further enhancement of the low-temperature activity can be achieved by extending the reduction beyond conventional surface modification to access distinct, metastable CoO surface terminations. These terminations spontaneously reconstruct under oxidizing conditions into oxygen-rich surface structures that exhibit enhanced lattice oxygen reactivity and are key to the improved lowtemperature activity. This work establishes programmed surface reconstruction through a defined reduction-oxidation sequence as a strategy for engineering highly reactive lattice oxygen sites in reducible oxides.

papers.title: Excitation-Dependent Spin-State Relaxation Mediated by Jahn–Teller Motion in a Mn(III) Complex
papers.abstract: Photoexcited transition-metal complexes exhibit complex excited-state dynamics arising from the interplay of electronic relaxation, spin-state conversion, and nuclear motion. Here, we use quantum dynamics to investigate the ultrafast photodynamics of the Jahn–Teller active complex Mn(terpy)Cl3. The high-spin d4 electronic configuration of Mn(III) produces strong coupling between electronic structure and molecular geometry, making this system an ideal platform for exploring nonadiabatic relaxation and spin-state evolution. Our simulations reveal that photoexcitation initiates coupled electronic and nuclear dynamics involving multiple excited states and spin manifolds. Population transfer is mediated by vibrational motion associated with the Jahn–Teller switching coordinate, which promotes both nonadiabatic transitions and intersystem crossing. We identify the dominant relaxation pathways, determine the key vibrational modes mediating population transfer, and establish the associated timescales. Importantly, the relaxation dynamics depend strongly on the initially prepared electronic-state composition, with different excitation energies accessing distinct regions of the excited-state landscape and leading to different decay mechanisms. These results provide a mechanistic understanding of excited-state relaxation in a prototypical Mn(III) complex and demonstrate how selective photoexcitation can influence spin-state evolution, offering insights relevant to the optical control of molecular magnetism.

papers.title: Supramolecular Polymers of Chiral and Achiral Rhodium and Iridium Complexes of N-confused Porphyrin
papers.abstract: A series of rhodium(III) and iridium(III) complexes of N-confused porphyrin (NCP) was synthesized and characterized by spectroscopic, electrochemical, and XRD methods. The results were analyzed and corroborated by DFT calculations. Insertion of the metal ions was carried out in the presence of primary alcohols (EtOH, n-PrOH), affording diamagnetic chiral square-pyramidal complexes, HNCPM(Acyl), bearing a C-bonded apical acyl ligand. By exploiting H-bonding between the apical ligand and 2-NH, in the solid state, the complexes formed 1-D polymeric chains composed of homochiral (for rhodium(III)) or heterochiral (for iridium(III)) monomers. The optical activity of these molecules in solution was established by CD for HPLC-separated enantiomers. Redox properties were studied by electrochemical and spectroelectrochemical methods. Relatively low first oxidation potentials of the NCP complexes of both metals allowed facile reaction with I2 as an oxidant and a source of the anionic ligands. The paramagnetic six-coordinated HNCPMI2 complexes formed in the solid state 1-D polymeric chains bridged by I2, interacting by halogen bonding with axial iodides. Analysis of the electronic structures of these complexes using EPR and DFT calculations revealed a predominantly π-radical character of the metal(III) complexes rather than tetravalent rhodium or iridium NCP species.

papers.title: Ge–N Cooperativity and Catalytic Hydrodefluorination by a Pyridine Dipyrrolide Germanium Platform
papers.abstract: p-Block elements are emerging as sustainable alternatives to transition metals in catalysis, but the development of new species capable of redox cycling poses a central challenge to achieving metallomimetic reactivity. Redox-neutral processes offer a powerful strategy to circumvent challenging reductive elimination steps. Despite promising early applications of germanium(II)–ligand cooperativity for stoichiometric bond activation, the use of germylenes in redox-neutral catalysis remains largely limited to hydrofunctionalization of polar unsaturated bonds.
