Herein, we report the synthesis, reactivity, and catalytic application of a welldefined pyridine dipyrrolide germanium(II) complex, ( tBu PDP)Ge . Stoichiometric studies reveal that ( tBu PDP)Ge activates substrates of varying polarity, including water, N-methylaniline, ammonia-borane, and phenylsilane via a Ge–N cooperative redox-neutral mechanism that bypasses high-energy redox cycling pathways. This germylene serves as a precatalyst for the hydrodefluorination of perfluoro(hetero)arenes. Mechanistic investigations, supported by experimental and computational data, establish a redox-neutral catalytic cycle. Isolation of a well-defined germylene hydride and other key intermediates enabled development of a milder, more efficient catalytic protocol by avoiding a sluggish precatalyst activation step.

papers.title: Molecular Engineering of a Small-Molecular Yellow-to-Orange Carbonyl-based Multi-Resonance TADF Emitter
papers.abstract: Red-shifting MR-TADF emitters via donor substitution is an established strategy; however, this typically results in broadened emission and reduced photoluminescence quantum yields (FPL). We report tBuInPZ-DiKTa, fusing an indolophenazine donor directly to the DiKTa core, achieving an unprecedented red-shift for fused DiKTa-based emitters while preserving narrowband emission and high FPL.

papers.title: Expanding the Cygnet Class of Solvents: Development of a Series of Bio-based Polar Aprotic High Boiling Solvents
papers.abstract: Polar aprotic solvents have many applications in organic chemistry, but there are few bio-based substitutes available. As legislation becomes more restrictive due to health and safety concerns, the need for safer and more sustainable solvents has become ever more pressing. Here, we have built on previous works to synthesise several derivatives of the cellulose-derived Cyrene through an environmentally friendly ketalisation reaction, resulting in a class of solvents called the Cygnets. Diol reagents were selected based on their bio-based origin, and four novel solvent structures were synthesised and comprehensively characterised using NMR, ( 1 H and 13 C), GC-FID, and HPLC-ESI-MS. The solvents were also shown to be non-toxic to skin cell lines HaCaT and BJ-5ta, presenting a viability above 70%. Finally, the presented structures show differing properties depending on the structure of the secondary ring formed. The presence of longer side chains results in a solvent with a lower boiling point, allowing it to be used in a wider range of reactions, and presents the interesting possibility to tune the final properties by modifying the used diol reagent.

papers.title: Colloidal Interactions in Low-polarity Dispersions of Permanently Magnetic Nanoplatelets
papers.abstract: Ferrofluids based on permanently magnetic nanoplatelets are attractive functional materials. However, their preparation in low-polarity media is particularly challenging because magnetic dipole–dipole interactions strongly promote agglomeration while conventional electrostatic stabilisation is weakened. Here, low-polarity dispersions of barium hexaferrite nanoplatelets were prepared by functionalising the particles with ricinoleic acid (RA) and dispersing them in low-polarity solvents of different chemical character. The resulting dispersions exhibited markedly different colloidal stabilities, ranging from stable ferrofluids in chlorinated solvents to unstable dispersions in toluene and decalin. Infrared spectroscopy and thermogravimetric analysis confirmed successful functionalisation with RA and indicated the presence of both chemisorbed and loosely bound RA species. Electrokinetic measurements revealed a clear correlation between colloidal stability and the development of a surface charge. Based on these results, we propose that stable dispersions are stabilised by an electro-steric-solvation mechanism that enables spatial stabilisation of charge in low-polarity media. A fraction of the RA is chemisorbed on the nanoplatelet surface, while loosely associated RA species, together with locally ordered solvent molecules, are proposed to stabilise the negative countercharge, thereby maintaining its separation from the positively charged nanoplatelet surface. This charge separation generates a repulsive barrier that counterbalances magnetic dipole–dipole attraction and prevents agglomeration. These findings highlight charge stabilisation in low-polarity media as a key requirement for preparing stable ferrofluids based on permanently magnetic anisotropic nanoparticles.

papers.title: Correlative super-resolution microscopy reveals preferential localization of quantum color center formation on carbon nanotubes
papers.abstract: Covalent quantum color centers, (CCs) introduced onto single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) create localized, red-shifted emission states with promising applications in quantum photonics, biosensing and bioimaging. Yet, the mechanisms governing where and how these color centers form on the SWCNTs remain poorly understood. To address this question, we mapped, in real time, the precise position of aryl CCs formed by photoinduced diazonium chemistry along individual (6,5) SWCNTs by combining, within a correlative framework, two complementary super-resolution imaging modalities: single-molecule localization microscopy of individual CC formation events and analytical reconstruction of the SWCNT backbone. We reveal that CC formation is not spatially random as CCs preferentially localize towards the central regions of nanotubes, away from their ends, and exhibit pronounced spatial clustering. Ruling out curvaturedriven effects, we attribute this clustering to non-uniform surfactant coverage along the nanotube, which creates locally exposed and chemically-reactive domains. These results establish nanotube surface heterogeneity as a key determinant of CC positioning and point toward strategies for the deterministic, spatially controlled engineering of quantum emitters on carbon nanotubes.

papers.title: Online Soil Column Chromatography Coupled with Mass Spectrometry for Studying Sorption of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances and Other Organic Contaminants
papers.abstract: Soil column chromatography (SCC) has been used to investigate the sorption of organic compounds in soils. However, its application has been restricted to compounds with UV or fluorescence activity, excluding many environmentally relevant compounds including numerous per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). Here, SCC was directly coupled with mass spectrometry (MS) to investigate the sorption of PFAS and other organic compounds. Using peat as model soil organic matter, the SCC–MS method demonstrated high repeatability and yielded organic carbon-normalized sorption coefficients ( Koc ) consistent with those obtained using UV detection. For neutral compounds and acids with high p K a , K oc values were minimally influenced by pH or electrolyte composition, indicating that SCC–MS with ammonium formate as the electrolyte can provide environmentally representative K oc data. In contrast, K oc of anionic compounds increased with decreasing pH and increasing ionic strength, consistent with enhanced charge screening and reduced electrostatic repulsion. For anionic PFAS, the K oc values measured here were lower than K oc values obtained with mineral soils and closer to those with peat in the literature. Together, these results demonstrate the applicability of SCC–MS as a tool for evaluating soil sorption, while highlighting the need to address limitations such as incompatibility with nonvolatile salts.

papers.title: Energy Transfer (EnT) Catalysed [4+2] Cycloaddition of Non-Symmetrical Dienes: From Mechanistic Anomaly to Fully Functional Reaction Pathway
papers.abstract: Harnessing the reactivity of triplet biradicals to selectively access unconventional cycloaddition pathways remains a fundamental challenge in energy transfer (EnT) catalysis. Herein, we demonstrate that systematic variation of diene substitution can redirect the intrinsic [2+2] reactivity of non-symmetrical dienes towards highly selective [4+2] cycloaddition. Notably, incorporation of a traceless vicinal BPin group invokes a non-conventional [4+2] pathway providing polysubstituted cyclohexenes with excellent regio- and diastereoselectivity. Mechanistic and computational investigations reveal that A-1,3-strain and geometric isomerisation shape the conformational landscape of the triplet biradical, accounting for the observed divergent reactivity. These findings establish substitution-controlled excited-state conformational dynamics as a key parameter for directing EnT-mediated cycloadditions beyond conventional [2+2] reactivity.

papers.title: Polarity-resolved imaging reveals active transport in catalytic Janus nanomotors
papers.abstract: Catalytic Janus motors that convert chemical energy into self-propulsion are promising platforms for targeted delivery, sensing, and environmental remediation. Miniaturizing these systems to the nanoscale is challenged by rotational diffusion (𝑫r ∝ 1/𝑹3) increasing faster than translational diffusion (𝑫t ∝ 1/𝑹), which destroys orientational memory. This raises the question of whether catalytic asymmetry can still bias the active displacement direction when orientational memory is short-lived. Answering it requires simultaneous knowledge of particle orientation and translational motion, yet current optical and ensemblebased methods cannot resolve catalytic cap orientation (particle polarity) of Janus nanomotors, leaving its relationship to propulsion direction experimentally inaccessible. Herein, we combine total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy to establish fuel-dependent activity under bulk conditions, with singleparticle visualization by liquid-phase transmission electron microscopy (LPTEM) to characterize active transport of platinum-polystyrene (Pt-PS) Janus nanomotors. TIRF measurements confirm fuel-dependent enhanced diffusion across a range of H2O2 concentrations (0 to 3 wt%). LPTEM analysis reveals superdiffusive transport (𝜶 =1.11) despite the heterogeneous interfacial energy landscape of the liquid-cell and identifies active intervals characterized by a Péclet number (𝑷𝒆) of ∼21. Frame-by-frame extraction of the platinum cap orientation during active displacements reveals a bias towards polystyrene-forward motion, consistent with self-phoretic mechanisms reported for Janus motors at the micron scale, while trajectory analysis yields an orientational persistence length of∼380 nm, corresponding to approximately three particle body lengths. These findings demonstrate that catalytic asymmetry continues to bias displacement direction even when thermal fluctuations limit orientational memory, providing a polarity-resolved mechanistic picture of Pt-PS propulsion at the 100 nm scale.

papers.title: Machine Learning for High-Throughput Reaction Yield Prediction in DNA-Encoded Library Synthesis
papers.abstract: DNA-encoded library (DEL) synthesis relies on efficient DNA-compatible reactions to ensure library fidelity and the reliability of downstream affinity selection. However, most existing reaction yield prediction models were developed for general organic synthesis and typically use full-atom representations of complete reactants and products. In DEL single-cycle synthesis validation, an appropriate model reaction is to focus on the exposed reactive handle, its local chemical environment, the incoming building block (BB), and the reaction type, rather than large constant backgrounds such as the DNA tag, linker, and pre-existing scaffold. Here, we propose a functional-group-centric machine learning framework for DEL single-cycle reaction yield prediction. The model uses only the exposed substrate functional group (FG) and its coarse-grained local environment, the incoming BB, and the reaction type as inputs. Benchmarking on a real-world high-throughput DEL single-cycle validation dataset shows that graph neural network (GNN) models based on this localized representation outperform traditional fingerprint-based baselines, with a graph attention network (GAT) achieving the best overall performance and showing strong robustness on highly imbalanced industrial data. These results indicate that foregrounding the local reaction center is not merely a simplification of molecular representation, but a task-aligned strategy that better reflects the chemistry and decision logic of DEL single-cycle transformations. This lightweight framework is readily compatible with practical DEL workflows and provides valuable supports on reagent quality control (QC), building block selection, high-fidelity library design, and retrospective analysis of anomalous results.

papers.title: TAME: Element-wise Mixture-of-Experts Fusion for Reliable and Interpretable Molecular Property Prediction
papers.abstract: Property prediction for molecules and materials is bottlenecked by label scarcity, and in this regime the operative failure mode is not a low mean but an unpredictable tail: individual training runs collapse. The three dominant molecular representations fail in complementary ways—physicochemical descriptors are exact but fixed, graph neural networks learn topology but degenerate under sparse supervision, and language models supply semantic context but cannot compute exact quantities— yet combining them is itself the learning problem, because modality-level scalar gating commits the whole model to one trust weight per source. We introduce TAME , a tri-modal encoder whose element-wise Mixture-of-Experts router assigns an independent modality mixture to every hidden coordinate, stabilized by a balance–entropy regularizer, a closed-form gate initialization (β = log τ ) that is intended to remove router burn-in, and two-stage self-supervised graph pretraining. On scaffold-split BACE (≈ 1.5k molecules, 100 seeds) we evaluate two fusion topologies, each against its own graph-only control. In both, adding the text and descriptor experts contracts the seed-to-seed distribution of the threshold-free metrics—ROC-AUC σ falls five-fold in the flat topology and 1.6-fold in the hierarchical one, whose control was already the tighter of the two—and the collapse tail reaching ROC-AUC ≈ 0.45 that the weaker single-modality configurations carry is absent from the fused models while accuracy is retained. Each comparison is matched on everything but the fusion stage, isolating its effect. The router allocates a distinct mixture to each coordinate, which no scalar gate can represent, and the entropy weight moves that allocation continuously between graded mixing and a near-binary regime in which each coordinate is claimed outright by one modality. Fused-representation alignment tracks encoder quality without supervision, shifting from text to topology once pretraining lifts the graph embedding out of rank-1 collapse. The same three experts map onto crystal graphs, composition–structure descriptors and literature-mined text. These three modalities recur unchanged across molecular and inorganic chemistry, so TAME is a single interpretable recipe for turning volatile low-data predictors into reliable, self-explaining ones, wherever data are scarce and every failed prediction costs a real experiment.

papers.title: Rapid, Reliable and Accurate XPS Depth-Distribution Functions from the Berger–Doggett method
papers.abstract: Two complementary rapid Monte Carlo methods for emission-depth distributions were introduced for Auger electron spectroscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy in 1993; the statistical weights method and the Berger-Doggett method. The statistical-weights method samples both elastic scattering directions and the distances between elastic events; the Berger–Doggett method conditions on the angular history and analytically averages over all such distances. These were much faster (by orders of magnitude) than previous methods and no less accurate. Besides reducing variance, the two methods should provide an unusually strong independent cross-check in their common domain of a homogeneous sample. As computer resources have progressively increased over the last 30 years, longer Monte Carlo runs have become practical, and in those a numerical instability can arise in the Berger-Doggett approach that we solve in this paper. We reformulate the original integral recurrence as a lower-bidiagonal system of linear ordinary differential equations with mixed boundary conditions. An ordered Schur decomposition selects the bounded invariant subspace and the required fluences are obtained from the action of a matrix exponential, avoiding the chance near-co-linear direction cosines that would occasionally frustrate the method published in 1993, and now allows very long Monte-Carlo runs to be performed quickly and reliably. In controlled tests the original method accumulated a relative error of 7.6 × 1010 at a cosine separation of 10−14, whereas the new formulation remained within 2.3 × 10−16 of a 120-digit reference. In a 500 angle-history recalculation using contemporary NIST SRD 64 elastic data, at a typical C 1s kinetic energy the old method gave a relative error of 6.2 × 1012 in the coefficient recurrence even though its closest pair of direction cosines differed by 1.15 × 10−4; the new formulation agreed with a 160-digit result to 1.6 × 10−16. This removes the need for extended or arbitrary precision without changing the underlying transport model. Routine Berger-Doggett calculations can now be done on a typical PC reliably and almost instantly, supporting also the statistical weights method by making it easier to verify implementations of it. This should be a significant step towards the automated extraction of all the information possible from nondestructive XPS depth-profiling. As an example of its wide applicability, the calculation confirms the physical basis of a previously proposed coaxial XPS geometry, producing a depth-distribution function with a subsurface maximum. Its considerable breadth, however, suggests enhanced subsurface selectivity rather than any general resolution of the ill-conditioning of depth-profile reconstruction.

papers.title: Exploring Architectural Decoupling of Molecular Span from Molar Mass: A Staged In Silico Design Strategy for a Polyolefin Antioxidant Candidate
Strong Light–Matter Coupling as a Photonic Substituent: Correlation-Enhanced Control of Regioselectivity in Nitrobenzene
papers.abstract: Strong coupling to the vacuum electromagnetic field of optical cavities has been proposed as a route to control ground-state chemical reactivity, enabling “photonic substituent effects.” Recent theoretical work predicted that cavity coupling can invert intrinsic regioselectivity in electrophilic aromatic substitution in nitrobenzene. Here, we revisit this prediction using correlated ab initio cavity quantum electrodynamics. QED-CCSD calculations reveal substantially enhanced energetic reordering of Wheland intermediates relative to previous approaches, indicating that regioselective control may be achievable under more experimentally feasible cavity-coupling strengths than previously predicted. QED-DMRG analysis shows that this effect arises from cavity-induced reweighting of resonance structures, reinforcing the idea of a photonic substituent effect that is similarly influential on molecular electronic structure as chemical substituents. Complementary ab initio molecular dynamics simulations driven by QED-DFT analytic gradients demonstrate that orientational fluctuations introduce a competing dynamical constraint on selectivity, suggesting conditions where canonical 100% meta selectivity could be modified to give mixtures of ortho and meta or para and meta electrophilic aromatic substitution products.

papers.title: Synergistic Multi-Heteroatom Doping in Three-Dimensional-Porous Iron Single-Atom Catalysts for Enhanced Oxygen Reduction Reaction
Mixed Computational/Experimental Screening for Aqueous Organic Redox Flow Battery Negolytes
papers.abstract: A library of 186 million drug-like compounds was constructed and screened using a combined computational and experimental approach to identify three scaffold structures previously unreported as organic redox flow battery (ORFB) negolytes. Candidate scaffolds were identified through computational screening of reduction potentials, triaged via literature search, and characterized electrochemically. Three scaffolds—pyrido[1,2-a]pyrimidine, saccharin, and thiopyran—showed measurable redox activity. Initial cyclic voltammetry of synthesized derivatives revealed the key challenges for each that must be addressed for development into viable aqueous ORFB negolytes.

papers.title: A Generalized Theory for the Structural and Spatial Mapping of Energy, Entropy, and Free Energy
papers.abstract: Systems in which the free energy density is nonuniform in space are familiar; the surface tension of a water droplet and the surface energy of a solid are good examples. Some such cases can be treated with prior theory, notably inhomogeneous solvation theory (IST), but IST is applicable only to liquids. Despite this limitation, IST has proven useful as a guide to the design of ligands to bind a targeted protein, based on the idea that ligands which displace high free energy water will tend to bind more tightly, other things being equal. Here, we present Generalized Thermodynamic Mapping (GTM) theory, a more general theory that is applicable to the entirety of a biomolecular or other chemical system, and which thus may provide additional guidance for molecular design. For example, it might highlight parts of a ligand whose local free energy rises on binding, thus suggesting where modifications could improve affinity. Starting from classical statistical thermodynamics, we derive structural decompositions that assign energy and entropy to individual atoms or to larger chemical components, such as amino acid residues, and spatial decompositions that define continuously varying thermodynamic densities throughout the system. The potential energy is decomposed via the multibody expansion, and the entropy via the mutual information expansion. The resulting thermodynamic densities satisfy key desiderata: their spatial integrals yield the correct total thermodynamic quantities, the densities vanish where the atomic number density is zero, and all entropy terms above first order go to zero in the absence of correlation. The entropy decomposition in GTM theory is closely related to that of IST, but it is simpler, largely because it expresses the entropy in terms of normalized probability density functions instead of non-normalized correlation functions. We show that, while GTM theory is formally exact for any number of particles, $N$, IST is not. The unified framework presented here enables thermodynamic mapping of solute and solvent alike and is expected to support a range of applications, including in structure-based drug design, protein design, the analysis of allostery, and materials science. The use of GTM theory to gain insight into protein-ligand binding is illustrated here with an initial case study.

papers.title: Triethoxysilane-Enabled Weak Lewis Acidic Boron Catalysis in Nitrile Hydroboration with Pinacolborane
papers.abstract: Triethoxysilane was an efficient precatalyst for the hydroboration of nitriles with pinacolborane (HBPin). The system accommodated a broad range of aromatic and aliphatic substrates, affording the corresponding diborylamines in excellent yields and tolerating both electron-donating and electron-withdrawing substituents. Notably, this transformation exhibited markedly different reactivity from the analogous reaction with alkynes. Competition experiments indicated that catalytic efficiency was governed primarily by steric effects, with minimal sensitivity to electronic variation. The use of the fluorinated analogue HSi(OCH 2 CF 3 ) 3 as a precatalyst, however, had only a minimal impact on the reaction rate. The presence of the N atom in nitriles was found to profoundly alter the nature of the catalytically active species, accounting for the significant differences in reactivity observed relative to alkynes and resulting in the identification of the in situ generated silylboronic ester PinB–Si(OEt) 3 as the predominant species involved in product formation. Changes in the chemical shifts upon addition of HSi(OEt) 3 or HBPin to 4-fluorobenzonitrile revealed a stronger preference of the nitrile for interaction with boron over silicon, consistent with a Lewis acid–base interaction between the B center of PinB–Si(OEt)₃ and the nitrile N atom that facilitates substrate activation during catalysis. The presence of the Si(OEt) 3 group in PinB–Si(OEt) 3 was found critical for efficient catalysis, suggesting that the silyl group may modulate the Lewis acidity and steric environment of the B center or participate directly in interactions with the substrates facilitating their activation.

papers.title: An Unexpected Application of the Negative Root Arising from the Use of the Systematic Treatment of Equilibrium in Calculating pH contribution from the Autoprotolysis of Water in Highly Diluted Strong Acid or Base Solutions
papers.abstract: In the undergraduate analytical chemistry curriculum, determining the concentration of hydronium ions (H + ) of a highly diluted strong acid or base solution (below 10 −6 M) is an important example to demonstrate the concept of the systematic treatment of chemical equilibria using applicable charge balance, mass balance and chemical equilibrium constants. In this case, to accurately describe the pH of the solution, the autoprotolysis of water must be considered in addition to the dissociation/protonation of the strong acid/base. Such systematic treatment yields a quadratic equation with [H + ], the concentration of H + , as its unknown. Solving the quadratic equation always yields a positive root equaling the total [H + ] of the solution and a negative one with no significant value. This article shows, based on the mass balance equations in such chemical system, that the absolute value of this negative root is the [H + ] from the autoprotolysis of water in the system. Our findings could be an interesting critical thinking activity in undergraduate curricula to assist students in their understanding of the principle and application of the systematic treatment of equilibria and practice critical thinking.

papers.title: Vicem: Automating Molecular Mechanics Modeling of Solvation Dynamics with Applications to Time-Resolved X-ray Scattering
papers.abstract: Time-resolved X-ray solution scattering (trXSS) probes molecular-scale structural dynamics in solution, but its interpretation requires efficient computational methodologies and models for assessing how changes in solute structure and charge distribution affect the surrounding solvent shell and the resulting scattering signal. We present VICEM, an OpenMM/ASE-based software suite for constructing solvated molecular models, running molecular dynamics simulations, inspecting and analyzing the resulting trajectories, while exposing solute geometry, partial charges, Lennard–Jones parameters, and bonded terms as editable variables for model refinement. VICEM includes an approximate restrained-solute model designed for rapid solvent-shell sampling around prescribed solute geometries, together with utilities for correcting the potential energy along selected intramolecular coordinates. We benchmark the restrained model against established force fields for 244 systems comprising neutral organic molecules, charged organic solutes, and transition-metal complexes. Across 5018 solute-water radial distribution functions, the effect of restraining the solute structure on the solvent shell is generally comparable to differences between established flexible force fields, and diagnostic cases are scrutinized to identify when reference geometry, nonbonded assignment, or suppressed solute flexibility controls the solvent response. For a prototypical iron complex, VICEM is used to scan candidate geometries and quantify the effect of the structure on solvent-shell radial distribution functions and the corresponding scattering signal, showing how VICEM can be used to tune molecular models for structural refinement. VICEM is therefore shown to provide a platform for reproducible solvent-shell modeling and targeted force-field refinement with particular focus on trXSS analysis.

papers.title: A molecular sewing machine
papers.abstract: Living molecular architectures adapt and evolve by continuously exchanging energy with their surroundings. To mimic this behavior, synthetic tools have been developed to switch 25 artificial systems between states; however, these systems generally relax toward thermodynamically inert equilibria. Creating “life-like” synthetic materials that operate far from equilibrium therefore remains a major challenge. Here, we show that attaching light-activated supramolecular “pumping” motors to polymer chain ends enables the “sewing” of these chains with complementary polymer units bearing multiple macrocyclic side chains. This directional 30 entanglement is sustained by a dissipative, non-equilibrium process and generates mechanically bonded nanogels that transiently store the input light energy processed by the molecular pump. This strategy paves the way to active soft materials capable of functioning over time and performing work on their environment.

papers.title: Decoupling additive manufacturing from virgin resource consumption through recyclable bio-composites
papers.abstract: Additive manufacturing could support decentralised, on-demand production, but it remains largely reliant on linear polymer systems that consume virgin resources and generate persistent waste. Here, we report a fully bio-derived composite platform for closed-loop additive manufacturing based on dynamic lipoic acid networks and renewable fillers. Printable inks containing hydroxyapatite or thiol-functionalized silica were processed by direct ink writing to produce robust three-dimensional structures. Unlike most sustainable 3D-printing strategies, which depend on biodegradation or downcycling through mechanical reprocessing, our lipoate matrix enables printed objects to be thermally recycled directly back into their original printable ink. This allows repeated cycles of fabrication, use, recovery and re-fabrication with minimal losses in printability, material recovery and mechanical performance. Life-cycle assessment shows that this circular materials design reduces impacts on human health, ecosystem quality and resource use, establishing a pathway to circular additive manufacturing that retains material value across multiple life cycles.

papers.title: Towards Reactive Electrochemical Transport Using the Lattice Boltzmann Method. Part II: Atomistically Informed Non-Ideal Species Transport
papers.abstract: The lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) provides an efficient framework for simulating species transport in electrochemical systems; however, conventional formulations commonly rely on ideal or dilute-solution descriptions that neglect molecular-scale non-idealities near solid–electrolyte interfaces. In this work, we extend our previously developed LBM formulation to incorporate non-ideal thermodynamic contributions through the excess chemical potential. The resulting formulation retains the original kinetic structure of the LBM, with non-ideal effects introduced through a modified source term in the species transport equation. This treatment provides a general thermodynamic closure through which steric interactions, species-specific interfacial free energies, and, more generally, excess free-energy models can be incorporated within the same transport framework. The formulation is demonstrated for the electrical double layer by progressively introducing finite-size effects and species-specific microscopic interfacial free-energy contributions. The results show that steric interactions substantially limit the large interfacial ion concentrations predicted by the classical point-ion Poisson–Boltzmann description, while microscopic free-energy contributions produce a further reorganization of the ionic distributions and, consequently, of the interfacial charge density and electrostatic potential. Using hypothetical short-ranged free-energy profiles, the calculations further demonstrate that molecular-scale thermodynamic information can generate an electrostatic response extending beyond the spatial range of the microscopic input through the self-consistent redistribution of charge. The present formulation therefore establishes the excess chemical potential as a natural bridge between microscopic interfacial thermodynamics and mesoscopic species transport. Although analytical free-energy profiles are employed here for demonstration, the framework is not restricted to a particular functional form and permits the direct incorporation of speciesspecific free-energy information obtained from molecular or atomistic simulations, providing a route toward atomistically informed LBM simulations of electrochemical transport.

papers.title: Harnessing TADF in iridium(III) complexes for nearly 20% external quantum efficiency in solution-processed OLEDs
papers.abstract: Our work presents three new di-iridium(III) complexes Ir-H, Ir-F, and Ir-CN displaying strong thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) behaviour. These complexes were obtained by variating the group R = H, F, CN at the 5-position on the pyrimidine-based bridging ligand. Our Ir(III) complexes emit green to orange photoluminescence in polystyrene film, with λPL in the range from 529 nm for Ir-H to 583 nm for Ir-CN and with unity photoluminescence quantum yield. They display clear negative solvatochromism in solution, in line with the metal-to-ligand charge-transfer (MLCT) nature of their excited states. Their TADF performance has been established in a temperature-dependent experiment with the ΔE S-T ranging 30-46 meV with the lowest value reported for orange emitter Ir-CN. Our work is complemented with a detailed computational study and modelling. We report the record high solution-processed organic light-emitting diode (OLED) external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 19.5% recorded for emitter Ir-F at luminance of 1000 cd m -2 . This remarkable achievement presents the highest EQE figure for any iridium(III) complex for which TADF has been reported and double the previous record. The low efficiency roll-off of this device is a result of extremely short PL lifetimes τ PL ~300 ns and high radiative decay rate constants k r ~3×10 6 s -1 of the Ir(III) TADF emitters.

papers.title: Advancing Fluorine Mass Balance Using Machine Learning-Based Quantitative Nontarget Screening
papers.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) often account for only a small fraction of the extractable organic fluorine (EOF) in fluorine mass balance (FMB) studies. Closing this fluorine gap requires identification and quantification of a broader range of fluorinated compounds, including low-fluorinated substances that are difficult to prioritize by nontarget screening (NTS). Here, a workflow combining fluorine-specific NTS with machine learning-based quantification (qNTS) to improve FMB closure was developed. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)-based qNTS models for electrospray ionization (ESI) + and ESI − were trained with 597 reference compounds (185 fluorinated) reaching mean absolute error of ×2.8 and ×2.5 on held-out folds, respectively. An independent validation set of 57 compounds previously unseen by the model reached a mean error of ×2.1. The workflow was applied to urban runoff extracts and AFFF-impacted soils. In sewage-associated runoff, fluorinated pharmaceuticals and their transformation products dominated the identified fluorine, whereas conventional PFAS (i.e. those containing a perfluoroalkyl chain) contributed <3%. Non-PFAS organofluorines (including many pharmaceuticals) contributed up to 48% of the EOF. Identified compounds explained 54–107% of measured EOF in sewage-associated samples but only 1–24% in street runoff, indicating a large fraction of unidentified fluorine in the latter. Application to aqueous film forming foam (AFFF)-impacted soils showed that qNTS performed well for anionic PFAS but was less reliable for cationic and zwitterionic PFAS, which were poorly represented in the training data. Overall, qNTS provided concentration estimates that enabled rapid identification of the compounds contributing most to EOF, thereby directing subsequent target confirmation and FMB closure.

papers.title: Electrochemical profiling of dietary supplements containing B-group vitamins
papers.abstract: The dietary supplement market is one of the fastest-growing sectors of the food industry. However, regulatory challenges and discrepancies between declared and actual composition raise concerns regarding product authenticity and consumer safety. Consequently, there is a growing need for rapid, reliable, and cost-effective methods for dietary supplement quality control. This study aimed to develop a novel electrochemical profiling method for dietary supplements containing B-group vitamins. To establish an effective fingerprinting strategy, cyclic voltammetry (CV) and differential pulse voltammetry (DPV) were performed using glassy carbon (GC) and boron-doped diamond (BDD) working electrodes. The resulting electrochemical responses were compared to assess the complementarity of the information provided by the different electrode materials and voltammetric techniques. The recorded data were analyzed using principal component analysis (PCA) to investigate the differentiation of dietary supplements based on formulation, revealing clear clustering of the investigated samples. Subsequently, two partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) models were developed for sample classification by product type and the presence of manufacturer-declared active ingredients, achieving classification accuracies of up to 100%. The proposed approach demonstrates the potential of electrochemical profiling as a rapid and cost-effective screening tool for dietary supplement quality control, supporting the assessment of sample consistency with manufacturer-declared composition and flagging samples that warrant further confirmatory analysis.

papers.title: Dual Ethylene and CS2 Insertion at an Amidoquinoline Nickel(II) Alkyl Complex Enables CS2-End-Capped Oligoethylene
papers.abstract: Combining olefin and heteroallene (e.g., CO 2 and CS 2 ) migratory insertion during chain-growth polymerization could provide a powerful route to polyolefin-like materials bearing chemically addressable functionalities and defined degradation sites. Herein, we report a neutral Ni(II)-methyl complex 1 supported by an amidoquinoline ligand that exhibits dual reactivity, mediating both ethylene oligomerization at 1 bar and 70 °C and, separately, CS 2 insertion at the Ni–CH3 bond at ambient temperature to afford the corresponding κ 2 (S,S)-dithioacetate complex 2. DFT calculations rationalize the rapid CS 2 insertion mechanism, proceeding through an η 2 –CS 2 pentacoordinate transition state with an overall barrier of 15.3 kcal mol–1. Remarkably, sequential ethylene oligomerization followed by CS 2 addition provides spectroscopic evidence for dithioacetate end-capped oligoethylene, demonstrating that the Ni–C bonds generated during ethylene chain growth polymerization remain competent for heteroallene insertion. Together, these results provide an important step forward toward the synthesis of chemically addressable polyolefin-like materials directly from small-molecules building blocks.

papers.title: Octahedral Molybdenum and Vanadium (Oxo)clusters as Dual Photoinitiators and Crosslinkers for PEGDA Hydrogels with Antibacterial Activity
papers.abstract: Covalent integration of inorganic clusters into polymer matrices opens the way to the creation of functional materials in which the identity of the cluster determines the behavior of the material. Here, Vanadium Lindqvist polyoxometalates [V6O13((OCH2)3CCH2-R))2]2– (abbreviated as V6-R, where R = OH, N3, mAcryl is (N3HC2)(C6H4)NHCOC(CH3)=CH2)) and octahedral molybdenum halide clusters [{Mo6I8}(X’6)]2– (abbreviated as Mo6-X’, where X’ is I or Acryl is O2CCH=CH2) demonstrate the unexpected behavior, and facilitate the poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEGDA) polymerization under mild UV irradiation. The V6-mAcryl and Mo6-Acryl clusters, which bear acrylate ligands grafted onto the inorganic core, fulfill both roles of photoinitiator and polymerizable building block at once, resulting in a composite copolymer network with PEGDA without any additional initiator, sensitizer, or chain-transfer agent. Operando infrared (IR) reaction kinetic monitoring and electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) studies reveal the markedly differences of mechanistic details, highlighting the important role of hexavanadate core photoreduction and ·OH radical formation in the vanadate mediated processes. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) reveals dramatically different hydrogel morphologies: Mo6-Acryl@PEGDA exhibits folded, “brain-like” thee-dimensional (3D) structures, while V6-mAcryl@PEGDA shows smooth, flat films. Mo6-Acryl@PEGDA exhibits potent antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli, whereas V6-mAcryl@PEGDA shows minimal bactericidal effect but moderate biocompatibility with L929 fibroblasts. This work establishes a tunable platform for integrating molecular inorganic clusters with metal–oxo and metal–metal bonds into polymer matrices, where cluster structure dictates morphology, kinetics, and biological function.

papers.title: Actinometric Methods to Assess Fluence for Ultraviolet Water Disinfection: A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Ultraviolet (UV) disinfection is a chemical-free treatment technology that is effective at inactivating a broad range of waterborne microbial pathogens. Ensuring safe and reliable disinfection performance for these systems requires accurate determination of the UV fluence delivered within the water treatment environment. Conventional fluence determination approaches, including biodosimetry and radiometry, exhibit limitations related to pathogen availability, spatial averaging, directional sensitivity, and applicability in enclosed systems. Chemical actinometry offers an alternative approach based on photochemical transformations that integrate the effective UV fluence within a system. However, its application in UV disinfection research remains fragmented, with limited guidance on selecting and implementing appropriate actinometric methods under different conditions. This systematic review aims to inform the application of chemical actinometers to assess the UV fluence for water disinfection systems. The review covers the application of commonly used actinometers, including potassium iodide/iodate, potassium ferrioxalate, uridine, and hydrogen peroxide, across a range of UV sources. The mathematical framework for deriving germicidal UV fluence from actinometric measurements is synthesized, with emphasis on wavelength-dependent behavior and experimental considerations. In addition, key limitations of chemical actinometry, including challenges in translating bench-scale methods to flow-through systems, are evaluated. These findings highlight current knowledge gaps and provide direction for improving the use of chemical actinometry to determine fluence in UV water disinfection systems.

papers.title: QUBO–SAMPLING–DRIVEN SELECTED CONFIGURATION INTERACTION
papers.abstract: Accurate solutions to the electronic Schrödinger equation remain a central challenge in quantum chemistry due to the exponential growth of the many-electron Hilbert space. Selected configuration interaction (SCI) methods mitigate this challenge by restricting the wavefunction expansion to a subset of important determinants, but their efficiency is limited by the quality/cost of determinant selection and Hamiltonian diagonalization. In this work, we propose QUBO-SCI, a novel approach that reformulates the selection step in SCI as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem. This formulation enables the sampling of low-energy electronic configurations as bitstrings using both quantum-inspired approaches and quantum annealing hardware. The sampled configurations are then incorporated into an iterative SCI framework using a perturbative importance criterion. We demonstrate the method on small benchmark systems, including H 2 , C 2 , H 2 O, and N 2 , showing that QUBO-SCI achieves near-FCI accuracy with a significantly reduced number of determinants. The results highlight the potential of annealing-based sampling as an efficient alternative to both conventional determinant selection strategies and circuit-based quantum SCI approaches in electronic structure calculations.

papers.title: How the Energy Gaps between Partners Rules ns-Scale Sensitization and Back-Energy Transfer in Lanthanide(III) Complexes?
papers.abstract: Molecular lanthanide complexes are widely utilized in optoelectronics and bioimaging due to their unique luminescence properties, which inherently rely on the light-harvesting antenna effect. While the ultrafast energy transfer (ET) dynamics of highly emissive ions like Eu3+ have been extensively investigated, mechanisms governed by uncommon kinetic regimes remain largely unresolved. Here, we investigate these ET processes within an isostructural series of lanthanide(III) complexes using nanosecond transient absorption spectroscopy (ns-TAS) under rigorously controlled oxygen concentrations. We provide (i) direct kinetic evidence for Yb3+ sensitization, demonstrating a slow (~40 ns) triplet-to-metal energy transfer that outcompetes intermolecular oxygen quenching, and (ii) elucidate the strong dynamic coupling between the ligand triplet and the Tb3+ emissive state via an ET/BET loop, directly linking oxygen-quenching to terbium(III) luminescence modulation. These results elucidate the complex kinetic picture of lanthanide(III) sensitization, highlighting the energy gap as the fundamental parameter that governs both photosensitization kinetics and the subsequent photophysical pathways. This study establishes ns-TAS as a critical tool to unravel such long-lived excited-state dynamics.

papers.title: Unifying Water Oxidation Chemistry of Iridium Oxide from Aqueous Model Systems to Proton Exchange Membrane Electrolysers
papers.abstract: Understanding how water-oxidation electrocatalysts operate under device-relevant conditions is essential for the design of advanced proton-exchange-membrane (PEM) water electrolysers. Although substantial progress has recently been made in elucidating the oxygen-evolution chemistry of iridium oxide in aqueous model systems, how these molecular insights translate to practical membrane–electrode assemblies (MEA) remains unclear. Here, we bridge this gap by combining operando hard and soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy with time-resolved optical spectroscopy to probe the intrinsic water oxidation chemistry of identical IrOx catalysts across three-electrode, catalyst–ionomer, and MEA configurations. We show that Nafion™ ionomers do not alter the intrinsic metal- and oxygen-centred redox transitions or the formation of electrophilic oxygen species that drives O–O bond formation. Instead, the ionomer content primarily affects mass transport through oxygen trapping and microbubble accumulation, which can obscure operando spectroscopic signatures. Operando Ir L3-edge XAS reveals higher average Ir oxidation states in MEA than in aqueous electrodes despite identical initial states, which is explained by higher catalyst utilisation in the MEA catalyst layers, even at substantially higher mass loading. Open-circuit decay measurements further reveal similar rapid and slow discharge regimes in both systems, demonstrating that IrOx remains in high oxidation states for hours in the absence of hydrogen crossover. These findings establish unified redox transitions and active species in aqueous and MEA environments, while identifying catalyst utilisation and transport effects as the dominant origins of MEA–aqueous discrepancies, thereby providing a general framework for translating molecular insights from model systems to device-relevant conditions.

papers.title: Online Soil Column Chromatography Coupled with Mass Spectrometry for Studying Sorption of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances and Other Organic Contaminants
ShapeAligner: Direct Molecular Superposition from Clique-Based Atom Correspondence
papers.abstract: Superposing one small molecule onto another is routine in ligand-based drug discovery. In atom-level correspondence methods, the pose the correspondence determines is only a starting point, and a subsequent search produces what is reported. We present ShapeAligner, a rigid aligner whose output pose is the superposition its maximal clique correspondence determines. Maximal cliques of an association graph over chemically typed heavy atoms each fix a reflection-free, equally weighted Kabsch transform in closed form. An analytic Gaussian shape-and-color volume overlap ranks the resulting poses. Nothing after the superposition moves the pose. Across 68,150 directed tasks from the LOBSTER cross-pair corpus, the top pose lands within 2.0 Å of the crystallographic pose in 30.98% of the tasks ShapeAligner covers, against 28.32% for the next-highest of six comparators. The median time is 0.214 s per task on one CPU core. Recovery depends strongly on the pair. It is highest when the larger ligand serves as the template, and the two ligands share at least 0.60 of the smaller ligand's volume. Below that threshold no method recovers more than 4% of the tasks it covers. The output is deterministic, and the correspondence it rests on is invariant to the input coordinate frame by construction. The implementation is released under the MIT license.

papers.title: Fatigue, Memory and Training in Thermo-Responsive Hydrogels
papers.abstract: Responsive materials are a cornerstone of functional soft matter. Their functionality relies on switching between equilibrium states, a process generally assumed fully reversible over repeated cycles. Here we show that thermo-responsive hydrogels can instead develop progressive fatigue and irreversibility during repeated volume phase transitions. Viscoelastic phase separation generates mechanical stresses that drive permanent network rearrangements and trap phase-separated morphologies, creating a non-volatile structural memory. Consequently, classical responsive hydrogels become adaptive materials whose structure and mechanics evolve with their thermal history. By varying chemical composition and network connectivity, we identify conditions governing the transition from reversible to adaptive behavior. Mechanochemical network remodeling thus provides a route toward materials that acquire durable memory through repeated stimulation, while revealing design and operation principles for fatigue-free switchable soft materials.

papers.title: Coupled Thermal Activation and Autocatalytic Cure Kinetics: A Theoretical and Computational Study of Delayed Reactive Transformation
papers.abstract: The delayed transformation of a reactive material into a solid phase is limited, in most thermal-management approaches, by a basic trade-off between transport stability and transformation speed. We formulate and computationally analyze a coupled zero-dimensional model in which (i) a lumped thermal energy balance governs the fluid element's temperature, including exothermic self-heating from the reaction itself; (ii) the release of a reaction-triggering species follows a physically motivated first-order relaxation toward a temperature dependent, Arrhenius-rate-controlled saturation level (a lumped analog to shell-diffusion-limited release), rather than a prescribed availability function; and (iii) the triggered reaction follows Kamal–Sourour autocatalytic kinetics. Four dimensionless groups — Λ=0.911 (release-to-reaction timescale ratio), Θ=0.454 (thermal-to-reaction timescale ratio), ψ=10.08 (reduced exothermicity), and Ar=18.9 (activation-sensitivity number) — are used to organize the parameter space. An objectively matched (not arbitrarily scaled) comparison against a first-order control, whose rate constant is root-solved for equal t50 rather than assigned an assumed scaling factor, shows that the coupled autocatalytic system is Pareto-optimal: across 60 sampled first-order rate constants spanning a wide range, none simultaneously matches or beats the coupled system on both premature conversion (α at t=25 min) and completion time (t90). A two-parameter regime map over (Θ, Λ) identifies thermally limited, release-limited, and reaction-limited regions, with the thermally limited region driving peak exothermic overshoots up to 204°C above the setpoint. Because complete suppression of conversion below the nominal activation threshold is a structural consequence of the idealized (zero-width) gate rather than an independent prediction, we reframe the falsifiable claim around a finite-width thermal gate: increasing the gate width from 0.5°C to 15°C is predicted to reduce premature conversion (α at t=25 min falling from 0.073 to 0.039) at the cost of slower completion (t90 rising from 34.1 to 40.4 min) — a quantified, directly testable trade-off. Vectorized Monte Carlo propagation of joint uncertainty across nine kinetic, release, and thermal parameters (N=20,000) indicates that 69.9% of the draws satisfy both a minimum induction time and a 75-minute completion target, with reaction-kinetics parameters (most notably Ea2, Spearman r=0.69) dominating the predicted variance over thermal or release-timescale parameters. Three falsifiable predictions, each paired with a standard dynamic-DSC or rheo-DSC validation protocol, are stated for future experimental testing.

papers.title: Incorporating Computational Chemistry into Introductory Courses with a No-cost, Installation-free Molecular Dynamics Activity in Python
papers.abstract: Molecular simulations have become indispensable in applications ranging from drug discovery to materials design and battery technology, yet students are typically not exposed to these techniques until upper-level physical chemistry courses towards the end of their undergraduate education. This late exposure to computational chemistry can limit opportunities for students to develop proficiency or participate in faculty-led computational chemistry research. Although Python-based molecular dynamics (MD) activities are increasingly incorporated into physical chemistry laboratories, they require students to simultaneously learn challenging chemistry concepts and computer programming, creating a substantial cognitive load. This work introduces computational chemistry earlier in the curriculum by integrating Python-controlled and Pythonanalyzed MD simulations into instruction on the ideal gas law. Designed for introductory chemistry, the activity is appropriate for first-year undergraduate and advanced high school students. Students completing this activity first learn foundational Python concepts before applying them to ideal gas law calculations and molecular simulations using the LAMMPS molecular dynamics package. The scaffolded activity progresses from basic Python programming to gas-law calculations and finally to analyzing Lennard-Jones simulations, allowing students to manipulate simulation parameters and compare real and ideal gas behavior while exploring the assumptions underlying the ideal gas model. The effectiveness of the activity was evaluated using anonymous preand post-activity surveys. All instructional materials are provided as publicly available Google Colab notebooks, enabling students to perform molecular simulations entirely through a web browser without software installation or specialized hardware. Because the simulations are run on Google’s freely available cloud computing infrastructure, the activities are freely accessible and can be completed on low-cost devices such as Google Chromebooks. Comparison of pre-and post-activity survey responses suggests that introducing computational chemistry through an accessible, scaffolded activity can increase students’ confidence in gas-law concepts, reduce barriers to computational chemistry, and stimulate interest in computational methods.

papers.title: THIOETHERS AS POTENTIAL ANTIBACTERIAL AGENTS AGAINST METHICILLIN-RESISTANT STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS (MRSA)
papers.abstract: The emergence and rapid spread of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) have created an urgent need for new antibacterial agents capable of overcoming established resistance mechanisms. Among the diverse sulfur-containing scaffolds, thioethers have attracted increasing attention because of their structural versatility and ability to modulate antibacterial activity through incorporation into different pharmacophores. This review provides a comprehensive overview of synthetic, semisynthetic, and natural or natural-product-derived thioether compounds evaluated against MRSA, with emphasis on their structural features, structure-activity relationships (SAR), antibacterial potency, and mechanisms of action. The major classes discussed include aminoglycoside-derived thioether amphiphiles, membrane-active small-molecule thioethers, quinazolinone and quinoline thioether scaffolds, pleuromutilin thioether derivatives, SecA-targeting thioethers, chalcone and oxazolidinone derivatives, FtsZ-targeting thioethers, anti-virulence and antibiofilm agents, antimicrobial peptidomimetics, and natural-product-derived thioether compounds. The studies demonstrate that sulfur-containing motifs can contribute to anti-MRSA activity through membrane disruption, inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis and targeting of essential non-ribosomal proteins. The available SAR evidence highlights the scaffold-dependent nature of thioether activity and supports their continued exploration as versatile structural motifs for the development of new therapeutic strategies against drug-resistant MRSA.

papers.title: Extensive A-Site Magnesium Solubility in Perovskite Oxides via Precursor-mediated Synthesis Pathways
papers.abstract: Incorporation of Mg 2+ on the A-site of ABO 3 perovskite oxides such as BaTiO 3 and SrTiO 3 has been limited by severe ionic size differences of the A-site cations with some reports claiming <1% substitution possible. Here, we demonstrate a precursor-mediated synthesis pathway to achieve extensive A-site Mg 2+ substitution in perovskite oxides – up to 50 mol%. By leveraging binary and ternary metal carbonates that are chemically mixed at the crystallographic scale, barriers associated with conventional solid-state reactions are bypassed. Specifically, we show that norsethite-type precursors such as BaMg(CO 3 ) 2 and Ba 0.5 Sr 0.5 Mg(CO 3 ) 2 react with TiO 2 to yield single-phase cubic perovskites Ba 0.5 Mg 0.5 TiO 3 and Ba 0.25 Sr 0.25 Mg 0.5 TiO 3 at temperatures as low as 640°C. This work highlights crystallographic-scale chemical mixing of carbonates as a generalizable route for accessing kinetically trapped, metastable oxides that are far from equilibrium.

papers.title: Spiral-Growth-Induced Nanosteps on Layered Oxyhalide Photocatalysts Enhance Anisotropic Charge Separation for Visible-Light Water Splitting
papers.abstract: Layered mixed-anion compounds are promising photocatalysts for solar fuel production owing to their visible-light absorption and suitable band-edge positions. However, their two-dimensional crystal structures hinder the spatial separation of reduction and oxidation sites because both photogenerated electrons and holes predominantly migrate in-plane along the layered frameworks. In particular, in plate-like particles reflecting this layered structure, charge carriers must travel relatively long lateral distances. Here, we overcome this limitation for the first time by introducing step structures on the basal planes, which shorten the lateral carrier migration while spatially separating redox sites. Using the layered oxyhalide Bi 4 NbO 8 Cl as a model photocatalyst, nanoscale steps are formed on the basal planes of plate-like crystals via screw-dislocation-driven spiral growth during flux synthesis. Subsequent acid etching converts the basal planes from photogenerated electron-rich to hole-accumulating surfaces, as revealed by surface photovoltage spectroscopy, enabling preferential photodeposition of reduction cocatalysts onto the electron-rich nanosteps. This asymmetric cocatalyst loading promotes anisotropic charge separation, resulting in a 16-fold enhancement in the photocatalytic H 2 evolution rate compared to the untreated sample and achieving one of the highest apparent quantum efficiencies reported for layered oxyhalide photocatalysts. Furthermore, etched samples with nanosteps exhibit enhanced photocatalytic water oxidation under visible-light Z-scheme water splitting, demonstrating the effectiveness of this surface engineering for solar water splitting. This study establishes spiral-growth-induced step formation combined with surface etching as a new design strategy for controlling carrier flow in layered photocatalysts, unlocking their potential for solar energy conversion.

papers.title: Interpretable Processing–Structure Relationships in Spirulina Bioplastics through Automated Spectral and Microstructural Analysis
papers.abstract: Algal bioplastics are emerging as a promising class of sustainable materials, but their development is limited by an incomplete understanding of how processing governs structure. Establishing principles connecting processing to structure is hindered by manual analysis and the complexity of structural data. Here thermomechanical processing conditions (time, temperature, and pressing force) are mapped to structural descriptors of Limnospira platensis (spirulina) bioplastics. Quantifiable features are derived from Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to summarize the chemical and physical structure. Informative FTIR regions are selected by principal component regression (PCR), and interpretable Gaussian bands are automatically deconvolved from the spectra. SEM micrographs are encoded using a self-supervised vision transformer (DINOv3), projected into two dimensions, and clustered. Overall, 201 features are combined into a structural fingerprint and fed to a gradient boosted model that is inverted to recover processing conditions. The inverted model reveals that temperature strongly influences the structural features, while pressing time acts as a secondary logarithmic modulator. Conversely, pressing force is recoverable only as a regime, behaving as a consolidation threshold near 5 kN. Together, these results demonstrate that complex structural signatures can be transformed into interpretable processing–structure relationships, enabling rational design of algal bioplastics.

papers.title: Temporal Programming of Interfacial States Reveals a Hidden Formate Pathway from CO2 Reduction on Palladium
papers.abstract: Controlling electrocatalytic selectivity requires not only tuning catalyst composition but also controlling the interfacial states that emerge during operation. Here, using bulk Pd as a model system for electrochemical CO 2 reduction reaction (CO 2 RR), we show that poor steady-state formate production emerges from time-dependent evolution of the electrochemical interface. Pd initially exhibits appreciable formate activity but rapidly accumulates strongly bound CO and evolves toward a CO-rich, formate-inactive state. Although substantial sorbed H persists during this evolution, its oxidation shifts to increasingly positive potentials with increasing CO coverage, indicating reduced electrochemical accessibility and reactivity of H at the CO-covered interface. Density functional theory shows that CO-rich configurations are thermodynamically favored under cathodic conditions, while increasing CO coverage destabilizes early intermediates of both the formate and CO pathways. Dynamic potential modulation temporally separates surface-state preparation from catalytic turnover: anodic excursions remove accumulated CO, and subsequent cathodic polarization repeatedly accesses a CO-depleted state that is not thermodynamically favored at the reaction potential. This strategy produces an approximately 230-fold enhancement in formate partial current density relative to static operation. Within this dynamically accessible low-CO regime, formate activity further correlates with sorbed-H availability. These results reveal a hierarchical interfacial control in which CO coverage gates pathway accessibility while hydrogen availability modulates formate activity, demonstrating how temporal control can access catalytic states and reaction pathways hidden under steady-state operation.

papers.title: Directed Evolution of a Non-Heme Iron Enzyme for Enantioselective Dearomative Nitrene Transfer: Synthesis of 3a-Aminopyrroloindoline Alkaloids
papers.abstract: Enzymatic nitrene-induced dearomatization represents an unexplored area of biocatalytic reactivity. Here, we report the directed evolution of AsqJ, a non-heme iron enzyme from aspoquinolone biosynthesis, to catalyze the first biocatalytic asymmetric dearomative nitrene transfer into indoles to furnish enantioenriched 3a-aminopyrroloindolines — a privileged scaffold in bioactive indole alkaloid natural products. Obtained through iterative semi-rational engineering and structure-informed mutagenesis, the final variant achieves up to 98% yield and >99% ee. The reaction accommodates a range of indole substrates, affording up to 86% isolated yield on preparative scale with consistently high enantioselectivity. Molecular dynamics simulations suggest that directed evolution established a new substrate-binding conformation that is distinct from the starting variant through a reorganized hydrogen-bonding network within a more preorganized active site. The synthetic utility of this platform is demonstrated through the total syntheses of two natural products, (+)-psychotriasine and (+)-psychotrimine. This work establishes asymmetric dearomative nitrene transfer as a new biocatalytic modality, extends the catalytic repertoire of non-heme iron enzymes to encompass asymmetric dearomatization, and provides a foundation for applying new-to-nature biocatalytic reactions in complex natural product synthesis.

papers.title: Structural and physicochemical dissection of the anticancer peptide PNC-27: a computational reassessment of its design logic
papers.abstract: PNC-27 (PPLSQETFSDLWKLLKKWKMRRNQFWVKVQRG) is a chimeric peptide in which p53 residues 12–26 are fused directly to a penetratin-derived cationic module. It was designed as an intracellular MDM2/HDM-2 antagonist, but the originating laboratory has since reported that its cytotoxicity does not depend on p53 status, and has proposed a membrane-associated mechanism in its place. This work re-examines PNC-27 as a peptide-engineering problem, using structural analysis of existing crystallographic data together with sequence-level biophysics. No folding, docking or molecular dynamics was used. Per-residue burial and contact analysis across ten receptor–peptide pairs drawn from seven MDM2/MDMX structures confirms the Phe19/Trp23/Leu26 hot-spot triad and puts numbers on it. Between 34.5 and 43.7 % of the buried interface lies outside the triad even in the tightest binders. Sequence-verified numbering (p53 = position + 11) places the buried hot spot Leu26 at PNC-27 position 15, immediately before the fusion point. Extrapolation of an ideal helix shows the C-terminal fusion vector to be sterically unobstructed, with no MDM2 atom within 5 Å over eight residues, whereas an N-terminal extension clashes at 1.82 Å. The cationic module proves to be a retro sequence of penetratin, with 14 of 16 residues matching reversed Antp 43–58. It is only weakly amphipathic (µH 0.272 against 0.455 for magainin-2 through the same pipeline) and appears to act as a solubilising element for the hydrophobic p53 head rather than as a lytic helix. Both the hydrophobic-moment maximum (µH 0.713) and the most helix-favourable segment straddle the inter-module junction instead of lying within either module. A seven-member insertion series shows that any linker abolishes the amphipathic maximum, while glycine-rich and rigid helical inserts diverge in their effect on junction helix propensity. Conventional flexible-linker insertion is therefore predicted to be counterproductive. Fifteen variants across six modification strategies are described, along with the specific measurements that would most efficiently discriminate between the competing interpretations. No therapeutic claim is made; every conclusion here is a structural or physicochemical hypothesis.

papers.title: Corridor Bonding Theory: A QTAIM-Based Density-Informed Graph Language for Teaching and Interpreting Chemical Structure
papers.abstract: Lewis structures, hybridization, the sigma/pi partition, and resonance hybrids remain the default teaching language of the chemical bond. They are useful representational tools, but they do not constitute a unique ontology of chemical bonding. This paper states Corridor Bonding Theory in its total form (CBT-T): a QTAIM-based density-informed graph language. An atom is a QTAIM basin. A corridor is a thresholded sharing contact; a large w is not by itself a binding energy, a force, or a reaction coordinate. The computational candidate set C(R*) is a finite screening rule, not a physical existence claim. G0 keeps screened pairs with w>eps (eps=1.0e-4). Gtheta keeps pairs with w>=theta. Unused capacity is a residual teaching label called a loop. Polarity is annotated by tau_q from QTAIM charges q=Z-N. A visually balanced cycle is a figure convention, not a theory of aromaticity. A reaction comparison is a difference of two stationary graphs, not a trajectory. The map is total: every stationary density yields G0, Gtheta, w and tau_q. There is no handshake that rejects a molecule, no post-hoc change of ports, and no unique integer bond order. w=delta(A,B)/delta(H,H) at one electronic-structure level. Appendix A2 reports that delta at PBE0/def2-TZVP for the protocol set, including CO2, open O3, SO2, SO3, B2H6, benzene, He2 and Ne2. Appendix C is a Wiberg-Lowdin proxy only.

papers.title: Systematic mapping of bimetallic catalyst combinations for floating catalyst chemical vapor deposition growth of single-walled carbon nanotubes
papers.abstract: Floating-catalyst chemical vapor deposition (FC-CVD) is a widely used method for the continuous synthesis of single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs), yet the rational design of multi-component catalyst systems remains limited by insufficient systematic mapping of secondary-metal effects. This work presents a systematic screening of 22 secondary-metal precursor combinations (spanning post-transition, transition and lanthanide metals) with a primary Fe catalyst to evaluate how secondary-metal chemistry influences SWCNT growth characteristics, including specific yield, SWCNT diameter, crystallinity, and bundle length. Statistical analysis revealed a moderate positive correlation between the bulk melting point of the secondary metal and specific yield, suggesting that thermal stability may contribute to improved SWCNT growth output under FC-CVD conditions. In addition, an effective activity parameter, N eff , was introduced to separate the contribution of characteristic nanotube dimensions from the measured yield and to compare the relative effective active-catalyst population among different precursor combinations. The resulting N eff –bundle length map showed that secondary-metal addition can shift the balance between effective active particle generation and sustained nanotube elongation. Notably, Fe-Ti exhibited a favorable balance between relatively high N eff (9.4%) and elongated bundle length (85.5%). Overall, this catalyst-property mapping provides a comparative framework for identifying promising secondary-metal combinations and guiding future FC-CVD catalyst design toward targeted SWCNT structures and assemblies.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Viscosity Gradients Shape Breakup and Relaxation in Non-Newtonian Drops
papers.abstract: Unlike elongated Newtonian drops, whose relaxation to a sphere is approximately exponential and governed by a single characteristic timescale, particle-filled drops can exhibit complex, multistage relaxation and may fail to recover a spherical shape. These dynamical features are important because they determine the morphology of particle-filled immiscible blends, which in turn controls their macroscopic properties. Our prior experiments demonstrated that, at sufficiently high particle loading, the initially rapid relaxation eventually slows down and appears to arrest at a finite, non-spherical deformation. However, the experiments could not resolve the spatiotemporal evolution of internal quantities such as viscosity, velocity gradients, and stress fields. Here, we investigate whether the retardation and subsequent apparent arrest of initially elongated drops can arise solely from strong shear thinning, without invoking fluid elasticity or a true yield stress. Motivated by experiments on particle-filled polyisobutylene drops, we perform axisymmetric, two-phase volume-of-fluid simulations in which the drop phase follows a Carreau–Yasuda constitutive law and the suspending fluid is Newtonian. The numerical method is first validated against classical predictions for Newtonian drop relaxation. We find that Carreau–Yasuda drops exhibit a two-stage response comprising rapid initial relaxation followed by pronounced late-time retardation. The onset, magnitude and rate of this slowing are governed by a dimensionless parameter S that compares the material shear-thinning rate scale with the characteristic capillary relaxation rate. Spatially resolved fields reveal that geometrically induced low-strain-rate regions near the retracting poles enter the high-viscosity regime before the remainder of the drop. These localized regions resist the flow required for continued shape recovery and act as viscous anchors, producing a self-reinforcing positive coupling between decreasing strain rate, increasing viscosity, and suppressed relaxation. Because the Carreau–Yasuda fluid never becomes truly unyielded, we introduce an operational stress-based criterion for apparent arrest using the characteristic stress η0/λ where η0 is the zero-shear viscosity of the Carreau–Yasuda fluid, and λ is the Carreau–Yasuda relaxation time. We demonstrate and rationalize via a stress balance argument that the deformation at apparent-arrest Darr ∝ S in this weak-to-moderate deformation regime. Taken together, spatiotemporal variations in the viscosity, strain-rate, and normalized-stress fields identify the microscopic origin of the arrested relaxation observed experimentally: a geometrically inherited low-strain-rate region near the drop ends, amplified by the shear-thinning constitutive response into a high-viscosity anchor, which couples back through positive feedback and stabilizes the drop at a finite arrested deformation.

papers.title: Tailoring carbon nitride nanoarchitecture and cellular interactions through hydrothermal alkaline etching
papers.abstract: Graphitic carbon nitride (g-C 3 N 4 ) is a versatile material for biomedical, energy, and environmental applications. Bulk g-C 3 N 4 is commonly used as a precursor for nanoscale objects, yet systematic links between synthesis conditions, nanostructure morphology, surface chemistry, and biological response remain limited. Here, we have fabricated a palette of carbon nitride nanostructures via hydrothermal alkaline etching. By varying the hydroxide (LiOH, NaOH, or KOH) and reaction conditions, etching yields carbon nitride quantum dots, carbon nitride nanowires and their networks, as well as larger flakes and sponge-like objects. Automated transmission electron microscopy image analysis supported this comparison by converting heterogeneous micrographs into object-level morphology and particle-size statistics. The hydroxide type also controls surface chemistry: LiOH and KOH promote stronger oxidative functionalization, whereas NaOH leads to a more hydrated and passivated surface. In immortalized human cervical cancer cells, the samples show little effect on metabolic activity after 24 h at 200 µg mL −1 , while cellular accumulation varies markedly with preparation conditions. Notably, smaller nanostructures do not guarantee higher cellular accumulation, suggesting that nanowire networks with entangled quantum dots may dominate membrane adhesion. Overall, this work provides a practical route to tune carbon nitride nanostructures for bioimaging applications.

papers.title: GNN-ωPBE: Range-Separation Parameters Learned from Three-Dimensional Structures
papers.abstract: Range-separated hybrid (RSH) functionals improve density functional theory (DFT) for modeling organic semiconducting molecules by reducing self-interaction and delocalization errors, but their accuracy depends critically on the range-separation parameter (ω). Although our previously developed ML-ωPBE functional generates molecule-specific ω values from topology-based descriptors, its applicability is limited for flexible molecules with rich conformational diversity. We introduce GNN-ωPBE, a second machine learned RSH functional that generates geometry-specific ω values directly from atomic numbers and three-dimensional (3D) atomic coordinates. Built on a graph neural network (GNN) representation, GNN-ωPBE encodes interatomic interactions through internal coordinates and distinguishes different conformers of the same molecule, enabling it to capture geometry-dependent variations inaccessible to topology-based molecular descriptors. Trained on a conformer-resolved dataset, GNN-ωPBE reproduces benchmark OT-ωPBE with a mean absolute error (MAE) of approximately 0.0072 a0−1. Our study advances machine learned density functional development from molecule-specific to geometry-specific modeling of conformational effects in electronic structures.

papers.title: pdb2reaction: End-to-End Reaction-Path Elucidation from PDB Structures Using Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Elucidating enzymatic reaction mechanisms requires a sequence of computational tasks comprising active-site extraction, minimum-energy path (MEP) search, transition-state (TS) refinement, intrinsic reaction coordinate (IRC) validation, and quasi-rigid-rotor harmonic-oscillator (QRRHO) thermochemistry—stages typically connected by ad hoc scripting and per-system tuning. We present pdb2reaction, an open-source Python command-line toolkit that automates this entire pipeline directly from a user-curated PDB using a single machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) backend. A GPU-accelerated pysisyphus fork is bundled to perform all Hessian-based heavy computations on the same CUDA device as the MLIP, minimizing data transfer overhead. This toolkit also implements a bond-change-driven recursive path-search algorithm, which successfully recovered the two-step reaction mechanism of the geranyl pyrophosphate (GPP) C6-methyltransferase BezA from a single reactant PDB and a minimal scan list.
