The identified mechanism comprises an S N 2-like methyl transfer followed by glutamate-mediated deprotonation via a cationic intermediate. A benchmark comprising 23 reaction steps across six different enzymes demonstrated that pdb2reaction recovered the literature mechanisms for 16 out of 23 steps using two of the five tested MLIP backends, with each successfully yielding transition states characterized by a single imaginary frequency. pdb2reaction enables rapid PDB-tomechanism elucidation on a single GPU, providing a high-throughput complement to higher-cost higher-cost DFT-based cluster-model calculations and full enzyme–solvent QM/MM calculations.

papers.title: The Structural and Dynamical Effect of Monolignol Coniferyl Alcohol on Biomembranes
papers.abstract: Monolignols are lignin precursors that must cross the plasma membrane before polymerization in the cell wall, but their interaction with lipid membranes remains poorly defined experimentally. In this work, we used Neutron Membrane Diffraction (NMD), Small-Angle Neutron Scattering (SANS), Neutron Spin Echo (NSE), and Quasi-Elastic Neutron Scattering (QENS) to examine the structural and dynamical effects of coniferyl alcohol (CA) in a DOPC/DOPE model membrane. Partially deuterated coniferyl alcohol (CA-D5) provided enhanced neutron contrast for probing changes in the transbilayer structure and possible distribution within the bilayer. NMD did not resolve CA-D5 at a specific bilayer depth over the nominal concentration range studied. Both NMD measurements of substrate-supported multilamellar bilayers and SANS measurements of unilamellar vesicles in solution revealed a small but clearly resolved bilayer thinning of approximately 1–2 Å, while the overall membrane architecture remained intact. Dynamically, CA-D5 softens the membrane at the collective length scale, as shown by a reduced effective bending modulus from NSE. At the molecular scale, QENS showed no systematic change in lipid lateral diffusivity, although the characteristic microscopic displacement length increased at higher CA-D5 concentrations. These cross-scale measurements show that CA produces measurable but limited changes in membrane structure and dynamics without major membrane reorganization. This membrane-compatible response is consistent with various proposed monolignol transport pathways, including passive permeation and vesicle-associated transport.

papers.title: High-Throughput Structure Determination Using Serial Electron Diffraction
papers.abstract: Atomic-scale structure determination is essential for product confirmation in chemical synthesis and for understanding material properties in chemistry, materials science, and pharmaceutical research. However, traditional techniques such as X-ray crystallography and Microcrystal Electron Diffraction (MicroED) are often limited by requirements for large crystals, cryogenic conditions, or complex goniometry, making them less suitable for beam-sensitive or agglomerated nanocrystalline samples. To address these challenges, we employ serial electron diffraction (SerialED) to determine the structures of twelve chemically and structurally diverse compounds at room temperature to demonstrate the generality of the method. The analyzed samples include metal-organic frameworks, pharmaceutical compounds, a perovskite, and various organic and metalorganic complexes. Additionally, we report the first de novo structure determination using SerialED by solving a previously unknown coordination polymer. Our method enables high-throughput diffraction data collection using commercially available instruments and low-dose exposures, circumventing the need for cryogenic preservation. Sub-angstrom resolution was achieved for all structures. Notably, the workflow from sample preparation to structure solution can be completed within an hour time frame using only micrograms of materials. These results demonstrate the versatility and practicality of SerialED as a routine tool for high resolution structure determination of nanocrystals at room temperature, overcoming key limitations of existing methods.

papers.title: Zinc Redox Catalysis in the Photochemical Borylation of Fluorocarbons
papers.abstract: Zinc compounds are ubiquitous in synthesis and materials. They find applications as reagents, catalysts, porous materials and as metalloenzymes — all of which rely on the properties of redox stable and electrophilic zinc(II) centres. In this paper we report the first clear example of redox catalysis involving reversible changes between zinc(I) and zinc(II) oxidation states. Under photochemical conditions a zinc(I) compound was shown to react with aryl fluorides. Turnover was achieved through addition of a diborane reagent, resulting in a catalytic borylation of the C(sp 2 )–F bonds of aryl fluorides. The reaction has a large scope including both electron-deficient and electron-rich aryl fluorides and tolerates a range of functional groups including ethers, amines, heteroaromatics, substituted alkenes and a strained ring-system. These findings were further exploited in the late-stage functionalisation of fluorinated molecules relevant to drug discovery and materials technologies, along the selective, stepwise, borylation of poly(fluorinated) arenes. Experiments and DFT calculations support a catalytic cycle involving changes between the zinc(I) and zinc(II) oxidation state. A zinc(II) boryl intermediate was isolated and shown to play a key role in reformation of the low-oxidation state zinc(I) species. The findings advance our fundamental understanding of redox catalysis with non-transition metal elements and set the foundation for further applications of zinc redox catalysts in challenging chemical transformations.

papers.title: Quantifying the Coherence Wall: FeMoCo Quantum Chemistry from 48 to 108 Qubits on IBM Heron r2
papers.abstract: We quantify the depth-dependent loss of many-body correlation information in FeMoCo-scale quantum chemistry circuits executed on IBM Heron r2. The workflow combines LUCJ circuit execution, Aurora-DD control, sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), DMRG prior construction, and ph-AFQMC refinement across 48-, 56-, 80-, and 108-qubit active-space instances. Rather than treating the 108-qubit energy as a chemical-accuracy claim, we separate statistical precision, systematic phaseless bias, and extractable correlation signal. The 108-qubit CAS(54e,54o) run reaches a ph-AFQMC statistical standard error of ±0.67 mHa, while the single-determinant phaseless bias remains approximately 1,103 mHa relative to DMRG M = 500. Conversely, a classical DMRG multi-determinant ph-AFQMC route reaches chemical accuracy at 48 qubits, with a residual phaseless bias of +1.07 mHa. Four-point spatial-correlation amplitudes decay from 0.226 at 48 qubits to 0.101 at 80 qubits and 0.045 at 108 qubits; fitting the 48-qubit amplitude gives a per-qubit scaling parameter ϵq = 0.0304 that predicts the 80- and 108-qubit amplitudes within 19–26% relative error without additional free parameters. Exhaustive Bayesian and machine-learning signal extraction yields an out-of-fold ceiling of r ≈ 0.03 at 108 qubits under the present Heron r2, shot-count, circuit-depth, and DMRG M = 800 reference conditions. We therefore define the observed coherence wall as a conditional hardware-characterization metric for this benchmark rather than a universal physical constant. The results suggest that residual incoherent noise channels, including TLS-associated loss and relaxation, now dominate over statistical sampling error in this regime.

papers.title: Machine-Learned Solid-State 13C Chemical Shifts for Structure-Resolved Analysis of Polymer Simulations
papers.abstract: Solid-state 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is among the most powerful probes of polymer structure, yet predicting solid-state 13C NMR spectra from molecular simulations has remained infeasible due to intractable computational costs. Here we introduce PNGWNN, a framework coupling molecular dynamics and machinelearned chemical shifts to efficiently generate solid-state 13C NMR spectra from molecular simulation. Trained on three polymer chemistries, PNGWNN achieves ∼1 ppm chemical shift prediction accuracy against density functional theory and transfers quantitatively to six chemically distinct test polymers across amorphous, crystalline, surface, multiphase, and copolymer morphologies. Moreover, predicted spectral features can be decomposed into atomically detailed contributions associated with specific conformations, hydrogen-bond motifs, and phase compositions, revealing structure–spectrum relationships without prior structural hypotheses. PNGWNN makes solid-state 13C NMR a computationally accessible observable, opening routes to simulation-driven structural inference and experimental design in polymers.

papers.title: Powering Hyperscale AI Data Centers with Off-grid Solar, Battery, and Hydrogen
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) data centers are emerging as a major source of electricity demand, driving interest in renewable-powered and off-grid energy systems as grid interconnection delays, generator shortages, and infrastructure constraints complicate high load factor operation. In this Perspective, we model a 1-GW off-grid solar-powered AI data center and show that battery-only systems exhibit rapid cost escalation at high load factor because of solar and battery overbuild, curtailment, and underutilized storage capacity. In contrast, battery + hydrogen systems suppress this behavior by allowing batteries to manage daily fluctuations while hydrogen provides long-duration and seasonal energy storage through underground hydrogen storage. Sensitivity analysis further shows that the economic advantage of battery + hydrogen architectures persists across wide hydrogen subsystem cost ranges. More broadly, this Perspective suggests that high load factor AI data centers may represent an early commercialization pathway for hydrogen-based seasonal energy infrastructure.

papers.title: Modeling Reaction Feasibility to Identify New Opportunities for Sigmatropic Rearrangements
papers.abstract: Defining the scope and limitations of synthetic methods enables bolder, lower-risk synthetic design. Computation can facilitate this if able to anticipate reaction success or failure. Herein, we combine a machine-learned interatomic potential with the TS-tools package for high-throughput prediction of transition state geometries and barriers for hypothetical reactions. We focus on sigmatropic rearrangements, which are of synthetic interest, enable non-obvious retrosynthetic disconnections, and are explicable by electronic structure theory. Benchmarking against reference theory and experimental kinetics establishes quantitative accuracy, and retrospective case studies illustrate utility in synthesis planning. Prospectively, we identify and experimentally realize a methylenation/Claisen sequence toward the natural product (±)-norbrachycoumarin and a UR-144 degradant. A coarse-grained kinetic study across ten substrates, seven installing all-carbon quaternary centers β to a ketone, reveals good agreement between computed barriers and experimental outcomes. Collectively, this work demonstrates how computational reaction feasibility modeling uncovers opportunities to apply existing methodologies to valuable chemical spaces.

papers.title: Oxidative C–C Bond Cleavage of 1,2-Diols by Mn-Doped CeO2 Catalysts
papers.abstract: The 1,2-diol motif is frequently found in biomass-derived compounds; thus, its direct and selective C–C bond cleavage is crucial for broadening the utility of biomass resources. In this paper, we report that CeO2 showed high catalytic activity for the C–C bond cleavage of 1,2-diols. Moreover, Mn-doped CeO2 demonstrated higher activity than pristine CeO2, enabling the efficient conversion of 1,2-diols into the corresponding carbonyl compounds in high yields. Mechanistic investigations revealed that the redox and surface basic properties of CeO2 was the key for facilitating catalytic C–C bond cleavage. The high reusability of the Mn-doped CeO2 catalyst underscores its potential for practical and sustainable synthetic applications.

papers.title: Role of ortho-functional groups in stabilizing catechol surface complexes on ferrite nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Molecular-level interactions of naturally occurring catechol derivatives with ferrite surfaces were investigated using permanently magnetic barium hexaferrite nanoplatelets and superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles. Catechol (1,2-benzenediol) and guaiacol (2-methoxyphenol) were selected as representative aromatic ligands relevant to catechol- and guaiacyl-containing natural compounds. First-principles calculations indicated facile proton transfer from the ligands to surface oxygen or hydroxyl sites and predicted strong H-bonding between the resulting surface-bound species and neighbouring surface groups. Consistent with these predictions, spectroscopic and thermal analyses together with zeta-potential measurements support a surface-complexation mechanism in which the complexes are stabilized by hydrogen bonds, also involving the ortho-phenol or methoxy group and an adjacent surface hydroxyl group. Ligand adsorption did not significantly affect the magnetic behaviour of either ferrite. Both nanoparticle systems remained chemically stable after the catechol adsorption at pH 10, while barium hexaferrite nanoplatelets were also stable under near-neutral conditions. In contrast, catechol derivatives accelerated the decomposition of barium hexaferrite nanoplatelets at pH 3. Moreover, barium hexaferrite nanoplatelets catalyzed the oxidation of catechols by molecular oxygen in aqueous dispersions. These results link proton transfer and hydrogen-bond-assisted surface complexation with the stability of ferrite nanoparticles and reactivity toward catechol ligands in aqueous environments.

papers.title: Computational Screening of Functional Nanocluster Precursors for Bottle-around-Ship Encapsulation in Metal-Organic Frameworks
papers.abstract: Monodisperse, Atomically Precise Nanoclusters (APNCs) exhibit distinct electronic and sizedependent properties, making them uniquely suited for catalysis, sensing, and drug delivery applications. However, their controlled synthesis remains a challenge since the existing methods struggle to reproducibly achieve atomic-level precision in their composition and geometry. Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOFs), particularly Zeolitic Imidazolate Frameworks (ZIFs) such as ZIF-8, have emerged as powerful templates for directing APNC synthesis via the bottle-around-ship strategy, in which the MOF framework self-assembles around the pre-formed Nanocluster Precursor (NCP). However, despite considerable experimental progress, no predictive framework exists to determine a priori which NCP-MOF combinations will undergo successful encapsulation and therefore yield well-defined monodisperse APNCs. Here, we develop a computational hierarchical screening workflow that systematically examines the chemical and structural factors that govern successful encapsulation of NCPs. The workflow evaluates four parameters: (i) ground-state spin multiplicity of NCPs, (ii) intrinsic structural stability of isolated NCPs, (iii) spatial compatibility of NCPs within the MOF cavity, and (iv) host-guest interaction energies along with the resulting structural responses in NCP@ZIF-8 composite systems. Applying this workflow to a chemically diverse NCP set spanning Chini-type, Pt-browns, and bimetallic Pt(M) carbonyl clusters, we correctly identify successfully encapsulated precursors. Overall, our strategy offers a cheap transferable route for screening existing and new NCP-MOF combinations.

papers.title: Spatially Differentiated Multi-Sectoral Mitigation Strategies Needed to Reduce PM2.5 Exposures in India
papers.abstract: Air pollution in India contributes to approximately 1 million deaths annually due to exposure to ambient fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ). Here, we demonstrate that interventions to achieve the goals of India’s National Clean Air Program require adopting a multi-sector, multi-scale approach to link air pollution sources to human exposure. To support this objective, we developed PAVITRA (Air pollution management and intervention tool for India), a computationally efficient and high-fidelity air quality management tool. The tool integrates the InMAP reduced-complexity air quality model tailored for India, with the SMoG (Speciated Multi-pOllutant Generator)-COALESCE emissions inventory. By deploying over 2,000 simulations, we established how emissions from multiple sectors at different spatial scales contribute to PM2.5 throughout India. We find dissimilar emission drivers of PM 2.5 exposure at regional, state, and city scales, with especially large spatial differences in the relative contributions of domestic, agriculture, and transport sources. We also find that targeted state-level interventions may be nearly as effective as uniform nationwide strategies. These results highlight the limitations of one-size-fits-all policies. Rather, we demonstrate the value of coordinated but differentiated mitigation strategies at regional, state, and city jurisdictional scales for effective air quality management in India. Reduced-complexity modeling tools such as PAVITRA present a way forward to support rapid evaluation of sector and scale-specific mitigation strategies for effective, science-based policy development.

papers.title: Deep Eutectic Solvents as novel food ingredients: biosafety assessment of water-based DESs (aquoDESs) extracts from spent coffee grounds
papers.abstract: The recovery of bioactive compounds, such as caffeine and chlorogenic acids, from spent coffee grounds (SCGs) represents a promising opportunity for developing functional food ingredients. However, the direct incorporation of extracts into food matrices requires rigorous safety validation of both the extraction solvent and the resulting extract. In this study, two food-grade water-based deep eutectic solvents (aquoDESs), trimethylglycine:water (TMG:H2O) and glycerol:water (Glyc:H2O) and their corresponding SCGs extracts at different dilutions (1:1, 1:5, 1:10) were evaluated in terms of chemical, biological and microbial safety. Antibacterial colony-counting assays, cytotoxicity screening on intestinal cell lines (Caco-2, HT-29, HCT116), furanic contaminant quantification, and INFOGEST static in vitro gastrointestinal digestion were investigated. The aquoDESs were designed to function not only as extraction media but also as potential food ingredients, thereby avoiding the need for solvent removal. Antibacterial activity was strongly concentration-dependent, with TMG:H2O-based formulations consistently outperforming Glyc:H2O ones against four foodborne pathogens. Cytotoxicity screening confirmed excellent biocompatibilities for all the samples; notably, TMG:H2O extracts stimulated cell proliferation at 1:5 and 1:10 dilutions. Furanic process contaminants (furfural, 5-methylfurfural, furfuryl alcohol, furfuryl acetate) were quantified: although TMG:H2O extracts contained higher levels than Glyc:H2O-SCGs extracts, all concentrations remained well below toxicological reference values. Finally, in vitro simulated gastrointestinal digestion demonstrated that phenolic compounds are bioaccessible after digestion of the extracts, reaching an intestinal bioaccessibility index of 51.91% (TMG:H2O-SCGs) and 70.19% (Glyc:H2OSCGs). These findings validate the investigated aquoDESs as safe solvents and their corresponding SCGs extracts as bioaccessible, ready-to-use functional food ingredients directly incorporable into food systems without solvent removal.

papers.title: Utilizing Electrosorption for Efficient Removal of Polyethylene Microplastics from Water: Critical Factors and Mechanistic Insights
papers.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) produced by human activities can enter the environment through wastewater systems. A significant quantity of MPs still reaches the environment via wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) effluent because the techniques commonly used in WWTPs are not effective at removing MPs, especially smaller particles. To address this, an electrosorption (ES) method was developed in this study to separate MPs (3–5 µm polyethylene particles) from water using graphite felt electrodes. Electrosorption experiments were conducted using a static water cell and a flow-through cell to examine the influence of hydrodynamic forces. Increasing voltage (up to 12 V) enhanced electrostatic attraction, accelerating removal. Higher flow rates improved MP transport to the electrode, boosting efficiency. The highest removal (96.9%) occurred at 80 mL/min, 12 V, and 20 mM KNO3 after 150 minutes. By analyzing the influence of various parameters on MP removal efficiency and exploring the underlying mechanisms through DLVO theory, this study research establishes a foundation for future advancements in ES for MP removal. Future studies could focus on investigating the removal of MPs using ES in more complex, real-world environments.

papers.title: Solvent-Dependent Self-Association of Chiral 2-Acetoxy-2-Phenylacetic Acid Revealed by Infrared and Vibrational Circular Dichroism Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: The solvent-dependent self-association of chiral 2-acetoxy-2-phenylacetic acid (APA) was investigated in CCl4, CDCl3, and DMSO-d6 solvents, using infrared (IR) and Vibrational Circular Dichroism (VCD) spectroscopy, supported by density functional theory calculations. Concentration-dependent IR measurements revealed progressive formation of self-associated species in CCl4 and CDCl3, whereas no significant concentration dependence was observed in DMSO-d6. Band-fitting analysis and comparison of experimental and calculated IR and VCD spectra indicate that hydrogen-bonded APA dimers with an antiarrangement of the phenyl rings are the dominant self-associated species in CCl4 and CDCl3. In contrast, the high polarity of DMSO-d6 suppresses self-association and favors a doubly hydrogen-bonded 1:1 APA–DMSO-d6 complex involving O-H…O and C-H…O interactions. The results demonstrate that solvent polarity strongly controls the balance between solutesolute and solute-solvent hydrogen bonding and highlight the sensitivity of VCD spectroscopy to molecular association and intermolecular interactions in solution.

papers.title: In situ light-coupled TEM separates photochemical and radiolytic degradation in halide perovskites
papers.abstract: Metal halide perovskites degrade under the same illumination that powers them, yet nanoscale observation of this photochemistry is confounded by electron-beam damage in transmission electron microscopy (TEM). We introduce an optical-fiber-coupled closed-cell TEM platform with independent control over electron dose rate, illumination wavelength and power density, and gas environment, and use it to decouple photochemical from radiolytic degradation in CsPbBr3 in real time. After establishing beam-safe imaging conditions, we find that above-bandgap illumination induces preferential emergence of PbBr2 domains, the dominant detectable crystalline product, primarily at grain boundaries. In contrast, the electron beam alone reduces Pb2+ to metallic Pb0, a chemically and spatially distinct pathway. Sub-bandgap illumination produces no detectable spectroscopic change, supporting photocarrier generation rather than optical power deposition as a dominant driver. Decoupling light from the electron beam is a prerequisite for real-time imaging photochemistry in beam-sensitive materials.

papers.title: Site-Specific Speciation of Vanadium Sites on γ-Al2O3 Facets and Edges from 51V SSNMR Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: γ-alumina (γ-Al2O3) supported vanadium oxide represent a notable class of heterogenous catalysts used for the direct oxidative propane dehydrogenation (ODH) reaction. However, while the presence of highly dispersed VOx (V5+) species has been established, understanding the exact structure of surface sites and the role of supports remains a pivotal objective for establishing structure-property relationships. Considering the structural complexity of γ-Al2O3 surfaces, where distinct surface sites emerge as a function of specific facets and edges, clarifying how the support dictates vanadium speciation remains a key objective. In this work, we employ Surface Organometallic Chemistry (SOMC) approach to evaluate the impact of the γ-Al2O3 nanocrystals morphology on the nature and structure of surface vanadium sites. Specifically, we grafted vanadyl isopropoxide (VO(OiPr)3) on tailored γ-Al2O3 nanocrystals, namely Rhomboids, Laths and Needles, exposing varying distributions of (110), (100) and (111) facets along with characteristic edges sites. Subsequent calcination yields supported, organic-ligand-free, monomeric vanadia sites. Advanced 51V solid-state NMR spectroscopy combined with DFT calculations reveals that grafting on γ-Al2O3 partially dehydroxylated at 500 °C directly generate bipodal VO(OiPr) species, whose structures depend on the underlying surface facets and edge sites. Furthermore, the supported vanadia sites formed upon calcination are also characterized by distinct V-O coordination numbers and hydroxylation states, which are quantitatively resolved across γ-Al2O3 morphologies. This work not only elucidates the complex speciation of V supported on γ-Al2O3 support, but also offers fundamental insights into the reactive surface sites on γ-Al2O3 that stabilize isolated metal species.

papers.title: ELECTROSTATIC MODEL OF COVALENT BONDING. A PARTICULAR SOLUTION OF THE HELLMANN – FEYNMAN ELECTROSTATIC THEOREM
papers.abstract: The purpose of this work was to create a model of a covalent bond based on quasi-classical electrostatic concepts. A three-center electrostatic model of a covalent bond has been proposed, which takes into account only the forces that occur along the axis connecting the nuclei of the bonded atoms. These electrostatic forces are represented as gradients of the potential energy of the atoms from their isolated state to their bonded state. According to the model concept, in the equilibrium state of a molecular system, the charges of the nucleus and the electron density, which is reduced to a point along the axis connecting the nuclei of the bonded atoms, are aligned in each of these atoms. In diatomic molecules, the force equilibrium between the bonded atoms is achieved by the equality of forces (and electrostatic potentials) between the nuclei of the bonded atoms and the electrostatic tension forces on the reverse side of the nuclei, ensuring zero ponderomotive forces on the nuclei. In polyatomic molecules, the electrostatic tension forces maintain equilibrium only for the nuclei of the terminal atoms. In polyvalent atoms, depending on the valence angles (α), these forces may be absent (α=180o) or partially realized (180o>α>90o). The revealed simple functional dependence of the electrostatic potentials of the bond atoms allows us to calculate the energy or length of a chemical bond for a known (or specified) value of the interatomic distance or bond energy, respectively, with an accuracy not lower than the error of their experimental determination. The results obtained indicate the promising nature of the study of molecular systems based on electrostatics, and may be useful in quantum chemistry to identify the difference in the topography of the electron density in chemically bonded and isolated atoms.

papers.title: Bioadhesive Linear-Dendritic Block Copolymer Hydrogels for Wound Closure and Localized Antibiotic Delivery
papers.abstract: Surgical adhesives have emerged as a less invasive alternative than classical sutures, yet many suffer from poor adhesion, poor compatibility with skin, and lack of antibacterial properties. To address these limitations, we developed a new class of dual-functional hydrogels combining strong tissue adhesion with localized antimicrobial activity. These hydrogels were formulated by blending catechol-functionalized linear-dendritic block copolymers (LDBC(cat)8) with UV-crosslinkable acrylate-terminated analogues (LDBC(acr)4), resulting in soft and interpenetrated hybrid network that combines hydrophilic/hydrophobic interactions with covalent crosslinking. Among the various hydrogel formulations tested, the one containing 15% of LDBC(acr)4 and 85 % of LDBC(cat)4 exhibited optimal mechanical performance and superior adhesion to porcine skin while biocompatibility assessments and swelling assays confirmed its suitability for biomedical use. Furthermore, the incorporation of water-soluble antibiotics, i.e. amoxicillin and moxifloxacin, enabled the hydrogel to act as a localized delivery system, with the antibiotic-loaded variant demonstrating potent antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. In vivo assays confirmed that these hydrogels could effectively close open wounds and that the presence of antibiotics did not alter such capability, positioning these biomimetic hydrogel platforms as promising candidates for next-generation surgical glues that not only seal tissue effectively but also combat infection.

papers.title: Energy Transfer (EnT) Catalysed [4+2] Cycloaddition of Non-Symmetrical Dienes: From Mechanistic Anomaly to Fully Functional Reaction Pathway
papers.abstract: Harnessing the reactivity of triplet biradicals to selectively access unconventional cycloaddition pathways remains a fundamental challenge in energy transfer (EnT) catalysis. Herein, we demonstrate that systematic variation of diene substitution can redirect the intrinsic [2+2] reactivity of non-symmetrical dienes towards highly selective [4+2] cycloaddition. Notably, incorporation of a traceless vicinal BPin group invokes a non-conventional [4+2] pathway providing polysubstituted cyclohexenes with excellent regio- and diastereoselectivity. Mechanistic and computational investigations reveal that A-1,3-strain and geometric isomerisation shape the conformational landscape of the triplet biradical, accounting for the observed divergent reactivity. These findings establish substitution-controlled excited-state conformational dynamics as a key parameter for directing EnT-mediated cycloadditions beyond conventional [2+2] reactivity.

papers.title: Antimicrobial and cytotoxic activity of 2-amino-4H-chromenes
papers.abstract: Although some 2-amino-4H-chromenes displayed moderate activity against S. mitis (1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, and 10), S. salivarius (3 and 9), and L. paracasei (1 and 6), most of the compounds displayed weak activity against most of the bacteria involved in dental caries and were inactive against C. albicans and C. krusei. On the other hand, compounds 4 (IC50 < 2.47 µM, SI > 2564) and 8 (IC50 = 37.74 µM, SI > 154.80) displayed the highest anticancer activity against the MCF-7 and HeLa cell lines. Although compounds 4 and 5 displayed only moderate activity against U-251MG cells, their high SI values (>82.78 and >81.60, respectively) make them promising candidates for further investigation as antiproliferative agents. Molecular docking simulations help us to rationalize potential molecular targets for compounds 1-10 reported herein. All molecules were docked into four receptors/enzymes (β-tubulin, CDK4/6, ERα, and EGFR), and in two of them (EGFR and CDK4/6), compounds 8R and 5R ranked favorably within their respective docking protocols and displayed relevant interactions with N842 and L83 residues in their respective active sites. These findings are consistent with in vitro cytotoxic assays and highlight the potential of compounds 1-10 to guide the design of more potent and selective anticancer candidates.

papers.title: Deep drug design for molecular scaffold hopping
papers.abstract: Structure-based virtual screening serves as a primary approach for ligand prioritization from large molecular libraries, but accurately predicting the activity of chemical entities on novel drug targets remains a formidable challenge. Here, we present an interactome-based graph transformer network for rapid bioactivity prediction and de novo ligand design. Integrating three-dimensional pocket geometry with two-dimensional ligand graphs yields a joint representation for direct affinity prediction, which generalizes well across sparse datasets. To validate practical utility, we performed a zero-shot generative ligand design to identify scaffold hops from the complex natural product ibogaine, a noncompetitive inhibitor of the serotonin transporter. The top-ranked design and its rational analogs were synthesized and exhibited equipotent isofunctional in vitro activity alongside favorable pharmacokinetic properties directly upon initial generation. This workflow establishes a blueprint for molecular engineering that seamlessly bridges the automated design of lead-like, synthetically accessible small molecules with efficient bioactivity prediction.

papers.title: Photochemical Carbamate Scission Redefines Metal-Based PhotoCORMs through Multi-Output Activation
papers.abstract: Metal-based photoCORMs (Photoactivatable carbon monoxide-releasing molecules) have traditionally relied on photolabile M–CO bonds, constraining modular design and limiting opportunities for integrating additional functions. Here we report a modular metalbased platform in which CO generation is encoded within a photolabile carbamate rather than a M–CO bond, enabling visible-light-controlled, spatiotemporal CO release while preserving the synthetic flexibility to integrate multimodal functions within a single molecular architecture. As a proof of concept, we constructed a fluorogenic, CA-IX-targeted Pt(IV) complex in which a naphthalimide chromophore is coupled to the metal centre through a carbamate CO-releasing module. Photoexcitation of the chromophore initiates a programmed cascade comprising carbamate scission for CO release along with fluorogenic activation of the CA-IX-inhibiting dye, and reduction of Pt(IV) to cytotoxic Pt(II), validating the modular design. More broadly, this work demonstrates that carbamate photolysis provides a broadly applicable route to programmable, stimuli-controlled CO release, independent of metal–carbonyl chemistry, integrated with modular multifunctional therapeutic architectures.

papers.title: Dynamic Evolution and Stability of Ketenes in MAPO-18 (M = Si or Mg): Molecular Insights into the Reaction Mechanism for CO2-to-Hydrocarbons
papers.abstract: AEI topology molecular sieves (MAPO-18) have shown promising properties as components of OX-ZEO type tandem catalysts, where the Brønsted acid sites (BAS) introduced by different framework substitutions lead to distinct catalytic mechanisms on the CO2-to-hydrocarbons conversion. Ketenes are key intermediates in the conversion of methanol to hydrocarbons. This study provides molecular-level insights into the reactions of three ketenes (ketene, methyl ketene, and dimethyl ketene) with the BAS in MAPO-18 (M = Si, Mg) molecular sieves at operando conditions through first-principles molecular dynamics (FPMD) simulations combined with enhanced sampling techniques. Free energy surfaces constructed from FPMD simulations revealed distinct kinetic and thermodynamic preferences, linking them to different reaction routes for the production of olefins. Prior studies suggested that ketenes and their protonated analogues are key intermediates in two different pathways to olefins formation, and the three ketenes exhibited higher kinetic stability than their protonated forms in H-SAPO-18 compared to H-MgAPO-18, suggesting a high tendency for olefin production via the (cyclo)addition-decarboxylation route in H-SAPO-18. In contrast, the increased stability of the cationic intermediates and low protonation barrier for methyl and dimethyl ketenes in MgAPO-18 favor their direct decarbonylation to olefins. Surface-bound species displayed decreasing stability from surface acetate to surface propionate to surface isobutyrate , aligning with established trends for surface alkoxides. Moreover, a comparison with static calculations demonstrates their limited ability to capture the entropic contributions and dynamic effects that dominate the behavior of active intermediates under realistic reaction conditions, highlighting the necessity of molecular dynamics (MD) approaches for accurate mechanistic modeling of catalytic reactions. Benchmarking against high-level random phase approximation (RPA) calculations further revealed that the density functional theory (DFT) method in combination with the revPBE-D3 functional used in the FPMD simulations may overestimate the stability of cationic intermediates and underestimate the protonation barriers of ketene. Together, these findings underscore the importance of combining dynamic simulations with accurate potential energy descriptions to reliably model active intermediates in confined microporous environments. Overall, this study provides key steps of ketene reactivity in zeolite frameworks, bridging computational and experimental insights into CO2-to-hydrocarbon conversion pathways. These results emphasize how subtle variations in the framework composition and substituents dictate the reaction mechanisms, offering guidance for the rational design of molecular sieves tailored for selective catalytic transformations.

papers.title: LCMD[db]: The Unified Chemical Data Hosting and Analysis Platform
papers.abstract: Chemical datasets used in computational chemistry are often distributed across separate repositories, stored in dataset-specific formats, and accompanied by heterogeneous metadata, property definitions, and structure representations. This fragmentation increases the manual preprocessing required to reuse datasets for molecular property prediction, reaction modeling, benchmarking, and machine-learning workflows. Here, we present LCMD-db, a chemical data hosting and analysis platform for organizing molecular, fragment, and reaction datasets within a common framework. LCMD-db represents data as datasets and self-consistent subsets, with explicit metadata, property definitions, structure mappings, and standardized ingestion pipelines. The platform supports molecular structures, fragments, equilibrium geometries, transition states, reaction participants, and computed properties linked to SMILES strings, molecular graphs, and three-dimensional structure files. For reaction datasets, LCMD-db stores molecular participants together with their chemical roles and reaction-coordinate relationships, allowing intermediates, transition states, reactants, products, catalysts, and other species to be treated as connected chemical entities rather than isolated files. The platform provides interactive visualization, property inspection, filtering, export of selected entries, and Python-native access to structured molecular and reaction objects. We demonstrate LCMD-db using in-house and external datasets spanning small organic molecules, transition-metal complexes, molecular fragments, and reaction datasets with thermodynamic or kinetic annotations. LCMD-db connects data hosting with analysis and modeling workflows by providing structured, searchable, and directly loadable chemical datasets.

papers.title: Product-Specific Isotope Effects as Constraints on Branched Catalytic Reaction Networks
papers.abstract: Rates and selectivities alone often cannot distinguish between competing mechanisms in branched catalytic reactions. Here, we use GC–IRMS at natural carbon-isotope abundance to measure the isotope compositions of both CO and CH4 formed during CO2 hydrogenation over SiO2-supported Ni and Co nanoparticles. Comparing the isotope effects of both products, rather than considering either product alone, allows us to test whether their pathways share intermediates and where the isotope-sensitive steps occur. An isotope-resolved carbon balance accounts for finite conversion, and a simple branching model separates isotope effects arising before and after the product pathways split. Across changes in selectivity, catalyst identity, and Ni particle size, the isotope effects of CO and CH4 change together and remain separated by an approximately constant difference. This behavior is inconsistent with fully independent pathways. Instead, it supports a dominant shared intermediate pool that is most plausibly derived from CO. Methane formation shows an additional normal isotope effect relative to CO formation, indicating that the stronger isotope-sensitive chemistry occurs during the C–O activation and hydrogenation steps after the pathways split. The isotope pattern remains similar across the Ni particle sizes, while Co shows a somewhat larger methane-side contribution. Paired product isotope measurements therefore provide an independent test of catalytic reaction networks that complements kinetics, spectroscopy, transient experiments, and theory.

papers.title: Same Substitutions, Opposite Residence Times: Target-Dependent Kinetic Inversion of Diazabicyclooctane 𝛽-Lactamase Inhibitors
papers.abstract: Reversible covalent inhibitors are governed by both formation and breakdown of the covalent complex, yet matched medicinal-chemistry modifications are often interpreted through affinity or potency alone. We performed an original quantitative reanalysis of published experimental kinetics and corresponding covalent crystal structures for four diazabicyclooctane (DBO) inhibitors—avibactam, FPI-1465, FPI-1523, and FPI-1602—against CTX-M-15 and OXA-48. Relative to avibactam, all three C2-modified analogues showed lower 𝑘2/𝐾𝑖 in both enzymes, but their effects on dissociation reversed sign between targets. FPI-1465, FPI-1523, and FPI-1602 dissociated 3.86-, 3.38-, and 4.91-fold more slowly from CTX-M-15, whereas they dissociated 68.8-, 3.12-, and 2.73-fold more rapidly from OXA-48. The corresponding cross-target interactions were 265.5-, 10.5-, and 13.4-fold. Eyring transformation mapped these effects to shifts in the reverse activation barrier of +0.72 to +0.94 kcal mol−1 in CTX-M-15 versus −0.59 to −2.51 kcal mol−1 in OXA-48. Static oxyanion-hole geometry did not encode the OXA-48 ranking: mean donor–carbonyl-oxygen distances changed by only 0.002–0.065 Å relative to avibactam despite 2.7–68.8-fold changes in 𝑘off. These findings identify a replicated target-dependent residence-time inversion and demonstrate that forward and reverse structure–kinetic relationships can diverge within a matched reversible-covalent series. Conformational ensembles and distributed electrostatics emerge as specific prospective mechanisms, but are not inferred as causal from the present static-structure analysis.

papers.title: The Mechanochemical Reset for Coordination Self-Assembly.
papers.abstract: Self-assembly is a canonical process for generating ordered, functional architectures, with the structural 'blueprint' encoded in the component design and interaction thermodynamics. While external stimuli such as concentration and chemical guests might shift the equilibrium between predefined ordered states, the structural memory remains embedded in the assembly (thermodynamic control). In this work, we employ mechanical force as a unique stimulus to dismantle thermodynamic order, accessing a structural “erasing” state and resetting the assembly landscape. Specifically, ball-milling of a thermodynamically-preferred Pd6L14 coordination cage (c-Pd6L14) drives it to a disordered, ligand-exchanged state (PdxL1y), which upon dissolution undergoes a conversion to a transient and metastable tubular Pd6L14 isomer (t-Pd6L14), thermodynamically inaccessible from conventional pathways from c-Pd6L14.We generalize such “mechanochemical reset” by transforming a complex double-walled Pd12L28 knot-like cage into a triply interlocked [Pd3L22]2 complex via a similar force-generated disordered PdxL2y state. To highlight the uniqueness of the reset process, this strategy was further employed in two confinement catalytic settings: 1) thermal; and 2) photochemical C-H oxidation reactions, where the analogous reactions suffer from product inhibition in conventional conditions. This work establishes mechanochemistry as not merely a green synthetic tool, but a powerful strategy for escaping deep thermodynamic minima and navigating the self-assembly energy landscape toward non-thermodynamic, otherwise-inaccessible states.

papers.title: First-principles Investigation of Reconstructions for the Polar CoO (111) Surface and the Impact on Nanoparticle Morphology
papers.abstract: Reconstructions of the polar CoO (111) surface defines critical properties that impacts application in catalysis, energy storage and electrochemistry. However, these surface reconstructions are relatively unexplored, compared to its isomorphic analogues, and greater understanding of CoO surfaces is needed to enable rational control of surface stability and reactivity. We investigate the surface reconstructions of the polar (111) facet of rocksalt CoO in equilibrium with an oxygen environment using first principles calculations in conjunction with surface thermodynamics. Surface reconstruction, which can expose high-index facets has received limited attention despite experimental evidence. Therefore, we have additionally considered high-index facets in our calculations to obtain a comprehensive understanding of CoO surfaces. Our results demonstrate that high-index facets, such as (331) and (311), are more stable than the oxygen terminated (111) surface and low-index (100) and (110) surfaces across a range of meaningful oxygen chemical potentials. The stability of the highindex surfaces is identified to be due to the crystal structure and strong interaction between the oxygen and cobalt atoms of the open high-index surfaces. Our results on stability of high-index facets shows that surface roughening could offer a mechanism to compensate the polarity of (111) surface. Polarity compensation mechanisms allow the occurrence of polar surfaces in experiments. Our work offers new insights into the stability of polar rocksalt CoO surfaces and provides a foundation for understanding and tuning the properties that govern its performance in catalysis, energy storage, and electrochemical applications.

papers.title: A dynamic active-site water molecule drives the photocatalysis in fatty acid photodecarboxylase
papers.abstract: Fatty acid photodecarboxylase (FAP) is a flavin-based photoenzyme that uses blue light to convert fatty acids into hydrocarbons, an attractive platform for sustainable fuel production. Its efficiency is set by a competition between photoinduced electron transfer, productive decarboxylation and unproductive back electron transfer, yet how the protein controls this competition at the atomistic level remains unresolved. Here, by following the coupled evolution of electrons and nuclei in real time with excited-state nonadiabatic dynamics simulations of wild-type FAP and an engineered variant, we show that a single water molecule in the active site acts as a dynamic switch rather than a static element of the hydrogen-bonding network. Rearrangement of its hydrogen bonding from the protein toward the flavin cofactor opens a predominantly adiabatic pathway for electron transfer. The resulting charge-transfer state is stabilized by a coupled protein–solvent response before decaying through competing back electron transfer and decarboxylation. Because electron transfer goes through a specific structural rearrangement, this mechanism cannot be fully captured by standard semiclassical Marcus theory. Our results show that the active-site hydrogenbonding network directly controls photochemical reactivity and indicate that photoenzyme engineering should target dynamic solvent interactions alongside amino acid residues.

papers.title: 4D-STEM Strain Mapping of Polycrystalline Core-shell Nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Metal nanoparticles play a key role in sustainable chemical conversions, energy storage and electronics. Lattice strain strongly influences the functional properties of these nanoparticles and enables precise tuning of their properties. Strain can vary substantially within single nanoparticles that exhibit defect sites and grain boundaries. However, experimentally evaluating local strain distributions within such polycrystalline nanoparticles is challenging and requires the development of new characterization methods. In this work, we successfully assess strain in complex polycrystalline nanoparticles with sub-nanometer spatial resolution by developing a novel 4D-STEM analysis method. For a strain-engineered trimetallic Pt-shell AuCu-core nanoparticles system, we show that most core-shell nanoparticles have homogeneous strain distributions, with slight strain relaxation in the shell regions. At defect sites and near grain boundaries, the local variations in strain become larger and the strain distribution significantly broadens compared to defect free crystal domains. We demonstrate that our method can be routinely applied to large numbers of polycrystalline nanoparticles and expect that our analysis method is applicable to a wide range of nanostructured materials, enabling detailed strain-functionality correlations in functional nanomaterials.

papers.title: Ancillary Ligand Engineering Controls Supramolecular Host Architecture
papers.abstract: Ancillary ligands (ALs) in coordination cages are commonly regarded as passive protecting groups whose primary role is to stabilize discrete cages and prevent formation of extended coordination networks. Here, we introduce ancillary ligand engineering (ALE) as a strategy for controlling the topology and dynamics of palladium-based coordination cages without modifying the metal or triimidazoylbenzene panel ligand. Systematic variation of substituents at the AL nitrogen atoms tunes both the rotational freedom of Pd-bound imidazole (Im) groups and the N–Pd–N coordination angle, thereby shifting the equilibrium between constitutional isomers with distinct tube- and capsule-shaped topologies. NMR spectroscopy reveals a gradual progression from a capsule-rich equilibrium with the smallest AL, ethylenediamine, to a strongly tube-biased equilibrium with the bulkiest tetraethylethylenediamine. Kinetic measurements further show that increasing AL bulk alters both intercage isomerization rates and the nature of the isomerization pathway. The capsule–tube equilibrium can be further shifted by guest encapsulation, with planar and tetrahedral guests favoring the tube and capsule hosts, respectively, thereby providing an orthogonal means to control cage architecture. ALE thus provides a simple and generalizable strategy for programming the topology and kinetic stability of coordination cages while leaving the primary cage-building components unchanged.

papers.title: Novel ebselen-based building block for the solid phase synthesis of selenopeptides
papers.abstract: Although some organic selenocompounds exhibit significant therapeutic potential, synthetic access to selenopeptides remains severely limited due to complex postassembly functionalizations strategies. To overcome these limitations, we developed a stable, ebselen-derived lysine compatible with standard Fmoc/tBu solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS). We synthesized the Fmoc-Lys(Ebs)-OH building block in five steps, characterizing it by HRMS and NMR spectroscopy. We then evaluated its chemical stability in standard SPPS conditions by assembling a test tripeptide and a diverse tetrapeptide library containing a variety of aminoacids. The novel Fmoc-Lys(Ebs)-OH demonstrated excellent coupling efficiency and high stability, tolerating repeated basic deprotections, couplings and strong acid cleavage to yield selenopeptides without degradation or byproducts. This novel building block enables the direct, site-specific incorporation of ebselen during SPPS, avoiding labor-intensive post-synthetic modifications to access to complex organoselenium peptides for biological and structure-activity relationship studies.

papers.title: Electroanalytical approaches for understanding the influence of applied potential on sensor biofouling
papers.abstract: Biofouling is a complex and dynamic process that remains a major limitation to continuous and longterm sensing in biological environments. Unlike passive biomaterials, electrochemical sensors operate under electrical control, yet the influence of applied potential on protein adsorption and the resulting electroanalytical response is insufficiently understood. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) with redox probes of different interfacial sensitivities was used to assess the influence of positive, open-circuit, and negative polarization during bovine serum albumin (BSA) incubation on the electrochemical behavior of gold and graphitic carbon electrodes. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) provided insights into interfacial blocking and charge transfer. Finally, electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation monitoring (EQCM-D) was used to directly investigate protein adsorption under polarized conditions. In general, suppression of redox responses, increased charge-transfer resistance, and larger changes in estimated adsorbed mass were observed at positive incubation potentials, indicating the formation of more electrochemically blocking protein layers. On the contrary, negative incubation potentials produced smaller changes in electrochemical activity and lower charge-transfer resistance, consistent with more open and accessible interfaces. These findings support a proposed model where applied potential, together with additional protein-surface interactions, affects not only the amount of protein adsorbed but also the organization and electrochemical accessibility of the resulting interfacial layer. Complementary electroanalytical techniques provide a practical framework for assessing sensor biofouling under operational conditions.

papers.title: Operating conditions redefine the governing principles of catalyst-layer fabrication
papers.abstract: Optimal catalyst-layer fabrication strategies for proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFC) are often developed under a single set of operating conditions, making it unclear whether the resulting design rules remain valid across different operating environments. Here, we show that operating conditions not only shift catalyst-layer optima but re-order the fabrication parameters governing performance. By combining application-relevant gas diffusion electrode (GDE) measurements with machine-learning analysis, we map the multidimensional fabrication–performance space of Pt/C oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) catalyst layers across humid low-temperature (30 °C, relative humidity (RH) > 80%) and dry high-temperature (120 °C, RH < 10%) regimes. The optimal catalyst-layer fabrication parameters change significantly between conditions, and their relative importance re-orders. While ionomer- and Pt-concentration-related parameters dominate performance under humid low temperature conditions, process- and deposition-related parameters become governing factors under dry high-temperature operation. These results demonstrate that catalyst-layer optimization is inherently condition-dependent and challenge the notion of universal fabrication rules. More broadly, this work establishes operating-condition-dependent design spaces as a fundamental principle of catalyst-layer engineering, providing a framework for developing electrodes optimized for the specific operating conditions of next-generation PEMFCs.

papers.title: Identifiability Boundaries in Dynamic GPCR Pharmacology: When Desensitization, Internalization and Persistent Signaling Become Mechanistically Indistinguishable
papers.abstract: Dynamic GPCR pharmacology increasingly relies on time-resolved signaling to infer receptor regulation, trafficking, and ligand residence, yet a kinetic response need not uniquely identify the mechanism that produced it. We developed minimal quantitative receptor-pharmacology models to determine when desensitization, internalization, persistent intracellular signaling, and slow receptor occupancy are distinguishable from a common downstream signal. We first derived exact input–output equivalences. Silent internalization is mathematically identical to desensitization for arbitrary time-varying receptor drive, whereas internalization with persistent signaling is exactly equivalent to a desensitization model under any single constant drive after an explicit parameter transformation. Across a 1,000system parameter ensemble, pulse–wash protocols broke the constant-drive equivalence but remained practically ambiguous after adversarial refitting: in 500 held-out systems, the wrong desensitization model had a median normalized error of 1.26% when downstream signal decay (kD) was unconstrained. Independent calibration of kD increased this to 11.90% and increased the fraction exceeding a 5% discrepancy from 11.4% to 80.0%. At 5% Gaussian observation noise, correct-model selection by BIC increased from 48.8% to 95.8%. An analytical kinetic blind manifold, kD = kr + qki, predicted where downstream-only discrimination failed. A single surface-receptor observation supplied substantially greater mechanism-specific information, with 95.5% of systems showing >20% surface loss after 5 min. Slow receptor occupancy also mimicked persistent intracellular signaling, but false trafficking fits made strongly divergent surface-state predictions. Published β2-adrenoceptor, AM2 receptor, and VIPR1 experiments provide independent pharmacological examples of the predicted information constraints and discriminating measurements. The resulting quantitative framework shows that mechanistic discrimination may depend more on independently constraining a downstream nuisance process or hidden receptor state than on collecting additional samples of the same downstream response.

papers.title: Oxygen-Necessitated Dissociation of Photoinduced Ground-State Charge-Transfer Complexes for Open-Air Synthesis of Block and Graft Copolymers
papers.abstract: Molecular oxygen is universally regarded as an inhibitor of radical photopolymerization, necessitating rigorous deoxygenation and introducing obligatory induction periods. Here we report that a persistent photoinduced ground-state charge-transfer complex (PCTC), formed between a naphthalimide acceptor and a tertiary-amine donor, undergoes selective dissociation upon exposure to molecular oxygen. This oxygen-triggered activation releases a donor-derived radical cation while regenerating the acceptor, converting ambient O2 from an inhibitory species into a functional trigger for radical generation. The resulting photopolymerization proceeds without metal catalysts, or external initiators under open-air conditions. Because the tertiary-amine functionality is preserved at the polymer chain end, the system supports sequential photocontrolled chain extension, enabling the synthesis of block and graft copolymers. Extension to α-methylene amine-functionalized polymer backbones affords brush architectures that function as high-performance photocurable adhesives (lap-shear strength up to 20.38 MPa), exhibit robust electrical insulation, and permit rapid photo-patterning with micron resolution in open air. These findings establish an open-air photocuring platform that overturns the long-standing requirement for deoxygenation in industrial radical processing, offering a scalable, metal-free route to advanced polymer materials in ambient manufacturing environments.

papers.title: Rational Design of a Red-Light Absorbing dinuclear Ruthenium (II) Complex with Photodynamic potential
papers.abstract: Conventional chemotherapeutic agents often suffer from systemic toxicity, poor selectivity, and the emergence of drug resistance, highlighting the urgent need for alternative anticancer strategies. In this context, light-activated therapies have emerged as promising minimally invasive approaches for controlled cancer treatment. However, the development of single molecular systems capable of integrating multiple photoinduced therapeutic mechanisms remains challenging. Herein, we report the rational design, synthesis, and comprehensive characterization of novel multifunctional bimetallic ruthenium complexes incorporating three photoactive units within a single molecular scaffold. The complexes exhibited favorable photophysical properties, efficient light absorption, and enhanced reactive oxygen species generation upon 690 nm LED irradiation. Computational investigations provided insight into the electronic structure and excited-state behavior, revealing potential photoinduced pathways associated with the multinuclear architecture. In addition, combined electrochemical analyses revealed the formation of Ru-DPP-Ru-DNA supramolecular assemblies, providing evidence of DNA binding while maintaining the electrochemical activity of the Ru(II) centers. ROS generation studies demonstrated a predominant Type II pathway involving singlet oxygen production, together with a minor contribution from Type I ROS. In vitro biological studies demonstrated neglible dark toxicity alongside moderate photocytotoxic activity under red light irradiation. This work presents the first example of DPP ligands scaffolds incorporated in a metal coordination sphere, a promising strategy for the development of next-generation bimetallic complexes as potential multimodal photoresponsive therapeutics for cancer treatment.

papers.title: Open Sesame! Simulation of the Adsorption Induced Phase Transformation Mechanism of MOF Nanocrystallites
papers.abstract: One of the most compelling features of certain MOFs is their ability to undergo stimuli-induced phase transformations with large changes in the accessible pore volume, leading to phenomena like “gate opening”. Theoretical simulations are an indispensable tool in order to understand such processes on a molecular level. However, adsorption phenomena are usually investigated within the approximation of periodic boundary conditions (PBC) and using Grand Canonical methods. This ignores the interface to the gas reservoir and any transport effects, which prevents the investigation of transformation kinetics. Previously, we developed methods to simulate explicit MOF nanocrystallites beyond PBC with the aim to understand size effects. In this work, the results of the natural next step, namely an in silico adsorption experiment for DUT-8 (Cu) nanocrystallites (about 10 nm edge length) in a reservoir of carbon dioxide are presented: Unbiased molecular dynamics simulations reveal a surprisingly rapid gate opening within a few nanoseconds. The first-order phase transition is initiated by a characteristic pore opening at an edge of the crystallite. The anisotropy of the pillared-layer MOF, with its channels along the crystallographic c-axis, leads to a rapid transport along these channels when the pore opening of the MOF proceeds. The simulations allow for an unprecedented view on the molecular mechanism, including the structural transformation of the MOF and the connected transport of the guest molecules into the MOF pores. Already this first attempt of a realistic adsorption simulation beyond PBC revealed the widening of a single channel at the obtuse angle edge of the NC as the secret “Open Sesame!” to open the gate. This confirms that for an in–depth view into the kinetics of adsorption induced phase transformations, an explicit interface between MOF and gas reservoir is pivotal and serves as a basis for further investigations with even larger systems and more realistic surface terminations to be performed in the future.

papers.title: Temperature-and potential-induced exfoliation of electrochemically produced solid carbon from CO2 on a Ce:GaInSn electrode
papers.abstract: Resource-efficient carbon dioxide removal from the atmosphere will require the development of new materials for processes beyond carbon capture and utilisation. One high-potential pathway for such negative emission technologies is the electrochemical reduction of CO 2 to storable products such as graphitic carbon. Although this can be achieved by employing an electrode made of cerium particles in a liquid gallium-indium-tin matrix, this electrocatalytic pathway currently suffers from comparatively low faradaic efficiencies (FE). In this work, we investigate the temperature dependence of electrochemical CO 2 -reduction to solid carbon on this liquid-metal. An increase in temperature of up to 50 ◦ C leads to significantly higher FEs. A variation of applied potentials leads to a temperature-dependent exfoliation of the product. Moreover, a change in the morphology of the solid carbon product species, from carbon black-like particles, over graphitic flakes to fibers can be induced by varying the operating conditions. From a practical standpoint, the temperature range, we find for optimum FE, lies in the range that can be achieved through thermal coupling with photovoltaic solar cells, suggesting co-benefits of photovoltaics-driven, electrochemical carbon dioxide removal.

papers.title: Engineering transparent-electrode surface chemistry for robust molecular interfaces in perovskite photovoltaics
papers.abstract: The chemical state of transparent oxide electrodes critically determines the formation and durability of selfassembled monolayer (SAM) contacts in perovskite photovoltaics. Although standard cleaning 1 (SC1) and ultraviolet–ozone (UVO) treatments are individually established approaches for oxide-surface modification, their complementary functions in regulating molecular interfaces remain poorly understood. Here, we show that sequential SC1 reconstruction and UVO activation create a distinct interfacial chemical environment: SC1 removes persistent surface contaminants and reorganizes the oxide coordination environment, whereas subsequent UVO activation eliminates treatment-derived residues and generates the highest hydroxyl-related surface fraction with enhanced thermal persistence. The resulting hydroxyl-rich oxide surface promotes SAM adsorption and strengthens oxide–SAM interactions, establishing a more homogeneous buried molecular contact. This reconstructed interface improves the crystallographic and compositional uniformity of the overlying perovskite absorber, reduces energetic disorder and non-radiative recombination, and suppresses opencircuit-voltage losses. Devices incorporating the reconstructed contact exhibit accelerated carrier extraction, prolonged carrier survival, reduced trap-assisted recombination, and enhanced photovoltaic performance and stability. The strategy further translates across flexible wide-bandgap devices, tin-based perovskite solar cells, and four-terminal perovskite/silicon tandems. These results establish the complementary coupling of SC1 reconstruction and UVO activation as a general strategy for engineering robust hydroxyl-mediated molecular contacts on commercial transparent oxide electrodes.

papers.title: Breakdown and Classification of Adiabatic-Connection Convexity in Coulomb Systems
papers.abstract: Convexity of the density-fixed adiabatic-connection integrand is widely observed but is not fixed by the variational structure of density-functional theory. We show that it is not universal for ordinary three-dimensional electrons with the bare Coulomb interaction. Equal-step third differences of the Levy functional give a derivative-free classification into convex, affine, concave, and mixed classes, while an exact response identity determines the local sign at regular fixed-density points. Opposite exactly solvable seeds—a closed-shell Hubbard ring and two-electron spherium—are transferred to smooth confining potentials in ordinary space. The resulting full-interval positive, negative, and mixed densities have N = 2, 6, and 8, respectively. For two distinct densities with the same particle number N = 6, one fixed four-point certificate is obtained with either sign. These deliberately engineered existence constructions do not imply that violations are common in molecular densities. Thus convexity is a property of density-preserving many-body response, not a universal exact condition.

papers.title: Atmospheric CO2 splitting using a visible light-driven Z-scheme photocatalyst in a gas-phase flow reactor
papers.abstract: Direct air capture (DAC) coupled to photocatalytic CO 2 splitting offers a route to simultaneously mitigate atmospheric CO 2 accumulation and produce sustainable fuels. However, integrations of DAC with photocatalytic CO 2 conversion have thus far relied on ultraviolet-light-absorbing TiO 2 and organic substrate oxidation, limiting solar energy utilisation and precluding a truly artificial photosynthetic reaction. Here, we introduce an integrated direct air carbon capture and utilisation (DACCU) system that couples under continuous flow nighttime atmospheric CO 2 capture with daytime gas-phase photocatalytic CO 2 splitting to CO and O 2 using a solid silica−amine adsorbent and a γ-Al 2 O 3 -supported visible-light-absorbing Z-scheme photocatalyst system, respectively. Gas-phase operation benefits CO 2 delivery and suppresses H2 evolution, achieving ~88% CO selectivity and ~100 h stability. Isotopic labelling confirmed that CO and O 2 originates from CO 2 and water, respectively. The DACCU prototype was operated outdoors over two consecutive day–night cycles, enabling continuous DAC at night with solar-thermal desorption and solar-driven conversion in the day. This work represents the first demonstration of producing solar fuels from only atmospheric CO 2 and moisture at low temperature and pressure and therefore provides a critical advance for the practical deployment of photocatalytic CO 2 splitting technologies.

papers.title: OptoMatKG: A Traceable Knowledge Graph Framework with Semantic Retrieval for Optoelectronic Materials Science
papers.abstract: Extracting and correlating knowledge from heterogeneous scientific publications poses a fundamental data engineering challenge for data-driven materials discovery. Traditional keyword search lacks semantic depth, while generic large language models (LLMs) are prone to hallucinated predictions. To address these limitations, we present OptoMatKG, a literature-scale data engineering system whose core contributions are threefold: (1) a domain-specific knowledge graph construction pipeline based on a nine-category fullworkflow ontology; the resulting graph comprises 2.62 million entities and 3.38 million typed relations; (2) a cascaded multi-stage retrieval pipeline that synergistically integrates LLM-based query normalization, semantic vector indexing and Materials Project pre-filtering to enhance metric-aware candidate ranking; and (3) an evidence-constrained auditing module that forces every output to anchor to DOI-supported reasoning chains, thereby enforcing end-to-end hallucination prevention. Using optoelectronic inverse design as a validation testbed, experiments verify that our entity extractor reaches a micro-averaged F1 of 0.971. Comprehensive tests over 2000 real-world queries further demonstrate that our system surpasses keyword-based and singlestage baselines in Recall@K and metric coverage. The system accurately quantifies multi-objective performance trade-offs while ensuring fully traceable inference. Although validated on photodetectors, the proposed solution provides a generalizable, pluggable engineering framework readily extendable to other functional material discovery pipelines.

papers.title: Nanocorrugation-Reorganized PEDOT:PSS Electrochemical Transistors for Ultrasensitive Biomolecular Detection
papers.abstract: Although electrolyte-gated organic transistor (EGOT) biosensors enable label-free volumetric biosensing, their sensitivity in physiological environments remains fundamentally limited by poor polymer microstructure ordering and inefficient ion–channel coupling. This paper introduces EGOTs with geometrically reconfigured mixed ionic–electronic transport enabled by nanocorrugated poly(3,4ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) channels. PEDOT:PSS films conformally deposited onto nanoscale corrugated SiO2/Si substrates undergo curvature-induced local chain reorganization and topography-guided nanoscale redistribution of PEDOT- and PSS-associated regions. These changes are associated with enhanced π–π stacking, improved polymer ordering, and more efficient gate–channel coupling. Compared with flat counterparts, the nanocorrugated devices exhibit improved ion accessibility, transconductance, and threshold-voltage modulation. The proposed platform enables ultrasensitive detection of nucleic acids and stroke-related protein biomarkers in buffer, serum, and whole blood, achieving a threshold-based measured DNA LOD of 20 aM in buffer, while statistically significant separation from negative controls begins at 200 aM; IL-6 is detected down to 1 fM under the tested buffer conditions. Electrochemical measurements and structural analysis reveal polymer chain alignment confined within the corrugation valleys and enhanced mixed ionic-electronic coupling. Overall, nanoscale corrugation enables a previously unexplored route to tune ion transport, reconfigure the polymer network, and enhance volumetric transduction in conducting polymer EGOTs, thereby facilitating robust biosensing under physiologically relevant environments.

papers.title: Pressing Mode Determines Densification Uniformity and Dimensional Stability in Sulfide Solid-State Batteries
papers.abstract: Pressure-assisted densification is essential for manufacturing sulfide solid-state batteries because electrochemical performance critically depends on intimate solid–solid contact within the electrode stack. However, how the applied stress state governs the co-densification of mechanically dissimilar layers and their electrochemical functionality remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the pressure-assisted consolidation of Li6PS5Cl separator/composite cathode bilayers under uniaxial and isostatic loading. Despite the contrasting mechanical response of the compliant separator and rigid composite cathode, all processing routes follow the same three-stage ceramic compaction mechanism. Isostatic loading and elevated temperature do not alter this mechanism but substantially improve densification efficiency and, more importantly, suppress the radial strain and center-to-edge density gradients inherent to uniaxial processing. The resulting lateral deformation compromises dimensional stability, which becomes increasingly critical for large-area electrodes and multilayer stacking. At the same time, locally under-densified edge regions provide mechanically weak, porous pathways for metal filament propagation and subsequent short circuiting. Warm isostatic pressing suppresses both lateral deformation and spatial densification heterogeneity, demonstrating that these limitations can be overcome by controlling the stress state during consolidation. These findings establish that a scalable densification process must provide not only sufficient average density, but homogeneous consolidation across the complete electrode while preserving its geometry, providing processing criteria for the development of large-area solid-state batteries.

papers.title: Understanding Aggregate Structures of Organic Donor-Acceptor Systems by Partitioning Repulsive Interactions into Orbital-Orbital Contributions
papers.abstract: Molecular Orbital-Pair Contributions to the Exchange repulsion (MOPCE) are used to elucidate the orbital origin of repulsive interactions and to understand their role in determining the stacking arrangements of organic donor–acceptor (DA) complexes. We investigate three DA complexes with planar monomers, benzene–p-benzoquinone (BZ–pBQ), benzene–tetracyanoethylene (BZ–TCNE), and tetrathiafulvalene–tetracyanoquinodimethane (TTF–TCNQ), which prefer distinct stacking geometries. Symmetry-Adapted Perturbation Theory (SAPT) is employed to decompose the intermolecular interaction energy into electrostatic, induction, dispersion, and exchange repulsion contributions. MOPCE partitions the latter into a sum of orbital-orbital interactions, Exr(a, b), where a and b stand for the occupied orbitals of the interacting systems. Thus, MOPCE also permits to identify the π-π-, π-σ-, and σ-σ-contributions to the exchange repulsion energy. Its π-π-contribution is shown to play a decisive role for the intermolecular energy landscape of π-stacked DA complexes, despite the attractive contributions are dominated by dispersion and electrostatics. The energetically most favorable slip-stacked structure of the BZ–pBQ complex is traced back to oscillations of a MOPCE term with similarly shaped orbitals that have a node orthogonal to the shift direction. The face-to-face arrangements preferred by BZ–TCNE and TTF–TCNQ can be rationalized by reduced orbital overlap due to the nodal patterns of the π-orbitals. The non-negligible role of electrostatic interactions is discussed. The MOPCE approach is shown to be an intuitive orbital-based description of exchange repulsion which provides a valuable framework for understanding and predicting arrangements in stacked organic π-systems in terms of the wave-function nature of the underlying electronic structure.

papers.title: Linear-response TDDFT simulations of K-edge resonant inelastic X-ray scattering in extended systems
papers.abstract: We present an implementation for the calculation of K-edge resonant inelastic X-ray scattering spectra based on time-dependent density functional theory in the CP2K package. The method evaluates the Kramers-Heisenberg cross section from transition dipole moments connecting the ground state, core-excited intermediate states, and valence-excited final states. The present implementation combines the existing linear response time-dependent density functional theory modules (XAS-TDP and TDDFT) within a unified framework. The resulting approach is computationally efficient and well suited for condensed-phase applications in combination with ab initio molecular dynamics. The implementation is validated against experiment and established reference calculations for gas-phase water and methanol at the oxygen K-edge. Its applicability to realistic condensed-phase systems is then demonstrated for crystalline kaolinite at the oxygen K-edge, and for aqueous ammonia at the nitrogen K-edge, where representative configurations are sampled from ab initio molecular dynamics trajectories.

papers.title: GLOSS: A Multi-Strategy Sampling Algorithm for Optimization in Vast Chemical Spaces
papers.abstract: Surrogate-based optimization accelerates closed-loop scientific discovery. In chemistry and materials science, however, sparse data over vast chemical spaces make surrogate predictions unreliable and undermine data efficiency. We develop GLOSS, a sampling algorithm that divides each batch across three complementary strategies: Global, Local, and Unexplored. Across multiple benchmarks, GLOSS reaches 95% of the optimum about twice as fast as Bayesian optimization and consistently outperforms genetic algorithms and random sampling, and its advantage grows more pronounced as the chemical space enlarges. By explicitly sampling unexplored regions rather than relying solely on surrogate predictions, GLOSS offers a scalable route to data-efficient closed-loop optimization in vast chemical spaces.
