A two-dimensional double-well pathway model then introduces a missing structural coordinate and shows that comparing observable sets can flag whether an omitted degree of freedom is structural or bath-like. With a three-coordinate conformational model, we then show that measuring multiple observables converts scalar memory analysis into a pathway-resolved description of delayed influence among measured coordinates. Variations in barrier height, bath time scales, observable set, and system-bath coupling patterns indicate that pathway power is more robust than assigning global memory periods to individual hidden modes. A hidden-mediator variant further highlights that pathway-resolved memory can reveal delayed communication produced by unobserved mediators, especially with the analysis of how pathway-resolved memory responds to perturbations. These results motivate observable-memory analysis as a framework for extracting mechanistic information from sparse experimental or simulation measurements, particularly in allosteric systems where hidden mediation and delayed communication are central to function.

papers.title: Photo-Physics of Halogenated-benzylidene-hydrazineyl-4-trifluoromethylthiazole combined Experimental and Computational study
papers.abstract: The photophysical properties of halogenated 2-(2-benzylidenhydrazinyl)-4-(trifluoromethyl)thiazole derivatives are reported based on combined experimental and computational methods. Structures were confirmed by NMR, IR, and high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS). Variation of halogen substituents (Cl, Br, I) enabled evaluation of substituent effects on electronic structure and excited-state behavior. Absorption and fluorescence measurements in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) revealed intramolecular charge transfer (ICT), driven by the electron-withdrawing trifluoromethyl group and conjugated hydrazone bridge. All three compounds undergo reversible deprotonation in DMSO, giving a red-shifted non emissive species that quenches the fluorescence. The 4-bromo-2-hydroxy substituted derivative (3b) additionally shows the most intense emission and smallest Stokes shift of the series, consistent with restricted excited state relaxation due to inter molecular Hydrogen bond. Computational analysis supported these findings by elucidating frontier orbitals and charge distribution. Notably, despite the presence of heavy atoms and calculated spin-orbit coupled states, no significant population transfer to the triplet manifold was observed neither experimentally or in simulations. These results demonstrate the impact of halogenation and electron-withdrawing substitution on the excited-state dynamics of thiazole-based chromophores.

papers.title: NEVPT2 Multiple Spawning Molecular Dynamics Simulations for Uracil
papers.abstract: The quasidegenerate n-electron valence state second-order perturbation theory (QD-NEVPT2) for complete active space reference wavefunctions has been implemented in the OpenMolcas package. The implementation utilizes the efficient formulation of Kollmar et al. for the electronic energy, which is extended here to the calculation of analytic derivatives. To demonstrate its utility, the method is applied to classical and non-adiabatic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of uracil. The non-adiabatic MD simulations describe the ultrafast deactivation of the initially excited bright ππ∗ state through the S 2 /S 1 conical intersection, demonstrating the applicability of the method to photochemical processes. Furthermore, a machine learning-based analysis of the trajectory data extracts key geometrical parameters that are associated with the magnitude of the time-derivative coupling.

papers.title: Model of the Henrys: Eyring, Frank, and the Foundations for Predicting Transport Coefficients
papers.abstract: Henry Eyring’s absolute rate theory provides a microscopic picture of liquid transport based on molecular jumps, while Henry Frank’s free volume theory relates entropy changes to an effective cage volume in condensed phases. In this work, we integrate these two frameworks to obtain the Model of the Henrys (MotH), a unified description of transport phenomena based on the (re)movement of molecules within a system. Starting from Eyring’s viscosity expression, we replace activation energies by residual energies, and express the free volume via Frank’s entropy–free volume relation using residual entropy. The resulting model contains a small set of molecule-specific parameters. We show that viscosity and self-diffusion of alkanes, alcohols, carbon dioxide, and water are described in good agreement with experimental and molecular dynamics data over wide temperature and pressure ranges, including the strongly interacting fluids that approaches such as entropy scaling struggle to capture. Transferring the free volume part of the model to thermal conductivity of alkanes serves as a proof of concept, validating the decomposition on which MotH rests. Analysis of the fitted parameters is consistent with Frank’s original idea that free volume is primarily controlled by molecular size, whereas activation energies are strongly family-dependent. Beyond the model itself, MotH provides a common origin for descriptions of transport that are usually treated as competing: Arrhenius/Andrade correlations and empirical entropy scaling are recovered as limits of the MotH model.

papers.title: Face saturation at ρ * = 4 ln 2: a universal threshold separating cooperative from individual relaxation in hydrogen-bonded liquids
papers.abstract: The non-Arrhenius crossover in the dielectric relaxation of liquid water near 35-45 • C has been documented for four decades. No existing model predicts the crossover temperature without a fitted parameter. We show that the crossover occurs at a topological threshold ρ * = 4 ln 2, derived from the 4-simplex (K5) and not adjusted. A periodic table of K5 hydrides (CH4, NH3, H2O, HF and their third-row analogues) reveals that water is the only simple hydride combining a permanent dipole with an effective hydrogen-bond density ρ above the threshold. The crossover at ∼ 40 • C is a direct consequence of this unique position. We test the universality of ρ * on a database of 11 hydrogen-bonding liquids with published temperature-dependent dielectric relaxation data. Using the measured number of hydrogen bonds per molecule nHB as the effective density ρ, the threshold classifies 10 of 11 liquids correctly: B19 • Regime II (ρ * < ρ < 2ρ *): cooperative. Water, formamide: 2/2. • Regime I (ρ < ρ *): individual. DMF, DMA, MeOH, EtOH, PrOH, DMSO, CH3CN: 7/7. • Regime III (ρ > 2ρ *): vitrification. Glycerol: 1/1. The single exception is N-methylformamide (NMF, nHB = 2.0 < ρ * , cooperative). Neutron diffraction shows NMF forms linear chains, not triangular clusters: its cooperativity arises from sequential bond breakage, a mechanism distinct from K5 face saturation. The gap between the lowest cooperative ρ (formamide, 3.08) and the highest individual ρ (ethanol, 1.5) straddles ρ * = 2.773 with no overlap. All nHB values are sourced from neutron diffraction or molecular dynamics; all τ (T) classifications are from the original authors. No existing model (Tanaka, Stanley, Poole) extends beyond water. D2O (nHB = 3.76) and ethylene glycol (nHB = 3.0-3.7) are predicted to show cooperative relaxation. Both are testable immediately. The threshold also predicts a critical concentration in water-alcohol mixtures: the non-Arrhenius crossover in τ (T) should disappear at x * MeOH ≈ 0.35 (25 • C) in water-methanol, and x * EtOH ≈ 0.39 in water-ethanol. B20 In the (T, nHB) plane, the cooperative-individual boundary is a horizontal line at nHB = ρ * , regardless of how nHB is varied (temperature, concentration, or pressure). Four K5 constants, together with one measured input (f coord), predict the relaxation time τ of 6 hydrides with τ free derived from geometry, and of 5 further molecules across three decades (3-1500 ps). All 11 predictions fall within a factor 3. B17 Companion script: 123 tests, 20 blocks, all PASS.

papers.title: On the acidity characterization of pristine and zinc-modified H-ZSM-5 zeolites: Comparison of adsorption-based characterization methods
papers.abstract: Unlike temperature-programmed desorption (TPD) of ammonia (NH 3 -TPD) and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy of adsorbed pyridine (pyridine-FTIR), where ammonia and pyridine adsorb and desorb without reaction, TPD of isopropylamine (IPAm-TPD) relies on a Brønsted-acid-catalyzed decomposition of isopropylamine to propylene and ammonia to selectively probe Brønsted acidity. Prior studies have reported altered IPAm-TPD responses for metals-modified zeolites relative to pristine zeolites, yet hypotheses on the cause have diverged. This work examined the acidity characterization results of pristine and zinc-modified H-ZSM-5 zeolites from IPAm-TPD against those from NH 3 -TPD, and pyridine-FTIR. For pristine zeolites, the IPAm-TPD data exhibited the expected Brønsted-site-related propylene desorption feature, with propylene amounts proportional to framework aluminium, strongly adsorbed ammonia in NH 3 -TPD, and Brønsted-associated pyridine in pyridine-FTIR. However, the IPAm-TPD data of the zinc-modified zeolites was more complex, with multiple desorption features. The mass spectrometry data and comparison of the quantitative IPAm-TPD results to those of NH 3 -TPD and pyridine-FTIR suggested contributions from a Brønsted-site-related propylene release, an additional, likely Lewis-site-related propylene release, and unidentified side products overlapping with typical propylene responses, possibly from dehydrogenation and aromatization reactions. When the Brønsted-site-related propylene response was quantified and compared to quantitative pyridine-FTIR results, the results seemed representative of Brønsted acidity despite the side reactions.

papers.title: Site-selective alkali ion alloying in double perovskites via liquid-assisted mechanosynthesis revealed by solid-state NMR
papers.abstract: Lead-free halide double perovskites are promising materials for light-emitting and photovoltaic applications. However, compositional tuning of their structural and optoelectronic properties has largely focused on B-site and halide alloying. In this work, we show that Cs + on the perovskite A-site of Cs 2 AgInCl 6 can be partly substituted with Rb + using simple apolar liquid-assisted mechanochemistry. By comparing Rb + with Na + substitution we show that ion size drives the site-selectivity of alkali ion substitution into double perovskites, with Na + preferentially occupying the perovskite B-site. By combining multinuclear solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy with X-ray diffraction, we show that Rb+ not only enters the double-perovskite site-selectively but also induces local symmetry breaking of the cubic structure, comparable to the effect of B-site Na + /Ag + alloying, with important implications for symmetry-forbidden photoluminescence emissivity. This work extends the tuneable compositional range of lead-free double perovskites to include A-site mixing while also establishing the site-selectivity of alkali ion speciation into the double perovskite structure.

papers.title: Some Thioester Syntheses Love DIC: A Case Study on Functionalizing Amino Acids with O-Protected Mercaptoethanol
papers.abstract: Thioesters can be made through the formal condensation of a carboxylic acid and a thiol. This is generally accomplished using the same activated ester intermediates employed for amide synthesis; however, the yields are often far lower for the thiols. As part of our effort towards generating new biocompatible polymers, we need to access thioesters of amino acids in high efficiency and found that literature conditions for analogous systems provided extremely poor yields. Consequently, herein, we report our coupling reagent screening study for making thioesters between functionalized carboxylic acids (in the form of differentially protected amino acids) and multifunctional thiols including TBS-protected 2-mercaptoethanol, Fmoc-protected cysteine, and various aliphatic and aromatic thiols. Although there is no universal answer, we found that DIC, supplemented (or not) with HOBt in DMF reproducibly, and in the hands of multiple experimenters provided only with the written protocol, produced the highest yield both on small (low mg) and multigram scale.

papers.title: Compositional Disorder Controls Bulk Ion Diffusion in Mixed-Ion Halide Perovskites
papers.abstract: Compositional mixing enables bandgap and phase-stability engineering in metal halide perovskites, but its effect on intrinsic ion mobility is obscured by surfaces, interfaces, and concurrent structural dynamics. Here, variable-temperature magic-angle-spinning NMR combined with machine-learning-accelerated molecular dynamics separates soft-phonon relaxation from vacancy-mediated diffusion across a Cs/Rb–Br/I composition matrix. Br/I mixing markedly accelerates bulk halide transport, whereas combined Br/I and Cs/Rb substitution produces a second, slower regime assigned to A-site cation diffusion. Linewidth and relaxation analyses yield consistent hopping barriers and an Arrhenius-extrapolated room-temperature bulk halide diffusivity of order 10−11 cm2 s−1, below values commonly inferred from electrical measurements of thin films. Simulations at fixed vacancy concentration reproduce the species-dependent mobility trends and indicate that static local distortions broaden the distribution of migration environments, creating locally accessible pathways for ion motion. These results distinguish intrinsic mobility per available defect from macroscopic ion redistribution, which additionally depends on defect abundance, interfaces, and thermodynamic or photoinduced driving forces. Enhanced per-defect mobility therefore need not imply rapid operational phase segregation, providing a framework for connecting compositional disorder with processing and stability in multicomponent ionic semiconductors.

papers.title: Specific Recognition of RNA Tetraloop in Tertiary Interactions of RNA
papers.abstract: GNRA tetraloops are ubiquitous RNA motifs that drive tertiary folding through tetraloop–receptor (TL–TLR) interactions. However, the mechanisms underlying their ion-dependent stabilization and mutational responses remain unclear. In this study, we performed atomistic molecular dynamics simulations of a minimal TL–TLR system containing a canonical GAAA tetraloop and a GAGA (A48G) mutant. Unbiased simulations combined with time-lagged independent component analysis (TICA) identify slow collective modes governing loop–receptor opening and closing, revealing Mg2+-dependent changes in the conformational ensemble. Enhanced sampling along these modes yields free-energy landscapes that describe Mg2+-mediated stabilization for the wild type. The A48G mutation, however, reshapes the landscape and stabilizes a competing non-native folded state, lowering the unfolding free-energy barrier relative to the wild type in the presence of Mg2+. These results provide an atomistic framework for understanding how divalent ions and sequence variations modulate RNA tertiary recognition and folding pathways.

papers.title: Fluorine-Free Gas Diffusion Media for Polymer Electrolyte Fuel Cells Part I: Silicone-based Microporous Layers
papers.abstract: The widespread use of fluoropolymers in electrochemical energy systems, coupled with increasing environmental, health, and regulatory concerns surrounding per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), is motivating the development of fluorine-free alternatives. Here, silicone-based resins are evaluated as fluorine-free binders for microporous layers (MPLs) and integrated into fully fluorine-free gas diffusion media (GDMs). Using Sylgard 184 silicone elastomer, the binder content was systematically varied, identifying 25 wt.% as the lowest loading that provided sufficient water repellency. At this loading, the influence of binder chemistry was investigated by replacing Sylgard 184 with KR-220L, a methyl silicone rigid resin. Although the resin chemistry strongly affected MPL thickness, porosity, and crack formation, its impact on fuel-cell performance was limited. Fully fluorinefree GDMs were then fabricated by depositing silicone-based MPLs onto carbon fiber substrates hydrophobized via organosilicon electrografting. Replacing a commercial PTFEtreated substrate with the fluorine-free electrografted substrate resulted in only a minor decrease in current density, from 4.2 to 4.0 A cm-2 at 0.3 V under high-humidity conditions; both exceeded the commercial fluorinated reference (3.8 A cm-2). Accelerated stress testing further demonstrated promising durability. Overall, silicone-based materials represent a viable route toward replacing fluorinated components in GDMs.

papers.title: Rapid acid-catalyzed synthesis and surface modification of isopropanol-derived carbon dots
papers.abstract: A rapid acid-catalyzed carbonization route was developed for the synthesis of carbon dots from isopropyl alcohol in concentrated sulfuric acid. Initial screening showed that reaction at 150–170 °C produced nanoparticles with narrow size distributions. The addition of water to the precursor mixture acted as both a thermal heat sink and a reaction moderator, suppressing overcarbonization and improving photoluminescence quantum yields. Box-Behnken response surface optimization identified a water-containing formulation that combined high quantum yield with reproducible synthesis, while selected conditions gave reaction yields up to 71.2%. Two representative base systems were modified with primary alkanols in a sequential 100 °C process. XPS and ATR-FTIR analysis indicated that surface functionalization proceeded mainly through sulfate/sulfite-related esterification or transesterification, accompanied by oxidative side reactions, rather than through classical carboxylic acid esterification. The modified carbon dots exhibited enhanced fluorescence quantum yields and reduced surface tension. Langmuir DPPC monolayer studies showed that, for the more oxidized water-derived base system, longer alkyl chains systematically increased membrane-insertion activity, with Δπ increasing from approximately 2.2 to 19.3 mN·m −1 as the modifier was extended from butanol to octanol. These results establish a tunable platform for controlling the optical, structural, and interfacial properties of carbon dots through synthesis optimization and post-surface modification.

papers.title: Counterpoise-Corrected Ab Initio Potential Energy Curves and Analytic Pair Potentials for Ag, Au, and Ni Interacting with He and Ar: A CCSD(T) Benchmark with Machine-Learning Comparison
papers.abstract: Accurate pairwise potentials for coinage-and transition-metal atoms interacting with noble gases are required for molecular dynamics simulations of metal clusters and matrix-isolation environments, yet such potentials are rarely benchmarked with counterpoise-corrected coupledcluster theory. In this work, potential energy curves of Ag, Au, and Ni interacting with He and Ar were computed at the CCSD(T) level using the aug-cc-pVTZ and aug-cc-pVTZ-PP basis sets, with full counterpoise correction and a wavefunction-stability-verified, orbitalcontinuity-chained self-consistent-field protocol. An initial dataset computed with Gaussian 16 was found to contain a spin-multiplicity error for nickel and uncorrected electronic-state discontinuities and was discarded in favor of a complete recomputation with ORCA 6.0.1. Basis-set superposition error was found to account for 59–166% of the well depth even at the aug-cc-pVTZ(-PP) level, and a genuine avoided electronic curve crossing was identified for the Ni–Ar pair near 2.6–3.0 Å, corroborated by both an energy discontinuity and a T1-diagnostic spike. The curves were fitted to the Lennard-Jones, Morse, Buckingham, and Improved Lennard-Jones (ILJ) forms, and to a Gaussian process regression model. The Improved Lennard-Jones and Morse forms were found most reliable classically, while the Lennard-Jones form was poorly constrained for every pair. The Gaussian process regression model outperformed every classical form on every pair. Well depths were found to follow the trend Au > Ag > Ni for both gases, and Ar wells were 11–16 times deeper than He wells, consistent with the larger polarizability of argon.

papers.title: Symmetry-Controlled Topological Phase Coherence Length as a Quantum Descriptor for Interfacial Charge Transfer
papers.abstract: Topological crystalline insulators (TCIs) provide a unique platform where crystalline symmetry protects spin-polarized surface states, enabling phase-coherent quantum transport. Here, we establish the topological phase coherence length () as a quantitative quantum descriptor that links symmetry protection, spin transport, and interfacial charge-transfer reactivity in SnTe-based TCIs. Structural confinement (SnTe@S) and vanadium (V) substitution (SnTe@V) are employed to tune the coherence of topological surface states (TSS). Low-temperature (7 K) electron spin resonance measurements reveal pronounced weak antilocalization (WAL) behavior in SnTe@V, exhibiting the highest WAL prefactor ( α) = 1.8 ± 0.2, and the longest phase coherence length ( = 12.5 ± 2.5 nm , signifying multiple coherent TSS channels stabilized by mirror-symmetry restoration. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations demonstrate that spin–orbit coupling (SOC) induced TSS enhance the local density of states and optimize hydrogen adsorption energetics through orbital hybridization between Sn and V, yielding the most favorable Gibbs free energy for hydrogen evolution. The direct correlation between the enlarged and accelerated charge-transfer kinetics identifies the symmetry-controlled topological phase coherence length as a fundamental quantum descriptor dictating charge-transport efficiency. This work establishes phase coherence length as a predictive quantum descriptor for catalytic charge transfer in topological materials.

papers.title: Interfacial Mechanisms of Reactive Dye Adsorption on a Waste-Cotton Derived PVA/TiO2/Cellulose Biofilm: A Molecular Dynamics and Physics-Informed Predictive Framework
papers.abstract: Textile dye effluents remain a major source of water pollution, and adsorptive bio-based composite films are attractive for their low cost and environmental footprint. This study identifies the interfacial mechanism governing reactive dye removal by a poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA)/TiO2/microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) biofilm, in which the MCC was extracted from waste cotton fabric (WCF) and citric acid served as the crosslinker, and shows that this mechanism can be captured in a predictive model. All-atom molecular dynamics simulations of the PVA–MCC–citric acid–TiO2dye system resolve an electrostatically dominated oxide interface together with an extensive PVA hydrogen-bond and hydrophobic-contact network that also explains the composite’s elevated glass-transition temperature; combined with the post-adsorption S=O infrared response and the TiO2 point of zero charge, this identifies attraction between the protonated surface and the dye’s sulfonate groups as the leading interaction. The resulting chemisorption-dominated picture is corroborated by two further approaches: classical kinetic and equilibrium analysis, best described by the pseudo-second-order (R2 = 0.998) and Freundlich (R2 = 0.978) models; and a physics-informed neural network constrained by the pseudo-second-order rate law, which achieved the strongest generalization among six benchmarked machine-learning models (leave-one-out R2 = 0.989, MAE = 0.021 mg/g). A four-parameter unified surface coupling the Freundlich isotherm and pseudo-second-order kinetics through a mass balance reproduces both datasets (R2 = 0.962 and 0.992) across dosages differing by a factor of 2.4, enabling prediction of performance under untested operating conditions. FTIR, XRD, particle-size analysis, FE-SEM/EDX, mechanical testing, DSC and swelling studies confirm composite formation and ester crosslinking, and the biofilm removed up to 49% of the reactive dye Avitera Light Red SE at 50 ppm within 170 minutes. Together these analyses offer a transferable framework for coupling molecular simulation with physics-informed machine learning in the study of bio-based sorbents.

papers.title: Graph attention networks for daily PM10 prediction at unmonitored European monitoring sites: operational scope, diagnostics, and outlier-robust training
papers.abstract: Air quality networks measure pollutant concentrations only at instrumented sites, leaving most locations unobserved. Graph-based virtual-node methods increasingly fill this gap, but are usually summarised by a single leave-one-station-out (LOO) R2 that leaves unstated where the model can be trusted and why it fails. Here, the operating envelope is the object of study. A graph attention network (GAT) combining multi-pollutant lags, ERA5 meteorology, MODIS aerosol optical depth, and land-use composition predicts daily-mean PM10 at unmonitored locations on the 18-station Styrian (Austria) network for 2020–2023. Under LOO cross-validation with disjoint years, the GAT reaches a median R2 of 0.52, seed-stable and ahead of Lagged-IDW (0.26), Lagged-Kriging (0.22), and Ridge-AR (0.45). At two stations whose PM10 distributions lie outside the training support, performance degrades sharply. Ablation and attribution trace the failure to one component: inverse-distanceweighted imputation of held-out lag features interacting with the persistence-residual head; graph topology is immaterial. An outlier-gated imputation policy raises pooled mean R2 from 0.31 to 0.38, node-masking training cuts per-station variance fourfold, and zeroing all auxiliary inputs lifts both outlier stations to positive R2: the partition is induced by the feature pipeline, not the architecture. The partition reproduces on NO2, and the model transfers to the 33-station Bavarian network (median R2 0.39, no negative folds). The outof-scope stations are clean-air sites under-represented in an urban-industrial network, and the worst is flagged in advance by a static-feature outlier detector: a deployable signal of where virtual-node estimates can be trusted and where the network must grow in regime diversity.

papers.title: Ion‐Selective Transistor Coupled Droplet Interface Bilayer with Short term Memory and Synaptic Plasticity
papers.abstract: The integration of sensing, memory, and learning within a single device remains a major challenge for bioinspired electronics. Here, we present an ion‐selective transistor coupled droplet bilayer (TCDB) that combines potassium sensing, ionic memory, synaptic plasticity, and associative learning within a unified iontronic architecture. The platform utilizes a valinomycin‐functionalized droplet interface bilayer that provides selective K+ transport while simultaneously serving as an ionic reservoir that electrochemically gates an organic electrochemical transistor, directly coupling ion transport to adaptive electronic responses, linking ion recognition with information storage and processing. The DIB incorporated OECT exhibits selective potassium sensing together with pronounced hysteretic memory behavior and activity‐dependent conductance modulation characteristic of artificial synapses. Unlike conventional ion‐selective OECT sensors that function solely as transducers, the proposed architecture exploits the intrinsic dynamics of ion transport across a biomimetic membrane to encode and retain information associated with previous ionic events. The resulting device demonstrates the coexistence of sensing, memory retention, and synaptic plasticity within a single platform without requiring separate memory elements or external processing circuitry. This work establishes a new class of adaptive iontronic devices in which sensing and computation emerge from the same ionic processes. The findings open new opportunities for intelligent bioelectronic interfaces, neuromorphic chemical sensors, and membrane‐inspired computing systems.

papers.title: Biochemical Investigation of the Role of Loop 1 Residues in LytM
papers.abstract: Infections caused by drug-resistant bacteria impact the lives of millions across the globe. To combat these infections, peptidoglycan hydrolases (PGHs) are gaining interest due to their ability to effectively kill these pathogens with low rates of evoking resistance pathways. One such PGH includes LytM, which is an autolysin produced by Staphylococcus aureus. While an engineered variant of this enzyme has shown antimicrobial activity, its mechanism is poorly understood. The loop 1 region was proposed to be responsible for a new cleavage site that has not been reported for other M23 enzymes. However, it is unclear what residues in loop 1 are key for catalytic activity. In this work, a biochemical analysis was used to identify sites that were important for activity. An alanine scan of the loop 1 region of the enzyme revealed key hotspots for hydrolysis. We then used site-saturation mutagenesis to identify the structure-function relationship of these sites. The function of these residues was then tested in a homologous enzyme, lysostaphin, to determine how well activity is conserved. Collectively, this work confirms residues that are important for activity of LytM and related enzymes.

papers.title: Active Sites in Motion: Principles, Materials Platforms, and Sustainable Applications in Heterogeneous Catalysis
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous catalysis stands as a cornerstone of modern chemical science, underpinning the sustainable production of fuels, chemicals, and materials across industries ranging from petroleum refining to environmental protection. This review provides a comprehensive, entry-level guide to the current frontiers of heterogeneous catalysis, structured to move from fundamental principles to advanced materials, characterization methodologies, and real-world applications. We frame the discussion around three linked questions: What is the active site? How is it measured under working conditions? And how can it be rationally designed for sustainable chemistry? Beginning with surface phenomena and classic kinetic frameworks, we examine the evolving conceptual landscape of active sites from isolated single atoms and dual-atom ensembles to dynamic, defect-rich interfaces that restructure under reaction conditions. A critical exposition of operando and in situ characterization methods reveals how the field is transitioning from static, ex situ descriptions to dynamic, site-resolved understanding. We then survey frontier materials platforms, including zeolites, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), metal oxides, single-atom catalysts, and carbon-based systems, illustrating how synthesis strategies such as defect engineering, confinement, and interfacial tuning enable precise control over reactivity and selectivity. These materials foundations are linked to sustainable reaction classes in biomass valorization, CO2 utilization, green synthesis, and energy conversion. We further discuss the emerging role of computational modeling, machine learning, and knowledge graphs in accelerating catalyst discovery, alongside the pressing need for reproducibility and standardized benchmarking. Throughout, we emphasize the integration of site-specific characterization, theoretical insight, and sustainability-driven objectives.

papers.title: SMART SENTINEL: Nondestructive Point-of-Need CRISPR-Cas12a Lateral Flow Platform for Rapid New World Screwworm Field Triage
papers.abstract: The recent re-emergence of the New World Screwworm (NWS) threatens the multibillion-dollar livestock industry, but current diagnostics require centralized morphological confirmation, creating severe 3 7-day testing bottlenecks due to an influx of non-target blowflies. To address this gap, we developed a rapid point-of-need (PON) CRISPR-Cas12a diagnostic framework for immediate NWS field triage. This assay features a nondestructive DNA extraction protocol that effectively isolates the target NWS cox1 gene while strictly preserving morphological integrity for mandatory federal verification. The assay uses the collateral cleavage activity of Cas12a to highly specifically cleave DNA probes upon Cas12a binding to the target cox1 gene via guide RNA. By combining a hand-held thermal cycler for target enrichment with lateral flow assay (LFA) readouts and portable digital imaging hardware, the integrated system couples molecular recognition with automated analysis to eliminate subjective field interpretation. To ensure biosecurity during development, we safely validated the pipeline using the Secondary Screwworm (C. macellaria) as a reliable congeneric surrogate proxy. Our assay demonstrates exceptional analytical sensitivity, establishing a limit of detection of 0.83 aM for synthetic targets, and exhibits absolute specificity against common distractor fly species, including Secondary Screwworms, Blue Bottle flies, Green Bottle flies, and House flies. Validation within a complex biological tissue matrix using a simulated beef liver infestation model confirmed robust diagnostic performance. Ultimately, this decentralized platform rapidly screens out negative samples, preventing the flooding of central reference laboratories and providing a critical biosecurity tool for swift epidemiological containment.

papers.title: A Composable 3D-Printed Platform for Rapid Sequential Sample Injection in Mass Spectrometry
papers.abstract: We developed a composable 3D-printed platform for rapid sequential sample injection in mass spectrometry. The platform works in a well plate-like format and allows direct loading of discrete sample droplets by micropipette or automated liquid handling. Droplets are separated by air gaps during transport and are directly coupled to MS through capillary vibrating sharp-edge spray ionization (cVSSI). Liquid-infused surface treatment was used to improve compatibility of the 3Dprinted microchannels with MS analysis. The platform was evaluated for device operation, throughput, quantitative performance, and carryover. A throughput of ~20 s per sample was achieved at 50 µL/min. Quantitative analysis of lysine gave a linear response with R2 = 0.9988, and carryover was evaluated across chemically distinct small molecules. These results demonstrate that the platform supports air-separated droplet transport, rapid sequential analysis of different samples, and quantitative MS measurements in a simple, modular, and customizable format.

papers.title: MoSeS Enables Autonomous Chromatography Operation through Programmable Analytical Expertise
papers.abstract: Chromatography–mass spectrometry is a central tool for chemical and biological analysis across a wide range of applications. However, its use in automated workflows has remained limited because instrument operation, chromatogram interpretation and method development have often relied on experienced users. Here, we translate key elements of this analytical expertise into programmable operations, and apply them across workflows of increasing analytical complexity. Most importantly, we show that autonomous, machine-learning-based chromatographic method development can be accelerated substantially by moving beyond black-box optimization and incorporating analytical expertise. We further demonstrate practical use cases from synthetic chemistry and materials discovery, including the automated annotation of complex reaction mixtures, and the autonomous development of a purification method for a target compound from a crude reaction mixture. These capabilities are provided through MoSeS, an open-source Python framework that integrates sample-by-sample instrument control, analyte-resolved data processing, cross-run analyte tracking, and physicochemical retention modelling within a common software layer. Together, these results show how analytical operations that are commonly performed by experts can be formalized into reusable computational workflows. This work provides both a usable software toolbox and practical demonstrations of integrating chromatography–mass spectrometry systems into automated laboratory routines – ranging from custom data analysis pipelines to AI-guided decision making in self-driving laboratories.

papers.title: Natural Product Chemistry in Sickle Cell Disease Therapeutics: Phytochemical Mechanisms, Pharmacokinetics, and Computational Docking Insights for Next-Generation Anti-Sickling Agents: A Comprehensive Review
papers.abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) — the most common severe monogenic disorder worldwide, affecting an estimated 7.74 million people and accounting for roughly 515,000 births each year, with nearly 80% of the global burden concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa — remains a disease for which the modern targeted-therapeutics pipeline has repeatedly underdelivered. Voxelotor, the first rationally designed small-molecule hemoglobin-oxygen-affinity modulator, was voluntarily withdrawn from every world market in September 2024 after post-marketing data suggested an unfavorable benefit-risk balance; crizanlizumab's European marketing authorization was revoked in 2023 after its confirmatory STAND trial failed to demonstrate efficacy; and the two FDA-approved gene therapies, Casgevy and Lyfgenia, remain inaccessible to the overwhelming majority of the global SCD population owing to million-dollar price tags and the specialized transplant infrastructure they require. Against this backdrop, natural product chemistry — long practiced empirically across malaria- and SCD-endemic regions, and increasingly interrogated with modern phytochemical, pharmacokinetic, and computational tools — represents a scientifically active and practically urgent alternative discovery axis. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of that literature. We first summarize the molecular pathophysiology of HbS polymerization and the specific structural targets (the T-state polymerization interface, the R-state Val1α allosteric pocket, and oxidative/membrane targets) that both synthetic and natural anti-sickling agents engage. We then catalogue the major chemical classes of natural anti-sickling agents — polyphenols and flavonoids, phenolic aldehydes exemplified by vanillin and its pyridyl derivatives, alkaloids, terpenoids, and standardized polyherbal formulations such as the Nigerian-developed Niprisan/NIPRD-94 — together with the specific plant sources (Cajanus cajan, Pterocarpus osun, Zanthoxylum zanthoxyloides, Carica papaya, Detarium microcarpum, Uapaca heudelotii, and others) from which they have been isolated. A dedicated section addresses the pharmacokinetic dimension explicitly requested for this review: the generally poor oral bioavailability, rapid conjugative metabolism, and short half-lives that most polyphenolic natural anti-sickling agents share, as well as the nanoformulation, derivatization, and polyherbal combination strategies being explored to overcome these limitations. We then synthesize the rapidly growing — but methodologically uneven — computational docking literature that has emerged over 2023–2026, tabulating the target structures, software, and binding-affinity results reported for natural-product ligands docked against sickle and carbonmonoxy hemoglobin structures, including direct comparisons to voxelotor as a co-docked reference standard. We close by proposing an integrated discovery pipeline — spanning extraction, in vitro anti-sickling assay, computational docking/ADMET triage, and pharmacokinetic-guided derivatization — for advancing natural-product leads toward genuinely next-generation anti-sickling agents, and by mapping the specific evidentiary and methodological gaps that currently separate this literature from that standard.

papers.title: Elucidating the Impact of Conductive Additives on Redox-mediated Reactions through a Porous Electrode Theory Approach
papers.abstract: *Corresponding Author Abstract While common to redox-mediated flow batteries (RMFBs), the role and influence of conductive composites vary widely, obfuscating pathways for performance improvements. In this work, we expand upon an earlier modeling framework to explicitly resolve the charge transport within composite active materials of RMFBs, combining porous electrode and mixed potential theories to describe the internal currents and charge transfer reactions produced by the “off-electrode” chemical redox reactions. The derived models elucidate the dynamics and spatial distributions of the mediator and solid half-reactions, highlighting differences in the driving force and mediator reaction rate associated with the active solid and conductive solid interfaces. The importance of conductive additives is found to be strongly tied to the relative rates of the active solid and “localized” mediator half-reactions occurring at the active solid interface, providing an explanation for the observed discrepancies in the observed improvements. A previously derived scaling relationship is adapted to capture trends in solid utilization for composite active materials in RMFBs. Together, these advancements provide newfound insights, offering guidance into the design and study of emerging redox-mediated systems.

papers.title: Reversible Electrochromic Materials Fueled by Shewanella oneidensis
papers.abstract: Developing synthetic chemical motifs responsive to biological metabolism allows us to expand the design space of functional biomaterials. The most basic metabolic feature in all living systems is respiration, the flow of electrons to an energy acceptor. Here, we demonstrate that viologens respond to extracellular electron transfer (EET)-mediated respiration of the facultative anaerobe Shewanella oneidensis. Through molecular engineering of the bipyridinium core to tune its reduction potential, we identified an asymmetric viologen structure that interacts with S. oneidensis EET and can be incorporated into biopolymers. Conjugation to a biopolymer also reduced cytotoxicity. The resulting hydrogels encasing S. oneidensis exhibited reversible and repeatable electrochromic switching behavior driven by bacterial metabolism, providing a visual readout. These findings expand the use of S. oneidensis EET beyond metal reduction and establish a reversible organic material interface with this electroactive bacterium.

papers.title: Studying Protein-Ligand Interactions with In-droplet Hydrogen-Deuterium Exchange Mass Spectrometry and Molecular Dynamics Simulations
papers.abstract: Native mass spectrometry (nMS) has been widely used for the characterization of biomolecules and their interactions with ligands under near-physiological conditions, yet connecting the change in conformational dynamics of proteins upon ligand binding remains challenging. In this work, the integration of capillary vibrating sharp-edge spray ionization based-nMS, in-droplet hydrogen deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provides a platform to characterize ligand binding and ligand-induced conformational changes of bovine carbonic anhydrase II (BCAII) upon interaction with its inhibitor, acetazolamide (AZM). cVSSI-based-nMS preserves the protein native-like state and facilitates the direct identification and determination of the apparent binding affinity of the BCAII-AZM complex. In-droplet HDX-MS measurements show a reduction in deuterium incorporation upon AZM binding suggesting ligand-induced structural stabilization of the holo BCAII. MD simulations of the apo and holo protein revealed ligand-induced suppression in backbone fluctuations and enhanced structural rigidity. A new model that uses protection factors (PF) and HDX scoring derived from MD trajectories that is based on solvent accessible surface area (SASA) and hydrogen bonding propensity is further refined. The model reflects experimentally observed trends in deuterium incorporation and offers atomic-level insight into structural stabilization of BCAII upon AZM binding. The combination of the cVSSI-based nMS, in-droplet HDX-MS and MD simulations provides a framework for identification and quantification of protein-ligand interactions and elucidation of ligand-induced changes in conformational dynamics of the protein.

papers.title: Bioelectric Design of Charged Hydrogels for Stem Cell Fate Control: Fixed-Charge Density, the Ionic Microenvironment, and the Path from Donnan Physics to Regenerative Medicine — A Comprehensive Review
papers.abstract: Regenerative medicine has, for two decades, instructed stem cell fate through two dominant biomaterial levers: biochemical signaling and substrate mechanics. A third, comparatively underexploited axis is now re-emerging with renewed mechanistic clarity — bioelectricity, the endogenous transmembrane voltage (Vmem) and associated ion-channel, pump, and gap-junction activity that non-excitable cells, including human mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (hMSCs), use to encode proliferative and lineage-commitment states. This review synthesizes the literature bridging three historically separate fields — cellular bioelectricity, polyelectrolyte/charged-hydrogel physical chemistry, and hMSC mechanobiology — to evaluate a specific, testable hypothesis: that the fixed-charge density of a hydrogel network can passively shape the local ionic microenvironment surrounding encapsulated cells through Donnan-type ion partitioning, and thereby shift membrane potential and lineage-specific differentiation without external electrical hardware. We trace the mechanistic foundations of bioelectric signaling from excitable to non-excitable tissue, detail the classical and recent physics of fixed-charge/Donnan equilibrium in synthetic and native charged gels, and catalogue the expanding landscape of charge-tunable hydrogel platforms — interpenetrating polymer networks, conductive polymer composites, piezoelectric and self-powered systems, and natural polyelectrolyte matrices — that could serve as delivery vehicles for this design principle. We give particular attention to the confounding pathways (electrostatic protein adsorption, growth-factor sequestration, adhesion-mediated cytoskeletal tension, and antifouling behavior) that are physically coupled to hydrogel charge and that any bioelectric hydrogel study must control for, and we review the measurement toolkit — voltage-sensitive dyes, patch-clamp electrophysiology, genetically encoded voltage indicators, and ion-channel/gap-junction expression assays — available to directly test the hypothesis rather than infer it from differentiation outcomes alone. A worked case study, drawn from a matched anionic/cationic/zwitterionic/neutral poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate interpenetrating-network hydrogel panel, illustrates how these principles translate into a concrete fabrication and validation pipeline. We close by mapping the current evidentiary gaps in the field, offering a research roadmap for establishing fixed-charge density as a validated, power-free bioelectric design parameter, and surveying the journals in bioelectricity, biomaterials, and stem cell biology where this convergent literature is actively being published. Taken together, the evidence reviewed here indicates that charge-mediated bioelectric signaling is a physically plausible and experimentally tractable, but not yet directly demonstrated, mechanism for hydrogel-based control of stem cell fate — positioning it as one of the more intriguing open questions at the interface of soft-matter physics and regenerative biology.

papers.title: Capacitance-based measurement of calcium-mediated vesicle fusion upon microinjection in droplet interface bilayers
papers.abstract: The droplet interface bilayer (DIB) offers a tunable and stable model membrane platform for studying transmembrane proteins (TMPs). Yet, the library of TMPs known to incorporate into DIBs remains limited to those that spontaneously self-insert from aqueous microdroplets. Moreover, incorporating TMP-decorated liposomes into DIB droplets prior to bilayer formation can disrupt lipid assembly and leave TMPs poorly protected from the oil-water interface. We overcome these hurdles by leveraging calcium-mediated vesicle fusion (CMVF) to deliver bilayer-stable TMPs into DIBs via post-bilayer formation microinjection. Departing from prior works, we employed capacitance-based measurements of intrinsic membrane potential to quantify fusion-induced changes in DIB lipid composition. Our results show that CMVF of symmetric, fusogenic liposomes with an asymmetric DIB reduces its transmembrane potential by an amount that corresponds to the fused area of the bilayer: injecting ~40 nL of fusogenic liposomes into one 400 nL droplet resulted in ~15% of the bilayer area becoming less asymmetric in leaflet composition. Moreover, repeated injections produced cumulative vesicle fusion, while omission of fusogenic lipids or Ca2+ ions abolished changes in membrane potential. After quantifying the CMVF process, we used it to enable and enhance the incorporation of multiple TMPs into DIBs. First, injection of proteoliposomes containing TREK-1 proteins, which do not readily insert into DIBs without fusion, consistently produced stochastic, multi-channel gating within minutes. TREK-1 channels exhibited bipolar voltage dependence and pharmacological activation by arachidonic acid, confirming native channel function. Separately, injection of proteoliposomes decorated with OmpF proteins yielded comparable increases in nominal membrane conductance to spontaneously-inserted OmpF proteins, but at half the driving voltage and despite delivering 10X less protein, indicating that fusion incorporates functional TMPs more efficiently than diffusion-limited protein insertion. Together, these results establish capacitance-based measurements and CMVF as a quantitatively verifiable route for improving TMP incorporation into planar lipid bilayers.

papers.title: Towards Sustainable Adipic Acid Production: Process Modelling of Conventional and Electrochemical Pathways
papers.abstract: Adipic acid (AA) is produced at more than 3 Mt annually, with approximately 95% of global capacity relying on a benzene-derived process in which nitric acid oxidation generates stoichiometric N2O emissions. Electrochemical alternatives, including electrocatalytic oxidation (ECO) of ketone–alcohol (KA) oil and electrocatalytic hydrogenation (ECH) of bio-derived muconic acid (MA), have shown promising cell-level performance, but their techno-economic feasibility has rarely been evaluated using fully integrated process models. Here, we developed Aspen Plus models for three 100 kt a-1 AA production plants located in the Rotterdam industrial region: the conventional nitric acid route with N2O abatement, an ECO route replacing nitric acid oxidation with an alkaline membrane electrolyser and electrodialytic KOH recovery, and a biomass ECH route converting clarified MA fermentation broth to trans-3-hexenedioic acid (t3HDA). All routes were evaluated using consistent feedstock, utility, cost, and emissions assumptions. The conventional process achieves a minimum selling price (MSP) of $1.58 kg-1 and emissions of 4.79 kgCO2e kg-1, consistent with current European AA prices. The ECO route reaches $2.33 kg-1 and 2.20 kgCO2e kg-1, while the biomass ECH route reaches $3.97 kg-1 and 1.18 kgCO2e kg-1. Importantly, electrolyser performance is not the dominant cost barrier. Electrolyte recovery, product concentration, crystallisation, and chilling account for a substantial fraction of capital and utility demand. MSP is particularly sensitive to electricity price, while process emissions strongly depend on grid carbon intensity. Neither electrochemical route is currently cost-competitive with the incumbent process. Moreover, upstream N2O abatement would substantially reduce the emissions advantage of ECO. These results identify downstream separation and product recovery, rather than catalyst performance alone, as the key constraints to economically viable electrochemical AA production.

papers.title: Atomic Decomposition and Mapping of Solute Thermodynamics
papers.abstract: Here we present theory, methods, and software that decomposes the free energy of a solvated solute into its energetic and entropic contributions and maps these quantities to solute atoms. Because the mapping is atomic, contributions can be summed over any set of atoms of interest, giving thermodynamic values for ligand functional groups, protein backbone and side chains, individual residues, or an entire binding site. Software implementing the energy decomposition is integrated into cpptraj in AmberTools and software introduced and described here. We illustrate the approach by atomistically mapping the energetic and entropic contributions of ligand 735 and of the binding-site residues of PPAR-α.

papers.title: Regio and Stereoselective Multicomponent Palladium-Catalyzed Carbonylative Heck-Stille arylation of allylic alcohols derivatives
papers.abstract: A reliable and operationally simple protocol for the regioselective and enantioselective carbonylative Heck-Matsuda arylation of protected allylic alcohols followed by interception of the acyl–palladium intermediate with alcohols and organostannane in a Stille-type coupling was developed. This intermolecular carbonylative Heck method provides access to highly functionalized esters and methyl ketones with the formation of multiple carbon–carbon bonds and the construction of an all-carbon quaternary stereogenic center in a single step from readily available starting materials in good to excellent yields. The reaction displays a broad substrate scope, affording products that offer opportunities for further derivatization, including their conversion into enantioenriched functionalized furans.

papers.title: Forced Reaction Redistribution in High-Loading Lithium-Ion Cathodes
papers.abstract: Classical secondary-current theory predicts a directionally neutral through-thickness reaction distribution when a porous electrode’s effective electronic and ionic conductivities are equal. In a working concentrated electrolyte, the salt-concentration gradient adds a thermodynamic contribution to electrolyte current that shifts this balance. A convention-consistent reduction of the porous-electrode equations shows that, in the quasi-steady weak-depletion onset limit, reaction skew vanishes when the electronic-to-ionic conductivity ratio equals 1/(1+ρe), or 0.390 for the reference electrolyte. Separator-favored reaction therefore persists well below the classical equal-conductivity condition. Full Doyle–Fuller–Newman (DFN) calculations reproduce ∼93% of the predicted boundary displacement across a 2.7-fold change in ρe, although the reduced theory overpredicts skew amplitude away from the boundary; the zero location is the more robust reduced-order result. The boundary does not prescribe the finite-time trajectory: across a 36-condition rate–thickness study, 8 of 17 evaluable trajectories show collector-ward centroid motion followed by separator-ward recovery, and nearly matched cutoff capacities conceal different internal histories. Finally, differencing two depth-resolved stored-lithium profiles at matched delivered capacities recovers the capacity-window-averaged reaction distribution from two states, with predicted through-thickness contrasts reaching ∼33% in 150 µm electrodes.

papers.title: Functional Biomaterials, Spatial Biosensing, and Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: Recent advances in bioengineering mark a paradigm shift from passive structural scaffolding toward dynamic, interactive platforms capable of modulating and continuously monitoring the cellular microenvironment. This review explores the convergence of functional biomaterials, spatial biosensing architectures, and artificial intelligence (AI) in decoding and steering complex cell behavior. Responsive hydrogels, nanozymes, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), and conductive scaffolds serve as information-generating systems that adapt to microenvironmental cues and produce measurable bio-signals. Concurrently, microfluidic organ-on-a-chip architectures integrated with continuous electrochemical, plasmonic, and field-effect transistor sensors enable real-time, non-destructive tracking of cellular secretions and metabolic gradients. To process these high-dimensional multimodal streams, machine learning models—ranging from explainable AI and neural networks to generative transformers and digital twins—are deployed for biomaterial optimization, label-free spectral fingerprinting, and spatial deconvolution. Finally, we highlight the application of these integrated bio-platforms in cancer modeling, liquid biopsy analytics, regenerative medicine, and closed-loop wound theranostics while addressing key hurdles in biofouling, dataset integration, and industrial scalability.

papers.title: Light-Driven Electron-Transfer Catalysis on Earth-Abundant CuFeS2 Nanocrystals Probed by Operando SERS
papers.abstract: Plasmonic nanoparticles possess a strong optical absorption but suffer from low catalytic activity and limited sustainability. Here, we demonstrate that earth-abundant chalcopyrite CuFeS2 nanocrystals (NCs) can serve as a dual-functional platform benefitting from a strong polaritonic absorption enabling surfaceenhanced Raman scattering (SERS), and providing at the same time high activity for light-induced electrontransfer catalysis. The nanocrystals exhibit a prominent optical resonance at 500 nm, originating from interband transitions into a Fe 3d derived intermediate band that drives the dielectric function toward the Fröhlich condition. This localized resonance yields a SERS analytical enhancement factor of ~ 3×103 for 1,2-bis(4-pyridyl)ethylene (BPE), validated by Discontinuous Galerkin Time-Domain (DGTD) electrodynamic simulations and Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations that motivates synergistic near-field and charge transfer contributions. In addition, the CuFeS2 NCs efficiently drive the selective photoconversion of p-nitrothiophenol (NTP) to 4,4′-dimercaptoazobenzene (DMAB). Crucially, wavelength-dependent SERS and kinetic measurements prove that both Raman amplification and surface reactivity follow the optical resonance profile. Power-dependent and substrate-heating controls further confirm that this reactivity is mediated by photoexcited electron transfer into adsorbate orbitals rather than photothermal heating. By integrating a polaritonic optical enhancement with long excited state lifetimes provided by the intermediate band electronic structure in a single earth-abundant material, this work establishes CuFeS2 nanocrystals as a versatile architecture for SERS diagnostics and non-thermal photochemistry.

papers.title: Rescuable Stagnation: A Diagnostic for Benchmark Suitability in LLM-Guided Materials Optimization
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly incorporated into closed-loop materials optimization, yet existing benchmarks provide little controlled evidence of what they contribute once Bayesian optimization stalls. We introduce a benchmark qualification criterion for rescue experiments—which we term rescuable stagnation—for determining, before the optimization comparison is run, whether a benchmark stalls while meaningful improvement remains available. Benchmarks that fail this test make it difficult to distinguish ineffective rescue strategies from saturated or non-stalling optimization. Qualifying a benchmark in advance therefore reduces the risk that null results reflect benchmark design rather than the method under evaluation. We demonstrate the approach on a benchmark constructed from Materials Project shear-modulus data, on which LLM-guided rescue gives no statistically significant improvement over heuristic injection—including a heuristic control provided with the same search information. The LLM nonetheless steers the search toward chemically distinct, high-modulus regions that conventional heuristics do not reach. This exploration behavior reproduces across two model capability levels and does not depend on the coherence of the model’s rationales, though it carries a substantially higher per-proposal cost. The LLM’s distinctive contribution on this benchmark is therefore in where it places exploration rather than in the optimization outcome it achieves, though this distinctiveness did not translate into a measurable advantage under the budget tested. More broadly, conclusions about LLM-guided discovery hinge on benchmark suitability—which qualifying the benchmark makes testable before experiments begin.

papers.title: Heteroatom-Tuned Acceptor Engineering for Red TADF Emitters and NIR-II Chromophores Beyond 1000 nm
papers.abstract: Achieving efficient deep-red and near-infrared (NIR) thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) emitters remains challenging due to the energy-gap law and the conflicting requirements of a small singlet–triplet energy splitting (ΔEST), strong spin–orbit coupling (SOC), and high radiative decay rates. In this work, a systematic acceptor-engineering strategy involving heteroatom substitution, cyano functionalization, and regioisomeric modulation was employed to investigate a molecular library of 31 donor–acceptor emitters, including 10 reported compounds and 21 newly designed analogues. Progressive stabilisation of the acceptor LUMO led to significant bandgap narrowing, extending absorption into the visible region and up to 1273 nm. The newly designed OPTC-6 and OPTC-7 acceptors exhibit exceptionally deep LUMO energies of –4.20 and –4.15 eV, respectively, representing some of the strongest acceptors reported for red/NIR TADF molecular design. ADC(2)/def2-SVP calculations predict emission maxima of 1020 and 1117 nm for OPTC-BOP-6 and OPTC-BOP-7, respectively, extending beyond the conventional NIR region into the NIR-II window. Excited-state analysis reveals that the APPTC and APTC families exhibit favourable ΔEST, SOC, and reverse intersystem-crossing characteristics, thereby enabling efficient TADF. At the same time, the OPTC derivatives exhibit the strongest bathochromic shifts due to pronounced charge-transfer stabilisation. Importantly, the investigated emitters exhibit a broad range of oscillator strengths (0.0003–0.551), radiative decay rate constants (7.25×102–7.01×107 s−1), singlet–triplet energy splitting values (0.002–0.589 eV), spin–orbit coupling constants (0.014–0.372 cm−1), and reverse intersystem crossing rate constants (1.27×10−7–2.90×106 s−1), highlighting the critical role of acceptor engineering in balancing radiative transition probabilities and triplet exciton harvesting efficiencies. Furthermore, descriptor analysis based on the ground-state energy gap (ΔEgs) and dipole moment (μgs) identifies a characteristic NIR-II descriptor space defined by ΔEgs ≤ 1.55 eV and μgs ≈ 9 - 11 D. These findings establish heteroatom-tuned acceptor engineering as an effective strategy for simultaneously developing red TADF emitters and discovering next-generation NIR-II organic chromophores with optical responses beyond 1000 nm.

papers.title: Concentration-dependent Transition in the Rate-determining Step of Hydrogen Evolution Driven by Pyridinium-tethered Mononuclear and Dinuclear Platinum Photocatalysts
papers.abstract: Our previous studies on the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) catalyzed by Pt(II)-based molecular catalysts often demonstrated a second-order dependence of the HER rate on the catalyst concentration, suggesting the importance of stabilizing a hydridodiplatinum(II,III) intermediate based on metal-metal bonding: 2Pt(II) + H+ + e− → Pt(II)-Pt(III)-H. However, we also noticed that some Pt(II)-based HER catalysts instead exhibit a first-order dependence of the HER rate on the catalyst concentration. The key factors governing the selection between these two distinct rate expressions have received limited attention. Here, we discovered a new class of Pt(II)-based HER photocatalysts that uniquely exhibit a transition in the rate law within a lower catalyst concentration regime. Three new photocatalysts developed in this study are abbreviated as [PtCl2(pBp)]2+, [Pt2Cl4(OpBp)]4+, and [Pt2Cl4(UpBp)]4+. Specifically, pBp2+ is a pyridinium-functionalized bipyridine, while OpBp4+ and UpBp4+ are dinucleating ligands wherein two pBp2+ fragments are doubly or singly bridged by phenylene moieties, respectively. Remarkably, all these photocatalysts exhibit two-successive pBp2+-based 1-electron reductions with a potential separation of 290-320 mV. These 2-electron-chargeable characters of the PtCl2(pBp)2+ fragments are enabled by the -conjugation of the two peripheral methylpyridinium moieties across the central bipyridyl ligand. All these complexes serve as efficient photocatalysts for the aqueous-based HER at pH 5.0 in the presence of EDTA as a sacrificial electron donor. Importantly, the HER rate exhibits a second-order dependence on the catalyst at lower concentrations ([Cat] < 20-30 M), indicating that a 2-electron-reduced species (Cat2−) is generated via a rate-determining disproportionation reaction (2Cat− → Cat + Cat2−) and serves as a key intermediate for H2 evolution (Cat2− + 2H+ → Cat + H2). Conversely, a first-order dependence is observed at higher concentrations, where the rate-determining step shifts to the photoinduced electron transfer process. Notably, because of the large comproportionation constants (Kc = 1.0-3.2 × 105), the Cat2− intermediate exists as a minor component (e.g., 0.2% of the total complex). Nevertheless, this low-abundance species dictates the overall reaction rate because its HER pathway possesses a ca. 0.3 eV higher thermodynamic driving force than that doubly driven by the Cat−/Cat couple, rendering the process kinetically highly favorable. While the dinuclear systems led to improved photocatalytic durability, they exhibit HER rates comparable to those of the mononuclear counterpart, suggesting that the HER in these systems does not benefit from the close proximity of the two Pt centers. Overall, this study provides new insights into the design principles for controlling the HER mechanisms of Pt(II)based molecular photocatalysts.

papers.title: Dual Fluorophore System for Direct Measurement of Acidity of Aerosol Particles
papers.abstract: Atmospheric aerosol particles exhibit diverse physical and chemical properties, depending on their composition and source, which are challenging to measure directly due to their chemical complexity. Aerosol acidity is a key chemical property that has significant implications for climate, heterogeneous chemistry, and human health. Here, we present a novel approach to measure aerosol acidity using carbon dots (CDs) as in situ fluorophores. The method uses a dual fluorophore system consisting of pH-sensitive CDs and pHinsensitive CDs incorporated into model aerosol particles, with the pH-insensitive CDs serving as an internal standard. Fluorescence microscopy was used to construct a calibration curve by plotting the ratio of fluorescence intensities of droplets of fluorophorecontaining standard solutions against pH. This calibration curve was used to determine the pH of model aerosol particles in the range of pH 1.5 – pH 3.5, demonstrating the e]icacy of this approach for real-time and direct measurement of the acidity. This approach holds significant potential to parameterize acidity in models, refine our understanding and predictions of aerosol properties such as heterogeneous chemistry, and aid in assessing the impact of aerosol particles on climate and health.

papers.title: Descriptors for orientation, induction, hydrogen donor, and acceptor intermolecular forces in mono-component non-ionic compounds and bridges between cohesion, COSMO, and free energy scales
papers.abstract: Solubility parameters are important properties for various substances because they serve as descriptors of the different kinds of intermolecular forces. These parameters guide the selection of proper solvents for different applications and can aid in predicting the behavior of substances in these solvents. The present work develops several non-experimental methods for calculating such descriptors with improved accuracy and predictability. Proton donor, proton acceptor, orientation, and induction interactions contribute differently to the cohesion and solvation behavior of mono-component non-ionic compounds, but the corresponding fractional descriptors are generally not available from standard Hansen solubility parameter tables. We develop methods for estimating Karger--Snyder--Eon (KSE)-like cohesion-energy descriptors, δo, δi, δa, and δb, from tabulated HSP values and common molecular/solvent data. The calculated descriptors were tested against data published in literature and showed useful predictive accuracy in estimating missing or uncertain fractional cohesion parameters. The orientation and induction components were evaluated by three complementary approaches: Keesom/Debye based method, Clausius--Mossotti and Lorentz--Lorenz based method, and comparator selection in Hansen/KSE descriptor space. Some of these methods were also used to compare cohesion-energy descriptors δo, δi with free-energy-based descriptors γoγi. These comparisons show that the cohesion-energy and free-energy parameters are related but distinct thermodynamic descriptors. The donor/acceptor hydrogen-bond split was further compared across free-energy, cohesion-energy, and COSMO scales. Analysis of 73 mono-component non-ionic compounds gave a strong empirical relationship between the proton donor and acceptor products αGβG (free-energy framework), δaδb (cohesion-energy framework), and COSMO, supporting the conclusion that three descriptor pairs encode related but non-identical aspects of hydrogen bonding. This provides a bridge between cohesion-energy, free-energy, and COSMO descriptors and formulates a practical method for estimating, checking, and predicting fractional intermolecular-force descriptors when direct experimental data are unavailable.

papers.title: Many-Body Interactions Resolve Halide Distribution at the Air/Water Interface
papers.abstract: Ion-specific surface propensities at the air/water interface remain debated. Here we use data-driven many-body energy (MB-nrg) potentials, which exhibit chemical accuracy across all phases, to compute Helmholtz free-energy profiles for the halides using a controlled model hierarchy. A polarizable baseline (TTM-nrg) reproduces the strong interfacial stabilization of I- (and smaller minima for Br-, Cl-) commonly found with empirical polarizable force fields. In contrast, the fully many-body MB-nrg treatment, which adds explicit 2-body and 3-body ion--water terms to many-body polarization, strongly suppresses interfacial adsorption across the series: only I- retains a shallow minimum on the order of kT near the Gibbs dividing surface, where k is Boltzmann’s constant. Decomposition of Helmholtz free-energy shows that this residual preference arises from a narrow energetic minimum in the water--water contribution at the interface that compensates ion--water desolvation, while an opposing entropic penalty compresses the net well. These results reconcile classical image-charge exclusion with polarizable-anion continuum and interfacial-fluctuation models, and identify the collective water response, captured only with a quantitative many-body description, as the mechanism that governs halide surface propensity.

papers.title: Polyvinylpyrrolidone-capped MAPbBr3 perovskite nanocrystals synthesized and processed in isopropanol
papers.abstract: Lead halide perovskite nanocrystals are promising candidates for many optical and opto-electronic applications due to their strong absorption, high photoluminescence quantum yields, and straightforward synthesis. However, the stability of these nanocrystals is unsatisfactory, and the synthesis and processing requires undesirable solvents such as DMF, and toluene. These drawbacks not only adversely impact environment, health, and safety, but also renders them incompatible with various industrial processes. To make perovskite nanocrystals widely applicable, an alternative synthesis is crucial, addressing these shortcomings while retaining advantageous properties. Herein, we present a practical, scalable method to synthesize MAPbBr 3 nanocrystals in isopropanol. The nanocrystals, capped with polyvinylpyrrolidone, are around 40nm in size, cubic, and show good optical quality. Polyvinylpyrrolidone capping enhances their stability, making the nanocrystals tolerant to suspension in isopropanol, moisture, and elevated temperatures. In contrast to conventional MAPbBr 3 nanocrystals, which are made in DMF or toluene and degrade in alcohols, these PVP-capped nanocrystals are synthesized, kept, and processed entirely in a green alcohol solvent. This environmentally and safety conscious method offers new routes for practical synthesis and processing of stable perovskite nanocrystals with advanced functionalities.

papers.title: C–N Coupling in Electrochemical Amino Acid Synthesis Occurs in Solution, not on the Catalyst Surface
papers.abstract: Amino acids are valuable targets for electrochemical synthesis, yet the mechanism of the central C–N bond-forming step remains unclear. Many studies assume that C–N coupling occurs on various electrocatalyst surface efficiently, an assumption that is difficult to reconcile with the strikingly diverse range of reported catalysts. Taking glycine synthesis from oxalic acid and hydroxylamine as a model reaction, we combine density functional theory with NMRbased experiments to investigate the origin of C–N coupling. The overall reaction can be described as three decoupled steps: (i) electrochemical reduction of oxalic acid to glyoxylic acid, (ii) a spontaneous solution-phase condensation that forms the C–N bond, and (iii) electrochemical reduction of glyoxylic acid oxime to glycine. For the C-N coupling step, calculations on model metal surfaces yield high barriers for this condensation, whereas a water-mediated proton-transfer pathway substantially lowers the calculated barrier in solution, consistent with the experimentally observed spontaneous oxime formation. We also observed this mechanism across a range of aldehydes and ketones, suggesting that effective electrocatalysts need to only drive reactant and oxime reduction rather than C–N coupling itself.

papers.title: When less is more: simplified models for interpretable materials design
papers.abstract: Simplified models have long played an important role in materials modelling, from hard-particle and lattice models to coarse-grained descriptions of molecules, polymers, colloids, and frameworks. The value of simplified models is not just computational efficiency. Reducing microscopic degrees of freedom while retaining macroscopic behaviour can reveal which physical and chemical ingredients are responsible for a material’s structure and properties. Simplified models can therefore occupy a middle ground between detailed simulation, which seeks to represent specific materials accurately, and abstract theory, which seeks general principles. In this Perspective, we discuss how simplified models can be used to understand emergent structure in materials. We consider the role of simplified models in deriving design principles across materials classes and their limitations. We argue that the most useful simplified models are tools for organising physical insight as they identify control variables, map regimes of behaviour and suggest which aspects of chemistry, geometry, or architecture are likely to matter for materials design. Their value for materials design therefore depends on identifying favourable regions of model space, and establishing how those regions can be accessed through chemical and synthesis conditions.

papers.title: Thermodynamically Controlled Mechanochromism Through Dynamic Boron–Nitrogen Bonds
papers.abstract: Covalent mechanophores use mechanical energy to facilitate thermal crossing of their activation barrier, resulting in color changes that are mostly governed by reaction kinetics. Here, we develop a B–N-functionalized donor-acceptor mechanochromophore based on a borylated thiophene benzotriazole motif that exhibits an extremely low barrier and fast switching kinetics. Thus, the thermal equilibrium between the B–N closed and open states is thermodynamically controlled, with reversion of the B–N open to the closed form in the absence of an external force taking place on the order of 10-10s. B–N coordination significantly perturbates the intrinsic charge-transfer character leading to strong mechanochromic changes. Force stabilizes the open form, shifts the equilibrium and increases the HOMO–LUMO gap. Increasing the steric demand at the boron center enables force control, rendering pN-scale forces detectable. Additionally, the B–N mechanophore displays photoswitching and enables selective solvent vapor sensing.

papers.title: Electrostatic Pre-solvation Enables Selectivity in Photoinduced Ligand Exchange
papers.abstract: Functional group compatibility remains a central challenge in photochemical C–H activation with metal complexes. Strongly donating groups preferentially coordinate to the reactive unsaturated metal and suppress weaker C–H coordination and σcomplex formation required for C–H bond activation. Controlling the initial coordination in photoinduced ligand exchange is therefore one approach to achieving selectivity in bond activation. Here, we resolve the elementary steps of photoinduced CO to acetonitrile ligand substitution for Rh(acac)(CO)2 with femtosecond-resolution X-ray absorption spectroscopy at the Rh L3-edge. We directly observe the formation of a hitherto undetected transient acetonitrile C–H s-complex and its subsequent rearrangement to the thermodynamically favored nitrogen-coordinated solvent complex. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the initial C–H coordination is enabled by electrostatic pre-solvation, which orients the acetonitrile methyl groups toward the metal center prior to CO dissociation. Our results point to a general strategy to direct selectivity in C–H activation by controlling coordination through pre-solvation.

papers.title: Multimodal PET/Fluorescence Imaging for the Preclinical Evaluation of Polysarcosine (pSar)-modified Dendrimers: Impact of pSar Length on in vivo fate
papers.abstract: Polysarcosine (pSar) is a promising stealth polymer in nanomedicine that has demonstrated a favourable stealth and safety profile preclinically. However, a detailed understanding of the impact that pSar functionalisation has on the longitudinal in vivo behaviour of nanoparticles is lacking. Here we use positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET-CT) to study the longitudinal biodistribution of a pSar-modified poly-L-lysine dendrimer (SDend) and explore the effect that pSar chain length has on biodistribution and pharmacokinetics. We describe the synthesis of three, 32arm SDends with either 28, 56 or 100 repeat units of pSar (SD28, SD56 and SD100) and their functionalisation with the chelator deferoxamine (DFO), the fluorophore Alexa Fluor 647 (AF647), and radiolabelling with zirconium-89 (89Zr).
