While physisorbed guest molecules in porous media are typically modeled as disordered fluids, CALF-20 is known to impart some order in the CO2 adsorbed phase. Here, we use solid-state NMR to resolve the dynamics underlying this ordering: as CO2 loading increases, the adsorbed phase undergoes a pressure-driven transition from rapid, isotropic tumbling to a rigid, orientationally locked state in which CO2 molecules align with the alternating electrostatic potential of the pore surface. GCMC and DFT simulations link this electrostatic templating to specific host-guest interactions and reproduce its pressure-dependent evolution. This cooperative, loading-dependent stabilization is accessible only to guests bearing a sufficiently strong electric quadrupole moment to couple with the template, providing a molecular basis for the framework's marked CO2/N2 selectivity. Comparison with structurally related frameworks indicates that electrostatic templating extends beyond CALF-20 to other materials with complementary pore electrostatics, pointing to a design principle for tailoring adsorbent selectivity to a guest's electronic signature.

papers.title: Beyond the Ground State: A Spin-Resolved Reaction Network for Oxygen Evolution Reaction on NiOOH
papers.abstract: Conventional theoretical models of heterogeneous electrocatalysis typically describe reaction mechanisms exclusively along the ground-state Born–Oppenheimer potential-energy surface (PES). However, this approximation is often insufficient for transition-metal-based catalysts with multiple coexisting spin states, where electronic excitations are energetically accessible at room temperature, and a weak spin–orbit coupling (SOC) hinders the reaction kinetics on the ground-state PES. In this work, we present a comprehensive spin-resolved reaction network for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) on a β-NiOOH (001) surface by combining hybrid density functional theory (DFT) embedded-cluster calculations with lattice kinetic Monte Carlo (kMC) simulations. We demonstrate that strictly restricting the reaction dynamics to spin-allowed processes under adiabatic spin conservation creates a severe kinetic bottleneck due to spin-trapping in long-lived intermediates. Crucially, incorporating nonadiabatic intersystem-crossing (ISC) transitions driven by weak SOC systematically dismantles these bottlenecks. At room temperature, thermal activation drives transitions into higher-energy electronic configurations. Once populated, these excited states activate a dense network of alternative, purely spin-allowed reaction pathways featuring substantially smaller thermodynamic barriers, which successfully drops the overpotential for the multilevel system to a calculated value of 0.58 V. Our findings establish the critical role of nonadiabatic spin-flip transitions and demonstrate that accounting for multi-spin pathways is essential for the realistic quantitative evaluation and rational design of highly efficient transition-metal-based electrocatalysts.

papers.title: Quantifying Michaelis–Menten parameter estimation errors across regression methods and experimental designs
papers.abstract: Michaelis–Menten kinetic analysis is widely used to estimate enzymatic parameters, but the accuracy of these estimations depends not only on the regression method but also on the experimental design. Although nonlinear regression is generally considered the reference approach, linear transformations remain frequently used due to their simplicity. However, the influence of substrate distribution, noise, and experimental conditions on parameter estimation accuracy remains insufficiently characterized. In this study, four regression approaches (Lineweaver–Burk, Hanes–Woolf, Eadie–Hofstee, and nonlinear regression) were systematically evaluated using simulated Michaelis–Menten datasets generated under various experimental conditions. A total of 307 scenarios were investigated, corresponding to 10,350 simulated datasets covering nine kinetic parameter combinations. The impact of noise level, number of experimental values, repetition number, substrate distribution relative to Km, and inhibition models on Vmax, Km, and Ki estimations was assessed using relative error analysis. Linearization methods showed increased sensitivity to noise and substrate distribution, with Hanes–Woolf consistently exhibiting the poorest performance, whereas Eadie–Hofstee and nonlinear regression generally provided the most reliable estimates. Across the tested noise, sampling, and replication conditions, estimates exceeding 20% relative error occurred in 9.2%, 22.2%, 8.2%, and 0.2% of cases for LB, HW, EH, and NL, respectively. In the most challenging conditions, the 95th percentile of Km​ relative error reached 89.3% for HW, compared with 8.7% for NL, highlighting the substantial differences in error magnitude between regression approaches. Their performances remained complementary depending on the parameter and inhibition model. Km​ estimation was generally more challenging than Vmax​ estimation, while increasing the number of experimental values or repetitions did not systematically improve accuracy when the substrate distribution was concentrated far from Km​. Experimental validation confirmed that substrate distribution strongly influences parameter estimation, particularly when experimental values are mainly located above Km​. Overall, this work demonstrates that robust enzymatic parameter estimation requires careful consideration of both regression strategy and experimental design. The results provide a framework for improving kinetic data acquisition and represent a step toward the development of more general guidelines for reliable parameter estimation beyond ideal Michaelis–Menten systems.

papers.title: Beyond Global Drug-Likeness: The FamDLike Framework as a Target Family-specific Druglikeness Score
Thermodynamic hydration boundaries guide storage and closed-loop recycling of sodium-ion battery cathodes
papers.abstract: Alluaudite-type sodium iron sulfate, Na 2.5 Fe 1.75 (SO 4 ) 3 (NFS), is a low-cost, high-voltage cathode material for sodium-ion batteries (SIB), but its sensitivity to atmospheric moisture challenges manufacturing, storage and transport. Here, we report the temperature- and water-vapour-pressure-dependent hydration behaviour of NFS and identify stability boundaries separating anhydrous, hydrated and deliquesced states. Hydration proceeds through discrete phase transitions, defining practical environmental windows for handling and processing. Exploiting this aqueous reactivity, we demonstrate the first closed-loop recycling of NFS via room-temperature aqueous leaching, recovering ~96.8 wt.% active material while retaining electrochemical performance comparable to the pristine NFS over 200 cycles. Life-cycle and technoeconomic analyses show that recycling reduces environmental impact and production cost relative to virgin NFS synthesis and compares favourably with established lead-acid, LiFePO 4 , and NCM cathodes. These results establish hydration boundaries as practical process-design parameters that guide materials handling, manufacturing and recycling across the cathode supply chain, enabling circular sodium-ion cathode manufacturing.

papers.title: Apparent Power as a Unifying Metric for Frontal Polymerization
papers.abstract: In self-sustained transformations such as frontal polymerization, the balance between power generated and power transfer governs propagation dynamics. Herein, we demonstrate the use of an experimentally practical apparent power expression to characterize frontal polymerization. We validated our expression by frontally polymerizing 1,5-cyclooctadiene, dicyclopentadiene, and 5-ethylidene-2-norbornene at various initiator loadings, finding a strong correlation between apparent power and reaction propagation. Raising a system’s apparent power drove a progressive transition in the observed front regime, from quenched through unstable to uniform. We further demonstrated that modulating apparent power influences backbone isomerization and polymer morphology. To further validate our expression, we used heat sinks to vary the reaction power, linking distinct front regimes with apparent power values. Geometric normalization extended this framework to literature examples and frontal radical polymerization, allowing for meaningful comparisons across variable reactions systems and mechanisms. This analytical tool offers a more holistic comparison of monomers and reaction mechanisms that otherwise differ in their thermodynamics and kinetics.

papers.title: Novel RiPP Cyclodehydratases from Thermophilic Bacteria Edit Folded Polypeptides
papers.abstract: Ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) often contain backbone-embedded oxazoline/thiazoline heterocycles that are installed by enzymes known as cyclodehydratases. These editing enzymes are of great interest as biocatalysts for biotechnology applications, as embedded oxazoline/thiazoline heterocycles can induce non-subtle structural and functional changes that alter bioactivity both directly and indirectly. However, the toolkit of existing cyclodehydratases with robust activity, stability, and well-defined sequence specificity is extremely limited. Herein, we apply a genome mining approach to discover two novel cyclodehydratases with improved thermostability: TcuD (from Thermomonospora curvata ) and TteD (from Thermocatellispora tengchongensis ). Notably, TcuD also displays exceptional substrate scope. Specifically, TcuD showed remarkable tolerance to mutations, insertions, and deletions to its substrate precursor peptide, TcuA , and it easily modified a diverse set of substrates whose sequences were derived from α-helical regions of structurally characterized proteins. This work expands the repertoire of cyclodehydratase enzymes available for polypeptide editing applications in biotechnology.

papers.title: In-gap states enhance the hydroxylation of c(6x2) terminated SrTiO3
papers.abstract: Strontium titanate (SrTiO 3 ) has been established as a model perovskite for studying fundamental surface-molecule interactions and mechanisms in photo-electrocatalysis. Here, we investigated the electronic structure and water adsorption behaviour of Nb-doped, SrO-enriched SrTiO surfaces prepared by HCl-HNO3 etching followed by high-temperature annealing in air. We compared low-doped (0.05 wt.% Nb) and high-doped (0.7 wt.% Nb) samples under both oxidising and reducing conditions before and after water exposure. Using Low-Energy Electron Diffraction (LEED), a c(6x2) surface reconstruction characteristic of SrO surface segregation was identified for both doping concentrations. This was induced by the high-temperature air anneal after etching, and was observed independent of subsequent reducing or oxidising treatments. Synchrotron-based X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) revealed that water adsorption is dissociative in all samples, leading to the formation of a hydroxylated surface. Furthermore, synchrotron-based XPS, X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), and lab-based He II ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) measurements identified Ti3d-derived in-gap states below the Fermi level. We demonstrate that the combination of high Nb-doping and thermal reduction results in a Fermi level of 3.15 eV above the valence band maximum and Ti3d states populate the bandgap close to the Fermi level. We propose that these near-Fermi level in-gap states serve as an electron reservoir that enhances the Lewis basicity of lattice oxygen anions by promoting Ti-O hybridisation, lowering the energy barrier for water dissociation, and stabilising surface hydroxyls.

papers.title: Orientational Order of Linkers Controls ZIF-8 Crystallization
papers.abstract: Zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 (ZIF-8) crystallizes through an amorphous intermediate, but the molecular events that triggers nucleation within this disordered phase have remained elusive. Here we introduce a dynamic-binding, implicit-solvent force field for the ionic building units of ZIF-8 that enables unbiased microsecond-scale molecular dynamics of the full crystallization pathway — from solvated monomers to a 10 nm ZIF-8 nanocrystal. Our simulations reproduce the experimentally observed multistep pathway: monomers and oligomers phase-separate into a solute-rich amorphous network with liquid-like dynamics, lower density, and predominantly three-coordinated Zn. Whereas crystalline ZIF-8 is defined by sterically constrained, near-tetrahedral Zn(mIm) 4 nodes, the amorphous network sustains a broad distribution of coordination environments and linker orientations. Nucleation occurs within this disordered phase through collective rearrangements that anneal misconfigured Zn(mIm) 4 nodes and couple linker rotational fluctuations to topological reorganization, locking in the four-connected framework. Crystal growth proceeds by the same defect-annealing mechanism. These results identify linker configurational dynamics as key for ZIF-8 nucleation, and provide a molecular foundation for understanding multistep MOF crystallization.

papers.title: Rapid and Selective Metal-Free O2 Reduction to H2O2 Using a Molecular CpN3 Electrocatalyst
papers.abstract: Hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) is a commodity chemical used broadly in the industrial sector that heavily relies on the 80+ year old anthraquinone process, requiring significant energy input in combination with precious metal catalyzed hydrogenation. We describe a metal-free molecular cyclopentadiene-iminium ([Cp N3 H] 2+ ) electrocatalyst for producing H 2 O 2 under ambient conditions with high Faradaic efficiency (up to 95%) and turnover frequency (TOF up to 10 4 s -1 ), surpassing some of the most active transition-metal based molecular catalyst systems. The amine-rich radical cation intermediate ([Cp N3 H] +• ) transfers a potent hydrogen atom (H•) to O 2 through an unusual radical-rebound mechanism to form a key hydroperoxyl intermediate ([Cp N3 OOH] +• ), with cutting-edge computational (DFT) and experimental mechanistic analyses in excellent agreement. This work demonstrates an innovative and sustainable molecular approach to furnish a valuable commodity chemical through an electrically driven process without the need for transition metals.

papers.title: Enhanced Oxygen Evolution Reaction by Cavity-Arrayed Electrodes
papers.abstract: Water electrolysis is a key technology for sustainable hydrogen production, which typically requires strongly acidic or alkaline electrolytes. In contrast, water electrolysis under near-neutral pH conditions remains challenging because reaction kinetics are limited by the intrinsically slow dissociation dynamics of water leading to the low availability of reactive ionic species. Here we investigate oxygen evolution reactions using cavity-arrayed electrodes designed to couple cavity modes with collective vibrational modes of water molecular ensembles. By combining high-throughput bubble imaging with kinetic analysis across more than 100 unique cavity structures, we observe pronounced structure-dependent enhancements in oxygen evolution activity under unbuffered conditions, reaching up to 10-fold increases in apparent OER kinetics. The periodic dependence on cavity length is consistent with resonant coupling to the vibrational modes of water. Intriguingly, activity enhancement is observed not only when overlapping with the OH stretching modes but also in bending or combination-mode regions, suggesting contributions from cooperative coupling with the cavity modes. Kinetic analysis further indicates accelerated water dissociation dynamics under resonant conditions. These findings suggest that collective modulation of water molecular ensembles can provide a strategy for controlling aqueous-phase chemical reactivities.

papers.title: 1 Investigating sodium hindering during electrochemical lithium extraction with LiFePO4 for Li-ion battery recycling
papers.abstract: Electrochemical Lithium-Ion Pumping (ELIP) stands as a promising technology for extracting lithium from leachates effluents, thus contributing to the lithium-ion battery recycling industry. This technology uses LiFePO4 electrodes to selectively insert lithium from these solutions, followed by deintercalation into a recovery solution which is being continuously enriched. As lithium (des)insertion mechanisms was thoroughly investigated, its competition with sodium insertion is specific to extraction technologies and is less understood. Previous works evidenced that co-cation presence in the electrolyte strongly decreases lithium insertion capacity, the reason being unclear. This however is a crucial point in improving ELIP technology to be competitive and efficient in lithium extraction industry, as both increasing lithium insertion capacity and rate-cycling performances will contribute to decrease the technology cost. By employing various electrochemical techniques and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, we found that sodium has a strong impact on lithium diffusion inside the electrode, even if sodium insertion stays below 5%. Calendering the electrodes helps to overcome this issue, increasing both lithium extraction efficiency and selectivity.

papers.title: Geometric Predictivity is Regime-Gated: A Combined-Diffusion Invariant for Fast-Charge Structured Lithium-Ion Electrodes
papers.abstract: Extreme fast charging is approaching the limits of what cell chemistry alone can deliver, so the next layer of gains must come from how the electrode is shaped. Structured (triply periodic minimal surface, TPMS) electrodes are widely expected to charge faster by shortening ion transport paths. We stress that this expectation is inherited rather than established: it rests on the reasoning that a bicontinuous network shortens transport paths, and it has been carried forward without being tested against extracted transport properties. If it holds, a single geometric number that ranks architectures would be a practical design tool. We test that expectation with a two-stage computational pipeline: we extract the transport properties of eight electrode architectures (five TPMS plus three reference geometries) directly from their meshes with the TauFactor solver, then evaluate fast-charge utilization for each with a one-dimensional Doyle-Fuller-Newman model in PyBaMM, across two lithium-ion chemistries under a pre-registered acceptance rule.

papers.title: Risk-Aware Design of Nanostructured All-Perovskite Tandem Solar Cells under Fabrication Variability Using Gaussian Process Surrogates and CVaR Optimization
papers.abstract: Designing efficient all-perovskite tandem solar cells requires optimization of photovoltaic performance, internal energy dissipation, and fabrication-induced geometric variability. Here, we develop a risk-aware optimization framework that integrates Finite Element Method (FEM) simulations, Gaussian process regression (GPR) surrogate modeling, stochastic fabrication-error analysis, and conditional value-at-risk (CVaR)-based optimization. Five monolithic two-terminal CsPbI3/CsSnI3 tandem architectures, including a planar, two NiO nanorod configurations, a NiO nanotube, and a NiO/MoTe2 core–shell configuration, are investigated. A dataset comprising 3,509 FEM simulations is generated to train GPR models for predicting VOC, JSC, and total power-loss responses of both subcells. The surrogate models reproduce the FEM responses, achieving R2 values above 0.99 for 19 of 20 outputs. The architecture-specific risk-aware designs are verified through FEM simulations and fabrication-variability analysis. The nanorod and nanotube architectures improve bottom-subcell energy utilization by reducing Joule dissipation and increasing electrical power extraction, whereas the core–shell design enables a thinner CsSnI3 absorber through additional MoTe2 absorption but introduces higher resistive losses. Sensitivity analysis reveals the dominant roles of absorber thickness and nanostructure geometry in governing voltage generation and internal energy dissipation. The proposed framework provides an uncertainty-aware pathway for identifying fabrication-tolerant all-perovskite tandem solar cells while elucidating the trade-offs underlying their performance.

papers.title: The SHEF1552 dataset: Fundamental trends and physical insights into halogen, chalcogen, pnictogen, and tetrel bonds
papers.abstract: The Sigma-Hole Energies and additional Factors (SHEF1552) dataset, a comprehensive collection of 1,552 σ-hole interactions (halogen, chalcogen, pnictogen, and tetrel bonds) is introduced. Each complex, formed by pairing 82 σ-hole donors with 19 Lewis bases, was analysed using explicitly correlated coupled-cluster interaction energies and symmetry-adapted perturbation theory (SAPT). Analysis of this dataset identifies key geometric and energetic trends. Pnictogen bonds are, on average, the strongest interactions, followed by tetrel, chalcogen, and halogen bonds. The interaction energy-distance relationship exhibits a distinct boomerang-like distribution, defining two regimes of contact strength. Geometrically, while halogen, chalcogen, and tetrel bonds require σ-hole angles approaching 180◦ for short contacts, pnictogen bonds are unique, displaying no requirement for linearity at short distances. Additionally, roughly 5% of the complexes exhibit appreciable interaction energies despite intermolecular distances exceeding the sum of their van der Waals radii, confirming that strict distance cut-offs are overly restrictive. Finally, SAPT analysis shows the strongest σ-hole interactions are electrostatically dominated, whereas the weakest are primarily dispersion-driven. Beyond these physical insights, the SHEF1552 dataset can serve as a wide-ranging computational benchmark for geometries and energies of σ-hole interactions.

papers.title: Total Synthesis and Preliminary Biological Evaluation of the Natural Glycolipids Cupacinoside and Dalberoside
papers.abstract: We report the total synthesis of the glycolipid natural products cupacinoside (1) and dalberoside (2), together with an alkynemodified analogue (3). The synthesis features two α-selective rhamnosylations and a β-selective glucosidation as key steps. Analague 3 was further derivatized to afford a BODIPY-labeled fluorescent glycolipid probe for functional and mechanistic studies. Prelinimary antimicrobial assays are reproted. We anticipate this work will facilitate synthesis and biological investigation of other glycolipid natural products and related chemical probes.

papers.title: Non-Coordinating Chemistry Enabled Highly Luminescent Perovskite Nanocrystals and Application in Micro-LEDs
papers.abstract: A facile route of synthesis for perovskite nanocrystals (PeNCs) via substitution of conventional strongly co-ordinating solvents with a compound solvent of Methylamine/Acetonitrile has been reported. It promotes the formation of stable, highly emissive PeNCs exhibiting a narrow photoluminescence (PL) peaked at 522 nm (FWHM ~27 nm), and a relatively high PLQY of ~70% in untreated thin films. Application of these PeNCs in LEDs has resulted in achievement of ~750 cd m-2 luminance. Their potential has been further explored by incorporating them in micropatterned LEDs using self-aligned photolithography. Micropatterned LEDs with 100 µm sized self-emissive pixels and a pixel density of 127 pixels per inch (PPI) show an external quantum efficiency comparable with unpatterned LEDs. These results demonstrate the first use of non-coordinating solvent approach for PeNCs emitting beyond red-NIR and their potential application for ultra high-resolution display, communication and AR/VR.

papers.title: Multi-material 3D Bioprinting of Complex Heterogeneous Constructs for In-vitro Mechanobiology Studies
papers.abstract: Multi-material bioprinting is a technology that enables the fabrication of complex, heterogeneous and/or multicellular constructs that can mimic the microenvironment of living tissues. These constructs can be used as models for in-vitro studies of stiffness-dependent cellular behavior, becoming highly relevant on disease states such as cancer or fibrosis, a disease where progressive tissue stiffening drives fibroblast activation, migration, and proliferation. In this study, PEGDA and GelMA-based biomaterial inks with varying polymer concentrations were used to demonstrate direct 3D bioprinting of double and triple-material constructs with defined soft, stiff, and/or extra stiff regions. Geometrically complex structures, including meshes, and cylinders were printed to show the versatility and precision of using these inks to create multi-material heterogeneous constructs with defined regions of stiffness. By having precise control over stiffness placement, these constructs provide a useful tool for studying how mechanical differences affect cellular behavior in a heterogeneous environment. As proof of concept of the use of these materials for mechanobiology studies, human lung fibroblasts (HLFs) were cultured on top of 3D printed constructs containing regions with three different stiffnesses. The results showed an increase in fibroblast activation with stiffness, characterized by α-SMA expression, F-actin organization, and increased cell density. When compared to single-material systems, multi-material constructs showed differences in fibroblast response across stiffnesses, highlighting the impact of mechanical heterogeneity in diseased tissue. This shows the potential of multi-material 3D bioprinting to address limitations of traditional single-material systems by providing a platform for modeling stiffness-dependent diseases, exploring cell-microenvironment interactions and advancing tissue engineering and regenerative medicine applications.

papers.title: Resolving Circuit Fitting Ambiguities of Impedance Spectroscopy in Light Emitting Electrochemical Cells using Distribution of Relaxation Times Analysis
papers.abstract: Light-emitting electrochemical cells (LECs) are gaining popularity as an easy-to-fabricate alternative to light-emitting diodes (LEDs). While Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) is the standard tool for probing LEC device dynamics, it suffers from a major analytical bottleneck when two processes occur at nearly the same time constants. This problem leads to ambiguous circuit fitting. Such non-uniqueness prevents the identification of the exact underlying physical mechanism, making the interpretation difficult. We address this by implementing the Distribution of Relaxation Times (DRT) analysis. We perform EIS across a range of bias voltages on LECs using the p-type conjugated polymer MEH-PPV (poly[2-methoxy-5-(2-ethylhexyloxy)-1,4-phenylenevinylene]) blended with an ionic liquid (IL). Using DRT, we successfully extract the distinct time constants of the various internal device processes. By comparing these DRT-derived time constants with traditional EIS fitting, we establish a way to get the true physical circuit.

papers.title: Stable Models, Unstable Candidates: Target Transferability in MOF Machine Learning for Gas Uptake Prediction
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) benchmarks for metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) often demonstrate high accuracy for a single adsorption condition; however, practical screening commonly reuses descriptors, models, or candidate lists across gases, pressures, operating conditions, and screening objectives. Here, we separate the conclusions that transfer from those that remain target specific. We benchmarked CO2 uptake at 0.015 and 0.15 bar and CH4 uptake at 5.8 and 65 bar at constant temperatures using an ARC–MOF-derived strict common cohort of 263,735 structures with compact geometries, enriched interpretable, and topology-augmented descriptors. The evaluation covered ridge regression, random forests, histogram gradient boosting (HGB), and neural network baselines under shared, repeated train/test splits. Target transferability was assessed through direct transfer with target-scale calibration, pretrain–fine-tuning transfer, and an independent per-target HGB baseline. Additional diagnostic analyses included residual overlap analysis, elite retrieval overlap, principal component analysis (PCA) of the descriptor space, and descriptor quantile profile. Descriptor/model rankings were highly stable across targets, with benchmark rank Spearman correlations of 0.85–0.99, and enriched or topology-aware random forests were consistently robust. Candidate-level conclusions are far less portable: residual overlap is selective, even when evaluated using a fixed enriched pore and topology descriptor with a Random Forest configuration across targets. Direct transfer often yields strongly negative ∆R2 values relative to target-specific scratch baselines, and the predicted top-5% overlap among test-set structures is sparse, except between the two CO2 pressures. In large-label regimes, reusing knowledge from another adsorption target is often less effective than training directly on the target, with many transfer variants yielding negative ∆R2 values relative to the matched scratch baselines. Thus, a single-target MOF benchmark can identify robust modelling choices without identifying reusable material shortlists. The workflow provides a reproducible and chemically interpretable reporting layer for safer multi-target adsorption ML and a more careful translation from benchmark accuracy to material selection.

papers.title: Learning from Nature: De novo Generative Design of Natural-Product-Inspired Opioid Agonists
papers.abstract: Developing safe and potent analgesics remains a critical global public health priority. Here, we show that generative de novo design can rapidly deliver novel opioid receptor agonists with high synthetic accessibility and desirable pharmacology. Inspired by the natural product mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, a complex metabolite found in traditional medicinal Kratom leaves, we leveraged its µ-opioid receptor binding characteristics to guide our generative computational framework. This deep learning approach successfully translated the partial agonism of the natural product and its G protein signaling bias into novel, structurally distinct chemotypes. One-third of the synthesized compounds exhibited potent receptor activation. Without requiring optimization, lead designs showed favorable pharmacokinetics, minimal off-target activity, and no β-arrestin recruitment. Cryogenic electron microscopy confirmed orthosteric receptor engagement, revealing that sub-pocket interactions alone do not account for their signaling behavior. By shifting away from stochastic high-throughput screening, this nature-inspired, artificial intelligence-driven workflow compresses discovery timelines while maximizing hit rates and molecular quality to deliver next-generation therapeutics.

papers.title: The Regularized Frozen Natural Orbital approach to CASPT2: extension to Restricted Active Space wave functions, different multiplicities and assessment of correlation effects
papers.abstract: The frozen natural orbital (FNO) method is a well-known approximation that significantly reduces the cost of many-body perturbation theory treatments for obtaining correlation energies in a systematic and controlled manner, enabling the simulation of larger and more realistic molecular systems. Here, we implement FNO on top of restricted active-space self-consistent field (RASSCF) wave function within second-order perturbation theory, leading to the FNO-RASPT2 method. To account for the additional approximations incurred when using restricted RASSCF wave functions, as well as to apply it to states of different molecular charge and spin multiplicity, we introduce a regularisation approach via a level-shift in the orbital deletion procedure, which helps avoid singularities resulting from vanishing denominators due to the reduced occupation of restricted (active) virtual orbitals and that we show does not significantly influence the final energies obtained. Numerical results on vertical excitation energies showcase the FNO to be up to ∼3.5 faster than the parent computation while retaining ∼95% of the dynamic correlation energy and being within 0.1 eV of the reference calculation, with the CASPT2 equations-the main bottleneck in large molecular systems-registering over an order of magnitude speed-up. An in-depth analysis shows the regularized FNO approach to retain electron correlation appropriately for internal and semi-internal contributions, while displaying larger deviations for the external term, which originates from the initial FNO truncation based on an approximated one-electron reduced density matrix. Ongoing efforts are directed towards improving and extending our current implementation to the calculation of analytic gradients and non-adiabatic couplings to enable faster non-adiabatic molecular dynamics simulations in larger and more realistic molecular systems.

papers.title: A Defect-Defect Feedback Loop Destabilizes MoS2
papers.abstract: Atmospheric O 2 spontaneously reacts with MoS 2 , but little is known about the mechanism. Herein, in-situ Raman spectroscopy during temperature sweeps under controlled environments show that MoS 2 is stable in O 2 -free environments, but O-substitution and MoO 2 formation occur in the presence of parts-per-million levels of O 2 , and oxidation to MoO 3 occurs at higher O 2 -levels. MoO 2 is stable at room temperature, but time-resolved experiments and density functional theory (DFT)-generated phase diagrams reveal it to be a metastable kinetic product that sequentially oxidizes at elevated temperatures, forming Mo 4 O 11 then MoO 3 . DFT calculations reveal that O-substitution makes both S-vacancy formation and O-substitution more favorable, creating a positive feedback loop that destroys MoS 2 . Experimentally, this feedback loop is embodied as formation of MoO 2 at progressively lower temperatures when either O-substitution or O 2 partial pressure in the environment are increased. These findings reveal that MoS 2 is inherently unstable in O 2 -containing environments due to synergistic effects of two defect types.

papers.title: Ultrafast Charge Separation Controlled by Aromatic Guests in a Perylene Dimer
papers.abstract: Engineering charge separation and recombination through non-covalent interactions offers a powerful route to functional photoactive materials without the need for covalent re-engineering. Here, we investigate the ultrafast excited-state dynamics of host-guest complexes formed between a valinolbridged perylene diimide (PDI) dimer macrocycle and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) guests using sub-50 femtosecond time resolution transient absorption spectroscopy. Macrocycle complexation with pyrene, perylene, and coronene introduces efficient charge-transfer pathways absent in the free host. Photoexcitation of the PDI dimer host leads to rapid quenching of stimulated emission and sub-picosecond formation of PDI radical anions, providing direct evidence for ultrafast hole transfer from the excited host to the PAH guest. The resulting charge-separated states persist for hundreds of picoseconds to nanoseconds before recombination. Analysis within the Marcus framework reveals that charge separation proceeds in a near-barrierless regime, whereas charge recombination lies deep in the Marcus inverted region, accounting for long-lived radical pair states. These results establish aromatic guest binding as a non-covalent handle for accessing fast, directional charge separation and long-lived charge-separated states in supramolecular donor-acceptor assemblies, relevant to light harvesting, photoredox catalysis and organic electronics.

papers.title: Head-to-tail cyclization of a peptide using a tethered homopolymer as a docking platform for ring-closing
papers.abstract: A physical extension to chemical procedures for head-to-tail cyclization of peptides at the single molecule level that uses a charged homopolymer (such as polyglutamate Em with m residues) as a tethered docking station to close a linear peptide at its N- and C-ends is proposed. The homopolymer may be anchored in one of three ways: 1) tethering one end to a nanopore in an electrolytic cell (e-cell); 2) immobilizing one end on a fixed glass slide similar to a flow cell surface in fluorosequencing and microarrays; 3) attaching it to and stretching it (fully) between two moveable platforms in an e-cell’s cis and trans chambers. The third option is similar to a recent proposal for general peptide modification (doi: 10.26434/chemrxiv.15006068/v1). Multiple molecules of the target peptide containing one internal Lysine (K) residue with unprotected side chain and the N- and C-ends capped are added to trans or the flow cell. Aided by a catalyst the K residue can form a lactam bond with any of the residues in Em; this docks the target onto Em. The target’s N- and C-ends are then uncapped to enable ring closing with the aid of a catalyst. Lactamization and ring closing can both be detected optically, the cyclized docked target can be cleaved from the homopeptide host orthogonally. Convergence of reactants was computationally simulated at a coarse-grained level; convergence occurs in a few milliseconds in both steps. Parallel head-to-tail cyclization can be done with an array of homopeptide anchors; with adequate peptide separation, docking and ring closing can occur without cross-talk. There are no solubility issues because of the tethering, so the purification required is minimal. The molar ratio of catalyst to target peptide in a reaction space 10 nm × 10 nm × (0.1-1.0) mm is 104-106; even though this is high virtually all of the excess products can be recovered and recycled. The method’s relative simplicity and low process complexity suggest that it may be suitable for the rapid construction of inexpensive macrocyclized peptide libraries.

papers.title: Programmable Regiodivergent Access to Non-natural α-Amino Acids via Cu/Pd-Catalyzed Asymmetric Propargylic Substitutions
papers.abstract: The ability to mimic nature’s efficiency in generating diverse, chiral molecules from simple precursors is a central quest in synthetic chemistry. Such divergence is crucial for rapidly exploring chemical space in drug discovery and biomaterial science, yet achieving it with man-made catalysts has been a formidable challenge. Here, we report a multisite programmable catalytic strategy that acts as a molecular “dial” to precisely steer chemical reactions down four distinct pathways from common starting materials. By leveraging a chiral copper catalyst to generate enantiocontrolled metalated azomethine ylides and, critically, distinct achiral palladium catalysts to regulate the reactivity of propargylic electrophiles, we achieve tunable control over chemo-, regio-, and stereoselectivity. This programmable platform delivers four distinct classes of chiral α‑quaternary α‑amino acids bearing alkyne, allene, alkene, or 1,3‑diene motifs in high yields and excellent enantioselectivity, thereby unlocking previously inaccessible chemical diversity.

papers.title: Imprinting chirality on a vibronic density of a non chiral vibrating molecule with a short femtosecond NIR chiral pulse
papers.abstract: Full quantum coupled electrons-nuclei dynamics show that electronic coherences resulting from multiphoton excitation by a femtosecond NIR chiral pulse drive the chirality of the vibronic density in the polar LiH molecule. The pseudoscalar, 𝑑(𝑡) = 𝝁(𝑡) ∙ (̇(𝑡)× ̈(𝑡)), built from the dipole vector, 𝝁(𝑡), and its first and second time derivatives, as well as the nonstationary electronic angular momentum 𝑳(𝑡) monitor the chirality both during and after the pulse. The electric field vector follows a 3dimensional temporal Lissajous curve. Reversing the pulse chirality flips the vibronic density chirality.

papers.title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Methods for Predicting Adiabatic Redox Potentials
papers.abstract: The prediction of the adiabatic potentials of one-electron oxidation and reduction processes, traditionally performed with DFT-based methods, is a computationally intensive and slow task. While predicted potentials can be utilized in various ways, such as assessing reactivity between molecules, the high resource requirements associated with their calculation limit their routine determination. Recently, machine-learning models have been adopted to predict these potentials, providing an simple and directly accessible alternative. The accuracy and precision of these models are heavily dependent on the underlying training data and the model architectures. These model architectures are usually selected based on intuition and rarely systematically compared with each other. Herein, we present a diverse and uniformly distributed dataset for reduction and oxidation potentials, the DFT-computed Adiabatic Redox Table (DART) dataset, covering 30 elements and molecules ranging from small (4 atoms) to medium size (54 atoms). We compare the novel dataset to the QM9 dataset, highlighting the diversity and uniformity of the DART dataset. We systematically evaluate molecular representations and model architectures, ranging from Morgan fingerprints to learned representations from machinelearned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), and from Random Forest to transformer-based models. Feed-forward neural networks with molecular representations derived from a MACE model trained on the OMol25 dataset (MACE-OMol) outperformed all other studied models, with MAEs of 0.078V for oxidation potentials and 0.112V for reduction potentials. This representation–architecture combination yields promising results on parts of the small experimental ROP-313 dataset out-of-the-box and improves further after fine-tuning models pre-trained on the DART dataset.

papers.title: Atomic Layer Deposition of Ferroelectric HfxZr(1-x)O2 from Metal-β-diketonate Precursors with Fine Cation Tunability.
papers.abstract: HfxZr1-xO2 (HZO) is a promising ferroelectric material for next-generation neuromorphic devices, where precise compositional control and complementary metal-oxidesemiconductor (CMOS) compatible processing are critical. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is particularly attractive for HZO integration due to its excellent conformality for future three-dimensional device architectures and possibility to control the composition. However, many widely used Hf and Zr precursors suffer from limited volatility and thermal stability. In this work, we exploit the robustness and favourable growth rates of the β-diketonate precursors Hf(thd)4 and Zr(thd)4 (thd = 2,2,6,6-tetramethyl-3,5heptanedionate) - with ozone co-reactant – to demonstrate the ALD growth of binary HfO2, ZrO2, and ferroelectric HZO thin films with finely controlled Hf/Zr cation ratios enabling the Hf/Zr composition required for ferroelectric thin films. Optimized binary ALD processes yield low growth-per-cycle (GPC) values of 0.085 Å/cycle for HfO2 and 0.12 Å/cycle for ZrO2, these low GPCs enable fine and reproducible control of the Hf:Zr

papers.title: Charge-State-Aware Machine-Learned Molecular Dynamics for Reactive Systems with Charge Transfer
papers.abstract: Conventional coordinate-based machine-learned interatomic potentials are single-valued, limiting their applicability to systems in which only a single charge state exists. Here, we introduce a charge-state-aware machine-learned molecular dynamics (MLMD) framework in which distinct charge-localized states are represented through alternative atomic labeling schemes within a unified machine-learned potential. Transitions between charge states are governed by energetic and configurational criteria learned directly from reference ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) trajectories. The method is demonstrated on the NH3 + NH3+ ion-molecule self-reaction, a system exhibiting competing proton transfer and charge (electron) transfer pathways. The resulting MLMD framework quantitatively reproduces AIMD charge-transfer event frequencies as well as relevant cross sections across all collision energies studied, while providing an approximately 1900-fold reduction in computational cost. The MLMD simulations also reproduce established state-selective trends, including the modest rotational dependence of proton transfer and the enhancement of charge transfer along with the suppression of proton transfer under umbrella mode excitation of the ammonia ion. These results demonstrate that conventional single-valued machine-learning interatomic potentials can be extended to describe reactive systems with evolving charge localization through learned transitions between distinct representations.

papers.title: Peptide Amphiphile-based Organelles for Fueled Synthetic Cells
papers.abstract: The bottom-up synthesis of life aims to replicate the characteristics of natural living systems from basic abiotic building blocks. In this context, synthetic cells based on liquid-liquid phase separation, such as complex coacervate droplets, have gained attention because they form spontaneously and readily take up molecules from their environment. More recently, we introduced fuel-dependent synthetic cells—coacervates that require fuel to form and decay unless periodically fueled. These synthetic cells are therefore under selection pressure to survive until the next fueling cycle. However, whereas natural cells rely on internal sub-compartments, complex coacervates typically lack structural heterogeneity. Here, we show that peptide amphiphiles can be activated in situ to generate discrete, phase-separated structures within complex coacervates. A chemically orthogonal stimulus enables spatiotemporal control over peptide assembly without disrupting fuel-driven phase separation. We further identify a reciprocal relationship: peptide assemblies alter the physical properties of the coacervate matrix, while the host compartment directs peptide morphology and assembly kinetics. These hierarchical assemblies function as artificial organelles within fueled synthetic cells. Together, they provide a strategy for integrating orthogonal supramolecular assembly with chemically fueled synthetic cells, enabling internal sub-compartmentalization, enhanced kinetic stability, and programmable morphology.

papers.title: From 'KGeP' to the Protonated P 4 -like Anion (HGe 3 P) 2− and the Endohedral Zintl Cluster [Mn@Ge 10 P 2 ] 3−
papers.abstract: Supporting information for this article is given via a link at the end of the document.

papers.title: Analysis of Rheo-SAXS Data from Dipeptide Micellar Dispersions Using CREASE-2D
papers.abstract: Rheology and small-angle X-ray scattering (Rheo-SAXS) combine the multi-scale structural information obtained from SAXS with rheological measurements enabling direct correlations between microscopic structure and resulting viscoelastic behavior. Under shear, soft materials can develop anisotropy in their structures as constituent molecules and/or assemblies reorganize in response to the shear. Although such anisotropy is captured in two-dimensional (2D) SAXS data, I (q, azimuthal angle), such orientational information can be lost if the 2D data are azimuthally averaged into one-dimensional, I(q) vs q form. To address this, recently a computational method called CREASE-2D (Computational Reverse Engineering Analysis of Scattering Experiments) has been developed to analyze directly the entire 2D SAXS data and interpret the structural arrangements including any anisotropy. CREASE-2D takes an input I (q, azimuthal angle) data and outputs all possible sets of structural features (i.e., mathematical descriptors of real-space structure) whose computed scattering matches the input scattering. In this paper, we extend CREASE-2D to interpret anisotropic SAXS patterns seen from dipeptide micellar dispersions under shear. Specifically, we analyze SAXS data that exhibit symmetric two-lobe patterns. We introduce an ( S 2 ) order parameter as a compact, rotation-invariant measure of two-fold anisotropy and incorporate it into CREASE-2D to preferentially sample sets of structural features that exhibit the same degree of orientational ordering as the experimental pattern. Furthermore, during comparison of computed scattering of structural features with input scattering, we introduce a wedge-focused structural similarity index metric (SSIM) that places greater weight on the angular sectors containing the scattering lobes while reducing sensitivity to the more isotropic regions of the scattering pattern. With these modifications in CREASE-2D we drive the optimization towards candidate sets of structural features that give a computed scattering that matches the lobe position, shape, and intensity of the input pattern. Together, these modifications enable more robust extraction of orientational ordering and morphology from anisotropic Rheo-SAXS data, providing a stronger connection between shearinduced structural evolution and macroscopic material response.

papers.title: Polyethylene conversion to mevalonate via catalyst-free autoxidation and bioconversion
papers.abstract: Hybrid chemical and biological processes are promising strategies to valorize recalcitrant plastic waste streams by generating soluble oxygenates that can be biologically converted into a single product. Here, we show that acetic acid-mediated autoxidation in the absence of metal catalysts can deconstruct high-density polyethylene (HDPE) to soluble oxygenates at 80 C-mol% carbon yield. These yields are a major improvement over metal-catalyzed autoxidation, and the chemistry readily translates to post-consumer substrates. Multiple analytical approaches enabled identification of major product classes, including dicarboxylic acids (DCAs), 2-oxocarboxylic acids (ketoacids), and -lactone acids. An industrially relevant bacterium, Pseudomonas putida, was engineered to efficiently utilize ketoacids via a unique β-oxidation pathway discovered via barcoded transposon insertion libraries and transcriptomics. P. putida was then engineered to convert HDPE-derived DCAs and ketoacids into mevalonate, an exemplary high-value chemical. Overall, this study demonstrates a carbon-efficient, catalyst-free process for solubilizing HDPE to mixed oxygenates and highlights the need to improve the bioavailability of polyolefin-derived intermediates from oxidation.

papers.title: Anion-templated Cu14 nanoclusters reveal ligand-controlled stability and catalytic evolution during electrochemical CO2 reduction
papers.abstract: Two atomically precise sulfide-templated Cu14 nanoclusters (NCs), [S@Cu14(4MBT)12(PPh3)6] (S@Cu14-4MBT) and [S@Cu14(3MBT)12(PPh3)6] (S@Cu14-3MBT), were synthesized and structurally characterized to investigate the influence of ligand engineering on the stability and electrocatalytic performance of Cu NCs during the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR). Single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis revealed that both NCs possess an identical S@Cu14 core architecture stabilized by twelve positionally different methyl substituted thiolate and six triphenylphosphine ligands, allowing direct evaluation of ligand effects without changes in core structure. Despite their structural similarity, positional variation of the methyl substituent generated distinct electronic environments, intermolecular interactions, and crystalpacking arrangements. The relatively electron-deficient Cu environment in S@Cu14-3MBT resulted in superior CO2RR performance, achieving Faradaic efficiencies of 52% for formate and 18% for CO at −1.4 V vs. RHE with suppressed hydrogen evolution, whereas S@Cu14-4MBT exhibited lower selectivity and stability. Post-catalytic analyses revealed degradation and ligand loss in S@Cu14-4MBT, whereas S@Cu14-3MBT remained structurally intact. These results highlight ligand engineering and anion templation as key strategies for tuning the stability and CO2RR performance of atomically precise metal NCs.

papers.title: Carbonate-Mediated Adsorption Switching Enables Alkaline Current Multiplication in Glycerol Oxidation on BiVO4
papers.abstract: Current multiplication in photoelectrochemical glycerol oxidation requires efficient electron injection from reaction intermediates into the metal centers that constitute the conduction band edge. On BiVO4, this demands intermediates coupling to V5+ sites, yet the intrinsic preference of glycerol for Bi3+ centers spatially separates intermediates from V sites and favors hole recapture. Here, we demonstrate that carbonate anions specifically adsorb on Bi3+ sites of BiVO4, blocking native glycerol binding and redirecting substrate adsorption to adjacent V5+ centers. This spatial switch anchors glycerol and its subsequent oxidation intermediates in direct electronic communication with the V 3d conduction band. Simultaneously, co-adsorbed carbonate acts as both a hydrogen-bond and a proton acceptor to accelerate dehydrogenation and facilitate deeper oxidation toward formate. When combined with a WO3 electron-transport layer, this interfacial adsorption switching boosts the photocurrent of the WO3/BiVO4 photoanode to 8.5 mA cm-2 at 1.2 V vs. RHE, achieving an incident photon-to-current efficiency of 157% at 400 nm and a formate production rate of 875 mmol m-2 h-1 with 89.1% selectivity. This work establishes anion-directed adsorption switching and electron-transport engineering as an effective strategy for promoting current multiplication in photoelectrochemical biomass valorization.

papers.title: The xenoreactome: where foreign chemistry becomes biological organization
papers.abstract: Biological systems can perform chemistry beyond their evolved reaction networks, but a reaction that is chemically possible does not necessarily occur in an intact system. I define the xenoreactome as the state-dependent network through which foreign chemistry enters a biological or cell-like system, is transformed and propagated, and is ultimately cleared or retained. The concept focuses on the factors that determine whether foreign chemistry is realized, including transport, localization, physiological state, downstream transfer and clearance. Xenoreactomes may remain entirely molecular, carry non-native chemical or elemental features through existing biological machinery, or support reaction sequences with no direct biological counterpart, such as sustained free-radical vinyl polymerization. In some cases, xenochemical products can also accumulate sufficiently to form polymers, condensed phases or other material states. For these systems, I introduce a simple quantitative criterion that relates xenochemical production and persistence to the threshold required for material formation. The xenoreactome provides a framework for asking which foreign chemistry biological systems can actually support, how far it propagates, and what ultimately happens to its products.

papers.title: Labelling of glycans using carbohydrate acetyltransferases via simple thioesters
papers.abstract: Glycosylation is a key modification on proteins and is present on at least 50% of the human proteome. The most common tools for glycan detection within complex biological matricies are affinity-based reagents such as antibodies and lectins. However, covalent labelling strategies could enable improved isolation methods as well as the introduction of bioorthogonal groups to the glycans. Here, we explore the engineering of acetyltransferases for the covalent tagging of specific carbohydrate structures. Acyl-coenzyme A (CoA) derivatives are readily accessed via thiol-thioester exchange between the free thiol of CoA and small-molecule thioesters. Using the galactoside acetyltransferase as a model system, we have demonstrated in situ acyl-CoA formation and enzymatic labelling. To access labelling of a more biologically relevant glycan, the polySia acetyltransferase NeuO was engineered to specifically transfer an azidoacteyl group from azidoacetyl-CoA onto polysialic acid (coliminic acid).

papers.title: Practical approach to improved temperature dependence of volatility for modeling partitioning of biomass burning organic aerosol
papers.abstract: Gas-particle partitioning of biomass burning organic aerosol (BBOA) depends strongly on temperature, so it is impacted by vertical transport. Atmospheric models commonly extrapolate vapor pressure and saturation concentration from a reference temperature using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, neglecting curvature associated with the constant-pressure heat capacity difference between the gas and liquid phases, ΔC p . Here, we compiled precise temperature-dependent vapor-pressure measurements for 100 oxygenated organic compounds and extracted vapor-pressure-encoded ΔC p values, examining their dependence on molecular size and functionality. All extracted ΔC p values are negative, with particularly large magnitudes for multi-oxygenated aromatic BBOA surrogates (average of −133 J K −1 mol −1 ), compared to mono-oxygenated phenolic compounds (average of −68 J K −1 mol −1 ). Incorporating negative ΔC p gives lower saturation concentrations upon cooling than conventional extrapolation and, consequently, greater particle-phase fractions, f. Representative ΔC p values of −100 and −150 J K −1 mol −1 , spanning much of the range observed for the BBOA surrogates, produce maximum shifts in f of roughly 8 and 12%, respectively, for cooling from 298 to 238 K, with the greatest effects for semi-volatile compounds near f = 0.5. Incorporating ΔC p therefore provides a practical, physically based refinement of volatility extrapolation of BBOA constituents during lofting.

papers.title: Activity and Photocorrosion of Cu2O-Modified N-Doped TiO2 in Photocatalytic Nitrate Reduction
papers.abstract: Photocatalytic nitrate removal depends on both catalyst composition and reaction conditions. Here, we systematically evaluated five variables for N-doped TiO 2 (N–TiO 2 ): nominal N/Ti precursor ratio, nitrogen source, calcination temperature, formic-acid concentration, and catalyst loading. All five showed non-monotonic effects on nitrate-N removal. The optimized sample, NT-1.0-400, achieved 90.6% removal after 2 h at a nominal N/Ti ratio of 1.0, 400 °C calcination, 80 mmol L⁻¹ formic acid, and 1000 mg L⁻¹ catalyst. Removal decreased to 18.3% without photocatalyst and 4.6% without formic acid, demonstrating the critical role of donor chemistry. XRD indicated predominantly anatase TiO 2 , while N 1s XPS features were assigned to Ti–O–N-related environments. Cu-containing modification nominally targeted as Cu 2 O gave 91.7, 93.2, and 82.5% removal at nominal Cu mass fractions of 5, 10, and 15 wt%, respectively. The highest value at 10% Cu represented only a modest increase over N–TiO 2 and coincided with a yellow-to-purple-red color change consistent with Cu-phase evolution. Without formic acid, removal fell to 7.8% and no comparable color change occurred. Because nitrogen products were not quantified, nitrate disappearance cannot establish denitrification or product selectivity. Overall, the results show that apparent nitrate-removal performance is governed by the coupled effects of catalyst preparation, donor chemistry, and catalyst stability, and should not be judged by endpoint conversion alone.

papers.title: Palladium-catalyzed C(sp3)-C(sp3) bond construction of benzylic alcohol derivatives using hydrazone umpolung chemistry
papers.abstract: Transition metal-catalysis for C(sp3)-C(sp3) bond formation has largely relied on the use of non-renewable chemical feedstock such as alkyl halides. In the recent years, efforts to switch to sustainable chemical feedstocks have become a critical topic in organic synthesis. Owing to its accessible and sustainable pathways for preparation, the use of benzylic alcohol and its derivatives in transition metal catalysis have emerged as an alternative to non-renewable fossil fuel-based building blocks. Herein, we report a palladium-catalyzed alkylation of mesitoyl derivatives of benzylic alcohols with umpolung hydrazones. Using hydrazones derived from readily available carbonyl compounds, the established method tolerates diverse functional groups as well as heteroaromatics while exhibiting good scalability. This protocol provides an efficient path for C(sp3)-C(sp3) bond formation from accessible starting materials catalyzed by a palladium-NHC complex.

papers.title: Exchange in transient covalent assembly
papers.abstract: The hydration of carbodiimides is commonly used to drive nonequilibrium chemical systems, often by converting carboxylic acids into transient aqueous anhydrides. This fuel reaction has found broad applicability in functional systems, from single-molecule motors to responsive bulk materials. The reaction cycle is usually presented in terms of activation (anhydride formation) and deactivation (hydrolysis) steps. Here, we investigate the additional role of exchange within the activated state. Slowly hydrolyzing anhydride dimers and polymers, representative of transient covalent assemblies, were generated using carbodiimide and then treated with distinct carboxylic acids. The formation of new anhydrides was monitored using 13 C NMR spectroscopy, allowing rate constants to be determined. The anhydrides exchange at an intermediate rate, with on the order of 10 exchange events per hydrolysis reaction under typical conditions. This process yields unique behavior. At long reaction times, the ratios of different anhydride assemblies do not trend toward the equilibrium distribution (fast exchange limit), nor are they determined solely by activation/deactivation rates (slow exchange limit). Instead, it is possible to favor distinct species because of the balance between exchange and deactivation. The implications of this result for the assembly of nonequilibrium species with covalent bonds is discussed.

papers.title: pH-Dependent Divergence of Oxidative Degradation Pathways in Verapamil Hydrochloride: A Forced-Degradation Study by LC-UV and High-Resolution Orbitrap Mass Spectrometry
papers.abstract: Verapamil hydrochloride is a phenylalkylamine calcium channel antagonist whose central tertiary amine constitutes its principal site of chemical vulnerability. Forced degradation studies conducted under ICH Q1A(R2) conventionally treat hydrogen peroxide exposure as a single oxidative stress condition. In this work, neutral and acidified peroxide stress were compared directly using reversed-phase liquid chromatography with diode-array detection coupled to high-resolution Orbitrap mass spectrometry. Verapamil hydrochloride was subjected to acidic, alkaline, thermal and oxidative stress, with the oxidative condition performed both at neutral pH and in the presence of added hydrochloric acid. No degradation was detected under acidic or mild alkaline hydrolysis. Under neutral peroxide stress, verapamil N-oxide (m/z 471.2853, +1.1 ppm) was the dominant degradation product; the combined chromatographic peak areas of parent drug and N-oxide accounted for 95–104 % of the area measured in unstressed samples, indicating near-quantitative conversion along a single pathway. Under acidified peroxide stress no N-oxide was detected, while a species assigned as the N-dealkylation product D617 (m/z 291.2067, −1.0 ppm following internal recalibration) was observed at 23.5 min. Norverapamil (m/z 441.2748, +1.4 ppm) was detected under oxidative stress but not in the unstressed control, indicating formation during degradation rather than presence as a process-related impurity. These findings indicate that solution pH governs which primary oxidation product is formed, and that peroxide stress conditions should specify pH when used to establish method specificity.

papers.title: A dual-criterion computational filter for the identification of selective MexABOprM efflux pump inhibitors: cross-family validation and control of MexRmediated derepression risk
papers.abstract: Drug repositioning against bacterial efflux pumps has classically relied on a single criterion: the predicted binding affinity for the target transporter. This approach overlooks a distinct failure modetranscriptional derepression of the pump's own expression, through inhibition of the associated transcriptional regulator. Here we propose a dual-criterion screening protocol, combining (i) a relative selectivity index between affinity for the MexB pump and affinity for its repressor MexR, and (ii) an absolute risk threshold calibrated on a documented derepression inducer (pyocyanin). The method was tested by molecular docking (AutoDock Vina) on 139 compounds spanning four independent chemical families (antidepressants, antipsychotics, H1 antihistamines, phytomolecules), against the MexB (PDB 3W9J) and MexR structures. The ΔG(MexB)–ΔG(MexR) correlation proved robust and generalizable across the four families (r = 0.834–0.924, all p < 10-7 after FDR correction), validated by bootstrap, permutation testing, and leave-one-out analysis. Controlling for molecular weight and LogP across the full dataset (n = 135) confirms a partial but non-exclusive contribution of molecular size to this correlation (partial r = 0.805 vs. raw r = 0.880). The dual-criterion filter revealed that 43.1% of the tested compounds, despite showing a good relative selectivity index, exceed the absolute risk thresholdamong them the historical reference compound PAβN and the previously proposed candidate vilazodone. Ensemble docking on three MexR structures (1LNW, 3ECH, 3MEX), performed on a subset of 14 priority compounds, quantified the associated structural uncertainty (mean standard deviation 0.512 kcal/mol): this test confirms the robustness of vilazodone's at-risk status, but reveals that a candidate initially classified as favorable (mianserin) becomes at-risk once this uncertainty is taken into account. These results indicate that filtering by relative index alone is insufficient to rule out derepression risk, and propose a reproducible methodological framework, including an uncertainty estimate, for drug repositioning in the context of combination therapy.

papers.title: Well-Mixed Dynamic Adsorber Model for Designing Cyclic Adsorption Processes
papers.abstract: The design and optimization of adsorption-based gas separations relies on process models that predict key performance indicators (KPIs) as functions of adsorbent properties and operating conditions. The one-dimensional axially-dispersed plug-flow (1-D ADPF) model is the established benchmark, but its computational cost limits its use in high-throughput tasks such as large-scale adsorbent screening and multi-objective process optimization. Existing simplified models achieve orders-of-magnitude speedups, yet the assumptions of a well-mixed adsorber and instantaneous equilibrium introduce large systematic errors in predicted KPIs. In this work, we present a dynamic well-mixed approximation of the 1-D ADPF model that retains the computational efficiency of prior well-mixed formulations while substantially improving predictive accuracy. The adsorber is represented by a well-mixed volume (or two in series for special cases). The formulation accounts for non-isothermal operation, finite heat and mass transfer rates, and linear pressure drop. The model is validated against experimental data and the 1-D ADPF simulations–including the solution of multi-objective optimization problems–across three representative applications: (I) pressure-vacuum swing adsorption (PVSA) for post combustion carbon capture; (II) temperature-vacuum swing adsorption (TVSA) for direct air capture; and (III) vacuum swing adsorption (VSA) process with light reflux for oxygen production from air. Across the first two cases, the well-mixed dynamic adsorption model predicts product purity and recovery, as well as specific energy consumption and productivity, with median deviations below ±0.35% while reducing simulation times by more than two orders of magnitude. Larger deviations were observed for the third case targeted towards light product recovery, but the well-mixed model correctly captures the overall trends in KPI trade-offs. The sensitivity of model accuracy to column geometry, mass transfer coefficient, and degree of bed utilization is systematically assessed, and practical validity boundaries are identified. These results establish a fast and accurate framework for adsorption process screening and optimization.

papers.title: A Continuous Parameter Model forChemical Bonds and the Bond Energy – Bond Length Scaling Law
papers.abstract: This paper reports two empirical findings in the field of chemical bonding: (1) The lattice energy of ionic crystals satisfies a linear relationship U = k_type·z1z2/d0 + 215 with ionic separation, achieving an equivalent mean error of 2.73% across 33 crystals, outperforming the classical Born-Landé equation (4.44%); (2) A systematic bond length differentiation exists in non-regular polyhedral coordination molecules. We define a "structural looseness" parameter δ = (d_max − d_min)/d_avg and establish a quick-reference table for 12 coordination geometry types. Extrapolation validation on BrF5 (not included in fitting) achieves endpoint prediction deviation < 0.3%. Additionally, the D·d product scaling law is verified on ~90 chemical bonds, and bond length prediction is extended to 82 bonds with equivalent mean error 3.1%. The model achieves calculator-level computational cost with industrial-grade accuracy, providing a complementary analytical framework to DFT.

papers.title: From Roughness to Reactivity: Platinum Nano-patches on Polymer Particles for PFAS Degradation and Defluorination
papers.abstract: Drinking water contaminated with polyfluoroalkyl and perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) poses a danger to human health due to their exceptional stability and chemical properties. Sometimes they are referred to as ”forever chemicals” because of their strong carbon-fluorine bonds, which make it very difficult to break their chemical structure. PFAS continue to exist in the environment, accumulate and grow over time, and are associated with serious health issues, including cancer, liver issues, immune system malfunction, and congenital disabilities. PFAS are chemically stable and resistant to natural deterioration. Drinking water tainted with PFAS may therefore be extremely dangerous to one’s health. In this work, real-time analysis of platinum-coated polystyrene (PS) particles shows how a homogeneous coating forms and emphasizes the significance of the reaction-aging effect. By generating reactive oxygen species during the catalytic reaction, the studded platinum nanoparticles, with their large surface area, degrade dissolved PFAS in water. Short-chain PFAS are more difficult to remove, although long-chain PFAS can decompose into short-chain molecules. Using heptafluorobutyric acid as a model PFAS chemical, this study examines the time-dependent development of platinum nanoparticles and the degradation of PFAS at concentrations ranging from 0.214 mg/L to 1.712 mg/L and to 10.7 mg/L, with a higher removal efficiency of 86.63% at 0.214 mg/L. Quantitative 19F NMR analysis revealed a fluorine removal efficiency of 54.5% with 10.7 mg/L, indicating substantial oxidative transformation under the applied reaction conditions. In situ FESEM analysis shows that 3 hours of platinum growth on polystyrene results in a smooth, uniform coating. The nanoparticle coverage indicates the influence of aging on the growth of platinum nanoparticles and their catalytic activity in removing heptafluorobutyric acid.

papers.title: Reprogramming Phosphorus(III) Chemistry Via Iminyl Phosphines Reactivity
papers.abstract: Polar phosphorus(III) chemistry is dominated by a limited number of well-established reaction pathways, restricting opportunities for fundamentally different synthetic transformations. Here, we uncover the reactivity of P(III) iminyl phosphines in aqueous media, establishing a versatile synthetic platform for the selective mono- and difunctionalization of electron-deficient substrates. These transformations proceed through the formal oxidation of phosphorus from P(III) to P(V), providing a mild strategy for installing phosphoryl groups into organic molecules. Water plays a decisive role by promoting a stepwise cyclization pathway, as supported by experimental and computational studies. The methodology displays exceptional scope and functional-group tolerance, enabling the functionalization of diverse bioactive substrates while providing direct access to valuable phosphorus-containing building blocks. The resulting products are readily diversified through downstream transformations. More broadly, our findings reveal that the reactivity of P(III) compounds can be profoundly transformed using iminyl phosphines, expanding phosphorus chemistry to previously inaccessible molecular scaffolds.

papers.title: Interplay of Depletion-Interaction and Viscosity Drives Non-Monotonic Ligand Binding to DNA G-Quadruplex under Crowding
papers.abstract: The study of ligand binding to G-quadruplex (G4) DNA under molecular crowding is essential for understanding its implications in cellular context; however, the underlying mechanism remains largely unresolved. Here we investigate the binding of TMPyP4 to parallel c-MYC G4 DNA under EG/PEG crowding using steady-state and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS). Ligand binding affinity (K) to G4 exhibits a pronounced non-monotonic, U-shaped dependence on crowder size – first decreasing due to viscosity-induced hindrance, then recovering for larger PEGs. Kinetic analysis of FCS data reveals that this arises from competing effects of crowder-induced viscosity and depletion interactions on ligand association (݇k on ) and dissociation (݇k off ) rates. A modified Collins-Kimball-Debye formalism, combined with hybrid MD simulations, shows that larger crowders create polymer-free depletion cavities that accelerate ligand/G4 association, counteracting viscous drag. These results provide a generalizable framework that connects polymer physics to nucleic acid-ligand recognition, useful for G4-targeted drug design in the crowded cellular milieu.

papers.title: Stability assay for screening non-aqueous redox flow battery materials.
papers.abstract: Non-aqueous redox flow batteries are a promising grid-scale energy storage platform; however, identifying stable redox-active molecules can be both time- and cost-prohibitive. To address these limitations, we developed a miniature-bulk electrolysis setup that can quickly assess cycling stability (e.g., discharge capacity and capacity fade) using milligram quantities and commercial glassware. This method can screen non-aqueous solvents, electrolytes, posolytes, and negolytes. By reducing waste and increasing efficiency, this new assay should streamline the discovery of redox-active molecules for redox flow batteries.

papers.title: C-H activation and C-C coupling of arenes promoted by a room-temperature-stable barium amidinate electride
papers.abstract: Carbon–carbon (C–C) coupling reactions are fundamental transformations in modern synthetic chemistry that are traditionally dominated by platinum group metal (PGM) catalysts. The scarcity, cost and toxicity of PGMs have inspired the quest for more sustainable alternatives. Alkaline earth (AE) metals have attracted a lot of interest due to their high earth abundance, though their applications in CC coupling reactions remain underdeveloped as a result of the limited redox chemistry of these metals. AE-electrides could offer a new strategy to fully unlock AE-mediated C–C coupling, owing to their higher accessibility with respect to low oxidation state complexes, and strong reducing power. Here we show how the pseudo-linear barium amidinate complex [Ba(L)2] (1-Ba, L = {C(Cy)(NDipp)2}–, Dipp = 2,6-diisopropylphenyl, Cy = cyclohexyl) was converted into the room-temperature-stable electride (RoSE) {K2[Ba(L)2]∙2e–} (2) via mechanochemical methods. The formation of an electride was confirmed via pulsed EPR studies that reveal magnetic communication between anionic electrons and ligand and metal spin-active nuclei (1H, 14N and 135,137Ba). Compound 2 activates arenes and performs

papers.title: Fluoropolymers Across Their Lifecycle: Why "Emissions Reduction" is not "Safe"
Molecular echoes of a hot Earth
papers.abstract: The effect of evolution on the fundamental thermodynamic properties of proteins has not been fully clear. Ancestral protein reconstruction has now revealed that Earth’s ancient high temperatures promoted entropy-driven ligand binding in a transcription factor family, while planetary cooling over billions of years led to favouring enthalpic mechanisms. Protein–ligand binding involves a complex thermodynamic balance. The binding free energy determines protein–ligand affinity and arises from two main factors: enthalpy, reflecting energy gained through specific interactions such as hydrogen bonds and electrostatic forces, and entropy, reflecting changes in disorder and the energetically favourable release of water molecules from hydrophobic surfaces. For decades, computational biology and drug discovery have primarily focused on enhancing enthalpic interactions by engineering complementary shapes and chemical groups to strengthen contacts. However, it has remained unclear whether evolutionary processes shape the fundamental thermodynamic contributions to binding and whether the physical environment can modulate these mechanisms.

papers.title: Chemical Similarity-Informed Machine Learning for Navigating Multi-Component Polymeric Material Design Space
papers.abstract: Chemical representation remains a central obstacle to applying machine learning (ML) in polymer science, and the difficulty compounds in multi-component formulations, where each polymer, solvent, and additive must be featurized independently and the inter-component interactions that often govern material properties go unencoded. Here we introduce a similarityinformed ML framework that, instead of encoding explicit chemical structures, represents each system by the pairwise chemical similarity between its components and uses these scalars as training features. Because it depends on relative similarity rather than on specific structural features, the representation is low-dimensional and inherently chemistry-agnostic. We validate the framework on block copolymer (BCP) thin films processed by non-volatile additive solvent annealing (NVASA) and blending, using high-throughput GISAXS analysis to assemble a dataset of over 700 nanoscale morphology measurements. Collapsing thousands of structural features into only 49 similarity descriptors, the framework matches the accuracy of the state-of-the-art full-feature and deep-learning baselines, with test R2 values of 0.986 for domain spacing and 0.835 for FWHM, while training in minutes rather than hours and yielding interpretability at the level of component pairs through SHAP analysis. An uncertainty-based active learning strategy reaches comparable accuracy using only 11% of the training data. Most importantly, the framework generalizes to 10 BCP thin films built from 5 previously unseen polymers and 2 unseen solvents (validation R2 of 0.928 for domain spacing) and transfers to an independent polymer solubility classification task, where it outperforms a Morgan-fingerprint benchmark on unseen chemistries. Together, these results establish a computationally efficient, interpretable, and generalizable representation of polymer chemistry for ML, enabling rapid exploration of vast chemical and processing spaces.
