We have shown that at high pH, when the positive charges are largely neutralized due to deprotonation of the amine groups in the lysine monomers, the strands show a clear tendency to form bundles of rigid and vertically elongated pLL molecules driven by intermolecular attractions caused by hydrophobic repulsion from the aqueous medium. On switching off the hydrophobic interaction, we see no bundle formation and the screened coulomb repulsions dominate pushing the strands away from each other, underscoring the essential role of hydrophobic interaction in pLL structuration. We see a similar tendency to move away from each other by keeping the charges fixed at high reduced temperatures as well. These results agree nicely with experimental observations of the different phases of pLL, in particular the formation of fibrils at high pH and room temperature. Once we established the pLL model, we introduced negatively charged single ATP beads. Based on the screened coulomb attractions between the polymers and the molecules, we could predict the crossover point where the repulsive regime gets converted into an overall attractive one leading to nucleation and growth, resulting into coacervation. We could, therefore, correlate the ATP/pLL ratio to the forces dictating the phase separation process – for the first time to the best of our knowledge. Additionally, we could find the radial charge and ATP and pLL bead density distributions which allows us to understand the internal structures of the condensates.

papers.title: Data-Driven Discovery of Boronic Acid Catalysts for Amidation Reactions
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly recognized as a powerful tool for catalyst optimization in organic synthesis. Yet, applications are often restricted by the need for large datasets, programming expertise, and specialized knowledge in model development. Boronic acidcatalyzed amidation reactions represent an attractive target for AI-guided optimization because of their synthetic relevance, detailed mechanistic understanding, and the need for improved catalysts for amidations. Here, an AI-guided workflow for catalyst optimization in boronic acidcatalyzed amidation reactions was established using the large-language model ChatGPT for code generation and workflow development. A dataset was generated by high-throughput screening of 459 arylboronic acids and combined with DFT-derived steric and electronic descriptors of the catalysts for model training. The model enabled the identification of the unprecedented catalyst FIBA with higher activity than the benchmark catalyst MIBA. In addition, detailed data analysis of the highly active but poorly predicted diboronic acid catalyst DBA led to the identification of a distinct activation mode involving higher-order boronate aggregates that activate and preorganize the amine nucleophile. Thus, improved catalyst performance and new mechanistic insight were obtained through an AI-guided workflow.

papers.title: From 2D Graphs to Sub-Unit pKa: Nine Iterations to Beat MolGpKa on Both Scaffolds and Sulfonamides
papers.abstract: Accurate pKa prediction for drug-like molecules remains a significant gap between com- mercial tools (Epik ∼0.5 RMSE, MoKa ∼0.4 RMSE) and open-source methods, particularly for sulfonamides and heterocyclic N–H compounds prevalent in medicinal chemistry. We present a systematic nine-iteration ablation converging on a routed ensemble that outperforms MolGpKa on both general scaffolds and sulfonamides simultaneously—the first open-source model to do so. Starting from a 2D molecular graph baseline (v1, SAMPL7 RMSE 3.48), we isolate each variable: global xTB descriptors help scaffolds but not sulfonamides (v2); data augmentation fails (v2-aug); per-atom Mulliken charges help sulfonamides but hurt scaffolds (v3); routing combines both (v4, SAMPL7 2.19). We then identify the architectural gap with MolGpKa: per-atom pKa output targets trained on microscopic data. Per-atom output alone fails with macroscopic labels (v5). Microscopic labels from Uni-pKa improve scaffolds but not sulfonamides (v6). Merging microscopic and macroscopic data with a mixed loss produces the first model with no tradeoff (v7, scaffold 1.31, SAMPL7 1.32). Adding full xTB charge coverage solves sulfonamides (v8, SAMPL7 0.535) but hurts scaffolds. The final routed ensemble (v9) achieves scaffold RMSE 1.255 (R2 0.878) and SAMPL7 RMSE 0.535 (R2 0.948)—beating MolGpKa by 62% on scaffolds and 45% on sulfonamides, with calibrated uncertainty and zero failure rate. All models trained on open data (IUPAC, ChEMBL, Uni-pKa) with open-source tools (xTB, RDKit, Chemprop).

papers.title: ChemMoB: Contribution-Aware Dynamic Multi-Modal Balance for Chemical Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Molecular property prediction underpins virtual screening, reaction design, and toxicity assessment, yet most deep learning models reason from a single molecular view—typically a two-dimensional graph or a SMILES string. Such single-modality representations discard complementary signals that chemists routinely exploit: the three-dimensional conformation governs quantum behavior, the textual description encodes sub-structural intent, and spectroscopic measurements provide direct experimental evidence. A further difficulty is that these modalities contribute unequally across tasks and training stages, so naive fusion lets a dominant modality suppress the others and fails when a view is missing. We propose ChemMoB (Chemistry-aware Multi-modal Balance), a framework that ports contribution-aware dynamic multi-modal balancing to chemical representation learning. ChemMoB encodes four complementary views of a molecule—a 2D graph, a 3D conformation, a SMILES/Transformer text stream, and a 1D spectroscopic signal—and fuses them through a Contribution-aware Dynamic Balance (CDB) module that re-estimates per-modality weights every epoch. To handle missing or noisy inputs, ChemMoB adds a generative spectral enhancement head, a static-to-dynamic lift that reconstructs an approximate 3D embedding from the 2D graph, and a provenance watermark that flags unreliable spectra. We evaluate ChemMoB on QM9 (quantum properties), ESOL (aqueous solubility), and ADMET binary tasks (blood-brain barrier penetration and hERG liability). ChemMoB consistently outperforms single-modality and fixed-fusion baselines, reducing QM9 average MAE by 12.0% over fixed fusion and improving BBBP and hERG AUROC to 0.873 and 0.831. Ablations confirm that the dynamic balance module and the static-to-dynamic enhancement are the principal sources of gain, and that ChemMoB remains robust when up to 30% of spectral inputs are dropped.

papers.title: Sustainable Synthesis of MIL-100(Fe) for Efficient Asphaltene Removal: Adsorption Performance, Reusability, and Data-Supported Mechanistic Insights
papers.abstract: Asphaltene precipitation and deposition remain major flow assurance challenges, yet solid adsorbents are often reported without sufficient links between uptake, model discrimination, uncertainty, and mechanism. Here we present green hydrothermally synthesized MIL-100(Fe) as a reusable nanoadsorbent for asphaltene removal from toluene model oil, supported by characterization, adsorption experiments, and a fully traceable data-analysis package. The material exhibited a BET surface area of 1950 m2 g−1, a pore volume of 1.63 cm3 g−1, and an average pore diameter of 3.3 nm. Adsorption approached equilibrium within about 60 min, reached 179.7 mg g−1 at the highest tested concentration, and achieved 83.2% removal under the low-concentration optimum. MIL-100(Fe) retained 72.1% removal after four cycles. Nonlinear isotherm fitting, information-criterion ranking, and bootstrap analysis supported Langmuir-type uptake at 298–318 K, while kinetic diagnostics indicated rapid pseudo-second-order behaviour with additional heterogeneous-surface contributions. Thermodynamic and molecular weight sensitivity analyses confirmed spontaneous, exothermic adsorption. FTIR shifts support pore filling, aromatic interactions, hydrogen bonding, and contacts with FeO/coordination environments. This work positions MIL-100(Fe) as a high-capacity, regenerable, and mechanistically auditable adsorbent for asphaltene mitigation.

papers.title: DNA Binding Metal-Peptidic Helicates as Minimal Coiled-Coil Mimics
papers.abstract: Metal-organic helicates are precisely defined nanoscale assemblies which have been widely used in biological applications due to their high stability, ready synthesis, and selective interactions with DNA. However, most have been formed predominantly from rigid aromatic panels or single, continuous pseudopeptidic chains, limiting their specific interactions with biological systems and potential for variation. Coiled-coils are common structural motifs in DNA binding proteins, enabling precise orientation of DNA binding a-helices. Herein, we merge these two concepts, creating metal-peptidic helicates (c. 3 nm long) which form from three individual, defined, a-helical architectures, with precisely controlled chirality, bridging the typical length scale of metal-organic helicates (1 nm) and coiled coils (c. 10 nm). We synthesise of a series of novel M2L3 metal-peptidic helicates (M = Fe(II) or Ni(II)) using bipyridine functionalised, Aib stabilised, a-helices, in which metal coordination brings together three individual peptide chains in a chiral, supercoiled, structure reminiscent of coiled-coil domains. By changing bipyridine substitution site, the handedness of the helicate structure (ΔΔ or ΛΛ) can be switched independently of peptide sequence. We demonstrate that these helicates possess exceptional stability in water, and are capable of selectively binding DNA three-way junctions (3WJs) over other DNA secondary structures – offering a highly tunable platform for developing selective binders for biological applications.

papers.title: Simulation of the Impact of Dust Particles on Carbon-Carbon Composite at Hypersonic Velocities in the Presence of Atomic Oxygen
papers.abstract: Comprehending the influence of reactive atomic species on the nanoscale mechanical response of Carbon-Carbon (C-C) nanocomposites remains a fundamental challenge in predicting coupled mechanical-chemical response in materials exposed to extreme environments. Specifically, leading-edge/nose-cone of hypersonic vehicles are exposed to extreme environments where shock-induced loading, particulate impact, and high-temperature oxidation occur simultaneously. Therefore, a detailed study of coupled synergistic thermo-mechanical and chemical processes occurring in thermal protection materials (TPM) is of great importance and poses significant challenges due to its complexity. In this work, reactive molecular dynamics (RMD) simulations are employed to study nano dust nanoparticle (~10 nm) impact at hypersonic velocity on a C-C composite surface, after traversing through a leading-edge shock layer. Unlike rain droplets, solid dust nanoparticles maintain their structural integrity while traversing through the shock layer, leading to concentrated momentum transfer and significantly deeper craters. The crater depth increases non-linearly with impact velocity ranging from Mach 6 to Mach 12, in accordance with hypervelocity impact theory. In addition, atomic oxygen (AO) interactions with the C-C composites’ surface are also examined, revealing oxidation-induced surface morphological reconstruction primarily characterized by CO production, resulting in C-C composite surfaces’ structural reordering. Interestingly, subsequent impacts from dust nanoparticle on the AO reacted C-C surface result in decreased crater depth due to AO induced morphological changes. A non-dimensional scaling law is established to correlate RMD predictions with experimental data, exhibiting consistent power-law behavior across different length scales.

papers.title: An analytical potential energy surface and variational transition-state theory kinetics of the NH3 + Br → NH2 + HBr hydrogen-abstraction reaction
papers.abstract: We report the first full-dimensional analytical potential energy surface (PES) and a variational transitionstate theory (VTST) study of the endothermic gas-phase reaction NH3 + Br −−→ NH2 + HBr, completing the halogen series (NH3 + F, Cl, Br) of the group’s analytical surfaces. Stationary points and energetics were benchmarked at the CCSD(T)/CBS level with the bromine 3d shell frozen; a −3.51 kcal/mol spinorbit correction was added to the NH3 + Br asymptote for the Br(2P) splitting. The benchmark locates a genuine, product-like (Hammond) saddle 17.6 kcal/mol above reactants but submerged 2.1 kcal/mol below the NH2+HBr asymptote (zero-point-and spin–orbit-corrected). A valence-bond/molecular-mechanics PES was calibrated to reproduce these stationary points to better than 0.25 kcal/mol; it retains an exact analytical gradient and dedicated van der Waals wells for the entrance (NH3···Br) and exit (NH2···HBr) complexes. Canonical variational theory with multidimensional tunneling (µOMT) yields forward rate constants over 200 K to 2000 K. Because the adiabatic barrier lies below the product asymptote, the tunneling coefficient is unity and the reverse reaction NH2 +HBr −−→ NH3 +Br exhibits a negative apparent activation energy, as measured for the carbon analogue CH3 +HBr. Quasi-classical trajectories on the same surface, once product zero-point leakage is accounted for, reproduce the variational forward rate as an independent check of the barrier. In the absence of experimental data, the forward rate constants are presented as predictions anchored to the high-level energetics.

papers.title: Temperature-Dependent Tensile and Fracture Behavior of Single-crystal and Polycrystalline Wurtzite GaN: A Molecular Dynamics Study
papers.abstract: The mechanical reliability of gallium nitride (GaN) power and optoelectronic devices depends on the intrinsic tensile response of the films, yet this response remains largely uncharacterized. Here, molecular dynamics simulations with the Nord–Albe–Erhart–Nordlund Tersoff potential are used to investigate the uniaxial tensile behavior of single-crystal and polycrystalline wurtzite GaN loaded along the [0001] direction. Polycrystals containing 10–40 Voronoi grains (mean grain diameter 5.8– 3.7 nm) are deformed at temperatures from 300 to 1200 K, and the single-crystal baseline is first validated against experimental and first-principles elastic data. Introducing grain boundaries reduces the ultimate tensile strength to 33–35 % of the single-crystal value (from 38.9 to 13.0–13.5 GPa) and the axial modulus to 65–72 % (from 329 to 213–237 GPa). Both quantities are essentially independent of grain number, a signature of the inverse Hall–Petch regime. Structural, atomic-strain, grain-rotation, and dislocation-extraction analyses consistently show that deformation is accommodated by grain-boundary sliding and shuffling rather than intragranular dislocation glide, with the crystalline grain interiors remaining intact up to failure. Temperature degrades the polycrystals far more than the single crystal, reducing their strength by 48 % and stiffness by 31 % because the disordered grain-boundary phase softens rapidly with heating. While the single crystal fails by abrupt brittle cleavage, the polycrystals fail by progressive intergranular void coalescence that becomes increasingly gradual at elevated temperature, revealing a brittle-to-quasi-brittle transition. These results identify the grain-boundary phase as the controlling factor for the strength, stiffness, and fracture of nanocrystalline GaN.

papers.title: Development and Validation of a Liquid Chromatography-Tandem Mass Spectrometry Assay for 4-Methylumbelliferone in Human Urine to determine the activity of Urinary β-Glucuronidase
papers.abstract: A method for quantitation of 4-Methylumbelliferone (4-MU), the aglycone of 4-Methylumbelliferone b-D-Glucuronide (4-MUG), in urine was validated. 4-MUG was spiked into urine samples, incubated at physiological temperature for four hours, and 4-MU concentration determined utilizing reversed phase Liquid Chromatography-Tandem Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Linearity was demonstrated over the concentration range from 10ng/mL to 1,000ng/mL. Matrix effects were not significant for the lots of urine used in the present validation. Percent accuracy ranged from 93.01% to 102.87%, and the coefficient of variation ranged from 0.89% to 7.26% for 4-MU over the concentration range. The results of the validation process described below illustrate the suitability of this method in the pursuit of urinary β-Glucuronidase (GUSB) activity quantification. This method represents a vast improvement upon currently available colorimetric or fluorometric assays for β-Glucuronidase activity, both of which perform poorly in urine samples.

papers.title: Automated Pharmacophore Hypothesis Generator for SILCS-Pharm: ph4gen
papers.abstract: Here we present ph4gen, a tool for the automated generation of pharmacophore hypotheses developed for use with the site identification by ligand competitive saturation (SILCS) technology. It builds upon the previously established SILCS-Pharm approach which generates the pharmacophore features from a given macromolecular structure, and SILCS-Hotspots which identifies potentially-druggable binding sites. The tool examines a set of pharmacophore features, typically 15-20, and ranks all permutations of hypotheses of a desired length, with default of 4 to 5 features per hypothesis. A diverse data set of seven proteins (namely, BACE1, CDK2, JNK1, P38, PTPT1B, Thrombin, and TYK2) and 336 ligands was used to train the logistic regression model which ranks these hypotheses and recalls at least one experimental pharmacophore hypothesis in four of seven cases in the top 10. The model was tested on a set of four separate proteins (namely FXR, HDM2, HSP90, and TRMD) and 354 ligands and recalls at least one experimental pharmacophore hypothesis in the top 5 in all four test systems, with mean precision and recall of 0.23±0.06 and 0.15±0.04, respectively. We show that the distribution of hypotheses generated is similar to that of the validated hypotheses, and that even in cases of near-misses, the pharmacophore hypotheses have similar chemical features to validated ones. The tool can also be tuned to provide greater or lesser chemical diversity when utilized in virtual screening. Ultimately, ph4gen is a useful tool as part of the SILCS workflow to identify druggable binding sites, generate drug-like pharmacophore hypotheses, and rank in silico hits for experimental validation.

papers.title: Profiling the N-Acyl L-Homoserine Lactone Landscape: How Acyl Chain Length (C1–C20) and 3-Oxo Modification Drive LuxR Receptor Activation and Inhibition
papers.abstract: Common bacteria coordinate group behaviors in a cell-density–dependent manner through quorum sensing. In Gram-negative bacteria, quorum sensing is typically mediated by LuxI/LuxR systems, where LuxI-type synthases produce N -acyl L-homoserine lactone (AHL) signals that are detected by LuxR-type receptors to regulate gene expression. Although AHLs share a conserved Lhomoserine lactone headgroup, receptor selectivity is encoded by the acyl tail, which varies in length and oxidation state. Here, we systematically interrogate the chemical determinants of AHL activity by synthesizing a set of 37 analogues spanning all acyl chain lengths from C1 to C20 with and without 3-oxo substitution. Evaluation of these compounds across seven LuxR-type receptors using cell-based reporter assays revealed detailed structure–activity relationships linking acyl tail architecture to receptor modulation. We identified distinct chain-length optima for agonism and antagonism and demonstrated that both parameters are strongly receptor-dependent. Interestingly, many of the antagonists displayed non-classical partial agonism behavior, with both antagonistic and agonistic activity on a receptor depending on concentration. Together, these results define several key chemical features governing LuxR:ligand recognition and establish generalizable principles for tuning AHL activity across some of the most studied LuxR-type receptors. This work also provides a framework for understanding how structural variation in native AHLs influences signaling specificity and for building hypotheses about the potential roles of LuxI/LuxR quorum sensing on interspecies interactions in complex mixed-microbial environments.

papers.title: Instantaneous Mechanical Programming of Polymer Microparticle Shape and Surface Architecture
papers.abstract: Structurally anisotropic polymer microparticles with controlled surface topographies are essential for applications in selfassembly, interfacial engineering, and responsive materials. However, practical methods for fabricating such complex morphologies remain limited. Here, we demonstrate an instantaneous mechanically driven strategy for simultaneously programming particle shape and surface architecture through a refined rubbing process. By optimizing particle plasticization, pressure distribution, and stress transmission, spherical polymer particles were transformed into cylindrical particles within only 10 s. Patterned silicon substrates enabled direct mechanical transfer of periodic surface structures, while variations in substrate topology and deformation pathway produced diverse anisotropic architectures. This simple mechanically driven process provides a straightforward platform for programming hierarchical polymer microparticle architectures.

papers.title: Quantitative Prediction of Skin Sensitization Potential of SNAr chemicals: A Quantum Mechanical Approach
papers.abstract: Skin sensitization is a critical endpoint in human safety risk assessment. Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (S N Ar) reaction substrates are classified as one of the chemical groups with high skin sensitization potential, capable of covalently binding with skin proteins and triggering a cascade of immune responses that lead to skin sensitization. In this study, we employed quantum mechanics and density functional theory (QM/DFT) methods to predict the skin sensitization potential of S N Ar substrates. We investigated the thermodynamic properties of the complete reaction pathways involving selected chemicals and protein surrogates, specifically, methylthiolate and methylamine, which serve as surrogates for cysteine and lysine residues, respectively. Our findings demonstrate a robust correlation (R 2 > 0.96) between activation energies derived from QM/DFT calculations and pEC 3 values obtained from the local lymph node assay (LLNA). The method can not only accurately distinguish between sensitizers and non-sensitizers (with 100% accuracy), but also can categorize chemicals’ skin sensitization potency with 90% accuracy. Furthermore, this research advances our understanding of the reaction mechanisms between S N Ar substrates and skin protein surrogates, providing valuable insights into Key Event 1 in the Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) for skin sensitization.

papers.title: Cellulose Microfibril Interfacial Sliding to Regulate Load Transfer in Plant Primary Cell Walls through Direct or Polymer-Mediated Contact: Insights from Molecular Dynamics
papers.abstract: Plant cell wall mechanics depend on molecular interactions between cellulose microfibrils (CMFs) and surrounding matrix polysaccharides. Here, classical molecular dynamics simulations and static energy calculations using the ReaxFF interatomic potential are used to investigate hydrated and unhydrated CMF/CMF, CMF/xyloglucan/CMF, and CMF/pectin/CMF interfaces across three crystallographic orientations. CMF/CMF interfaces exhibited facet-dependent interfacial energetics and sliding resistance. In vacuum, the hydrophilic (110)/(110) interfibrillar interface had the most favorable dry work of adhesion, whereas in water the hydrophobic (100)/(200) interface exhibited the most favorable hydrated association. However, interfacial work of adhesion and sliding resistance were not directly correlated. The maximum calculated shear stresses for the (100)/(200), (110)/ (110), and (11̅0)/(11̅0) interfaces were 530, 209, and 839 MPa, respectively, which are consistent with experimentally correlated values and supporting interfibrillar sliding as a dominant mechanism for plastic deformation of the plant primary cell wall. Polymermediated interfibrillar interfaces exhibited less favorable hydrated interfacial energetics and reduced shear sliding resistance, suggesting that matrix polysaccharides modify CMF contact geometry, hydration, and sliding pathways and not as load-bearing connectors under our modeled conditions. Overall, these results connect interfacial chemistry and mechanical response, providing new insight into the molecular origins of load transfer and plastic deformation in plant cell walls.

papers.title: Pareto-guided Monte Carlo tree search explores multi-objective trade-offs missed by scalar antimalarial generation
papers.abstract: De novo molecular generation often collapses multiple design objectives into a single scalar reward, obscuring trade-offs between potency, synthetic accessibility and drug-likeness. We present a Paretoguided Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) framework that maintains a non-dominated front across multiparameter optimisation (MPO), synthetic Bayesian accessibility (SYBA), resistance-resilience (RRS) and polypharmacology-network (PNS) scores, guided by a scaffold-aware fragment policy derived from ChEMBL27 frequencies and Tanimoto compatibility. A four-method benchmark across 20 independent seeds (fixed search budget) shows that random search achieves the highest mean reward (0.733 5), followed by MCTS (0.727 6), deterministic greedy search (0.721 1) and a genetic algorithm (0.702 7); the MCTS–random gap is small (mean ∆ = 0.005 9, 95% CI [0.000 8, 0.011 0], paired t19 = 2.41, p = 0.026). MCTS is therefore competitive on scalar reward and, within our fragment-vocabulary oracle design, is the method that returns a multi-objective Pareto front of non-dominated candidates (four solutions, hypervolume 1.236 6) spanning the potency–accessibility trade-off, including the high-potency / low-accessibility extreme that fixed-weight scalar aggregation discards. To our knowledge this is the first Pareto-guided MCTS to fold resistance-resilience and polypharmacology-network scores into the generation objective, in contrast to generic affinity/drug-likeness metrics in prior Pareto-MCTS generators, with the honest caveat that in the present front these domain scores remain comparatively homogeneous. Component ablations identify the scaffold-aware policy (∆ = +0.148) and the Pareto front itself (∆ = +0.108) as the dominant drivers of performance. All code, molecule sets and score tables are deposited under an open licence. These results position MCTS as a complementary multi-objective explorer rather than a universal single-objective optimiser. Scientific Contribution: We introduce a Pareto-guided MCTS framework for de novo antimalarial design that maintains a non-dominated front across potency, synthetic accessibility, resistance-resilience and polypharmacology-network scores, guided by a scaffold-aware fragment policy. Against a four-method benchmark across 20 seeds, MCTS is competitive with random search on scalar reward while uniquely recovering a multi-objective Pareto front spanning the potency–accessibility trade-off. Component ablations identify the scaffold-aware policy and the Pareto front itself as the dominant drivers of performance.

papers.title: AutoSolvate 2.0: Automated End-to-End Explicit-Solvent Molecular Simulation for Chemically Diverse Molecular Systems
papers.abstract: Electronic-structure calculations in solution often require explicit solvent to describe hydrogen bonding, ion pairing, charge transfer, and solvent reorganization. However, preparing explicit-solvent simulations remains labor-intensive because force-field generation, system construction, molecular dynamics (MD) sampling, and quantum-chemical calculations typically rely on multiple software packages. Here, we present AutoSolvate 2.0, a modular, open-source framework that automates end-to-end explicit-solvent simulation workflows for chemically diverse systems. A new AutoMCPB module automates the MCPB.py parameterization workflow for transition-metal complexes, while generalized system representations enable mixed solvents, multiple solutes, and multicomponent electrolytes at arbitrary compositions. AutoSolvate 2.0 integrates force-field generation, solvated-system construction, MD simulations, and microsolvated-cluster extraction through standardized software wrappers. It also provides complementary JSON, interactive command-line, and Model Context Protocol interfaces for high-throughput calculations and integration with large language model (LLM) agents. We demonstrate these capabilities through three applications of increasing complexity. AutoSolvate 2.0 reproduces the solvent-dependent absorption spectrum of an aqueous transition-metal photosensitizer, the microsolvation structure of water–acetonitrile mixtures, and the ion-pairing structure of a multicomponent redox-flow-battery electrolyte. These results show that AutoSolvate 2.0 can generate simulation-ready explicit-solvent models across diverse chemical environments while substantially reducing manual intervention, providing a versatile platform for solution-phase quantum chemistry and AI-assisted computational workflows.

papers.title: Accelerated Green SN1 Reactions of the 9-Phenyl-9-fluorenyl Group
papers.abstract: Unimolecular nucleophilic substitution (S N 1) reactions are expedited by resonant acoustic mixing (RAM). 9-Phenyl-9-fluorenyl (PhF) halides were rapidly made from PhF-OH by RAM of concentrated toluene - mineral acid mixtures. By RAM of PhF-Br and Et₃N in environmentally benign propylene carbonate, N-PhF-amino esters were synthesized from hydrochlorides including serine and hydroxyproline esters without alcohol side chain protection. Ester saponification with RAM gave efficiently N -PhF-amino acid. The RAM-assisted S N 1 chemistry proved proficient for greener PhF installation.

papers.title: Chemical Control of Quorum Sensing Rewires Mixed Bacterial Communities
papers.abstract: Microbial communities are central to host and environmental health, yet their dysregulation can drive disease. Chemical strategies to selectively reprogram community composition remain limited. Here, we show that agonists of the accessory gene regulator ( agr ) quorum sensing system provide a powerful, non-bactericidal approach to reshape Staphylococcal biofilm communities. In mixed biofilms of multiple Staphylococcus epidermidis strains, selective agr activation produces pronounced, sequence-dependent shifts in community composition in vitro . This targeted remodeling enhances susceptibility of the community to antibiotic treatment. Extending this strategy to interspecies systems, we demonstrate that agr agonists reduce the abundance of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus by >95% in mixed biofil ms with S. epidermidis , without relying on bactericidal activity. Notably, the efficacy of agr -mediated community control is modulated by iron availability, revealing an environmental layer of regulation. Together, these findings support quorum sensing agonism as a chemically precise strategy to manipulate microbial communities by exploiting intrinsic signaling differences, with implications spanning human health and agriculture.

papers.title: Generalising metallaphotoredox alkyl and aryl methylation with photoactive quinoline-based organoaluminium
papers.abstract: Herein, we report a quinoline-based photocatalyst that enables the highly important yet challenging metallaphotoredox methylation with high efficiency and generality, accommodating diverse coupling partners, including derivatives from carboxylic acids, alcohols, amines, halides and arenes. Central to this breakthrough lies the rational design of a hydroxylated diarylquinoline as a non-innocent ligand, thus in situ evolving photocatalytically active aluminium complexes. Such a distinct paradigm not only formulates a dynamic platform uniquely suited to produce and tailor the otherwise elusive methyl radical for downstream cross couplings, but also establishes a privileged photocatalytic scaffold that could expand the synthetic repertoire of less explored main-group elements. Of equal importance, our diversity-oriented strategy demonstrates broad translational utility in drug discovery by late-stage methylation of pharmaceutically relevant compounds. These efforts eventually culminated in a methylated analogue with potent antitumour activity in vitro and in vivo, which remained unknown in the current literature and was synthetically challenging using existing methods.

papers.title: N-Arylation of Inosine and 2’-Deoxyinosine with Diaryliodonium Reagents and Atropisomerism of the Products
papers.abstract: The first examples of arylation reactions of inosine and 2’-deoxyinosine by diaryliodonium salts are described herein. Because the amide moiety in these purine nucleosides is an ambident nucleophilic site, the first consideration was whether aromatization of the purine ring would lead to aryl ethers or whether reactions would occur at the ring nitrogen atom. Using appropriate experiments, the nitrogen atom was shown to be the reaction center. Reactions of the two nucleosides proceeded well with Cu(OAc) 2 and Cs 2 CO 3 , in PhMe at 60 o C. That Cu I is a likely catalytic species was demonstrated via the in situ formation of CuOAc. Reactions with five symmetric and fourteen asymmetric diaryliodonium salts were performed. Of the latter five contained a non-transferred (dummy) ligand. In all cases, N -arylation was predominant, although minor O -arylation was observed in some cases. Reactions also provided insight into the impact of electronic and steric differences on the transfer of aryl rings from the iodonium salts, effect of TfO – versus TsO – counterion, as well as reactivity differences between the ribo and 2’deoxyribonucleoside precursors. In some cases, atropisomers were evident due to axial chirality resulting from the newly-formed N–C bond. In one case, the atropisomers were chromatographically separable, but the products re-equilibrated even at –20 o C in solvent. In a second case, the atropisomer mixture was analyzed by NMR spectroscopy. It was found that this phenomenon can result due to the saccharide OTBS protecting group and/or the substituent on the introduced aryl ring. This work is the first demonstration of reactions of nucleosides with diaryliodonium salts, product distributions in these reactions, and the N–C axial chirality that can be observed in some of the ensuing products.

papers.title: Covalently Grafted Molecular RuBda Catalyst on Pristine and S-doped gC3N4 for Controlled Photocatalytic Ammonia Oxidation
papers.abstract: Across various fields, interest in hybrid heterogeneous molecular materials is steadily increasing due to their tunability and versatility. Selective ammonia oxidation represents an attractive strategy for nitrogen-cycle closure, concomitantly generating proton equivalents relevant in hydrogen-related energy conversion processes. Here we report the first hybrid system capable of conducting photocatalytic ammonia oxidation (AO), consisting of a molecular ruthenium catalyst (RuBda; Bda = 2,2′ bipyridine 6,6′ dicarboxylate) covalently anchored onto graphitic carbon nitride (g C3N4, CN) and Sulfur-doped g C3N4 nanoparticles (10P, 50P). The resulting hybrid photocatalysts (CNRuBda, 10PRuBda, 50PRuBda) combine the light harvesting properties and robustness of C3N4 with the well-defined reactivity of Ru in the catalytic centre of the RuBda moiety. Covalent grafting via surface –NH2 defects enables high Ru loadings (up to 5.5 wt%) while preserving the structural integrity of the C3N4 framework. Electrochemical studies show that immobilised RuBda retains its intrinsic AO activity, exhibiting a ~0.33 V (vs NHE) cathodic shift of catalytic onset and turnover frequencies up to 5.6 s-1 (CNRuBda). Under Xe lamp irradiation, all hybrid catalysts oxidise NH3 to N2 and H+, with CNRuBda producing up to 9.09 µmol N2 in 3 h, a TOF of 1.55 × 10-3 s-1, and a cumulative TON of 44 over three cycles. Accompanying minor NO2- formation and background N2 evolution highlight the intrinsic complexity of AO. Overall, this work establishes the first proof-of-concept molecularly functionalised C3N4 photocatalysts for selective AO.

papers.title: Structural Dynamics and Optical Spectra of the Phycobiliprotein PC612 Complex
papers.abstract: Phycocyanin 612 (PC612) is a light-harvesting complex found in cryptophyte algae, characterized by its distinct open structure and flexible protein conformation, allowing the algae to survive in low-light aqueous environments. Although cryptophyte algae are known to show a diverse range of spectroscopic properties, the complex electronic structures and photophysical properties of their pigment molecules, known as bilins, are not yet fully understood, particularly in terms of how the surrounding protein environment influences them. In this study, we performed quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics simulations with excited-state calculations utilizing a numerically efficient density functional tight-binding method to examine the structural dynamics and optical features of bilin molecules within an open-form PC612 complex. Our results indicate that the protein matrix significantly controls the fluctuation of excitation energies and excitonic couplings of the pigment network. Very different from (bacterio)chlorophyll containing systems, thermal fluctuations induced by the environment have a minimal effect on the pigment spectral densities due to similar electron density distributions in the ground and excited states. The computed absorption spectra calculated at different temperatures are in reasonable agreement with the experimental counterparts, accurately predicting the relative peak positions and confirming the validity of our findings.

papers.title: Lignin self-photocatalytic depolymerization
Gold-Catalyzed "Anti-Baldwin" Cyclization of Unactivated Alkenes
papers.abstract: Owing to the unfavorable orbital alignments and geometric constraints, 5-endo-trig cyclizations are kinetically disfavored as stated by Sir Jack Baldwin. Consequently, reports of such cyclization are scarce and primarily rely on the use of activated alkenes. Herein, we report a rare example of "anti-Baldwin" cyclization of unactivated alkenes. The key to the success of this transformation is that the kinetically favored 4-exo-trig cyclization is reversible, thereby enabling equilibration to the thermodynamically favored 5-endo-trig cyclization intermediate which then undergoes reductive elimination to form the product.

papers.title: Comparative Computational Analysis of Selective vs. Non-Selective NSAIDs.
papers.abstract: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs represent one of the most widely used classes of therapeutic agents globally [1]. While traditional non-selective drugs inhibit both cyclooxygenase-1 and cyclooxygenase-2, second-generation selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors were rationally designed to minimize gastrointestinal toxicity [2]. However, the secondary effects of these structural changes on pharmacokinetic profiles and tissue distribution are not fully explored. In this study, an integrated computational workflow combining ADME profiling and molecular docking simulations was applied across eight representative drugs divided into five non-selective agents and three selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors. Molecular docking into crystal structures of cyclooxygenase-1 (PDB ID: 1EQG) and cyclooxygenase-2 (PDB ID: 6COX) confirmed that selective inhibitors bind with significantly stronger affinity to cyclooxygenase-2 compared to non-selective agents (p = 0.023), resulting in a pronounced selectivity differential (p = 0.004) [3, 4]. Inferential statistical testing revealed that targeting the secondary active-site pocket of cyclooxygenase-2 requires bulky, polar extension groups that significantly increase molecular weight (p = 0.012) and topological polar surface area (p = 0.041) [5]. Consequently, while all evaluated compounds retained high gastrointestinal absorption and complete Lipinski rule compliance, every selective inhibitor was excluded from crossing the blood-brain barrier [5, 6]. These findings highlight a fundamental biophysical trade-off in drug design, showing that engineering structural selectivity for peripheral gastroprotection inherently limits central nervous system penetration.

papers.title: Small details with large impacts: guidelines for reproducible NaBH4-mediated syntheses of surfactant-free colloidal gold nanoparticles at room temperature
papers.abstract: The controlled synthesis of nanomaterials remains a general bottleneck, often related to challenges in reproducibility. A range of seemingly non-relevant parameters can crucially impact the outcome of a synthesis. In particular, gold nanoparticles can be very easily obtained at room temperature in seconds by simply using water, HAuCl4 and NaBH4 without the need for other chemicals. Despite the very promising features of this surfactant-free colloidal approach, its potential remains largely under-exploited. Here, we first detail the strong influence of the type of the reaction vessel used, the impact of different suppliers of the chemicals, the influence of direct or sequential addition of NaBH4, the effect of using inert gas and the impact of temperature on the resulting size of the gold nanoparticles obtained. It is found that the synthesis is rather reproducible but particularly sensitive to the geometry of the vessel used, mixing of the chemicals and chemicals used. There is no benefit to use a controlled gas atmosphere or high temperatures to achieve small size nanoparticles. The sequential addition of NaBH4 is a convenient original approach to achieve size control for this synthesis. Finally, the nanoparticles are shown to be readily active catalysts for Congo Red degradation and to study size effects. The results clarify important pitfalls for improved reproducibility in this synthesis strategy for a wider use of this convenient approach and to make the most of the resulting materials.

papers.title: BN-Sequence Extension of Heterophenalene Analogs via the Sugasawa-type Double Annulation: Single-Atom Sequence Perturbation Controls Molecular Binding in Isoelectronic Scaffolds of BN-Embedded Aromatics
papers.abstract: It is important to understand how a contiguous sequence of boron and nitrogen atoms in aromatics (BN sequence) modulates sp 2 /sp 3 interconversion at a boron center upon molecular binding, particularly for metal-free catalysis. However, suitable model compounds remain scarce due to limited synthetic access. Here, we report a strategy based on the Sugasawa reaction to extend the BN sequence from boron diaminonaphthalene (Bdan) with an NBN pattern to a branched sequence along two zigzag directions, embedding a BN 3 unit as a binding site. This approach is also applicable to an NCN-patterned heterophenalene analog based on diazaphenalene (DAP), affording the same 24π-electron scaffold and enabling a direct comparison of single-atom-perturbed BN sequences in molecular binding behavior. NMR analyses revealed sequence-dependent sp 2 /sp 3 interconversion of boron, consistent with solvatochromism and thermochromism. Calculations indicated that the BN sequence modulated not only the LUMO but also the delocalization circuits. A global 22π-diatropic circuit was observed in the sp 2 state of the Bdan-derived molecule, but not in the DAP-derived molecule, supporting the distinct sp 2 /sp 3 interconversion of the boron centers. This work extended BN sequences from stable heterophenalene precursors along two zigzag directions for the first time, elucidating the impact of single-atom perturbation on BN sequences.

papers.title: Towards Reactive Electrochemical Transport Using the Lattice Boltzmann Method. Part I: Electrostatics, Hydrodynamics, Species Transport, and Electrokinetic Benchmarking
papers.abstract: This work presents the first stage in the development of a lattice Boltzmann framework for reactive electrochemical transport. The present study focuses on the verification and validation of electrostatics, hydrodynamics, ionic species transport, and coupled electrokinetic phenomena using analytical benchmark solutions. A modular lattice Boltzmann framework is developed in Fortran, in which independent distribution functions are employed to solve the Poisson equation, Navier–Stokes equations, and Nernst–Planck equations within a unified computational framework. The numerical solutions are systematically compared with the corresponding analytical solutions, demonstrating excellent agreement for the electrostatic potential, electro-osmotic velocity, ionic concentration profiles, and the fully coupled electrokinetic system. The benchmark presented in this work establishes a robust and extensible numerical foundation for future developments toward reactive electrochemical transport and multiscale electrocatalytic simulations.

papers.title: Unlocking Net-Negative Methanol Synthesis: Reactive Capture and Conversion Enabled by Computational Amine Screening
papers.abstract: Net-negative methanol production has long been constrained by an energy penalty. The thermal energy required to release captured CO2 (desorption) often offsets the net carbon benefit of the entire conversion cycle. We address this issue through a staged Reactive Capture and Conversion (RCC) process. This system bypasses the energy-intensive desorption step by directly hydrogenating the captured CO2 within the capture solvent. The captured carbon is converted to methanol through staged reactions, each carried out in its own optimal chemical environment. To identify optimal amines that mediate each stage, we screened 176 million compounds using a graph neural network (GNN)-based molecular screening framework. We identified piperidine as the key mediator, which facilitates the rate-limiting C–N bond cleavage and markedly raises the methanol yield. Our system achieves a single-pass methanol yield of 56%, which is more than three times the yield of conventional CO2 hydrogenation and double that of industrial coal-to-methanol synthesis. It delivers net-negative emissions while achieving a minimum selling price of $0.55/kg, which is competitive with fossil-based market prices. Comprehensive techno-economic and life-cycle assessments across 24 major countries further confirm that the proposed RCC platform remains robust under diverse supply scenarios. These findings demonstrate how molecular-level engineering can be translated into a globally deployable strategy for carbon-negative manufacturing.

papers.title: A guideline to FAIR data reporting for metal-organic frameworks
papers.abstract: Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are porous, crystalline materials with tunable properties that have shown to be effective for gas storage, separation, and catalysis. Their chemical and structural versatility yields materials with enormous surface areas that are promising for the generation of clean energy, environmental remediation, and advanced chemical processes. To make MOF syntheses reproducible and to facilitate the transition from the lab bench into industrial applications, reliable and standardized data reporting is crucial. In this work, we propose a generic, format- and system-agnostic guideline on how to describe MOFs and their syntheses with the aim to foster the generation of ‘FAIR MOF’ data. The described approach offers a fundamental set of recommended information to be provided for MOF synthesis, description, and characterization, and it suggests details on how the information should be reported, e.g., by proposing default units or by defining the conditions under which a certain information should be provided. Those guidelines build on previous work and includes, complements, and harmonizes existing approaches developed by other researchers in the field. Our work forms the basis for a comprehensive scheme on how to report and publish MOF-related scientific work, aiming to support reproducible and comparable data collection and publication as well as the development of well-structured, comprehensive databases.

papers.title: Modular synthetic approach for crane corroles
papers.abstract: The chemistry of corroles has experienced a resurgence in recent years and has gained importance for potential applications in catalysis, as chemical sensors, and as therapeutics in medicine. This is due to the versatility of corroles in forming stable complexes with a wide variety of transition metal ions, thereby exhibiting diverse properties. To enhance the activity of the molecules, post-functionalization is required, which can present synthetic challenges. This paper describes a very simple method for synthesizing a variety of functionalized corrole molecules from an easily synthesized corrole via a Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling reaction. The yields range from 42 % to 96 %. Furthermore, first investigations of intramolecular interactions with the corrole core were performed.

papers.title: ALIGNing Learned Representations: Domain-General Models Triangulate Physicochemical Interactions in Analytical Separations
papers.abstract: Despite rapid progress, foundation models for chemistry have yet to consistently deliver broadly transferable, experiment-grounded representations for structure-to-measurement tasks in practice. This reflects both the scarcity and fragmentation of experimental datasets and the weak alignment between common molecular representations (e.g., SMILES and graphs) and measured chemical behaviour. Here, we formalize domain-general models: pretrained models constrained across multiple measurement contexts within a physically coherent domain to learn transferable chemical representations that capture how molecular structure gives rise to experimental observables. Using liquid chromatography as a testbed, we develop ALIGN and show that it outperforms conventional baselines, including foundation models and transfer learning approaches, across diverse chromatographic contexts while retaining performance in data-limited and chemically out-of-distribution settings. By training across multiple chromatographic methods, ALIGN triangulates an underlying physicochemical interaction space, with each method providing a complementary projection that constrains the learned representation. We show that ALIGN learns embeddings consistent with physicochemical properties and chromatographic principles and provide evidence for a mechanism underlying improved method-specific adaptation. These representations transfer to related analytical modalities, including GC, CCS, and DMS, suggesting that these measurements encode overlapping physicochemical relationships. Together, these results demonstrate the value of physically grounded representation learning and suggest that domain-general approaches may extend to other fragmented scientific domains.

papers.title: Conversion of 5-Hydroxymethylfurfural to 2,5-Furandicarboxylic Acid with an Engineered Alcohol Dehydrogenase
papers.abstract: The conventional synthetic organic wisdom emphasizes and exploits molecular fragment chemistry, the division of reactant into partitioned fragments (e.g., functional group and appendage groups) as distinct reactivity effecting units, for reaction development. The loosely coordinated and limitedly defined reactivity manifested in direct reaction or reaction under chemical catalysis translates to the narrow reactivity effecting scope and minimum range of reactivity. We propose herein a synthetic organic logic of molecular totality chemistry, the utility of totality of reactant as integral reactivity effecting unit. The precisely coordinated and expansively defined reactivity manifested in reaction under biological catalysis (e.g., enzymatic catalysis) translates to the broad reactivity effecting scope and maximum range of reactivity. In particular, an engineered alcohol dehydrogenase has been developed herein for the enzymatic catalysis conversion of 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) to 2,5furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA), featuring the hitherto elusive, simultaneous operation of two pathways: HMF to 2,5-diformylfuran (DFF) to 5-formyl-2-furancarboxylic acid (FFCA) to FDCA and HMF to 5-hydroxymethyl-2-furancarboxylic acid (HMFCA) to FFCA to FDCA. The catalytic isolation and orthogonality of HMFCA-to-FFCA conversion herein, as against the rest of the pathways, exemplifies the very essence of molecular totality chemistry and promises its powerful synthetic organic utility in reaction development.

papers.title: Risk-controlled battery parameterization from electrochemical impedance spectroscopy for model inputs and measurement planning
papers.abstract: Physics-based parameterization from electrochemical impedance spectroscopy increasingly supplies parameters to battery models, yet a spectrum constrains some parameters far better than others. Across 87 spectra from 13 commercial lithium-ion cells, fits that are indistinguishable in residual disagree on diffusion quantities by 1.6 to 3.3 orders of magnitude while the ohmic resistance is essentially unchanged. A low fitting error therefore cannot license a complete parameter set, and we treat parameterization as a decision made one parameter at a time. For a 48-parameter porous-electrode impedance model, each parameter is estimated by whichever of eight regularized fits its own diagnostics favor, and is reported only when out-of-sample evidence supports it under a stated error budget. On model-generated spectra this recovers 28 of 48 parameters, replicated on three independently generated panels, and certifies about 10 parameters per run with 96 percent of them correct. Measurement design matters more than estimator strength: a balanced grid of 7 temperatures and 7 states of charge gives the certified yield of a full-frequency sweep using 36 percent of the impedance points. Applied to the 13 measured cells, the same rules return an auditable conditional parameter record and name the missing measurement for every parameter they decline.

papers.title: Identifiability-aware battery EIS parameterization with empirical risk-controlled hand-off
papers.abstract: Battery models can be degraded by EIS-derived parameters that fit spectra well but are not uniquely constrained: across 87 measured spectra from 13 commercial cells, equal-residual fits disagree on diffusion by 1.6–3.3 decades. We convert this hazard into risk-controlled parameter hand-off and measurement allocation: a coordinate-wise router selects each of 48 coordinates among eight regularized estimators, and an empirical risk controller accepts individual claims under a false-claim budget, behind out-of-distribution and frequency-support vetoes. Routing lifts development-panel recovery to 28.0 of 48 and replicates at 27.78, 26.82, and 27.82 on three disjoint, truth-isolated model-consistent panels generated after hash-freezing; the best validated point yields 10.38 correct claims per run at 0.960 realized precision. In a locked within-class transfer study, hand-off cuts median unseen-condition error from 0.163 to 0.018 versus documented defaults, yet the best predictor is a single prior-anchored fit recovering far fewer coordinates than routing: prediction accuracy does not certify parameters. A balanced 7 × 7 temperature–state-of-charge design matches full-frequency enrichment within the prespecified equivalence margin using 36% of the impedance points. On the measured cells the pipeline returns an auditable conditional record per cell while vetoing out-of-domain certification; real-cell parameter truth and hardware battery-management benefit remain the decisive open experiments.

papers.title: Chlorinated Byproducts in Diisocyanates Synthesis from 35Cl Nuclear Quadrupole Resonance
papers.abstract: Chlorinated impurities in industrial diisocyanates production significantly impact product quality and stability, yet their speciation remains an analytical challenge. This study demonstrates that 35Cl NQR spectroscopy, supported by DFT calculations, provides a powerful framework for identifying byproducts in these processes. We show that NQR frequencies effectively categorize chlorinated species—such as amino hydrochlorides and carbamoyl chlorides—into distinct chemical families, with signal shifts driven by local electronic structure, intermolecular interactions, and conformation. Applied to commercial 4,4'-MDI, this analytic ruler successfully identifies the presence of specific byproducts and establishes 35Cl NQR as a uniquely sensitive tool for monitoring byproducts and thereby the quality of industrial diisocyanate streams.

papers.title: Experimental and DFT insights into phase-dependent performance of NiIn1-xSnx (x=0.5 and 0.8) intermetallic catalysts for acetylene hydrogenation
papers.abstract: Intermetallic catalysts offer a unique platform for the hydrogenation reaction of acetylene, as their well-defined crystal structures and precise stoichiometry enable atomic-level control over active-site composition, geometry, and electronic structure. In ternary intermetallics, the addition of a third element in varying amounts can alter the crystal structure, thereby changing the stable crystal facet(s) and, consequently, the active-site electronic structure, demonstrating an intriguing strategy to boost product selectivity. The site-specific substitution of Sn in NiIn 1- x Sn x ( x =0.5, 0.8) exhibits two distinct phases belonging to hexagonal ( x =0.5) and orthorhombic ( x =0.8) crystal systems. Density Functional Theory calculations show that (0001) and (010) facets of hexagonal and orthorhombic phases, respectively, are the most stable. Catalytic performance for the acetylene hydrogenation reaction confirms that the hexagonal NiIn 0.5 Sn 0.5 is more catalytically active and selective towards ethylene than the orthorhombic NiIn 0.2 Sn 0.8 . The Nudged Elastic Band calculations reveal a significant difference in the kinetics of the conversion reactions, making the hexagonal phase more selective than the orthorhombic phase. Thus, this study combines both experimental and theoretical approaches to understand the superior catalytic performance of the hexagonal phase over the orthorhombic phase, which mainly originates from differences in the atomic arrangement of the most stable surface, which significantly influences the reaction kinetics of acetylene hydrogenation.

papers.title: Revisiting Deep Learning DTA Methods from the Dataset Viewpoint
papers.abstract: In this work, we present a study revisiting deep learning drug-target affinity models, which are otherwise used as benchmark methods in the literature to compare more complex and heavy-weighted architectures. We focus on training and testing these models using pKd values from BindingDB, a dataset that presents binding affinity information of a high variety of ligans and proteins. These activity data need a proper pre-treatment and curation prior to actually using them for production tasks, a factor that is often overlooked in the literature. We show that a combination of a thorough curation of the dataset and a proper hyperparameter tuning of slight modifications of the revisited models (e.g, by using pretrained protein embeddings to describe the proteins) provides beyond state of the art performances at a much lower computational cost, with respect to more demanding deep learning models. We study the distributions of the protein and ligand learned (or eventually, pre-trained) embeddings, to observe how they classify the proteins depending on the (super)families they belong to (for the former), and how they distribute in the embedding space depending on the values of their binding affinities, with respect to a given protein (for the latter). We take advantage of the graph representations of the ligands to further approach explainability at an atom-wise level, by computing the directional derivative of the model with respect to each of the atoms of a ligand. This method, unlike other derivative-based approaches such as Grad-CAM and variants, turns out to be extremely useful for regression tasks of binding affinities, as this provides direct means of assessing which atoms contribute to an increase/decrease of the binding affinity, depending on both the sign of the directional derivative, and on its absolute value-an indication of how steep the function is with respect to each atom.

papers.title: Rapid, Reliable and Accurate XPS Depth-Distribution Functions from the Berger–Doggett method
papers.abstract: Two complementary rapid Monte Carlo methods for emission-depth distributions were introduced for Auger electron spectroscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy in 1993; the statistical weights method and the Berger-Doggett method. The statistical-weights method samples both elastic scattering directions and the distances between elastic events; the Berger–Doggett method conditions on the angular history and analytically averages over all such distances. These were much faster (by orders of magnitude) than previous methods and no less accurate. Besides reducing variance, the two methods should provide an unusually strong independent cross-check in their common domain of a homogeneous sample. As computer resources have progressively increased over the last 30 years, longer Monte Carlo runs have become practical, and in those a numerical instability can arise in the Berger-Doggett approach that we solve in this paper. We reformulate the original integral recurrence as a lower-bidiagonal system of linear ordinary differential equations with mixed boundary conditions. An ordered Schur decomposition selects the bounded invariant subspace and the required fluences are obtained from the action of a matrix exponential, avoiding the chance near-co-linear direction cosines that would occasionally frustrate the method published in 1993, and now allows very long Monte-Carlo runs to be performed quickly and reliably. In controlled tests the original method accumulated a relative error of 7.6 × 1010 at a cosine separation of 10−14, whereas the new formulation remained within 2.3 × 10−16 of a 120-digit reference. In a 500 angle-history recalculation using contemporary NIST SRD 64 elastic data, at a typical C 1s kinetic energy the old method gave a relative error of 6.2 × 1012 in the coefficient recurrence even though its closest pair of direction cosines differed by 1.15 × 10−4; the new formulation agreed with a 160-digit result to 1.6 × 10−16. This removes the need for extended or arbitrary precision without changing the underlying transport model. Routine Berger-Doggett calculations can now be done on a typical PC reliably and almost instantly, supporting also the statistical weights method by making it easier to verify implementations of it. This should be a significant step towards the automated extraction of all the information possible from nondestructive XPS depth-profiling. As an example of its wide applicability, the calculation confirms the physical basis of a previously proposed coaxial XPS geometry, producing a depth-distribution function with a subsurface maximum. Its considerable breadth, however, suggests enhanced subsurface selectivity rather than any general resolution of the ill-conditioning of depth-profile reconstruction.

papers.title: Many ligands, many signals: The diverse transduction landscape of the 5-HT receptor 2A
papers.abstract: The 5-HT receptor 2A (5-HT2AR) is a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) activated by serotonin and one of the main targets for the development of antipsychotic drugs, e.g. against schizophrenia. There is evidence that the activation of certain transducers downstream of the receptor over others may lead to fewer side effects. For the development of new drugs with a more favorable side-effect profile than existing medications, therefore, a deep understanding of the correlations between the chemical structure of 5-HT2AR ligands and the panel of transducers that are activated after ligand binding is necessary. In this work, we have computationally screened large databases for previously undescribed ligands of the 5-HT2AR and pharmacologically assessed four transducers–activation of Gq, G15, Gz and recruitment of β-arrestin–with BRET assays. Each molecule was tested in agonist-and antagonist mode, resulting in diverse transducer engagement profiles for 37 ligands of different chemotypes. Receptor:ligand interactions were investigated through Molecular Dynamics simulations and Protein-Ligand Interaction Fingerprints. Our data highlight how the vastness and density of chemical space enable incredibly diverse texture in the signaling outcome, namely that even molecules similar to serotonin itself show vastly divergent signaling outcomes, occasionally even with pathway bias. This opens doors for exploring new pharmacology.

papers.title: Reactivity of Diethylstilbestrol toward Electrogenerated Superoxide in N,N-Dimethylformamide through Proton-coupled Electron Transfer
papers.abstract: The superoxide radical anion (O2 •−) scavenging mechanism of diethylstilbestrol (DesH2) was investigated using in situ UVvis spectroelectrochemistry, cyclic voltammetry, and DFT/TD-DFT calculations. While thermodynamic evaluation indicates that all tested stilbene derivatives possess favorable free energy changes for scavenging O2 •−, comparative cyclic voltammetry revealed that only DesH2 and 4,4′-dihydroxystilbene exhibit distinct scavenging waves. On the electrochemical timescale, effective scavenging requires a 1:1 stoichiometric proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) mechanism involving the transfer of two protons and one electron from a single molecule. Thermodynamic and mechanistic analyses supported this PCET pathway. Crucially, the diethyl substituents in DesH2 stabilize the generated radical anion and maintain the structural integrity of the stilbene core, enabling further two- to four-electron oxidation. Furthermore, subsequent chemical steps (e.g., adduct decomposition or OH addition) pull the reaction equilibrium forward to dynamically drive the initial PCET process.

papers.title: Immunological Evaluation of Conformationally Constrained Tn and sTn Analogues
papers.abstract: Conjugate vaccines, targeting tumor-associated carbohydrate antigens (TACAs), have met clinical challenges that have been attributed to heterogeneous TACA presentation on the surface of tumors cells and low vaccine immunogenicity. A promising strategy to improve immunogenicity is to lock the target antigen in its biologically active conformation, improving presentation in antigen presenting cells. In this study, Tn-Thr and sTn-Thr conformationally restricted TACA mimics were conjugated to the low immune interfering, high-loading, entirely carbohydrate vaccine carrier, PS A1, followed by in vivo evaluation. According to ELISA and FACS data analysis of raised antibodies in C57BL/6J mice, a Tn-Thr-PS A1 mimic conjugate proved to be better in comparison to a Tn-PS A1 control. However, the sTn-Thr-PS A1 mimic conjugate did not benefit from Tn restricted conformation, hinting at a less prominent role of the core D-GalNAc moiety in immune recognition.

papers.title: Mapping Molecular Universe
papers.abstract: The success of large-language-models highlighted the importance of datasets, whose quantity, quality and diversity dictate the accuracy and creativity of artificial intelligence (AI) systems in learning and inferring. However, in scientific domains, such datasets required for domain-specific AI/machine-learning (ML) models do not exist for most of the fields. In this perspective, by examining the logics and rationales behind the construction and mapping of a universe for small organic molecules (108~1012), we explore what new capabilities AI can bring to the materials discoveries. We identify the elusive structure-property relationship as a core challenge for new materials design and explore the possibility AI tools could enable us to design based on targeted properties instead of the structural derivation. In broader context we further discuss what challenges and limitations AI-driven material sciences still face and envision possible avenues into the future of AI4Materials.

papers.title: Anharmonic Vibrational Structure and Bound States of the He-CO2 van der Waals Complex
papers.abstract: We present a new flexible-monomer two-body ab initio potential energy surface (PES) for the He–CO2 van der Waals complex, building on studies for noblegas systems including Ar–CO2, Ne–CO2 and Kr–CO2. As the least polarizable member of the series, helium provides an extreme benchmark that isolates how weak anisotropic interactions shape both intramolecular spectroscopy and lowfrequency intermolecular dynamics. Using vibrational structure methods, including vibrational self-consistent field and vibrational configuration interaction, we compute excitation energies spanning intra-and intermolecular coordinates and reproduce the experimentally observed blue shift of the CO2 ν3 band origin upon complexation. The calculations also capture the monomer’s characteristic Fermi-resonance structure in this region and show that the corresponding features in the He–CO2 complex are very similar. To treat the strongly anharmonic intermolecular motion beyond a local-mode picture, we additionally solve the full bound-state problem on the anisotropic PES and compare the resulting level spacings with available experimental results and literature benchmarks. Finally, we provide a quantitative prediction for the lifted intramolecular bend degeneracy of ∼0.03 cm−1, with the out-of-plane component lying above the in-plane component.

papers.title: Development of an algorithm for assessing peak irregularities in two-dimensional chromatographic separations
papers.abstract: Chromatography is a powerful method for separating complex mixtures and has become ubiquitous in the analytical chemistry laboratory. The quality of chromatographic separations, in both liquid chromatography (LC) and gas chromatography (GC), are assessed with standard Gaussian distribution-associated figures of merit—such as full-width at half maximum (FWHM), signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), resolution, number of theoretical plates, peak capacity, and tailing and fronting factors—in which computation is straight-forward. Comprehensive two-dimensional (2D) chromatographic separations, such as LC×LC and GC×GC, provide improved chromatographic resolution and increased peak capacity, making them attractive to researchers in fields such as metabolomics and environmental chemistry, but currently lack a standardized set of figures of merit. Peaks in 2D separations are ideally represented as Gaussians following normal distributions in both dimensions; however, in practice, peaks are often tailing, fronting, and/or rotated. Quantifying peak phenomena across samples is crucial in chromatographic quality control (QC), and there is currently no available tool to efficiently perform these operations in 2D. Here, using singular value decomposition (SVD), we have developed a methodology to assign new axes to 2D peaks in the direction of data variance along principal components, allowing for the measurement of major and minor peak widths and consequential decomposition of data onto these coordinate axes. Further computation allows for numerical description of skewness and rotation and provides a means to perform statistical analysis directly in both dimensions despite peak irregularities. The algorithm computes peak widths with > 95% accuracy to ground truth while accounting for peak distortion and rotation. Application to large data sets provides a method for tracking and analyzing peak metrics across multiple injections, thus establishing the foundation for automated QC in multidimensional separations.

papers.title: Electrostatic templating and the dynamics of physisorbed CO2 ordering in CALF-20
papers.abstract: Reducing CO2 emissions requires adsorbents combining high selectivity with large capacity, however the molecular origins leading to such properties remain poorly understood. Physisorbents are desirable for their low regeneration energy but they often lack the selectivity needed for efficient large-scale CO2 separation. While physisorbed guest molecules in porous media are typically modeled as disordered fluids, CALF-20 is known to impart some order in the CO2 adsorbed phase. Here, we use solid-state NMR to resolve the dynamics underlying this ordering: as CO2 loading increases, the adsorbed phase undergoes a pressure-driven transition from rapid, isotropic tumbling to a rigid, orientationally locked state in which CO2 molecules align with the alternating electrostatic potential of the pore surface. GCMC and DFT simulations link this electrostatic templating to specific host-guest interactions and reproduce its pressure-dependent evolution. This cooperative, loading-dependent stabilization is accessible only to guests bearing a sufficiently strong electric quadrupole moment to couple with the template, providing a molecular basis for the framework's marked CO2/N2 selectivity. Comparison with structurally related frameworks indicates that electrostatic templating extends beyond CALF-20 to other materials with complementary pore electrostatics, pointing to a design principle for tailoring adsorbent selectivity to a guest's electronic signature.

papers.title: Does the Substrate Affect the Attenuation Length in an Overlayer? Not Significantly in Practical XPS Film Thickness Measurements
papers.abstract: We develop a simple one-dimensional model of elastic backscattering in samples consisting of a thin overlayer on a homogeneous substrate. The model isolates the additional influence of the substrate on the apparent attenuation of photoelectrons in the overlayer—the “Substrate Backscatter Effect”—from the separate geometrical effects of elastic scattering that become important at large emission angles. The treatment yields closed-form expressions which complement more rigorous Monte Carlo and transport-theory calculations and provide a direct physical interpretation of the trends they predict. For the common case in which overlayer thickness is determined from attenuation of a substrate signal, the Substrate Backscatter Effect produces no error within the accuracy of the present zero-and single-backscattering model. For thickness measurements based on overlayer intensity, the predicted error for the population of typical XPS lines is usually below 1% and seldom exceeds about 4%; deliberately extreme combinations of substrate and overlayer scattering properties can give errors of order 4–7%. Thin-oxide measurements based on chemically shifted substrate and overlayer peaks are particularly insensitive because the relevant photoelectrons have nearly identical kinetic energies and similar elastic-scattering properties. These results explain why attenuation lengths determined for homogeneous materials can normally be used in practical XPS film-thickness measurements without introducing a significant additional uncertainty associated with the identity of the substrate. The effective attenuation length remains dependent on the measurement geometry and quantitative procedure, but under normal XPS conditions the substrate contribution is generally negligible compared with other sources of uncertainty.

papers.title: Experimental validation of quantitative soft X-ray ptychography at the carbon K-edge
papers.abstract: Quantitative accuracy of soft x-ray ptychography (SXP) was tested using polystyrene nanospheres measured at five selected energies around the Carbon K-edge. Reference phase and optical density maps were calculated from STXM (scanning transmission x-ray microscopy) derived optical constants and a blurred spherical particle model. The reconstructed images preserved the particle morphology and spherical trend but both phase and absorption amplitudes were systematically underestimated. Phase showed higher spatial agreement than absorption, while the absorption comparison was more robust near the π* resonance. These results demonstrate the usefulness of the workflow for identifying, rather than eliminating, quantitative errors in SXP.

papers.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Generate Your Next Textbook?
papers.abstract: College students have been immersed in classrooms where technology is integrated throughout the learning process, even as early as elementary school. Viewing content and turning in assignments through a learning management system (LMS), contacting instructors by email, reading online news articles, creating shared documents in group work, and conducting research on online platforms are all common ways they use technology to learn and share. All the while, their textbooks remain static, almost like what their predecessors would have used in college decades prior. College textbooks have been criticized for their cost, their inability to present emerging topics, and on the grounds that they are static and do not allow a student to delve deeper into a topic that might be of interest. This article contains a model for questions that generate content that mimics aspects of a textbook with the additional benefit of no cost and adjusting to student input. This unique format utilizes only questions to generative artificial intelligence (GAI) that have been tested, and the faculty member can adjust topics as needed. This would benefit both students and instructors, by not only decreasing the cost of instructional materials in higher education but also creating material that is fluid with new approaches and discoveries in science.

papers.title: Neutron Resonance Computed Tomography of Tungsten-Ditelluride in Tellurium Flux
papers.abstract: Exfoliable single crystals of tungstenditelluride (WTe 2 ) play a critical role in the investigation of novel phenomena in condensed matter physics and the development od nextgeneration electronic devices. Production of this material requires chemically informed synthesis to control crystal size and shape. In-situ imaging of crystal growth experiments has been shown to excel at relating processing conditions to robust spatial data sets. Such experiments are challenging when applied to the synthesis of WTe 2 , given the high reaction temperature, small crystal volumes, and the dense and opaque tellurium (Te) flux. Computed tomography (CT) produces data sets in three dimensions, providing the highest quality description of synthesis environments. Conventional CT based on X-rays is incapable of revealing growth behavior inside highly dense metal fluxes. We demonstrate that neutron resonance CT is well suited to studying the spatial organization of WTe 2 grown in Te flux. These results suggest that WTe 2 crystals occupy both the ingot bulk and the ingot surface, which requires further investigation to determine the nucleation conditions. Descriptors of length and volume of the largest crystals are extracted from the computed volume rendering, which will inform future interrogations of optimizing synthesis for crystal size. This work provides the foundation needed for real-time in-situ observations of flux growth of high-density materials.
