Here, we present an activation-mapped kinetic modeling workflow combining density functional theory (DFT), machine-learning cluster expansion (ML-CE), Metropolis Monte Carlo (MMC), and kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) to trace processing-driven structural evolution in L1 0 and L1 2 Pt–Fe nanoparticles. We define the activation-derived ensemble as the statistically sampled Pt-skin configurations generated by high-temperature ordering, selective Fe leaching, vacancy-mediated restructuring, and room-temperature activation. This ensemble construction links processing history to subsurface composition, surface morphology, and site-resolved catalytic response. Within the modeled activation sequence, phase-dependent Fe leaching produces an inversion in second-layer Fe enrichment relative to the ideal ordered references and changes the dominant active-site families, making L1 0 -derived nanoparticles terrace-controlled, whereas L1 2 -derived nanoparticles become comparatively edge-controlled. When coupled to steady-state *OH coverage kinetics, these activation-derived ensembles recover the experimental oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) activity ranking and reveal phase-specific size–activity trends missed by ideal models. More broadly, the results show that the activation-derived structures, rather than pristine phases alone, govern catalyst ranking and highlight how ordering-dependent subsurface reconfiguration can reshape static-model predictions.

papers.title: Generator-Collector enhanced Square Wave Voltammetry for Acetaminophen detection
papers.abstract: While generator-collector (GC) electrochemistry using traditional electrochemistry methods, such as cyclic voltammetry, has been employed to enhance the detection of a number of analytes, little work has been done on coupling this phenomena with pulsed techniques. These techniques, such as square wave voltammetry (SWV), have been shown to enhance the detection capabilities of sensors, when employed without the use of GC mode. In this work, the effects of enabling GC mode on an interdigitated electrode array coupled with SWV are presented. Subsequently sensor surfaces were modified, via electroplating of gold, to further enhance the performance. The effect of varying key operational parameters for SWV, such as frequency and amplitude, as well as the applied potential bias to optimise GC mode were also studied. This sensor was subsequently utilised for the detection of acetaminophen in buffered samples, demonstrating the signal enhancing effects of GC SWV.

papers.title: Reinventing the Mitsunobu Reaction with Iminophosphorane Reagents
papers.abstract: The Mitsunobu reaction is one of the most celebrated reactions in organic synthesis, enabling stereospecific C–O, C–N, and C–S bond formation from abundant alcohol feedstocks. However, its widespread use is constrained by explosive reagents, laborious product purification and a pronucleophile p K a window that precludes C–C bond formation. Herein, we disclose iminophosphoranes as a new class of reagents for the Mitsunobu reaction that readily overcome these limitations. The key iminophosphorane reagent is rapidly and quantitively formed in situ from commercially-available 1-azido-4-methoxybenzene and a trialkylphosphine, allowing the construction of C–O, C–N, C–S and, notably, C–C bonds from primary and secondary alcohol substrates with vastly simplified product purification. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the direct use of a solution of pre-formed iminophosphorane eliminates end-user azide handling altogether. The utility of the reaction was demonstrated through reaction scale-up and late-stage functionalisation of pharmaceutically-relevant compounds.

papers.title: Openclatura–an Open-Source Nomenclature Framework for Rule-Based Molecule Naming
papers.abstract: Naming molecules systematically remains an open challenge in cheminformatics. The reverse task—converting names to structure—has been largely solved for over a decade by OPSIN, yet no open-source tool performs the forward direction. Here we introduce Openclatura, which generates IUPAC names from molecular structures. The rule set was constructed by an agentic system that exhaustively enumerates naming rules, with each candidate name checked for structural round-trip consistency against OPSIN. Across three challenging benchmarks (QM9, PubChem, and ZINC22), Openclatura produces valid names for 98% of molecules, compared to 95% for the deep-learning baseline STOUT, while running on a single CPU core (40 times faster). We further present Robomoleculographer, an extension that generates natural-language descriptions of molecular graphs, bringing to chemistry what robocrystallographer offers to materials. Openclatura is fully deterministic and exposes an inspectable decision trace for every generated name.

papers.title: Light drives bidirectional two-electron transfer between paired dynamic redox molecules
papers.abstract: We demonstrate closed photoredox systems in which light alone drives a net two-electron transfer between pairs of dynamic redox (dyrex) switches. The same pair can be cycled between two thermodynamically stable states using light of orthogonal wavelengths, so the direction of two-electron transfer is set optically rather than by an external bias. The system is closed, requiring no sacrificial oxidant or reductant. The quantum yield of two-electron transfer exceeds unity through a combination of photoexcitation and potential inversion of the dyrex pair. This system provides directional, multi-electron control by light at the molecular level, a capability with no precedent in molecular redox chemistry.

papers.title: Determination of reduced nitrogen by 4-Toluenesulfonyl Chloride (TsCl) Derivatization and HPLC-MS
papers.abstract: The potential environmental and health impacts of reduced nitrogen have drawn significant research interest in recent decades. While various analytical techniques exist for detecting specific reduced nitrogen compounds in air and liquid matrices, given the diverse research interests across scientific disciplines, there remains a need for a widely applicable, selective, and affordable method. In this work, a high-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS) method that incorporates a simple precolumn derivatization procedure using p-toluenesulfonyl chloride (TsCl) was optimized for the analysis of small reduced nitrogen compounds. This derivatization method is selective for the N–H bond and exhibits high sensitivity and calibration linearity for a diverse range of reduced nitrogen compounds. Key derivatization parameters, including reaction pH and time, were optimized, and the stability of the derivatization products was investigated. This derivatization method was further applied to particulate matter samples collected from a poultry research center and biomass burning samples from wood combustion. Using an ultra-high resolution MS and its MS2 function, we identified MS2 fragments unique to TsCl derivatization. This finding enables the detection of various reduced nitrogen compounds in complex environmental matrices.

papers.title: Nanoplastic Standards
papers.abstract: Open questions about the potential effects of nanoplastic particles have driven researchers to a frontier of measurement science, where they seek answers without the full support of metrological standards. Documentary and material standards improve the reliability of measurement results but are slow to develop, while researchers are eager to explore and publish. This mismatch motivates efforts to exploit any potential utility of existing standards and to elucidate emerging needs for new standards. Accordingly, we consider possible applications of microplastic and engineered nanomaterial standards to support nanoplastic analysis, and the many challenges of developing new nanoplastic standards. We study corresponding issues in four research activities—physicochemical measurements, reference materials, weathering methods, and toxicity assays. Our integrative perspective elucidates challenges and opportunities. We identify topics that can limit progress, such as measurement uncertainty propagation and process–product–purpose constraints. A focus review of recent literature shows uneven progress in addressing these issues. We suggest opportunities to expedite progress, such as feedback loops for measurand prioritization and uncertainty budgeting, timely development of imperfect standards, and metrological innovation to obviate current constraints. Our study informs the research, development, and application of nanoplastic standards to reliably answer open questions and to support other technological ventures.

papers.title: Beyond Multiscale: A Neural Network-Unified Molecular Model for Asymmetry-Free Dynamics Simulation
papers.abstract: Adaptive multiscale simulations, such as adaptive QM/MM, are indispensable for investigating complex solution dynamics but historically suffer from a fundamental dilemma: the dynamic exchange of identical solvent molecules across different model resolutions introduces a physical asymmetry. This asymmetry forces a prohibitive trade-off between severe structural distortions and the violation of Hamiltonian conservation (continuous energy drift). To definitively resolve this issue, we propose the ”Integrated Molecular Model,” a paradigm-shifting framework that mathematically unifies multiple resolutions into a single, dynamically consistent potential. By employing a neural network that takes only the multiscale weight functions as input descriptors, our model learns to systematically cancel the non-physical transition forces originating from spatial discontinuities. As a proof-of-concept, we validated this unified framework on bulk water, aqueous ionic solutions, and reactive hydronium ions. Our approach not only faithfully restores artifact-free solvation structures but also strictly conserves the Hamiltonian, enabling unprecedentedly stable, long-term simulations under the microcanonical (NVE) ensemble. Consequently, the model successfully eliminates artificial thermostat-induced breathing modes, allowing for the rigorous evaluation of intrinsic dynamical properties such as diffusion coefficients. Furthermore, owing to its physically informed network design, the correction potential introduces less than 2\% additional computational overhead and demonstrates remarkable zero-shot transferability across chemically similar ionic species. By fundamentally eradicating the inherent asymmetry of adaptive multiscale modeling, this highly scalable framework establishes a robust foundation for high-fidelity simulations of complex condensed-phase phenomena, including reactive dynamics at solid-liquid interfaces and ion transport in battery electrolytes.

papers.title: Negative Charge Activation of Surface H₂O Molecules as a Proposed Trigger for Evaporation and Phase Transition
papers.abstract: Evaporating water droplets are known to acquire net charge, and the air–water interface to carry a collective net negative charge; yet the causal role of charge in evaporation itself has received comparatively little attention. While prior studies have addressed charge separation via ion diffusion at the phase front or external-field-induced polarization, these approaches treat charge as a consequence of — or an external input to — the phase transition, rather than as its trigger. Here, we propose that when charge is redistributed at the hydrogen-bonding sites of interfacial H 2 O molecules — specifically at the hydrogen atoms connecting to the oxygen atoms of sub-interfacial H 2 O molecules below — by external influences such as electric fields, contact, or thermal agitation, the resulting negative charge activation generates Coulombic repulsion sufficient to sever the hydrogen bond and expel the molecule into the gas phase. To test this hypothesis, we conducted four experiments: (i) container opening geometry, (ii) a modified gold-leaf electroscope, (iii) closed-circuit bottle configurations, and (iv) applied low voltage (0.10–0.20 V). The gold-leaf electroscope experiment indicated net charge transfer during phase transition; the closed-circuit copper wire experiment showed that charge dissipation suppressed evaporation by ~18%; and the low-voltage experiment showed that evaporation progressively increased (+0.063% → +0.275%) with stepwise voltage increase (0.10 → 0.20 V). These results indicate that charge redistribution at the hydrogen-bonding sites of interfacial H 2 O molecules is a factor influencing evaporation, with implications for evaporation-driven energy harvesting.

papers.title: Pre-Analytical Integrity in Ignitable Liquid Residue Casework: Decision-Grade Reporting
papers.abstract: Ignitable-liquid residue (ILR) analysis can provide powerful chemical evidence, but its forensic meaning depends on the integrity demonstrated before analysis. Volatile loss, alteration, contamination, transfer, background contribution, sampling limitations and missing context may restrict how far an observation from the analysed material can defensibly extend. Drawing on standards, forensic guidance and ILRspecific literature, this narrative review develops a claim-restriction framework for decision-grade reporting. The framework uses five record-based dimensions—identity, continuity, condition, context and control—to support four case-specific statuses: demonstrated integrity, administrative nonconformity, qualified deficit (NR-Qualified) and blocking deficit (NR-Fatal). These statuses indicate whether an observation can support an item-level, scene-linked or broader forensic claim, or whether the claim must be qualified, restricted or withheld beyond observation. The proposed chain is evidence condition → integrity status → permissible claim space → reporting language. The framework does not replace validated analytical methods, laboratory quality systems, probabilistic interpretation or expert judgement. Nor is it a sampling protocol, reporting template or automatic decision rule. Its purpose is to make explicit the boundary between analytical validity and evidential integrity. Where the record supports the intended claim, probative value should not be diluted unnecessarily. Where a relevant deficit remains bounded or unbounded, reporting should remain within the corresponding defensible claim space. Decision-grade reporting therefore aligns what was analysed, what was demonstrated and what is finally claimed.

papers.title: Guest Protonation Gates Hydrogen-Bond-Driven Selectivity in Native Cyclodextrin Molecular Recognition
papers.abstract: Cyclodextrin inclusion is often described primarily in terms of hydrophobic displacement of cavity-bound water, a framework that explains volume-dependent affinity but does not account for why closely related guests exhibit distinct stabilization within the same host cavity. Hydrogen bonding is increasingly recognized as an additional recognition element in macrocyclic hosts, but whether this principle operates within an unmodified, native cyclodextrin cavity—and whether it can be switched reversibly—has not been established. Here, we show that guest protonation supports switchable encapsulation behavior, using albendazole and fenbendazole as structurally matched benzimidazole drugs that allow hydrogen-bond donor–acceptor character to be tuned independently of the hydrophobic scaffold. Solubility measurements across native α-, β-, and γ-cyclodextrin show that protonation enhances association in all three hosts, while NMR spectroscopy, variable-temperature thermodynamic analysis, and semiempirical molecular dynamics simulations focused on β-cyclodextrin reveal that this enhancement reflects two mechanistically distinct outcomes. Although both protonated guests form 1:1 complexes with comparable hydrophobic cavity occupancy, albendazole achieves deeper cavity insertion that positions its protonated benzimidazole to engage a broader network of hydrogen bonds at the host rim, yielding a larger enthalpic gain offset by greater entropic compensation. Comparison with simplified benzimidazole fragments lacking the hydrophobic anchor shows that hydrogen bonding alone cannot sustain stable association in water, establishing that hydrophobic anchoring is a prerequisite for productive protonation-dependent recognition. These results identify protonation as a general, structurally contingent switch for redistributing enthalpic and entropic contributions to host–guest stabilization in native cyclodextrin systems.

papers.title: Quantifying the physical complexity of chemical architectures through electron-density topology
papers.abstract: Quantifying molecular complexity is a longstanding challenge with profound implications for chemical discovery, biological organization, and materials design. Existing descriptors typically rely on 2D graph-theoretic connectivity or empirical heuristic rules, thereby failing to capture physically encoded structural organization and three-dimensional electronic environments. Here, we introduce the Quantum Assembly Index (Aρ), a parameter-free descriptor that defines molecular complexity through real-space electron-density topology and its associated assembly constraints. The index is constructed from shortest-path organization within QTAIM-derived topology graphs, integrated with ring and cage contributions extracted directly from electron-density critical points. Across a chemically diverse benchmark dataset spanning simple inorganic species, organic compounds, biomolecular motifs, coordination clusters, and extended frameworks, Aρ scales logically with molecular size while resolving substantial complexity differences among systems of identical atom counts. In binary classification tasks, Aρ significantly outperforms widely used traditional cheminformatic metrics (including Bertz complexity and QED) and markedly improves predictive performance when integrated into combined models, demonstrating that it captures unique physical signals blind to standard descriptors. Rigorous validation via cross-validation, holdout testing, and permutation controls confirms the robust stability of the framework. By grounding complexity metrics within quantum-mechanical observables, this work provides a physically grounded, broadly applicable route for quantifying organized molecular architecture, offering an extensible framework for reaction networks, automated machine-learning workflows, and the discovery of complex functional materials.

papers.title: Stapline: Development of a Force Field Library for Stapled Peptide Residues
papers.abstract: As of 2026, more than 150 peptides are in clinical development as therapeutic candidates and molecular biology tools, and more than 120 therapeutic and diagnostic peptides have already been approved, representing a growing area of medicine. Stapled peptides are chemically constrained to retain their secondary structure to provide enhancements in binding affinity, membrane permeability and proteolytic resistance, and have emerged as promising solutions for the disruption of protein-protein interactions implicated in a variety of diseases. Molecular dynamics simulations have proven to be a powerful tool for exploring peptide secondary structure. However, the lack of readily available accurate force field parameters for a broad range of staple chemistries, as well as the computing cost of predicting the secondary structure of stapled peptides, have limited the accessibility of stapled peptide MD simulations. To facilitate greater adoption, we have developed the Stapline pipeline for the parameterisation of popular stapled peptide moieties and implemented an efficient MD simulation protocol to obtain stapled peptide secondary structure preferences. The protocol’s applicability is demonstrated on a series of hDM2-binding stapled peptides, successfully reproducing experimental α -helicity trends.

papers.title: GQR–X: The Quantum Loom of Life on Earth Uniting Isotopic, Chalcogenic, and Protonic Resonance at the Quantum–Critical Boundary
papers.abstract: Following the isotopic bifurcation observed in GQR–IX, the Gated Quantum Resonator (GQR) framework is here extended to sulfur–substituted analogues (H 2 S, D 2 S, T 2 S) within the same photosystem II (PSII) geometries. Time–domain simulations reveal systematic frequency compression relative to water while maintaining a shared field–geometry envelope. The combined isotope–chalcogen phase map exposes a universal resonance–shield boundary that separates collective from localised tunnelling modes. A new interpretation emerges: the low–medium–split frequency pattern reflects a dual-phase charging process, in which vibronic energy is absorbed, stored, and redistributed between two coherent channels prior to turnover. Transient hydronium clusters (H 3 O + , H 5 O +2 ) act as heavy–proton mimics, bridging isotopic and chalcogenic effects under a single quantum–critical law. Together these findings show that PSII catalysis operates at a tunable boundary where mass and polarizability co-regulate tunnelling, unifying the principal schools of catalytic theory within one Hamiltonian landscape

papers.title: GQR–IX: Quantum–Gate Bifurcation in Photosystem II Deuterium Suppression and Field–Tuned Resonance Switching at 8F4I
papers.abstract: The Gated Quantum Resonator (GQR) framework interprets catalysis as a circuit-Hamiltonian network in which vibronic tunnelling channels are dynamically modulated by structural and electromagnetic gates. Here, attosecond-femtosecond time-domain simulations of the photosystem II oxygen-evolving complex (OEC) reveal a reproducible isotopic bifurcation at geometry 8F4I. Deuterium exhibits a pronounced suppression of its dominant gate frequency (∼0.45 PHz) while protium and tritium remain coherent near 2.3 PHz, marking a non-monotonic inversion of kinetic-isotope ordering. This behaviour constitutes a quantum-gate bifurcation — a transition between collective and localised tunnelling regimes — driven by the interplay of mass, field, and hydration topology. The result links enzymatic water-splitting dynamics to the same resonance-switching principles that underpin quantum-critical materials and ultrafast electronic devices. Beyond biological insight, it establishes a design framework for field-tuned, isotope-adaptive quantum catalysis and for artificial resonators that exploit controllable coherence-decoherence thresholds.

papers.title: Detecting Catalytically Competent Surface-Bound Hydrogen on Electrocatalysts with Weak Acids
Metal Nanoclusters for Electrochemical Nitrate Reduction
papers.abstract: Nitrate ion (NO3−) in agricultural and industrial wastewater is a cause of groundwater and river contamination. The electrochemical NO3− reduction reaction (eNO3−RR), in which nitrate is reduced to ammonia (NH3) using electricity derived from renewable energy sources, has been attracting increasing attention as a means of detoxification and valorization of these nitrates. Among the various available catalysts, ultrafine (~ 1 nm) metal nanoclusters (MNCs) are of interest. These MNCs possess distinctive electronic and geometric structures that differ from those of relatively large metal nanoparticles because they have discrete electronic states that arise from quantum size effects. MNCs are expected to enable highly selective NH3 synthesis while suppressing competing reactions and side reactions of the eNO3−RR. In this review, we summarize recent studies on the eNO3−RR using MNCs and present design guidelines for this research field.

papers.title: Label-Free, Quantum-Mechanically Informed Scoring of Protein–Ligand Complexes with Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Virtual chemical libraries now exceed billions of compounds, placing joint demands on the scoring tools used to prioritize candidates for accuracy and scalability. Supervised affinity models meet scalability demands but remain vulnerable to dataset memorization and train-test leakage. Here we introduce AIMNet2(Score), a physics-informed scoring framework built on AIMNet2 machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) that uses no experimental binding-affinity labels. The score combines three energetic terms evaluated on a single bound structure: a protein–ligand interaction energy from AIMNet2(2025), a ligand desolvation penalty, and a local conformational strain penalty, the latter two computed with AIMNet2-CPCM. On KIN66, a new kinase benchmark of ~1,000-atom active sites with interaction energies at three DFT levels, AIMNet2(2025) reproduces its B97-3c training reference to 3.13 kcal mol-1 RMSE and transfers to systems larger than those used for training. On eight FEP+ congeneric series and a curated co-crystal set (HiQBind), the label-free score ranks affinities on par with or ahead of docking, semiempirical, and deep-learning baselines. On raw docked poses, all methods including ours perform comparably, isolating pose fidelity rather than scoring physics as the accuracy ceiling for single-structure scoring. AIMNet2(Score) thus provides a label-free, QM-informed route to candidate ranking and defines where such scoring succeeds and fails.

papers.title: Enhancing Ion Yields in MALDI-2-MSI Using Dopant-Assisted Post Ionization for High-Resolution MS-Imaging of Lipids and Metabolites
papers.abstract: Matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization mass spectrometry imaging (MALDI-MSI) is the most widely used label-free method for mapping the molecular distribution of lipids and metabolites from tissue sections and cell cultures. To mitigate the problem of partially low MALDI ion yields for several of these analyte classes, different post ionization techniques have recently been developed – for example, MALDI-2, where a second UV-laser pulse intersects the initial particle plume to generate additional charges. Here, we show that the MALDI-2 signal intensities of important lipid classes can be further increased upon introducing reactive dopant vapor into the MALDI-2 ion source. We tested acetone, anisole, toluene, 2-propanol, and chlorobenzene as dopants. Acetone as a dopant proved to be the most effective and robust choice for the given setup and MALDI matrix. We demonstrate that with dopant-assisted (DA-)MALDI-2, a signal increase of up to 5 orders of magnitude, as compared to regular MALDI, is, for instance, achieved 2 for several classes of sterols, glycerophospholipids, and sphingolipids. Both the intensities of signals for abundant lipids as also the total amount of annotated signals (based on MS1) were majorly increased. Dopant assistance as an optional add-on was realized in prototype-form on MALDI-2 ion sources of a Spectroglyph Injector-Orbitrap MSI set-up and a timsTOF fleX MALDI-2 instrument. We demonstrate the potential for biomedical imaging applications with the examples of murine spleen and cerebellum sections analyzed in the positive and negative ion mode.

papers.title: Opto-Thermophoretic Printing of Gold Nanosphere Assemblies with Tailorable Packing via Ligand Chain Length
papers.abstract: The ability to control nanoparticle assembly on substrates using light offers unique opportunities for the fabrication of functional nanostructures. Herein, the opto-thermophoretic patterning of gold nanoparticles is mediated by carboxylated thiol ligands with varying chain length, revealing how ligand structure governs assembly dynamics and final morphology. Upon laser irradiation of a gold nanosphere dispersion in the presence of ω-mercaptocarboxylic acids, localized surface plasmon resonance creates a temperature gradient that promotes ligand exchange while attracting nearby particles, leading to thiol-functionalized nanoparticles that can bind to a glass substrate. Comparing short (C3), intermediate (C12), and long-chain (C16) ligands, we demonstrate that ligand length plays a critical role in nanoparticle-nanoparticle and nanoparticle-substrate interactions under non-equilibrium conditions. The criteria to pattern gold nanosphere layers with hexagonal packing symmetry was established, providing highly uniform surface enhanced Raman scattering signal across the patterned assembly. This work provides new insights into light-driven nanoparticle patterning, showcasing the potential of simple ligands for regulating opto-thermophoretic patterning. This will broaden the scope of potential materials that can be printed by opto-thermophoresis, opening avenues for the design of tailorable nanostructured materials.

papers.title: A protein-water interaction model for one-site water: incorporating the effect of water polarity to capture hydrophilicity and hydrophobicity at atomic resolution
papers.abstract: Coarse-grained water models have been developed to reduce the size of simulating systems and their computational cost. One-site water models have clear benefits over cluster models, including finer granularity, but they may face challenges when applied to biomolecular systems, such as protein complexes, because water molecules are electrically neutral. In this work, we propose a mathematical model that describes interactions between protein atoms and coarse-grained one-site water molecules, by incorporating the effect of water polarity to describe interactions with charged protein atoms. This model is developed based on observations made in this work and in our previous work. First, at the atomic level, protein-water interactions are mostly controlled by electrostatic interactions between protein atoms and waters’ hydrogens and by the collective dynamics of all waters’ hydrogens. Second, interactions between protein atoms and water molecules can be composed of three components: (i) interactions by statistical preferences of the water orientations around protein atoms, (ii) perturbations of those interactions by neighboring protein atoms, and (iii) interactions with bulk water. Our results show that the proposed model accurately captures the hydrophilic and hydrophobic properties of protein atoms, including force profiles that indicate potential energy wells and repulsive walls, respectively, and reproduces the hydrophilic, hydrophobic, and amphipathic properties of amino acids at the atomic level. This work explains how individual protein atoms can exhibit hydrophilic or hydrophobic behavior. The proposed model has the effect of screening protein-water electrostatic interactions and the potential to significantly reduce the computational cost of the molecular dynamics simulations. In this work, we additionally propose the least-squares closest-distance (LSCD) fitting method, which has slight advantages over least-squares (LS) fitting by avoiding the overweighting of large-magnitude values, maintaining accuracy for values close to zero, and reducing the need for extremely small thresholds when fitting functions have complex forms.

papers.title: Negative Fragmentation Approach to investigate the backbone hydrogen-bond energies for protein secondary structures
papers.abstract: The Negative Fragmentation Approach (NFA), incorporating counterpoise correction for basis-set superposition error (BSSE), enables site-specific evaluation of intra- and intermolecular interaction energies using quantum chemical calculations, even for covalently connected or embedded molecular sites. Here, we applied NFA to quantify BSSE-corrected hydrogen-bond (H-bond) interaction energies between the backbone carbonyl and amide groups in peptide models in various secondary structures: α-, π-, and 3 10 -helices, and parallel and antiparallel β-sheets. The NFA-calculated H-bond energies in the whole second-structure peptide models were compared with those in the corresponding minimal H-bond (minHb) models composed of two separate Nmethylacetamide molecules, which isolate a single donor-acceptor H-bond from the other backbone groups. The differences between the whole and minHb models indicate conformation-dependent reduced or enhanced polarization of H-bond donor and acceptor groups by neighboring backbone polar groups. The NFA-derivd H-bond energies were also compared with those obtained using the AMBER classical force field.

papers.title: Show me your moves: a comprehensive in silico analysis of the dynamics of the CXCR4 receptor
papers.abstract: Current understanding of C-X-C chemokine receptor type 4 (CXCR4) activation relies on many crystal structures, which mostly represent a small fraction of this receptor’s conformational landscape. We performed extensive MD simulations of CXCR4 receptor to elucidate its dynamical behaviour. We updated previous CXCR4 activation model that shows H294 7.45 conformational rearrangement was not consistent with its role determined experimental mutagenesis by comparing the dynamical behaviour of two different models of CXCR4’s binding site, with H294 7.45 simulations either neutral or positively charged states. Positively charged H294 7.45 recovers the sodium binding site conformation observed in CXCR4 experimental structures and shows better agreement with in silico mutations than its neutral counterpart.

papers.title: Role of Early-Stage Chemistry and Reactor Environment in Carbon Nanotube Formation by Floating Catalyst CVD
papers.abstract: Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are key carbon nanomaterials for a range of energy-related applications. The performance of these applications strongly depends on the electrothermal properties of CNTs, which are governed by the structure developed during synthesis. Here, we investigate how early-stage chemical reactions evolve for different hydrocarbon precursors and how carrier gas and reactor-environment effects influence CNT formation in floating-catalyst chemical vapour deposition (FCCVD). In this work, experimental observations were correlated with reactive molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of early-stage reaction pathways, as well as FEM and CFD simulations of temperature distributions and gas-flow behaviour inside the reactor. FEM/CFD modelling revealed spatially confined growth zones and reactor-scale thermal asymmetries that strongly influence precursor decomposition and CNT deposition. CNTs were synthesised using aromatic and linear hydrocarbon precursors, including toluene and C6–C16 alkanes, at temperatures between 760 and 960 °C in an argon atmosphere. The results show that increasing alkane chain length enhances carbon availability and nanotube yield but reduces crystallinity and increases structural disorder, whereas moderate temperatures improve structural quality. Reactive MD simulations reveal that aromatic precursors promote stronger Fe–C interactions and stable iron cluster formation, favourable for ordered CNT formation, while longer alkanes generate intermediates that weaken catalyst clustering and increase structural heterogeneity. These findings suggest that differences in CNT structure originate already during the earliest stages of precursor decomposition, Fe clustering, and carbon-species evolution, prior to fully developed nanotube growth, and are governed not only by feedstock composition but also by reactor-scale effects.

papers.title: mioXpektron: a modular Python toolkit for ToF-SIMS spectral recalibration, preprocessing and analysis
papers.abstract: Time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS) generates chemically rich profile spectra whose interpretation depends on the mass coordinate and on documented preprocessing. Small errors in the channel-to-m/z transformation can alter peak assignment, integration, and cross-sample alignment, while preprocessing choices can change the resulting feature matrix. We describe mioXpektron, an open-source Python toolkit that brings referenceion-based recalibration, denoising, baseline correction, normalization, peak detection, area integration, tolerance-based alignment, diagnostic plotting, and statistical analysis into a module-oriented workflow. Recalibration routines locate user-specified reference ions, fit selectable time-of-flight models, and report in-sample residuals together with retainedcalibrant counts and fit warnings. Denoising, baseline, and normalization evaluators compare user-defined candidate settings while retaining method-specific quality metrics, and peak detection exports detector and integration semantics with aligned peak-height and peak-area matrices. Illustrative evaluations on the example cohorts show how model flexibility and preprocessing choice affect internal fit diagnostics, peak-position dispersion, local signal-tonoise estimates, baseline metrics, and label-informed normalization scores. A constructed fivegroup example exercises the analysis interfaces. These evaluations are deliberately bounded: fitted ions are not independent check ions, normalization scores are descriptive for the example cohort, and the synthetic example is not biological validation. The contribution of mioXpektron is therefore an inspectable, provenance-oriented implementation for ToF-SIMS profilespectrum processing, with explicit assumptions and auditable outputs, rather than a claim of universal method superiority or independently validated analytical performance.

papers.title: Research-informed coherence in chemistry teacher education: PCK, inquiry, and student agency across aligned curriculum
papers.abstract: This paper analyses the chemistry teacher education pathway at the University of Jyväskylä, examining how its course architecture systematically develops pedagogical content knowledge, inquiry‑ and phenomenon‑based pedagogy, student agency, and assessment literacy. By mapping study‑guide descriptions against contemporary research in chemistry education, we identify a coherent competence profile that integrates representational and modelling skills, inquiry design linked to assessment for learning, contextualisation and sustainability, laboratory safety and digital practices, and research‑informed professionalism. The analysis shows that these competences are explicit design targets rather than incidental by‑products, resulting in strong alignment with the aims of Finnish chemistry curricula. The paper concludes with recommendations for programme development that emphasise evidence‑based refinement, strengthened assessment coherence, and continuity across the bachelor–master continuum.

papers.title: Microsoft Skala’s One-Electron Performance: Self-Interaction Error in a Machine-Learned XC Functional
papers.abstract: Benchmarking the machine-learned Microsoft Skala functional against H+ 2 dissociation reveals significant improvements regarding self-interaction error (SIE). Unlike Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE), which exhibits severe SIE, Skala substantially reduces this error. The results demonstrate that Skala reaches the correct dissociation limit of −0.5 Eh by 5.0 Å. This suggests Skala’s neural network implicitly learned to correct fundamental physical errors absent in standard semi-local functionals, offering efficient, improved accuracy.

papers.title: ROBUST TRANSFER LEARNING FOR BAYESIAN OPTIMIZATION OF CHEMICAL REACTIONS
papers.abstract: Transfer learning offers a promising route to accelerate Bayesian optimization (BO) by reusing knowledge acquired during related optimization tasks. In chemical reaction optimization, this most naturally arises during search-space expansion, where previous optimization campaigns involving related–but distinct–substrates, ligands, catalysts, or optimization objectives create opportunities to accelerate the exploration of new chemical systems. Despite the practical importance of this setting, BO-based transfer learning for chemically relevant search-space expansion has received comparatively little attention. Here, we systematically investigate the factors governing successful transfer learning using representative high-throughput reaction optimization benchmarks. We show that robust transfer learning depends not only on the transfer strategy itself, but also on the underlying Gaussian Process (GP) model. In particular, well-calibrated, dimension-aware hyperpriors substantially improve transfer performance over legacy default priors, while hidden-space molecular representations become increasingly advantageous as optimization campaigns are transferred to larger sets of previously unseen chemical species. More importantly, we highlight that the central challenge of transfer learning lies in balancing positive and negative transfer. Across the benchmark datasets considered here, direct reuse of historical observations proves remarkably effective, whereas deliberately constructed stress-test scenarios reveal that misleading prior information can substantially impair optimization performance when source and target campaigns differ sufficiently. Motivated by these observations, we introduce a simple two-phase transfer protocol that initially exploits historical observations before transitioning to task-aware transfer once sufficient target-task evidence has been collected. Although no single strategy is universally optimal, our results establish practical guidelines for selecting transfer-learning strategies according to the expected similarity between historical and target optimization campaigns, while identifying the proposed two-phase protocol as a robust default when this similarity is uncertain.

papers.title: Topology-Driven Molecular Recognition through Constitutional Isomerism
papers.abstract: Constitutional isomerism is among the most fundamental forms of molecular structural variation, yet how it governs molecular recognition across multiple physicochemical scales remains largely unexplored. Here we establish a multiscale computational framework to uncover how constitutional isomerism reprograms host-guest recognition in carbohydrate macrocycles by comparing cyclodextrins and their constitutional isomers, cyclodextrans. Using force-field reparameterization, equilibrium enhanced sampling, nonequilibrium alchemical simulations and quantum-mechanical energy decomposition analysis, we systematically investigate cyclodextrins and cyclodextrans of varying sizes and 130 host-guest complexes involving these carbohydrate macrocycles. We show that replacing α-(1→4) with α-(1→6) glycosidic linkages fundamentally reshapes conformational landscapes, transforming rigid preorganized cavities into highly adaptive recognition architectures with multiple competing binding pathways. Despite this pronounced structural heterogeneity, thermodynamic predictability is preserved when conformational ensembles are rigorously resolved. More importantly, constitutional isomerism rewires interaction fingerprints and establishes distinct physicochemical recognition classes despite identical monosaccharide composition. These findings reveal a topology-driven mechanism that propagates from molecular connectivity to conformational dynamics, recognition mechanisms and interaction physics, providing general design principles for programmable molecular recognition in flexible supramolecular systems.

papers.title: Reactivity of Water Dimer Radical Cations toward Inert Molecules: DFT Approaches for the Realistic Calculation of Ground- and Excited-State Reaction Profiles
papers.abstract: For the last quarter of century, the topic of chemistry of radical cations (RACs) is expanding at an extreme rate. Produced via single-electron transfer by photo-redox or electrochemical methods, RACs attract attention of organic chemists due to the diversity of possible chemical rearrangements. Thorough theoretical description of RACs is a key to better understanding their properties and predicting chemical behaviors. Unfortunately, the currently available quantum chemical methods were mostly parameterized on the ground-state neutral closed-shell system. As a result, their behavior in RACs remains hard to validate. Our literature analysis indicates that the accuracy of many commonly used methods is rather low, thus putting the chemical interpretation under question. Here we explain the methodology that could be used to evaluate the reliability (and modification, if necessary) of the density functional theory methods to produce realistic models of chemical rearrangements involving RACs. We used water dimer radical cations (WDRACs) as a model system. Recent experimental studies have shown that WRDACs display rather unexpected reactivity toward inert molecules, including catalytic-free nitrogen fixation, or ambient methane-to-methanol conversion. We demonstrate that the properly chosen broadly available models show reasonable agreement with experimental data and help to visualize excited-state chemistry behind RAC-transformations.

papers.title: Computational Discovery of Antimalarial Candidates from African Natural Product Chemical Space
papers.abstract: Virtual screening of antimalarial targets typically requires tens of thousands of docking runs per target, a computational cost that restricts discovery in resourcelimited endemic regions. We developed a centroid-based screening framework that combines variational autoencoder clustering with dual-filter consensus docking (AutoDock Vina + DiffDock) and multi-parameter optimization, reducing screening cost by 99.3 % while maintaining discriminatory power against the MMV Malaria Box positive-control benchmark (consensus-score ROC-AUC 0.924 to 1.000). An independent prospective DEKOIS validation (PfDHFR, AutoDock Vina only) confirms that single-method docking yields near-random enrichment (ROC-AUC 0.450), motivating the ML-based consensus rescoring that underpins the observed performance. Application to a 65 856molecule hybrid library derived from 396 African natural products and 454 synthetic antimalarials yielded 19 913 computationally predicted synthesizable leads, comprising both single-target optimized and multi-target candidates. All 850 screened seed molecules with valid predictions showed a predicted selectivity index > 10, and the full dataset is deposited as an open-access community resource (Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19608875).

papers.title: SmartReact: An Open-Source Python Package for Scalable Forward Synthesis Enumeration Built on Interpretable SMARTS Templates
papers.abstract: Predicting which products can be made from a set of building blocks underpins library design, analogue generation, and synthesis-constrained generative modelling. Reaction templates encoded as SMARTS patterns are the standard tool for this forward synthesis enumeration task. However, existing approaches force a trade-off between chemical coverage, specificity, and the computational cost of applying large template sets at scale. We present SmartReact, an open-source Python library that resolves this trade-off through a template set built on SMARTS-RX, a hierarchical functional group ontology. The same ontology that gives each template a precise chemical environment also drives exact pre-filtering of incompatible reactant pairs, keeping enumeration fast as the template library grows. Every prediction is traceable to a named reaction template and an explicit set of functional group requirements, making results directly interpretable by chemists and straightforward to validate or audit. New reaction types can be incorporated by specifying a SMARTS pattern and its functional group requirements, making the library easy to extend. A case study enumerating 524,911 unique products in under a minute from 1,000 building blocks demonstrates real-world utility at scale. Scientific Contribution: SmartReact contributes both a large, expert-refined SMARTS reaction template library and a scalable open-source Python package designed to use it efficiently. The library’s 9,594 templates spanning 36 medicinal chemistry reaction types are grounded in the SMARTS-RX functional group ontology, giving them high chemical specificity and non-redundancy that auto-extracted libraries lack. The same ontology drives exact pre-filtering of incompatible reactant-template combinations, yielding a 43-fold algorithmic speedup that combines with near-linear parallel scaling and a classify-once API to reach over 11,000-fold throughput relative to single-core brute-force matching on a 32-core server.

papers.title: CoreMeta4Cat: Guidelines for Metadata Standards in Catalysis
papers.abstract: Catalysis is a key technological pillar of the global chemical industry, enabling energy-efficient, sustainable and climate-friendly chemical production. Despite the maturity of the field, the reproducibility, interoperability and reuse of experimental and computational data remain limited because primary data are often insufficiently contextualized through structured metadata. This challenge is further compounded by the exceptional diversity of catalysis research, which spans multiple disciplines, including molecular chemistry, materials science, reactor engineering and computational science. The absence of a broadly applicable metadata framework capable of accommodating this breadth of catalytic systems, experimental workflows and simulation approaches further hampers the transition towards data-driven and digital catalysis. As a result, valuable datasets frequently remain difficult to interpret, compare, reproduce and integrate into computational workflows. Here we present CoreMeta4Cat, a community-driven metadata framework developed within the National Research Data Infrastructure for Catalysis-Related Sciences (NFDI4Cat) in Germany to enable standardized metadata management in catalysis research. CoreMeta4Cat defines the essential metadata required to contextualize primary experimental and computational data and introduces a structured, machine-readable and semantically interoperable framework that supports interoperability, data integration, and computational analysis. The framework combines hierarchical metadata organization, metadata fields classified according to their criticality, and controlled terminology to ensure consistent documentation across diverse catalysis domains. CoreMeta4Cat provides a foundation for reproducible and interoperable catalysis data, thereby accelerating the transition towards data-centric and digital catalysis.

papers.title: Electronic Energy Migration in Protein Polymers Associated with Neurodegenerative Diseases
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are primarily characterized by the accumulation of misfolded protein aggregates in the brain. In addition to their pathological roles, these aggregates have been proposed to transduce photochemical stimuli into biochemical responses. The lattice-like structure of closely spaced aromatic residue chromophores in protein aggregates has raised the possibility of electronic energy migration over large distances, similar to photosynthetic light harvesting. Here, we investigate electronic energy migration in proteins associated with major neurodegenerative proteinopathies across three different states: monomers, fibrils, and extended polymeric assemblies using kinetic Monte Carlo simulations on structures extracted from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) to predict the distances over which electronic energy migration (characterized by the photoexcitation diffusion length; LD) can 2 take place in these structures. We find that repeated energy transfer ’hopping’ in the singlet state (through Förster resonance energy transfer; FRET) occurs over characteristic diffusion lengths of up to approximately 2.0 nm, with the longest values observed for the multiple system atrophy (MSA) associated α-synuclein structure (PDB 6XYO) in the polymeric state, whereas triplet state migration (through Dexter electron transfer; DET) is maximized in the fibrillar state (up to 0.85 nm) in the Alzheimer’s disease Aβ42 fibril structure (PDB 7Q4M) and is substantially reduced in polymers. We observe substantial variation in LD across monomeric, fibrillar, and polymeric states, indicating that the supramolecular organization strongly influences electronic energy migration. Because the calculated diffusion lengths are considerably smaller than the dimensions of protein assemblies, incoherent electronic energy migration is likely to remain localized within protein polymers associated with neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Direct solvothermal growth of TaS2 on substrates enables stable self-supported hydrogen evolution electrocatalysts
papers.abstract: Layered transition metal sulfides, such as TaS2, have emerged as promising electrocatalysts for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). However, the solution-phase synthesis of TaS2 remains challenging and underdeveloped. Herein, we present an effective solvothermal protocol for the growth of TaS2 on different substrates, including Ta plate and carbon cloth, enabling the fabrication of self-supported electrodes. By employing ligands during synthesis, the morphology of TaS2 can be tailored from nanodisks (NDs) to nanosheets (NSs), while preserving a highly crystalline single-phase 1T structure. HER evaluation under acidic conditions reveals that both the catalyst morphology and the underlying substrate significantly influence the electrocatalytic performance. Among the electrodes, TaS2 NSs grown on a Ta plate exhibit the best HER activity, with an overpotential of 377 mV at 10 mA cm-2, a Tafel slope of 110 mV dec-1, and stable hydrogen production for over 45 h at 10 mA cm-2. We demonstrate that the developed synthetic approach enables morphological control for tuning catalytic activity. Furthermore, all self-supported electrodes demonstrate excellent long-term stability regardless of morphology or substrate. Our work highlights the developed solvothermal route as a versatile approach for the direct growth of morphology-controlled TaS2 self-supported electrodes with high stability and efficient HER performance.

papers.title: Physics-guided neural networks for pure-liquid viscosity prediction: Controlling structural and temperature extrapolation through derivative regularization
papers.abstract: Data-driven property models support chemical process and molecular design, yet reliable prediction remains difficult beyond sampled chemical and operating-condition domains. Using pure-component viscosity, we diagnosed structural-and temperature-extrapolation errors and tested axis-specific, physics-guided derivative regularization. We analyzed 21,616 measurements for 2,501 compounds in a leakage-controlled comparison across linear and nonlinear model classes, treating descriptor selection as part of nested hyperparameter optimization without access to outer test data. When similar compounds were distributed across training and test sets, a standard neural network matched kernel ridge regression; however, its error increased more sharply than those of kernel and tree models as structural similarity decreased. Analysis of its descriptor-space prediction surface suggested that off-domain curvature contributed to this deterioration. Hessian regularization reduced median pathwise curvature by 43.2% and achieved the lowest compound-weighted mean absolute error among all evaluated models. For temperature extrapolation, a neural network with a soft penalty on deviations from inverse-temperature linearity provided the strongest performance across the 20 and 50 K tasks among the standard neural network, kernel ridge regression, and a network enforcing exact Arrhenius behavior. Notably, it yielded lower aggregate errors than compound-specific local Arrhenius fits, suggesting that shared molecular information enabled data-supported corrections to strict Arrhenius extrapolation. Combining the structural and temperature regularizers yielded the lowest mean integrated score. Together, these results show that axis-specific derivative regularization can translate neural-network flexibility into robust extrapolation, offering a transferable strategy for property prediction across chemical and operating-condition domains.

papers.title: Nonthermal Plasma-Assisted Methane Dehydroaromatization to Alkyl Aromatics
papers.abstract: The non-oxidative conversion of methane to aromatics is an attractive alternative to conventional petroleum reforming, yet practical implementation remains hindered by thermodynamic constraints, severe coke formation, and rapid catalyst deactivation at high temperatures. Here we demonstrate that nonthermal plasma-assisted methane dehydroaromatization (PAMDA) exhibits substantially lower deactivation rates than conventional thermal conditions, with Fe/ZSM-5 catalysts achieving higher aromatic yields under plasma than the corresponding thermal operations. Notably, PAMDA produces alkyl aromatics (e.g., toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylenes) at rates ~6x greater than benzene under optimized conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that monitoring of plasma electrical diagnostics in operando enables real-time tracking of coke formation, enabling insights into the nature of plasma-catalytic deactivation. This diagnostic is extended to track carbon removal during plasma-assisted oxidative catalyst regeneration. This work highlights a direct electrified pathway to valorize methane to aromatics and provides a facile methodology to probe plasma-catalyst deactivation in coking systems.

papers.title: Objective-Dependent Biasing of Markov Networks for Relaxation and First Passage
papers.abstract: Enhanced-sampling simulations accelerate rare molecular transitions by adding a bias potential, but a bias that accelerates one kinetic quantity need not accelerate another, and a strong bias can reshape the transition pathway it is meant to characterize. Here we formulate bias design on a reversible Markov state generator under a local-detailed-balance state-potential tilt, deriving per-state gradients of the spectral gap and of the A → B mean first-passage time (MFPT) and comparing these kinetic objectives with a heuristic umbrella-coverage score on a common feasible set. Exact two-and three-state models and multidimensional networks show sharp objective dependence: on a nine-well landscape the spectral optimum accelerates global relaxation 357-fold but the targeted transition only 1.16-fold, whereas the MFPT optimum gives a 2.4 × 104-fold transition speedup at the same bias budget. To quantify how much an accelerating bias deforms the reaction pathway we introduce transition-paththeory diagnostics—a normalized reactive-current overlap and a current-weighted edgerate distortion—and apply them, as a model-conditional analysis, to Ras phosphateunbinding trajectories generated under an adaptive MFPT bias.

papers.title: Triarylhydrazone Photoswitches with >360 nm Absorption Maxima, Highly Enriched Photostationary States, and Modular Scaffold Engineering
papers.abstract: Hydrazone-based molecular photoswitches have emerged as one of the most promising classes of light-responsive systems, particularly owing to their straightforward synthesis and broad structural tunability. However, only a limited number of hydrazone motifs combine efficient and stable photoswitching with absorption beyond 360 nm, a prerequisite for many emerging optical technologies and biological applications. Furthermore, the photochromic properties of hydrazones are often highly sensitive to structural modifications, making rational tuning challenging. Herein, we report a family of quinoline-containing triarylhydrazone (triaryl-HZ) photoswitches that exhibit absorption in the UV region above 365 nm. The prepared photoswitches display well-separated absorption bands (approximately 60 nm), minimizing spectral overlap between the switching states and enabling high photoconversions. Designed triaryl-HZs allow versatile structural modifications on both phenyl rings, with only a minor influence on their photochromic behavior. These results identify quinoline-based triaryl-HZs as a versatile platform for the development of robust and spectrally addressable molecular photoswitches.

papers.title: Departing Pathways in Aza-Diarylethene Photoswitching: Elucidating the Role of the Central Ring Allows Reprogramming of the Photoresponse
papers.abstract: Aza-diarylethenes (aza-DAEs) are an emerging class of molecular photoswitches that allow reversible C-N bond formation and cleaving upon irradiation. They show not only high potential as T-type photochromes but offer exciting opportunities for the exploration of unique reactivity control. Two types of these photoswitches are currently investigated, which differ substantially in the nature of their metastable states. While classical DAE behavior is found in perfluorinated thiazole derivatives, an unexpected zwitterion formation and concomitant aromatization is observed for non-fluorinated pyrimidine derivatives. The latter offer reversible control over intramolecular charge-separation and intrinsic three-state photoswitching. Their metastable state unleashes thiolate reactivity, which can be harnessed e.g. in photoinitiation applications for smart polymer generation. Despite this highly promising progress, the reason for the divergent photochemical behavior in aza-DAEs is not understood right now. Here we show that substitution of the central five-membered ring is responsible for the different photochemical outcomes and nature of the metastable state. Guided by theory, we deliver a comprehensive mechanistic explanation why the different behavior occurs. We then use this knowledge to reprogram thioazole-derivatives and render them into zwitterion-forming aza-DAEs. With these results, predictable and rational design of aza-DAEs is enabled, which can now be radically changed in their photoresponses and tailored to specific desired properties and applications.

papers.title: From One-Dimensional Chains to Single-Crystal Nanoelectronic Devices: Linking Structure, Band Energetics and Ambipolar Transport in an Ammonia-Based Magnus-type Salt
papers.abstract: Ammonia-based Magnus-type salts have long been recognized as highly insoluble coordination compounds whose one-dimensional chain structures give rise to unusual optical and electronic properties. Despite nearly two centuries of study and persistent debate, a unified understanding connecting structure, band energetics, and charge transport remains elusive. Here, we combine experimental and computational approaches to elucidate such relationships. A reproducible crystallization protocol enabled single-crystal X-ray diffraction characterization of [Pd(NH3)4][PdCl4] (2, Vauquelin salt), [Pt(NH3)4][PdCl4] (3), [Pd(NH3)4][PtCl4] (4), and [Pt(MeNH2)4][PdCl4] (5), along with new high-quality crystallographic data for [Pt(NH3)4][PtCl4] (1, Magnus green salt). Despite minimal structural variations across the series 1–5, periodic DFT calculations reveal pronounced modulation of band energies arising from cation–anion electrostatic effects and closed-shell metallophilic interactions. Single crystals of 2 were integrated into dual-gated field-effect transistors using nanolithography techniques, enabling the first unambiguous demonstration of ambipolar transport in an ammonia-based Magnus-type salt. The semiconductor band gap was experimentally determined to be 0.65 eV, closely matching the DFT prediction (0.61 eV, PBEsol functional), thereby establishing a quantitative link between crystal structure, band dispersion, and device-level electronic response.

papers.title: Synthesis and adsorption at the air/solution interface of new pH-responsive dicephalic and quadruple-head cationic surfactants
papers.abstract: Two groups of novel multifunctional surfactants branched on a nitrogen atom, i.e., dicephalic 2,2’-(alkylimino)bis(N,N,N-trimethylethanammonium) dibromides (Cn-DNNMe3Br, n = 12, 14, and 16) and quadruple N,N,N-bis(2-(N,N,N-bis(2ammoniumethyl)amino)ethyl)dodecylamine tetrabromide (C12-DNQNNMe3Br) have been synthesized in divergent synthetic routes and characterized by 1H NMR and 13C NMR, ESI-MS as well as by elemental analysis. Surface tension isotherms of their aqueous solutions in the absence and with the addition of NaBr, HBr and NaOH (at pH = 3 and pH = 11, with ionic strength fixed by addition of NaBr), reflecting the protonation/deprotonation of the tertiary amine present in the Cn-DNNMe3Br and C12-DNQNNMe3Br structures, were evaluated using the modified surface quasi-two-dimensional electrolyte (mSTDE) model of ionic surfactant adsorption. To account for protonation/deprotonation equilibria and the formation of transient multicharged surfactant–counterion complexes, we proposed the concept of effective charge, which we substantiated with data from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The results indicate that the difference between surfactant nominal charge and effective charge increases with the number of charges at the hydrophilic headgroup, a combined effect of counterion complexation and enhanced screening of electrostatic interactions. The use of MD tools, combined with a thermodynamic model approach to multicharged surfactant adsorption, can explain some experimentally observed phenomena and provide a basis for the development of novel materials for various applications. This type of complementary approach, integrating experimental data, molecular dynamics simulations, and a thermodynamics-based model, is relatively scarce in the literature.

papers.title: Near-Unity Sodium Metal Cycling without an Anion-Rich Interphase
papers.abstract: Sodium metal anodes promise high energy density at low cost, yet they show poor reversibility in common carbonate electrolytes. The prevailing design strategy, inherited from lithium metal research, holds that reversibility requires a dense, anion-derived, NaF-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). Yet we find that NaF in the SEI impedes Na+ transport and raises interfacial resistance, limiting reversibility and rate capability. Here, we expand prevailing Na SEI design principles by showing that 1 M NaPF6 in diglyme (G2) enables Na plating and stripping at an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.9 percent over more than 1,000 cycles by forming a thin, self-limiting, oxygen-rich organic layer almost immediately upon exposure to electrolyte and maintains ultralow resistance throughout cycling. Across in-situ impedance spectroscopy paired with distribution of relaxation times analysis and post-mortem cryogenic X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, solid-state NMR, and cryogenic electron microscopy, anion-derived phases are non-existent or minimal in the G2 interphase. We find that the limiting interfacial resistance arises

papers.title: In Silico Screening of Drug-Like Compounds Against the TcBDF2 Bromodomain of Trypanosoma cruzi: Identification of Potential Inhibitors for Chagas Disease Treatment
papers.abstract: Chagas disease affects 6 to 8 million people worldwide and has no effective treatment for its chronic phase. The two available drugs, benznidazole and nifurtimox, were developed in the 1970s and cause significant side effects. New therapeutic targets are urgently needed. This study performs molecular docking of 28 drug-like compounds against TcBDF2, an epigenetic bromodomain protein essential for Trypanosoma cruzi survival, using the crystal structure deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB: 6NP7). Six compounds demonstrated binding energies below -8.0 kcal/mol. All six passed Lipinski's rule of five, indicating predicted oral bioavailability. Interaction analysis using PLIP identified a conserved binding pharmacophore at residues ASN73, GLN77, GLU84, and TYR120. Apigenin scored -8.806 kcal/mol with a clean drug-like profile and no pan-assay interference alerts. Vorinostat, an FDA-approved epigenetic inhibitor, scored -8.166 kcal/mol and showed the richest interaction profile of any compound tested, supporting its evaluation as a drug repurposing candidate. These results provide a computational basis for experimental validation of TcBDF2 inhibitors as novel Chagas disease therapeutics.

papers.title: Polarity-Directed Vapor Organization in Hierarchical Metal-Organic Frameworks
papers.abstract: The spatial organization of guest molecules within metal-organic frameworks strongly influence adsorption, transport, separation, and reactivity, yet controlling guest location across chemically and structurally distinct pore environments remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate that local pore polarity directs vapor-phase guest positioning within the interconnected hydrophilic and hydrophobic pores of NU-1000. Water and heptane were selected as representative polar and nonpolar guests, respectively. Water preferentially occupies hydrogen-bonding-rich pore environments before populating the hydrocarbon-rich pores, whereas heptane exhibits the opposite filling sequence. Vapor-phase adsorption isotherms, combined with powder X-ray diffraction-derived differential electron density analysis, reveal these polarity-dependent guest distributions and filling pathways. These findings establish pore polarity as a key design parameter for programming guest organization in hierarchical MOFs and provide a foundation for creating confined environments that enable phase separation, interfacial reactions, and other spatially controlled chemical functions.

papers.title: Experimental molecular assembly estimations for space exploration using gas chromatography mass spectrometry
papers.abstract: Most biosignature methods are biased by what we know about life on Earth. However, an agnostic approach would be more beneficial when looking for life on other planets. Molecular Assembly (MA) is an experimental agnostic biosignature method that could help to look for unknown life. To date, there has been no experimental test employing MA with an instrument type that is spaceflight ready. To explore whether MA can be used for biosignature detection on flight-like instrumentation, we used gas chromatography-electron impact-mass spectrometry (GC-EI-MS) to estimate MA in a range of different samples. We have demonstrated how GC-EI-MS can be used for experimental EI-MA estimation, showing that we can replicate trends from previous MA experimental work with volatile organic compounds and distinguish samples from abiotic and biotic origin. This is the first extensive laboratory experimental study, demonstrating how EI-MA can be used for measurements on instruments that are spaceflight ready and already deployed in space, showcasing a direct route 2 of how MA could be deployed for life detection measurements in the future. This work is a significant step towards making molecular assembly measurements in situ, advancing the search for unknown life in our solar system.

papers.title: Reconstructing Electronic Property Distributions from the Coarse-Grained Resolution with Conditional Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Coarse-grained (CG) simulations efficiently sample the mesoscale morphologies that govern charge, ion, and exciton transport in soft electronic materials, but they integrate out the atomistic degrees of freedom needed to evaluate electronic properties. Recovering these properties conventionally requires expensive backmapping to atomistic structures followed by quantum chemistry. Electronic coarse-graining (ECG) circumvents this by directly learning the conditional distribution of an electronic observable given each CG configuration. Here we introduce conditional flow matching (CFM) as a scalable and distributionally flexible framework for ECG. Unlike Gaussian-process approaches, CFM imposes no functional form on the conditional distribution and trains at a cost that scales linearly with dataset size. Using the HOMO energy of a substituted oligothiophene (ST3M) and the intermolecular HOMO–HOMO coupling of condensed-phase BTBT dimers as benchmarks, we show that CFM accurately captures heteroscedastic, skewed, and heavy-tailed conditional distributions and reconstructs the ensemble electronic distribution upon marginalizing over the equilibrium CG ensemble. We further show that a temperature-conditioned CFMmodel learns a smoothly evolving family of transport maps, enabling accurate interpolation and extrapolation of electronic distributions to unseen temperatures from only a few reference temperatures. Together, these results establish CFM as a scalable, temperature-transferable, and assumption-free framework for recovering electronic property distributions directly from CG simulations.

papers.title: Quantifying Ternary Complex Stability Through Binding Free Energy Calculations in the Geometric Route
papers.abstract: Molecular glue induced targeted protein degradation is a powerful emerging therapeutic modality that exploits the ubiquitin-proteasome degradation pathway to break down proteins associated with disease proliferation. At the structural level, degradation proceeds through the formation of a ternary complex induced by small molecules between the target protein and an E3 ligase. Unlike PROTACs, molecular glues do not require a chemical linker and tend to stabilise pre-existing native protein-protein interactions. Computational screening of novel glues is challenging, in large part due to the complexity and high degree of cooperativity involved in the formation of the ternary complex interface. Here, we present a rigorous Molecular Dynamics based simulation protocol that uses Umbrella Sampling to calculate the ternary complex binding free energy. The protocol follows a geometric thermodynamic cycle with conformational and Boresch-style orientational restraints to drive the system from bound to unbound. Our framework demonstrates excellent sensitivity (R2 = 0.95) to predict the effect of single point interface mutations on lenalidomide induced degradation of CK1α through recruitment of the CRBN E3 ligase. We also study a series of systems related to the BRD4 degraders IBG1 and IBG3, which recruit the DCAF16 E3 ligase. We rank various complexes engaging DCAF16 by their binding free energies, and achieve ordering that is consistent with the trends observed in biophysical assays. Of particular note is our ability to assert the reliance of BRD4 selectivity on a single interfacial glycine residue, which alternative MM/GBSA or HADDOCK scoring methodologies fail to achieve. Overall, our protocol shows promise as a generalisable approach to predicting ternary complex binding affinity, which provides a strong indication of the degradation potency of novel glue candidates.

papers.title: AtomFormer: A Simple Model for Any Mixture Odor Prediction and Beyond
papers.abstract: *Corresponding author: yangxiao_ztri@foxmail.com Abstract. Odor prediction has relied on two implicit assumptions: that a closed set of expert-defined labels is necessary for training, and that individual molecules must serve as the encoding unit—forcing mixtures to be decomposed into constituents, predicted separately, then aggregated through ad hoc fusion. Here we show that both assumptions can be eliminated simultaneously. We introduce AtomFormer, which uses GIN layers as a molecular tokenizer and Transformer self-attention to enable atoms from different molecules to interact directly in a single forward pass, eliminating the need for separate mixture aggregation. On a rigorously decontaminated test set of 6,260 binary mixtures, AtomFormer achieves macro-AUROC = 0.9347 with 16.9M parameters. Beyond odor perception, we validate this architecture on predicting excess enthalpy of mixtures, where it achieves Pearson R = 0.937 with 1.18M parameters. Across these two distinct tasks, AtomFormer achieves strong performance with zero pretraining and end-to-end prediction, demonstrating the generality of the framework across diverse mixture prediction domains.

papers.title: Modulation of Open-Shell Character in Dibenzoazaborine Dications through Amino-Substituent Modification
papers.abstract: Oxidation of dibutylamino-substituted dibenzoazaborine Bu₂NDBAB afforded the air-stable dication [ Bu₂NDBAB ](SbF 6 )₂ in 83% yield, with an NIR absorption band at 943 nm. Structural analysis revealed pronounced oxidation-induced quinoidal distortion. Unlike the previously reported diarylamino-substituted analogue [ Ar₂NDBAB ]²⁺, the present dication exhibited well-resolved ¹H NMR signals, and no ESR signal attributable to the dication was detected. Although the broken-symmetry open-shell (BS-OS) solution was the lowest-energy solution, its small diradical character ( y = 0.122, compared with 0.324 for [ Ar₂NDBAB ]²⁺) indicates only a limited open-shell contribution. Spin-density and natural spin-population analyses showed that replacement of the Ar₂N groups with Bu₂N groups suppresses peripheral spin delocalization, resulting in a singlet ground state with predominantly closed-shell character. Nucleus-independent chemical shift (NICS) calculations further indicated increased antiaromatic character of the azaborine ring in the present dication. These results demonstrate amino-substituent control of open-shell character in DBAB dications.

papers.title: Ensemble π‑Stacking Landscapes of 33 NBOH Derivatives: Mapping Functional Signatures at 5‑HT₂A
Advancing polypharmacology-based drug discovery using deep generative models
Strain-Engineered Colloidal Quantum Dots for Nonclassical Light Emission
papers.abstract: Photonic quantum information processing stands to benefit from the realization of scalable, customizable emitters. While colloidally synthesized quantum dots address the challenge of scalability, better control over their properties remains desirable before the customizability challenge is fully addressed. To this end, better structure-property correlations need to be established in colloidal materials for these to be usable interesting for photonic information processing. Here we develop a synthesis of colloidal quantum dots that show reduced surface strain profiles. To show that this can be realized on arbitrarily engineered excitonic level structures, we further introduce additional layers to realize core wavefunction engineering. We specifically employ a recently reported motif that allows us to enhance single photon emission probability even at high laser excitation powers. We show that unlike ordinary QDs that exhibit strain at surfaces, these materials show suppressed luminescence intermittency. We show the potential of these QDs for photonic information by using these as deterministic sources of single photons with high purity in successive excitation pulses without employing spectral filtering or external cavities.

papers.title: De Novo Design of Enantioselective Artificial Metalloenzyme Photocatalysts Containing Metal Polypyridine Cofactors
papers.abstract: The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis. Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins. In this study, we show that generative protein design can be harnessed to create de novo scaffolds that selectively accommodate one enantiomer of a metal polypyridine photocatalyst as a cofactor. The resulting ArMs enable efficient, enantioselective photocatalysis, highlighting a broadly applicable route for programming stereocontrol into metalloenzyme catalysts. High total turnover numbers are achieved, the ArMs can be recycled by simply extracting reaction products and reusing the aqueous ArM solution for subsequent reactions, and even commercially available racemic cofactor can be used for ArM formation.
